#10198. How Product Teams Can Use AI User Research to Test Assumptions Before Sprint Planning

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sprint planning is on Thursday, and the top of the backlog rests on three things nobody has checked. Users want the feature, they will find it, and they will understand what it does when they do. Each belief is plausible, and each has already been written into a ticket.

AI user research uses language models to simulate or analyze user conversations, so a team can put a question to a modeled audience in minutes instead of recruiting people for weeks. Used well, it gives a product team a cheap first check on backlog assumptions. Used badly, it produces confident-sounding agreement. This guide covers a two-day routine that gets the benefit and avoids the trap.

An assumption is worth testing when the plan depends on it and a wrong answer would change the ticket. "Users like clean interfaces" fails that test. "Analysts re-apply the same filters every session" passes, because if it is false the saved-filters feature shrinks or disappears.

The timing matters because planning leaves little room for research. The Scrum Guide says Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and the first question the team answers is why the Sprint is valuable. Checks run before that meeting inform the answer. Checks run during it eat the time meant for deciding.

Write each risky item as a short card that names the belief, the consequence of being wrong, and the decision it feeds. A card forces the team to say what would change its mind, which most tickets never do. Here is an example:

Aim for three to five cards. A team that tries to test the whole backlog will test none of it, and the cards on the riskiest items give the best return.

AI user research comes in two forms. The first analyzes data you already hold: clustering support tickets and summarizing interview transcripts. It works on real evidence, so its main risk is a sloppy summary.

The second form interviews simulated people. AI user research of this kind builds a panel of modeled personas matched to your target profile, asks them your questions, and reports the themes. It needs no recruiting and returns results quickly, which fits a two-day window. Its output comes from a model of users and not from users, and that distinction should appear in every planning document that cites it.

A simulated audience helps most when you want to sharpen a question, and least when you need proof. Nielsen Norman Group's 2024 review of synthetic users found them useful for generating hypotheses and preparing interview guides. It warned against using them for final decisions or concept validation, and for niche populations, because AI tends to please and "every idea is often seen as a good one."

Spend Tuesday collecting answers and Wednesday reading them skeptically. On Tuesday, put each card's question to the modeled audience in neutral wording, and ask what would make them not use the feature. A question phrased as "Would saved filters help you?" invites a yes, while "Walk me through setting up your weekly report" does not.

On Wednesday, compare the answers with what you already know from support tickets and analytics. Mark each assumption as supported, contradicted, or unclear. Treat a unanimous answer with suspicion, because real audiences rarely agree on anything. Also be wary of lists in which the modeled users "seem to care about everything," which is how Nielsen Norman Group describes their weak prioritization.

Whatever stays unclear or high risk goes to real people. Jakob Nielsen's classic analysis found that five users find about 85% of usability problems, assuming comparable users, and he recommended several small rounds over one large one. An AI check is a good way to decide what those five people should be asked.

Each mark maps to a different decision. A contradicted assumption means the ticket is cut or reduced to its smallest useful version. A supported assumption that rests only on simulated evidence is not yet safe, so schedule a real-user check as the first task in the sprint, ahead of the build work that depends on it. An unclear assumption should not receive full scope.

The cost of skipping this step is real. A 2019 analysis of 615 product subscriptions by a product analytics vendor found that about 12% of features generate 80% of daily usage volume, and 80% of features are rarely or never used. That is one vendor's customer base, and the figures cover features that customers chose to track, so treat them as a rough guide. They still suggest that most of a backlog is a bet.

AI user research cannot replace talking to real users. Nielsen Norman Group found that synthetic users gave overly optimistic accounts of their own behavior, such as claiming to finish every course in a study, and that they cannot supply real past experience. It also called presenting synthetic findings as real-user findings "an unethical way to share what you've learned."

Two habits keep a team honest. Label every piece of evidence in the planning document as modeled, observed, or reported, and require that any feature built on modeled evidence has a real-user check scheduled. The review also warned that teams starting with synthetic research may get comfortable and skip the real kind, so put the real check on the calendar before the first AI result arrives.

Can AI user research replace interviews with real users? No. It is a cheap first pass that helps you write better questions and spot weak assumptions. Anything that drives a significant build still needs real people.

How many assumptions should a team test before planning? Three to five. Pick the ones where a wrong answer would cut or reshape a ticket.

How do I stop simulated users from just agreeing with me? Use neutral, open questions, ask what would make them avoid the feature, and treat unanimous answers as a warning sign.

What should I do with results I cannot verify? Mark them as modeled, give them less weight than observed evidence, and schedule a real-user check before committing full scope.

Sources: Scrum Guide, Sprint Planning; Jakob Nielsen, "Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users" (March 18, 2000); Nielsen Norman Group, "Synthetic Users: If, When, and How to Use AI-Generated 'Research'" (June 21, 2024); 2019 Feature Adoption Report (615 product subscriptions, vendor-reported).

PaddleOCR 3.5 brings OCR and document parsing tasks closer to the Hugging Face ecosystem. With this release, supported PaddleOCR models can run with Hugging Face Transformers as an inference backend by setting:

PaddleOCR continues to provide OCR model series such as PP-OCRv5 and document parsing model series such as PaddleOCR-VL 1.5, while Transformers becomes one of the supported backends for running them.

Try the live demo on Hugging Face Spaces: https://huggingface.co/spaces/PaddlePaddle/paddleocr-3.5-transformers-demo

PaddleOCR 3.5 introduces a more flexible inference-engine interface. Developers can select the backend through the engine parameter and pass backend-specific options through engine_config.

This release is mainly about the inference backend layer: PaddleOCR continues to provide OCR and document parsing capabilities, while Transformers gives supported PaddleOCR models another backend option that fits naturally into Hugging Face-centered environments. The larger Document AI workflow remains in the hands of developers and application builders.

For RAG, Document AI, and document agent applications, the hard part often starts before the LLM.

Developers first need to turn PDFs, scanned documents, screenshots, tables, charts, formulas, and complex page layouts into reliable structured data. If this ingestion step is weak, the downstream LLM workflow may miss key information, retrieve the wrong context, or produce unreliable answers.

PaddleOCR helps address this document ingestion challenge by providing OCR series models such as PP-OCRv5 and document parsing series models such as PaddleOCR-VL-1.5.

With PaddleOCR 3.5, these capabilities are now easier to connect with Transformers-centered stacks. Supported PaddleOCR models can run with a Transformers backend, while PaddleOCR continues to manage the OCR or document parsing pipeline behind the scenes.

For developers, this means less integration friction and a more natural path from documents to downstream RAG, agent, search, analytics, or automation workflows.

Install PaddleOCR 3.5, PaddleX, Transformers, and a compatible PyTorch build for your hardware.

For CPU, ROCm, or other environments, install the PyTorch build that matches your target hardware.

The Hugging Face Space uses float32 for broad compatibility. For your own hardware, you can tune backend-specific options through engine_config:

The best configuration depends on your model, hardware, and deployment environment.

Use the Transformers backend when you want PaddleOCR’s OCR and document parsing capabilities to fit more naturally into a Hugging Face-centered stack.

This is especially useful if you are building RAG, Document AI, search, analytics, or agent applications and already rely on PyTorch / Transformers infrastructure for model loading, experimentation, deployment, or model artifact management.

The Transformers backend is a good fit when you want:

When maximizing OCR or document parsing throughput is the priority, PaddleOCR’s default paddle_static backend is usually the recommended choice.

This release is not about replacing one backend with another. It is about giving developers more flexibility: use PaddleOCR for OCR and document parsing capabilities, and choose the inference backend that best fits your stack.

#10194. AI-Powered Pentesting for DevSecOps: 7 Checks Developers Should Make First

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Security testing used to happen once or twice a year, usually after a release had already shipped. That rhythm does not fit teams that deploy daily. AI-assisted tools now promise testing that runs continuously, chains steps together on its own, and writes up what it found.

For developers, the interesting question is not whether these tools are impressive. It is what has to be true in your pipeline before you let an automated attacker loose on your own systems. This article covers seven checks to make first, each with a pass condition, and one short code example you can run. Some checks, such as written authorization and cost tracking, usually belong to a security lead or manager. For those, the developer's job is to confirm they exist, not to own them.

Testing systems you do not have permission to test is not a gray area. Make sure someone with authority has approved the targets and the time window, and keep that approval with your records. Run the first tests against staging with test data. Production comes later, once you know how the tool behaves and what load it creates.

Pass: The approval is on file, and the SOC knows the window and source IPs.

An automated tester should never decide for itself what it is allowed to touch. Define scope in a file that your pipeline can check: which hosts are in bounds, when testing may run, and whether anything destructive is allowed.

SitePoint's article on security patterns for autonomous agents uses an open-source AI penetration-testing agent as its case study. It covers sandboxed execution, tool permissions scoped to each role, approval gates for high-risk actions, and audit logging. Scope enforcement belongs in that same family of controls. Here is a minimal check that refuses any target outside the allowlist or time window:

Call this before every scan job, and log the result. A tool that is out of bounds should fail loudly instead of quietly continuing.

Pass: An out-of-scope target fails the job, and egress outside the allowlist is blocked.

Findings are only useful if they reach the people who can fix them. Most teams already have a place where security results show up in pull requests or a security tab. SitePoint's walkthrough on automating DevSecOps static analysis with GitHub Actions shows how results written in the SARIF format appear as inline annotations and can block a merge when severity crosses a threshold. If your pentest tool can export SARIF or a similar format, send its findings to the same place.

Pass: The tool exports SARIF or similar, and results show up in PRs or the security tab.

An AI tool can produce a long list of findings. To judge whether they are complete and sensible, you need a reference for what good web security testing covers. The OWASP Web Security Testing Guide is a free, widely used checklist of test categories for web applications. It covers web applications only, so APIs and network services exposed to the internet need their own coverage. Map the tool's findings against it, and note which categories it never touched.

Pass: You know which OWASP WSTG categories you expect the tool to cover.

Vendors describe AI pentesting in similar terms: agents plan attack steps, try them, and verify what works. For a view of how a security vendor explains the approach, CyCognito's overview of AI penetration testing walks through a workflow from scoping to autonomous testing, validation and reporting, and notes that human review stays part of the process. All vendor claims need testing in a demo against your own systems before you rely on them.

Ask the same questions of any tool you evaluate: What does it test beyond known checks? How does it confirm a finding is real? What does it send to external services?

Pass: The vendor has clear answers, including where the target list comes from.

Automated findings need review. A person should confirm that a reported path is exploitable, judge its business impact, and decide the fix order. Make sure this is set up before the first run. Without it, a team can end up with a long backlog of unverified findings and little trust in the tool.

Pass: There is a named reviewer and time set aside each cycle.

Running agents continuously can add up, especially when they call large models. Make sure you can track what each run costs and how many real issues it finds, so you can compare it with other approaches. You also need to be able to rerun the specific test that found a problem after a fix ships and keep the result. A finding is only closed when the retest passes.

Pass: Both are possible before you commit to running the tool continuously.

Does AI pentesting replace manual penetration testing?

Not entirely. Automated testing can run more often and cover more ground, but people are still needed for scoping, complex attack paths and judging impact.

In staging, with test data, inside a written scope and time window.

What should I do with findings from the tool?

Send them to the same place as your other security results, have the named reviewer check them, and retest after fixes.

AI-assisted pentesting can give development teams faster and more frequent security feedback, but only when it runs inside clear limits. Before the first run, check that targets and the window are approved, scope is enforced by your pipeline, findings will land where developers work, you have a baseline to judge the output, you know what the tool tests and sends out, someone owns the review, and you can measure cost and retest. The scope check above is small, but it makes sure the tool stays inside the lines you set.

#10193. Introducing the Ettin Reranker Family

Today I'm releasing six new Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder rerankers, state-of-the-art at their respective sizes, built on top of the Ettin ModernBERT encoders, together with the data and full training recipe that produced them:

The models were trained with a distillation recipe: pointwise MSE on mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 scores over cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, which is a subset of lightonai/embeddings-pre-training mixed with a reranked subset of lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning.

Our six rerankers paired with google/embeddinggemma-300m on MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval. See Results for five more embedder pairings.

If you're new to rerankers and want the "why" first, jump to What is a reranker, and why pair one with an embedder?. If you just want to plug a model in, jump to Usage. If you want to train your own, jump to Training.

I bootstrapped the training recipe below with the new train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. Install it with hf skills add train-sentence-transformers [--global] [--claude] and ask your AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...) to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data.

A reranker (a.k.a. pointwise cross-encoder) is a neural model that takes a (query, document) pair and outputs a single relevance score. Unlike an embedding model, which encodes the query and document separately and computes their similarity from the two embedding vectors, a reranker lets the two texts attend to each other through every transformer layer. That joint encoding is more accurate but also more expensive: the model has to be run once per (query, document) pair rather than once per text.

Because cross-encoders are too expensive to run over a full corpus, the common production pattern is retrieve-then-rerank: a fast embedding model retrieves the top-K candidates (cheap), then a cross-encoder re-orders just those K with high accuracy. The total cost stays bounded while the final ranking is much closer to what an exhaustive cross-encoder pass would produce.

Throughout this blogpost I'll use "reranker" and "cross-encoder" interchangeably.

The released models are normal Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder models, so you can use them with just 3 lines of code:

For a query and a list of candidates, you can also use rank to get back sorted indices and scores:

You can swap cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-32m-v1 for any other size to trade quality for speed. All six accept up to 8K tokens of context (useful for long-document reranking) thanks to ModernBERT's long-context pre-training.

It is recommended to install kernels and set model_kwargs={"dtype": "bfloat16", "attn_implementation": "flash_attention_2"} for the highest throughput. See the Speed section below for more details, but in general you can expect a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over default loading depending on model size and sequence length.

A complete example with a fast embedder for retrieval and the reranker for the final ordering:

This is the same shape used by most modern search systems. The retriever decides what enters the funnel, the reranker decides what wins.

All six rerankers share the same architecture and differ only in their backbone size. The backbone is one of the six Ettin encoders from Johns Hopkins University's Ettin suite. These are ModernBERT-style models with unpadded attention, RoPE positional encodings, GeGLU, and 2T tokens of open-license pre-training, supporting up to 8192 tokens of context.

On top of each encoder, the reranker uses a 4-module classification head that mirrors ModernBertForSequenceClassification but is built from Sentence Transformers' modular components. The underlying Transformer is a plain AutoModel rather than AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which lets us use sequence unpadding for variable-length inputs for Flash Attention 2. At medium-document sequence lengths this is a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over fp32+SDPA depending on model size (see Speed for the full benchmark):

In my ablations, CLS pooling outperformed mean pooling. That was a little surprising. ModernBERT uses global attention only every third layer and the other two-thirds use local-window attention that cannot reach CLS from distant positions. Empirically, those few global layers carry enough signal to make CLS the better pooling choice.

All six models are released under the Apache 2.0 license, matching the Ettin encoders.

I ran each released model through the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark (10 tasks, top-100 reranked) using MTEB's two-stage reranking flow, pairing each reranker with six embedding models that span the speed/quality spectrum:

The dashed retriever-only line in each chart below is the headline number to beat. Anything below it means the reranker actively hurts the pipeline on average:

Mean NDCG@10 over the 6 embedder pairings, sorted descending. Our six models are in bold, and the teacher mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 is underlined.

† Capped to max_seq_length=8192 (the 4B Qwen3-based rerankers don't fit on a single H100 80GB at native context). Native-context evaluation is likely higher.

NanoBEIR is a fast 13-dataset subset of BEIR that uses 50 queries per dataset against up to 5000 documents each. NanoBEIR is what metric_for_best_model was set to during training (see Evaluation), and what I used to guide the experimentation.

The smallest model I'm releasing, our 17M, beats the 33M ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2 by +0.051 NDCG@10 (0.5576 vs 0.5066) on MTEB and +0.038 (0.6746 vs 0.6369) on NanoBEIR at roughly half the parameter count. The 32M beats the 568M BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 by +0.025 (0.5779 vs 0.5526) on MTEB, a 17x parameter gap. If you've been using one of the legacy MiniLM rerankers as the default in your retrieve-then-rerank stack, swapping in our 17M (or 32M) is a low-risk drop-in replacement, with a noticeable quality bump on both benchmarks.

Moving up the table, our 150M is the strongest reranker I tested in the under-600M range on MTEB, edging out the recent Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (596M) by +0.005 (0.5994 vs 0.5940) and beating every BAAI bge-reranker variant by 0.03 to 0.05. The 68M is also worth a mention: at 0.5915 it lands almost exactly on Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (0.5940) while using a ninth of the parameters.

At the top of the released range, our 1B model closely tracks its teacher. It comes within 0.0001 of the 1.54B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 on MTEB (0.6114 vs 0.6115) and within 0.008 on NanoBEIR, despite distilling from a model 54% larger than itself. The distillation effectively closes the gap to the teacher, which is what I was hoping to see going into this release.

The overall strongest reranker in the comparison is Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-4B at 0.6367 MTEB, +0.025 above our 1B model. Closing that gap from the current recipe would likely require distilling from a stronger teacher (our teacher itself sits below Qwen3-Reranker-4B). For most retrieve-then-rerank workloads, our 1B at a quarter of the parameters (see Speed) is a much more practical pick.

Quality numbers are only half of what matters for a reranker. The other half is whether its latency fits inside the budget you have between retrieval and showing results to the user. Let me walk through what I measured.

I benchmarked all six released models against thirteen public rerankers (strong baselines up to about 1B parameters) on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB. The queries and documents come from sentence-transformers/natural-questions at its natural document-length distribution: most NQ answers are short, some are long. Documents are truncated at max_length=512 to avoid giving the older models an unfair advantage. Each model uses its best supported attention implementation: Flash Attention 2 wherever the architecture supports it (BERT, XLM-RoBERTa, ModernBERT, Qwen2), SDPA where it doesn't, and eager for DeBERTa-v2 (which currently has neither FA2 nor SDPA support in transformers).

For every model an auto-batch search starts at batch size 8 and doubles until the GPU runs out of memory. At each batch size I run three timed passes and keep the median throughput, so a single unlucky run doesn't drag the number around. The reported throughput is at whichever batch size won.

Table 1. Throughput in pairs per second, all in bfloat16. Our six rerankers are in bold.

Our 17M is the fastest reranker in the whole comparison, at 7517 pairs per second. That's almost twice the throughput of ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (3817) and faster even than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (4029). And as you saw in the MTEB table earlier, our 17M is also more accurate than every MiniLM variant. If you're currently running a MiniLM cross-encoder, swapping to our 17M is a one-line change that improves both your latency and search quality.

Our 150M is an even more interesting comparison, because there are two direct architectural peers at exactly 150M parameters: Alibaba-NLP/gte-reranker-modernbert-base and ibm-granite/granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2. Both are built on the same ModernBERT-base backbone. Our 150M runs at 3237 pairs per second, while the two peers come in at 1418 and 1404 respectively, for a 2.3x speed gap.

All three 150M models use Flash Attention 2, but the two peers load through AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which keeps the inputs padded. So attention itself runs the FA2 kernel, but the rest of the model is still doing dense compute on padding tokens that don't contribute anything. Our modular Transformer module (see Architecture Details above) propagates unpadded inputs all the way through the model, so every layer only spends compute on real tokens. That's the difference between getting some of FA2's benefit and getting all of it.

At the bottom of the table, our 1B model hits 928 pairs per second, which is 2.4x faster than the 1.54B teacher mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (387 pairs per second) while matching its MTEB score within 0.0001. The teacher is Qwen2-based with a prompt-template overhead per pair, so the distilled student inherits the teacher's calibration and judgement but skips all the runtime baggage. This is honestly the most satisfying single number in the whole release for me.

One unfortunate note: the DeBERTa-v2-based mxbai-rerank-{xsmall,base,large}-v1 series ends up much slower than the rest of the table because DeBERTa-v2 currently supports neither Flash Attention 2 nor SDPA in transformers. The 70M mxbai-rerank-xsmall-v1 runs at 2636 pairs per second, about half the throughput of our 68M at almost the same parameter count. The models themselves are perfectly fine, they just don't get to use modern attention kernels.

If you're self-hosting on a consumer card rather than a datacenter GPU, here's the same throughput sweep on an RTX 3090. Same benchmark setup as Table 1: bfloat16, best-supported attention per model, three-trial median throughput at the largest batch that fits.

Our 17M is still the fastest model in the table at 9008 pairs per second, actually higher than its H100 number, which suggests that at tiny sizes raw compute isn't the bottleneck and the H100's extra muscle doesn't translate. The middle of the table reshuffles a bit, with the MiniLM rerankers overtaking our 32M and 68M, and the 1B slipping behind mxbai-rerank-base-v2 (189 vs 221 pairs per second). Our 150M model still holds a solid lead over the two 150M ModernBERT-based peers, and the teacher-replacement story still holds, with our 1B at 2.7x the throughput of the 1.5B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (189 vs 69 pairs per second).

On CPU, we can't take advantage of bf16, Flash Attention 2, or unpadding, so the latency story is a bit simpler: the higher the parameter count, the slower the model. The 17M model is considerably faster than ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (267.4 vs 143.9 pairs per second) and even faster than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (206.2). As expected, our 150M model lands alongside the two 150M peers (14.0 vs 14.5 and 14.7 pairs per second) now that unpadding no longer applies. If you're CPU-bound, our 17M and 32M are the practical picks.

To explain where the speed comes from, the next table sweeps fp32+SDPA, bf16+SDPA, and bf16+FA2 for our six models using the same bench config. The FA2 column is split in two: one with the inputs still padded (what a wrapped model would see) and one with unpadded inputs (what our modular Transformer actually does). The rightmost column is what our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

Table 2. Precision and attention ablation for the six released sizes at max_length=512 on natural NQ documents. Each cell shows pairs / second with the multiplier relative to fp32+SDPA in parentheses, and peak GPU memory on the second line. The rightmost column (in bold) is the configuration our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

The total speedup from bf16+FA2 w.o. padding over the fp32+SDPA baseline grows sharply with model size, from 1.71x on the 17M to 8.26x on the 1B. Most of that growth comes from bf16 alone: the fp32+SDPA to bf16+SDPA step gives the 17M only a 1.03x speedup but gives the 1B a full 5.60x speedup, also due to the lowered memory cost allowing for bigger batch sizes. In short, bfloat16 is the biggest single contributor to the overall speedup.

Unexpectedly, turning on FA2 while the inputs are still padded is actually slower than bf16+SDPA at every size in the release. The FA2 kernel prefers an unpadded format, and when you feed it padded inputs you pay the bookkeeping overhead of converting between formats while still spending compute on the padding tokens themselves. So the bf16+FA2 w. padding column is roughly what you'd measure if you swapped sdpa for flash_attention_2 in model_kwargs without changing anything else about the model loader. This is the situation that gte-reranker-modernbert-base and granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2 from Table 1 are in.

Lastly, going from bf16+FA2 w. padding to bf16+FA2 w.o. padding is worth between 1.78x (1B) and 2.45x (68M) of additional throughput, and it also cuts peak memory considerably, allowing for higher batch sizes.

So my recommendation is simple: enable bf16 and FA2 together. The six Ettin rerankers will use unpadded inputs by default, since that's what the modular Transformer module from the Architecture Details section is set up for. The full snippet is the same as in the Usage section above:

Use pip install kernels to install FA2. It ships pre-built kernels for a wide range of GPU architectures, CUDA versions, and operating systems.

One caveat for other CrossEncoders: the full speedup is only available for models built with a modular Transformer like the Ettin rerankers. Applying the same two flags to a CrossEncoder that loads through AutoModelForSequenceClassification lands you in the slower bf16+FA2 w. padding column of Table 2 instead.

The training script below started as the output of the new train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill, shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. If you use an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...), you can install the skill and ask it to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data. The skill carries version-aware guidance for base model selection, loss and evaluator choice, hard-negative mining, distillation, LoRA, Matryoshka, multilingual training, and static embeddings, plus template scripts for each model type.

A prompt like "Fine-tune a cross-encoder reranker on (query, document) pairs from my dataset, mine hard negatives, and push to my Hub repo" will produce a runnable script you can then iterate on. That's how I started working on the recipe below.

All six rerankers were trained with the same single-stage recipe. Only the learning rate and the per-device batch size vary per model size. The full training script is ~150 lines and uses one published dataset.

The recipe converged after a single sweep across model sizes. Each size's learning rate was tuned by a small grid search on a ~15% subset of the final training data, and the resulting LRs transferred cleanly to the full-data runs without re-tuning. No per-size tuning beyond LR was needed.

Most published reranker recipes train on human-labeled relevance triples (a query, one positive document, and optionally hard negatives) with a contrastive, pointwise, pairwise, or listwise loss like MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, RankNetLoss, or LambdaLoss, respectively. See my earlier Training and Finetuning Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost, for example.

But this approach has a few practical and theoretical drawbacks. First, positives need to be human-labeled, which is expensive and slow to scale across many domains. Second, the model only ever sees a label for the small subset of (query, document) pairs that someone went through. Especially after hard negative mining, you end up with a lot of false negatives, e.g. as shown in Hard Negatives, Hard Lessons. Third, the binary nature of this labeling doesn't match reality, where some documents are simply more relevant than others.

I took a different route here: pointwise MSE distillation from an existing strong teacher reranker. The setup is simple enough to describe in three lines:

I've released the training data as a single Hugging Face dataset, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, assembled from two sources. Each source is kept as its own split so the provenance is transparent:

Total: ~143M (query, document, score) triples, plus a held-out 5K-row eval split (the tail of quora) that drives the in-training eval loss.

Most hyperparameters are constant across model sizes:

Only the learning rate and global batch size very per model size.

global_batch_size is per_device_batch_size x world_size x gradient_accumulation_steps. On a single 8-GPU node, the 1024 global batch for 17m means per_device=128. On 8 nodes, it means per_device=8. The training script computes per_device_batch_size from global_batch_size // world_size so the same script works at any node count. The global batch size could be made more consistent, but I found that the above values worked well and didn't want to retune them just for the sake of consistency.

I monitored NanoBEIR mean NDCG@10 during training (eval every 5% of steps) and used it as the metric_for_best_model for load_best_model_at_end. NanoBEIR is fast, so I could afford it 20 times per training run. After training, I evaluated both the best checkpoint (according to NanoBEIR) and the last checkpoint on the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark. The final release checkpoint was the one that did best on MTEB. The NanoBEIR-preferred checkpoint won for all sizes except 68m, where the last checkpoint was slightly stronger.

The complete script (what every released model was trained with) is a single file. Only ENCODER_SIZE changes per run, and everything else is automatic:

For multi-node training (anything past 17m/32m), launch the same script with torchrun:

The ettin-reranker-v1 family, trained with a single simple recipe, is state-of-the-art at every released size up to 1B parameters. Pointwise MSE distillation from a strong teacher onto a broad-domain and retrieval-specific mix scales cleanly from 17M to 1B parameters, with only the learning rate and per-device batch size changing between sizes.

Every ettin-reranker-v1 model beats the ms-marco-MiniLM-L*-v2 family by a comfortable margin on MTEB and NanoBEIR. cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-150m-v1 is the strongest mid-tier reranker I tested in the under-600M range, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-400m-v1 lands within 0.0024 of the 1.54B teacher's MTEB score, and cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-1b-v1 matches that teacher within 0.0001.

If you build something on top of these, please let me know! I'd genuinely love to see what people do with them, and if you manage to train better rerankers using the released data, even better. The recipe is intentionally simple, partly so that there's plenty of headroom for someone else to improve it. Train a stronger teacher and the same script can keep producing better students.

I'd like to thank the Ettin team (Orion Weller, Kathryn Ricci, Marc Marone, Antoine Chaffin, Dawn Lawrie, and Benjamin Van Durme) for building the base encoders that these rerankers are built on, the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for their work on the training data collection, and the Mixedbread AI team (Xianming Li, Aamir Shakir, Rui Huang, Tsz-fung Andrew Lee, Julius Lipp, Benjamin Clavié, and Jing Li) for their work on the teacher model.

If you use the ettin-reranker-v1 family or any of the released artifacts, please cite this blogpost:

This is a fantastic read, thank you for the hard work and for sharing the recipes!

Great work! Really learnt a lot from this blog.

Great work! Love that you used stratified sampling.It's great to see its power on cross-encoders, too!

Definitely! I tried a few variants, and in my tests, a mix of top and stratified worked best, but I sampled from 2048 docs, so fully stratified means the 2nd doc is already pretty far from the most similar.

What a clean release, congrats @tomaarsen !

Thanks Maxime! You know, I bet the training script would apply pretty cleanly on LFM models as well 👀Although maybe the model prefers a generative architecture with a chat template that asks the model to generate either "yes" or "no", and the difference in raw logit scores for those tokens are used as the prediction. That's what's used for the teacher model's Sentence Transformers integration, and it works quite well: https://huggingface.co/mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2

Fantastic work! In information retrieval, rerankers are often used in real-time pipelines, so a compact reranker with strong performance is exactly what many of us have been waiting for. Thank you for the great work!

Yess, exactly. In my opinion, rerankers have been getting too big to keep them usable. Hopefully this'll inspire others to make smaller models as well. Plus, the Ettin base models are just amazing, that helps a lot.

Since I often use TEI (text-embeddings-inference) in production, I opened a pull request adding Ettin support to TEI, though I’m not sure if it will be merged.

With this, Ettin can be served as a stable API service through TEI, and I observed around a 1.5x inference speedup in my tests!

Amazing work @tomaarsen , thanks for everything you do for open source !May I ask some questions on the recipe ?

If I understand well, you are mixing lightOn hard negatives data (with Jang et al. stratified sampling) with broader lightonai/embeddings-pre-training - which (i think) doesn't include mined negatives

Correct on all counts. They're different data formats initially. I took:

Yes, I did try various mixes. Specifically, I tried multiple approaches for the second subsampling (256 -> 64), e.g. grabbing 16 random docs, grabbing top 8 + 8 random, top 16 + 16 random, top 16 + 16 uniformly sampled, top 32, top 64, and what worked best for me: 32 top + 32 uniformly subsampled.

I also tried different mixes of the pre-training data vs the embeddings-fine-tuning data. As you can see https://huggingface.co/datasets/cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data#lighton-pre-training-32-configs, I limited the largest sources from embeddings-pre-training to 5M and smaller ones to 2.5M, but during my tests I also tried limiting the largest to 1M and the smallest to 500k. Expanding to the larger number of rows was beneficial. I might also benefit from going larger, but that was exceeding my training time goals. I only experimented with the number of embeddings-fine-tuning data by updating its sampling (e.g. the top 64 has 2x as much fine-tuning data as the top 32 test).

I ended up not wanting to do too many experiments on the data mixture, as I was wary that I might start to overfit on my evaluation benchmark (NanoBEIR), which would only result in better NanoBEIR scores but worse overall MTEB scores. So I didn't do too much.

In ST, you advise to discard Arguana and Touché when using Nanobeir13, I guess it works best with those at the end ?

In truth, I probably should not have excluded these 2 from the default CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator, as people might run the dense and reranker evaluators side by side and expect to be able to compare them, which you now sadly can't do. But in short: At the time, my opinion was that Arguana and Touche2020 didn't really match the usual usage for rerankers. For example, in ArguAna the query is just a big paragraph, and in Touche the documents are a bit vague (i.e. not as confident information sources but instead opinions). I think these might make them less suited as benchmarking datasets for reranker models, and I suppose also less interesting as training datasets for training rerankers. In the blogpost, I included them, as I want the scores to be easier to compare to the dense NanoBEIR13 scores from a standard embedding model.

#10191. Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond

End to end walkthrough of the new Agents CLI Extension System, with a worked LangChain example and a custom deploy policy

When we launched Agents CLI at Google Cloud Next '26, we built it around one strong opinion: going from an idea to a production agent on Google Cloud should take a single unified command surface. For teams building with Agent Development Kit (ADK), that opinionated path has worked. You run agents-cli create, write the agent logic, and ship to Cloud Run with observability and evals wired up, in about thirty minutes.

The agent framework landscape has grown more diverse in the months since. In addition to ADK, developers today pick between LangChain and LangGraph, specialized newcomers like Deep Agents, or in-house frameworks tailored to a specific business domain. Different teams prefer different frameworks, and the right choice for a greenfield prototype is rarely the right choice for a production migration. Enterprise admins may also have governance policies they want to enforce across the ADLC for all of their development teams, such as: a compliance scan, an SSO gate, a Model Risk Management hop.

Can a team benefit from the deployment, evaluation, and observability work in Agents CLI without being forced to adopt ADK, or without being forced to accept the default behavior of every command? Starting with version 1.5.0, the answer is yes. Agents CLI now ships with an Extension System that lets developers override or add commands without forking the tool. Version 1.8.0 ships the first-party LangChain extension, which replaces the framework-coupled commands with their LangChain equivalents and leaves the rest of the lifecycle untouched.

We will walk through two journeys below. First, to show you the ADLC with LangChain agents, we'll show you how you can scaffold, run, deploy, and evaluate a LangChain agent through the Agents CLI lifecycle using the first-party extension. Then we build our own small extension that wraps the deploy command with a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) scan, demonstrating the pattern enterprise platform teams can use to enforce their own policies across every project. Both journeys use the same mechanism.

Most agent development toolchains available today share a limitation: they are opinionated about one specific framework, and the surrounding capabilities (deployment targets, CI/CD pipelines, evaluation harnesses, observability wiring) assume the developer has adopted that framework. When your framework matches the tool's assumption, the opinionated path works. When it does not, you're left with three bad options.

The first is to fork the CLI, maintaining a divergent copy and re-syncing it on every upstream release. You pay a permanent maintenance tax, and every upstream improvement has to be hand-merged into the fork. The second is to wrap the CLI behind custom scripts, building a parallel command surface that invokes the underlying tool. The problem is that developers (and their coding assistants) forget about the wrapper and call the underlying tool directly, bypassing the intended abstraction. The third is to walk away and build everything from scratch, which can consume several engineer-months of work that the team had not planned for, and which rarely produces tooling as polished as the upstream project.

The problem shows up in two scenarios. One is enterprise customers adopting Agents CLI: in regulated industries, a central platform team often requires that every deploy invocation be wrapped with a compliance check, that login route through corporate single sign-on, or that evaluations flow through a Model Risk Management pipeline. Each of these requirements, implemented today, means either forking the CLI or building a wrapper layer. The other is teams that use ADK most of the time but need to run a non-ADK framework on a specific project. Within the Agents CLI command surface, six commands assume the ADK runtime: playground, run, and four eval subcommands. The other eighteen or so (scaffold, infra, deploy, publish, login, and friends) are framework-agnostic. Without extensions, choosing a non-ADK framework for a single project meant losing access to all twenty-four.

The Extension System handles both with one mechanism.

An Agents CLI extension is a directory in a Git repository that contains a single file called agents-cli-extension.yaml. The file declares which built-in commands the extension overrides and which new commands it adds. From the official documentation:

Extensions take two shapes, described in the Using Extensions page. A command override replaces the behavior of a built-in like playground, deploy, or eval generate. The overridden command receives the user's arguments verbatim, so the user experience stays consistent with the native command. A new command exposes a workflow the CLI does not currently provide as agents-cli . Both shapes can coexist in the same extension, and most non-trivial extensions use a combination of the two.

Extensions are distributed through Git repositories rather than through a dedicated package registry. The design draws from the extension model used by the gemini-cli project. There is no central index to publish to, no package format to maintain, and no ownership roster to apply for. Any directory inside any Git repository can serve as an extension, and Git handles the versioning, pinning, and distribution. For enterprise platform teams, this means creating an internal platform-extensions repository and pointing their developers at it, with no external registry to coordinate with.

An extension can be referenced in several ways, depending on where it lives and how the developer wants to use it:

The # syntax lets a single Git repository hold multiple extensions, with the fragment identifier selecting one of them. Enterprise platform repositories often bundle together a family of related extensions (one for deploy, one for login, one for scaffold create) under a single repo with shared ownership and release cadence.

Extensions install at two scopes. The default is the project scope, where the extension and its lockfile entry are committed to the project's own repository. Teammates and CI pipelines pick it up on checkout. The alternative is the user scope, enabled via the --global flag, where the extension is stored in the user's home configuration directory and applies to every project on the machine. The user scope is the one you reach for when an extension needs to be available before any project exists, such as a framework bootstrap extension that configures agents-cli create itself.

When both scopes define the same command, the project scope wins, and agents-cli info surfaces the source of each active command. Scoping is deliberately explicit: the Extension System will not silently merge or override extensions, and any conflict surfaces to the developer at install time or in the extension list output.

The Extension System follows the discipline of package managers like uv or npm: it resolves a Git reference to an exact commit SHA at install time, records the resolved SHA in a lockfile, and uses the lockfile to re-materialize the exact reviewed code on every fresh checkout. The agents-cli install command restores the vendored working copy from the pinned SHA without advancing the pin, which guarantees that CI and local development run bit-for-bit identical code. To advance a pin to the latest commit on the tracked reference, the developer runs agents-cli extension update, which re-resolves the reference and re-prompts for third-party trust. The complete lifecycle is in the Using Extensions → Lifecycle section.

The Extension System is marked experimental in v1.8.0. The manifest schema and the command surface may still change in breaking ways before the system is finalized, so teams depending on it should pin their Agents CLI version.

The LangChain first-party extension is a project template: one command scaffolds a working LangChain agent wired into the Agents CLI lifecycle. The resulting project has zero google-adk dependency and deploys to Cloud Run through the same code path an ADK project uses. The template's own description reads:

In modern LangChain (version 1.0 and later), the state management layer is provided by LangGraph, so the three frameworks share a common graph representation. The template serves all three communities with the same code.

A Google Cloud project with billing enabled is also required. If you do not have one yet, it can be created at console.cloud.google.com.

If Agents CLI is not already installed on the development machine, it can be installed in a single command:

Finally, we authenticate with Google Cloud and enable the APIs the agent will depend on at runtime:

Scaffolding and extension installation are the same operation. Rather than installing an extension first and then scaffolding a project, we point agents-cli create directly at the extension's template, pinned to a specific release tag:

The output confirms the scaffold succeeded:

The scaffolded project already contains an agents-cli-extension.yaml at its root, which is auto-loaded at project scope the next time any command is invoked. There is nothing to install manually, because the project itself is the extension's installation. A developer scaffolding a LangChain project does not need to know the Extension System exists. The command looks and feels like a native agents-cli create invocation that happens to produce a LangChain project instead of an ADK one.

The structure looks similar to an ADK project: same app/, same tests/, same Terraform under deployment/, same manifest at the root. The two differences are the agents-cli-extension.yaml at the top (which carries the LangChain overrides) and the langgraph.json file (which configures the LangGraph dev server used by the local playground).

The main agent definition lives in app/agent.py:

The agent is created with the langchain.agents.create_agent helper, which compiles into a LangGraph CompiledStateGraph. The type annotation on root_agent makes this explicit. Modern LangChain uses LangGraph as its state management layer, which is why the template is positioned as supporting LangChain agents, LangGraph graphs, and Deep Agents through the same lifecycle: all three compile to the same underlying graph.

The scaffolded project contains no dependency on the Agent Development Kit. We can verify this directly:

The grep returns no matches, and the exit code of 1 confirms the absence of ADK references. The google-* packages that do appear in pyproject.toml are the ones any Google Cloud Python project would include: google-cloud-aiplatform[evaluation], google-cloud-logging, langchain-google-genai, and the OpenTelemetry Google Cloud exporters.

Behind the scenes, Gemini-3.8-flash on Vertex AI has invoked the compiled graph in-process, called get_weather("San Francisco"), received the simulated foggy response, and reasoned the final sentence back to the user. The warning line tells us which extension commands are active, with one entry per overridden command. The warning is deliberate: an override quietly changes native behavior, so the loader always announces which commands are being intercepted and by whom.

For a local inspector, agents-cli playground boots LangGraph Studio on port 8080, replacing the ADK web UI that would otherwise appear.

To confirm which commands the extension has modified, we can inspect the help output:

The [↑ langchain] suffix is the Extension System's way of signalling that a command has been overridden, together with the name of the extension responsible. Both human developers and coding assistants reading the terminal can tell at a glance which commands behave differently in this project.

For a complete inventory, agents-cli info lists every active extension together with the exact command vector it executes:

Six overrides total, falling into three categories: four framework-coupled replacements (playground, run, eval.generate, and publish.gemini-enterprise), two explicit refusals (eval.dataset and eval.optimize need an ADK agent object to introspect, so the LangChain project refuses them cleanly rather than producing invalid results), and the publish.gemini-enterprise override additionally refuses only on the Agent Runtime deployment target while delegating to the native command on Cloud Run and GKE. The First-party frameworks page has the official breakdown.

The deploy command is not overridden by the LangChain extension. Deploying a LangChain project to Cloud Run uses exactly the same code path as deploying an ADK project:

The underlying mechanism shells out to gcloud run deploy --source . against the project's Dockerfile, which includes:

That CMD is identical to the one in an ADK project's Dockerfile. The LangChain template serves A2A (Agent-to-Agent) protocol traffic over FastAPI, exposing the application under app.fast_api_app:app. The deployment path does not need to know which framework is powering the agent, because uvicorn and gcloud run deploy operate on the FastAPI contract.

The same holds for infra, scaffold enhance, scaffold upgrade, install, info, setup, lint, and login. All unchanged in a LangChain project. A year of Agents CLI work on these commands lands in LangChain projects for free, with no divergence to maintain between the ADK and LangChain code paths.

Evaluations in a LangChain project follow the familiar pattern from the ADK walkthrough, with one difference: the eval generate step is overridden to drive the LangChain graph, while the subsequent evaluation steps use the native commands:

The overridden eval generate command produces output in the standard EvaluationDataset format, which the native eval grade, eval compare, and eval analyze commands know how to consume. The evaluation service and the grading rubrics are framework-agnostic.

If a developer invokes one of the refused eval subcommands, the extension responds with a clear explanation rather than failing silently:

A clear refusal is more useful than a silent failure, especially when a coding assistant is driving the terminal and would otherwise retry a broken command multiple times before giving up.

The LangChain template is the first-party demonstration of the Extension System, but the same mechanism is open to any team that wants to customize the Agents CLI command surface. Enterprise platform teams can author and distribute extensions internally, encoding their policies as code and shipping them through the Git infrastructure they already use for everything else. Every developer on the team then follows the same checks by default.

To illustrate the pattern, we will build a small extension called sbom-deploy that wraps the deploy command with a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) scan, refusing to deploy if any critical vulnerabilities are found. The authoritative reference for the manifest schema is the Authoring Extensions page.

We begin by creating a directory for our extension and adding the manifest file at its root:

The manifest contains five top-level keys, and no others are allowed. The schema uses strict validation, so a typo like reqires: fails install with a did-you-mean suggestion rather than silently dropping the override.

The schema field identifies the manifest schema version. The name field is a single path component (slashes and parent-directory references are rejected) and becomes the directory under extensions/ where the vendored copy is stored. The requires block declares which versions of Agents CLI the extension supports, together with a policy (warn or error) that controls behavior on a version mismatch. The commands block is where the actual overrides and additions live.

The Rules that matter section of the authoring docs enumerates additional constraints worth knowing about. Two in particular: you can override a specific subcommand (such as eval.generate) but not a top-level command group (such as eval as a whole), and run: is a command vector, not a shell command, so any chaining of commands has to happen inside a wrapper script rather than inside the manifest.

Because run: is a command vector executed without a shell, chaining multiple operations means writing a wrapper script that sequences them explicitly:

AGENTS_CLI_DISABLE_OVERRIDES=1 is what makes this work. Agents CLI sets it in the environment of any script invoked through an override. When our wrapper calls agents-cli deploy recursively, the call lands in the native deploy command rather than looping back to our own override. No special syntax, no recursion.

We can verify this directly. For demonstration, we swap the SBOM scan for a few echo statements that confirm the environment and arguments:

The --project foo flag passed through to the wrapper verbatim, and the environment variable was set by the loader before our script began executing. The wrapper has everything it needs to delegate to the native command.

With the manifest and wrapper in place, we can install the extension. During development, point at the local path:

Once the extension has been pushed to a Git repository, the same syntax works with a remote reference:

After installation, we verify the extension is active by listing the installed extensions and inspecting the help output:

The [↑ sbom-deploy] tag next to each overridden command is the Extension System's user-facing signal that the behavior has been modified.

Behind the scenes, extension add resolved our Git reference to an exact commit SHA and recorded the resolution in a lockfile at the project root:

Both the lockfile and the vendored working copy under extensions/ should be committed. On a fresh checkout, agents-cli install re-materializes the exact reviewed code from the pinned SHA, the way uv sync or npm install restore pinned dependencies. The install command never advances the pin, so an extension cannot change its behavior between two deployments of the same commit.

To advance the pin to the latest commit on the tracked reference (branch, tag, or SHA), the developer runs agents-cli extension update sbom-deploy. To switch to a different tag or branch, re-run agents-cli extension add with a new --ref. The complete lifecycle is detailed in the Using Extensions → Lifecycle section.

Agents CLI began life as an opinionated path to shipping ADK agents on Google Cloud. With the Extension System in place, those opinions are now yours to override, replace, or augment.

Install Agents CLI and scaffold a LangChain agent in two commands:

Then explore the official documentation: the Extensions overview, Using extensions, Authoring extensions, and First-party extensions. The full source code of Agents CLI, including the first-party templates, is at github.com/google/agents-cli.

#10190. Retrying a send is harder than sending

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every integration that moves something out of your system has the same weak point, and it is

not the happy path. It is the second attempt.

Your code posts a document to a provider. The connection drops before the response arrives. You now hold no job id, no confirmation and no idea whether anything left the building. The timeout told you about your network. It told you nothing about theirs.

So you retry, and you either send the thing twice or you never send it at all. Pick one, because

without help from the API you cannot have both.

The first instinct is a client-side guard. Hash the payload, keep a table of what you have already

That works until the duplicate attempt comes from a different process, a different container, or a

queue worker that started after a deploy. Your table is local state defending against a distributed

The second instinct is to ask the provider whether the job exists. That means listing recent jobs

and matching on something, usually the recipient and a timestamp window. It is a search, and

searches have false positives. Two legitimate sends to the same recipient a minute apart look exactly like one send and one retry.

The third instinct is to make the operation naturally idempotent. That works beautifully for a database upsert and fails completely for anything that leaves your control. A document that has been transmitted cannot be un-transmitted by a second call.

An idempotency key, generated by the caller, attached to the request, and honoured by the

The contract is simple. The caller invents a unique string per logical operation. Every attempt

carries the same string. The first request to arrive does the work and records the result against that key. Every later request carrying that string gets the recorded result back instead of doing the work again.

The important part is where the state lives. It is on the server, which is the only place that knows

whether the job exists. Your retry loop stops needing to be clever. It just needs to reuse the key.

Stripe popularised this pattern and the reason it spread is that the alternative is unbounded.

Without it, every caller writes their own deduplication, badly, and the failure only shows up under load.

Document and messaging APIs are where it matters most, because the side effect is visible to

someone outside your company. Fax for Agents is a current example of the pattern taken

seriously. It requires an Idempotency-Key on every mutating call, so a retry hands back the

same job instead of creating a second one.

Idempotency solves the duplicate. It does not solve the other half, which is that you still do not know what happened.

Most integrations model this as a boolean. Sent, or not sent. That is wrong, and you discover it

the first time a transmission half completes.

A useful state machine for a send has more room in it. Fax for Agents publishes six states:

queued, active, partial, failed, unknown and delivered. Two of those are the interesting ones.

unknown means the provider has not said. Not failed, not delivered. The correct response to

unknown is to wait. A retry loop that treats unknown as failure needs rewriting, because that is

how you produce duplicates even with idempotency in place.

partial means some of it arrived. Resending the whole document would deliver the first pages

twice, so partial is a state that must never be retransmitted automatically. It needs a person, or a

And delivered should be the narrowest word in the vocabulary. In that API it is written only when

the provider's evidence for the attempt supports it, never when the request was merely

accepted. The gap between "we accepted your job" and "it arrived" is where most false

Four questions, answerable from the documentation before you write a line of code.

Does it accept a caller-supplied idempotency string on every mutating call, and for how long

How many terminal states does a job have? If the answer is two, the API is hiding something

Is there a state meaning "we do not know yet", and does the documentation say what you should do when you see it?

When a webhook arrives, can you verify it came from them? Signed delivery with an event id is

the difference between a webhook handler and an open endpoint.

None of that is exotic. It is the difference between an integration that degrades and one that

#10189. OlmoEarth v1.1: A more efficient family of Earth observation models

🧠 Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/olmoearth | 📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth_v1_1 | 💻 Code: https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain

We released OlmoEarth (v1) in November 2025. Since then, partners have applied it across a wide range of tasks, from tracking mangrove change to classifying drivers of forest loss to producing country-scale crop-type maps in days, scaling deployments to national, continental, and global areas. Every release moves us closer to our mission: bringing state-of-the-art AI to organizations and communities working to protect people and our planet.

When OlmoEarth processes satellite imagery to make predictions across tens to hundreds of thousands of square kilometers, efficiency shapes what’s possible. Over the full lifecycle of running OlmoEarth – data export, preprocessing, inference, and post-processing – compute is by far the highest cost. A more efficient model means we can support more partners on the OlmoEarth Platform, and that anyone running OlmoEarth on their own can leverage this technology faster and at lower expense.

That’s why we built OlmoEarth v1.1: a new family of models that cuts compute costs by up to 3x while maintaining OlmoEarth v1's performance on a mix of research benchmarks and tasks we’ve constructed with partners.

The OlmoEarth models are transformer-based models, one of the dominant architectures in machine learning today. To process remote sensing data, we first convert it into a sequence of tokens the model can ingest.

Two important levers control efficiency in transformer-based models: model size (this is why we release a family of models, so users can pick the size that fits their compute budget) and token sequence length. Compute costs scale quadratically with the token sequence length, so even small reductions can meaningfully cut the cost of running the model.

MACs, or multiply-accumulate operations, estimate the computation needed for one model forward pass; lower MACs generally mean cheaper, faster inference. The y-axis is inverted because lower average rank is better. Labels show model family and size. All plotted points use the pasted MAC/rank values.

This raises an important question for transformer-based remote sensing models: what should a token represent?

Take Sentinel-2 imagery, a common modality we process. A Sentinel-2 input will be some tensor with a height and width (H, W representing the latitudinal and longitudinal pixels), a temporal dimension T, and 12 Sentinel-2 channels ([H, W, T, D=12]).

Currently, we split the data into resolution-based patches. Concretely, this means that we will pick some spatial patch size p, and split our overall Sentinel-2 image into patches of size p x p:

For each patch, we create a token per timestep per resolution. So a Sentinel-2 input with 2 timesteps yields 6 tokens per patch (2 timesteps x 3 resolutions, 10m, 20m, and 60m).

In total, a[H, W, T, D=12] Sentinel-2 input will yield H/p x W/p x T x 3 tokens.

Using a unique token per resolution is a common technique when processing Sentinel-2 data—Galileo and SatMAE both take this approach, and SatMAE shows significantly better results when doing it. However, it is not universal: CROMA is a model that only uses a single token for all bands, regardless of resolution. Because token counts compound multiplicatively, collapsing resolutions into a single token produces three times fewer tokens and material savings across pretraining, fine-tuning, and inference.

Naively combining the tokens in this way leads to significant performance drops, including a 10 ppt drop on m-eurosat kNN (a common benchmark task for remote sensing models). We hypothesize that separating Sentinel-2 bands into different tokens makes it easier for OlmoEarth to model important cross-band relationships.

Merging tokens without impacting performance required us to modify our pre-training regimen. We describe those changes in detail in our paper.

The result is a model family that does more with less. At every size, OlmoEarth v1.1 runs up to three times cheaper than OlmoEarth v1, making frequent, planet-scale map refreshes more affordable for every team running OlmoEarth. If you're using a model from the original OlmoEarth family, try OlmoEarth v1.1. It provides similar performance to OlmoEarth v1 while requiring one third of the compute, though we have seen some regressions (see our technical report for more details). If it works for your task, you should see a significant speedup during fine-tuning and inference.

Pretrained remote sensing models have many degrees of freedom, which makes them hard to study. When performance shifts, is it the architecture, the dataset, or the pre-training algorithm?

We train OlmoEarth v1.1 on the same dataset as OlmoEarth v1, so any differences between the two isolate the effect of methodological changes. We hope this advances understanding of scientific principles when pretraining models for remote sensing.

Check out the OlmoEarth v1.1 weights and training code, including the weights for our Base, Tiny, and Nano models.
