#10167. Adding MCP Tools to Reachy Mini

The Reachy Mini conversation app can now use tools hosted in public Hugging Face Spaces, called over MCP. You can give your robot a new ability, like checking the weather or searching the web, by adding a Space from the Hub instead of editing the app. The tool keeps running in the Space itself, so no code is downloaded onto your machine. And you can publish your own tools for other people to use.

Below, we look at what a tool is, how profiles control what the robot can use, and the current limits of the remote path.

When you talk to the robot, what you get back isn't only a voice, it's a system that reacts to the conversation: the robot can move and respond non-verbally, when it's applicable. The part we want to focus on here is the tools that make that possible. A tool is something the model can do during a conversation: play an emotion, move the head, look through the camera. Each tool has a name and a short description. The model reads those, decides when one is useful, calls it, and uses what comes back.

Today every tool is local and ships inside the app, and most of them are about the robot's body:

A tool in the code isn't usable until it's enabled in a profile, a folder with two files that matter here: instructions.txt (the prompt) and tools.txt (the tools that are turned on).

The default profile enables the full set:

If a name isn't in tools.txt, the model can't call it.

You can also write your own tool: add a Python file to the profile (or external_tools/), give it a name and description, and list that name in tools.txt.

Today there are built-in tools and custom local tools, and tools.txt decides which are active. This works well for the robot's body and keeps the trusted core small.

The constraint here is that every tool has to be local Python. For move_head or play_emotion that's right: they talk to the hardware and belong in the app but a lot of useful things have nothing to do with the body, like web search, weather, or lookups. For those, keeping everything local is mostly friction:

Remote tools add a third kind, alongside the built-in and custom local tools you already have, for capabilities that are easier to publish, share, and update on their own:

We started with two canary tools, small test tools to exercise the new flow:

They're enough to exercise the whole feature: install from the Hub, discover the remote tools, enable them per profile, and let the realtime backend call them exactly like built-in tools.

To use both at once, add each Space and their tools stack in the same profile:

Now the robot can search the web and check the weather in the same conversation, which is exactly what the canary_web_search_weather profile below does.

add validates the Space on the Hub, probes the MCP endpoint, discovers its tools, and by default appends the tool IDs to the active profile's tools.txt. The active profile is default unless you've set REACHY_MINI_CUSTOM_PROFILE. Use --install-only to skip that step.

tools.txt is the gatekeeper: a remote tool is only active if its ID appears in the profile's tools.txt, alongside whatever built-in tools you want.

Each installed Space gets a local alias derived from its slug, with hyphens, dots, and slashes collapsing to underscores:

Remote tools are then namespaced with a double underscore:

This keeps remote tool names from colliding with built-in ones and lets multiple Spaces coexist in the same profile.

The implementation also strips redundant Space-name prefixes when possible, so a verbose remote tool name becomes a cleaner local ID. If stripping would cause a collision between two tools from the same Space, the code falls back to the fully namespaced name.

There is also a duplicate safety check at registry level: Tool.name values must be unique across the entire merged tool set. The app fails fast if two sources claim the same name.

For this work we created two focused canary profiles to isolate the MCP experiment from the full embodied tool set.

The first keeps a few expressive tools (emotions, head movement) and adds web search on top:

The second is the same, plus the weather tool alongside search:

The small physical tool set means Reachy Mini can still react expressively while answering current questions from the web.

The remote-tool plumbing gets the tools into the model. The prompts decide how the model uses them.

That was especially visible in the search-plus-weather canary. A combined question like:

can be handled in at least three ways: weather first then search, search first then weather, or both in the same turn. If the prompt is vague, the model serialises the calls and creates unnecessary latency. So the canary prompts became part of the feature, not just incidental configuration.

Two things are worth calling out. First, the Space has to actually behave like an MCP server; if tool discovery fails, the install fails. Second, prompt instructions can encourage parallel calls but cannot guarantee them. If deterministic orchestration matters for a use case, that logic should move from the prompt into code.

If you want others to use your tool, publish it as a public Gradio Space that exposes the standard MCP endpoint, and keep the tools stateless so they work well over the network. Whether a Space installs depends on this runtime behavior, not on tags.

Tags aren't required for installation, but they help people find compatible Spaces:

The app now has three kinds of tools sharing one registry: built-in, local custom, and remote MCP tools, and profiles still decide which of them a given assistant can reach. A small, trusted core stays at the center while the optional capabilities around it can be added, tested, and swapped without touching the app itself.

What we're most curious about now is what people build. If you publish a tool Space, tag it reachy-mini-tool and mcp so others can find it. We'd love to see what Reachy Mini ends up able to do!

Acknowledgements: Many thanks to Fabien Danieau for proofreading this post and helping test the workflow, to Andres Marafioti for helping test it, and to Remi Fabre and the Pollen Robotics team for the ideas and feedback that shaped the remote tools workflow.

MCP Space for Reachy Mini weather briefs.

Great work on making Reachy even easier to customize!How can I add these MCP tools on a wireless Reachy Mini with a preinstalled conversation app?

The tools.txt approach makes the MCP integration especially clear. I like how remote tools are kept separate from the built-in robot tools while still being enabled per profile. The distinction between installing a Space and actually activating its tool IDs in tools.txt also seems important, particularly when multiple remote tools are being used together.I’m also using an MCP server on my site, https://tinid.ph/, to work with AI agents, and it has been really useful for me. In particular, it has helped a lot with identifying and fixing technical issues on the site. The idea of keeping tools accessible to AI agents through MCP, rather than building every capability directly into the application, makes a lot of sense.

#10166. From Containers to Sandboxes: Developer Trust in the Agentic Era

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

What the 2026 Stack Overflow Developer Survey tells us about where trust goes next

If you’ve followed Docker lately, you know we’re all-in on sandboxes. We’ve spent a ton of time talking about the difference between sandboxes and containers, and helping our customers and the industry as a whole understand when to use which. In fact, Docker president Mark Cavage dedicated his opening keynote at WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America to this exact topic, using live demos to show why sandboxes (and not containers) provide the level of isolation required to contain autonomous agents.

To be clear: none of that means we suddenly think less of containers or the vital role they will continue to play in the software development process and ecosystem. We are Docker, after all. And lest anyone forget, as the just-released 2026 Stack Overflow Developer Survey confirmed yet again, when it comes to containers, there’s Docker, and there’s everyone else. Docker is the most used (59%) and most desired (38%) tool in the survey’s cloud development category.

Now, we can all agree that the tech industry is inundated with surveys these days. Vendors, analysts, research firms, everyone’s got a groundbreaking new survey. So, if your reflex response to reading about new survey results is to roll your eyes and think here we go again, well, I get it.

But the annual Stack Overflow Developer Survey isn’t just another survey. When it comes to the developer community, it’s arguably the survey, the one developers themselves pay attention to. Over the course of 16 years, it has become something of a de facto standard for those of us interested in truly understanding how developers think and act. Released earlier this month, the 2026 survey reached more than 30,000 respondents across 169 countries.

Of course, this year’s survey did more than just remind us of Docker’s continued container dominance. It painted a picture of an industry in transition as developers grapple with one of the biggest questions in technology right now: how to bridge the gap between what they want to do with agents and what they can securely and confidently run in production.

Put it all together, and the missing ingredient is clear: trust. Developers want to tap into everything agents make possible without crossing their fingers and hoping “everything” doesn’t include a catastrophic security failure.

I didn’t point out those earlier Docker numbers just to brag (though, hey, I’m a marketer, so it was at least part of it). I mentioned them because they’re a reflection of trust — trust earned across more than a decade helping developers make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure.

Today, we’re building on that foundation and extending that trust into the agentic era. At WeAreDevelopers, you saw the first steps. We launched Docker Cloud Sandboxes, published the next-generation Sandbox Kit specification (which we’ve committed to submitting to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation), and built nearly everything we showed around one idea: helping developers manufacture trust for AI agents.

If it all looked and felt like a slightly different Docker, that was intentional. We’re at the start of a transformative era for Docker, and you’ll see a lot more from us in the coming weeks and months.

But no matter how much the industry changes, and no matter how much we evolve along with it, one thing won’t change. Docker will continue to run on trust.

If you’d like to see what that looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes (and get a $250 credit if you sign up before Oct. 31). You can start an agent on your laptop, ship longer jobs off to the cloud, and bring the results back. We’d love to hear what you think.

Docker’s WeAreDevelopers keynote shows how Sandboxes, Kits, and Cloud Sandboxes give AI agents strong isolation and reproducible authority.

PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise landed in the same week. Docker published a fixed PHP image within 24 hours and rebuilt the trust store across the catalog.

On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Docker began tracking two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, commonly known as PHP2Shell.

#10165. All the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Amazon Prime Day 2026 was exclusively for Prime members and ran June 23–26, 2026 with millions of deals across more than 35 categories.

As part of our annual tradition of sharing how AWS powered Prime Day (2016, 2017, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025), I want to share the services and chart-topping metrics from AWS that made your amazing shopping experience possible.

Prime Day 2026 – all the numbers As always, Prime Day was powered by AWS. Here are some of the most interesting and/or mind-blowing metrics:

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) and AWS Graviton – During Amazon Prime Day 2026, AWS Graviton powered up to 49% of the Amazon EC2 compute used by Amazon.com.

Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon EBS, our high-performance block storage service, peaked at over 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving over an exabyte of data daily.

AWS Lambda – AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS) and Fargate – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, representing a 47.7 percent increase from the previous year’s Prime Day average.

Amazon CloudFront – Amazon CloudFront delivered over 2.1 trillion HTTP requests during the global week of Prime Day 2026, a 5 percent increase in total requests compared to Prime Day 2025.

Amazon DynamoDB – Amazon DynamoDB, a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database, powers multiple high-traffic Amazon properties and systems including Alexa, the Amazon.com sites, and all Amazon fulfillment centers. Over the course of Prime Day 2026, between June 23 and June 26, 2026, DynamoDB processed over 59 trillion requests. DynamoDB maintained high availability while delivering single-digit millisecond responses and peaking at 192 million requests per second.

Amazon Aurora – On Prime Day, Amazon Aurora, a relational database management system (RDBMS) built for high performance and availability at global scale for PostgreSQL, MySQL, and DSQL, processed hundreds of billions of transactions, stored 5,491 terabytes of data, and transferred 1,194 terabytes of data.

Amazon ElastiCache – During Prime Day, Amazon ElastiCache peaked at serving over 2.3 quadrillion daily requests and 2.1 trillion requests in a minute.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams – Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, a fully managed serverless data streaming service, processed a peak of 988 million records per second during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS) – Amazon SNS, a fully managed pub/sub messaging service for application-to-application and application-to-person communication, delivered 5 trillion messages in a single day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) – Amazon SQS, a fully managed message queuing service for microservices, distributed systems, and serverless applications, received a peak of 213 million messages per second during Prime Day 2026

AWS CloudTrail – AWS CloudTrail processes billions of API activity events per day for governance, compliance, and operational auditing. During Prime Day 2026, that volume surged to 3.6 trillion events in just four days, a 44% increase over Prime Day 2025.

Amazon CloudWatch – Amazon CloudWatch processed over 2.15 quadrillion metric observations per day during Prime Day 2026.

Amazon GuardDuty – During Prime Day 2026, Amazon GuardDuty monitored an average of 14.08 trillion log events per hour, a 59% increase from last year’s Prime Day.

AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) – We ran over 44,000 AWS FIS experiments – more than six times what we conducted in 2025 – to help ensure Amazon.com remains highly available on Prime Day.

Prepare to scale If you’re preparing for similar business-critical events, product launches, and migrations, I recommend that you take advantage of AWS Countdown Premium. From retail peak seasons to major sporting events, elections, and healthcare enrollment periods, we help you deliver flawless experiences when it matters most. Our experts help you manage your infrastructure to handle massive traffic spikes while maintaining security and performance. We work alongside your team to scale infrastructure, optimize costs during demand surges, strengthen security measures, and monitor real-time demands. To learn more, visit AWS Countdown Premium for business critical events.

I look forward to seeing what other records will be broken next year!

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#10164. Direct Preference Optimization Beyond Chatbots

In April, we released DharmaOCR, our specialized structured OCR model (available on Hugging Face) along with a paper detailing the methodology behind it and a benchmark demonstrating its superior quality and cost efficiency. The paper benchmarked leading vision-language model families - both open-source and commercial - on a structured document extraction task: OCR on Brazilian Portuguese text. Among the reported metrics was text degeneration rate: the frequency with which a model produces a repetition loop instead of a transcription.

Across the tested open-source families, vanilla degeneration rates ranged from below 1% to above 33%. Supervised fine-tuning reduced those rates for most models - but rarely to production-acceptable levels. The pattern points to a structural limitation: SFT optimizes for correct outputs, but does not explicitly penalize degeneration. There appears to be a ceiling on how much task-focused fine-tuning alone can reduce this failure mode (Text Degeneration Article).

A second training stage - applied after supervised fine-tuning (SFT), on the same documents, using the same model - reduced text degeneration in every family tested. No exceptions. Average reduction: 59.4%. Best case: 87.6%.

Figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

That second stage was Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Almost all published DPO applications target chat alignment - models trained on human judgments about helpfulness or harmlessness (example: Rafailov et al., 2023). OCR carries none of that subjectivity: the task is objective, and there is no conversational context. There is, however, a clear preference signal. A correct transcription is chosen; a degeneration loop is rejected. DharmaOCR used that binary to construct a DPO training set, testing the technique not for alignment, but as a direct mitigation tool for a specific failure mode.

The training signal came from the model itself - specifically from the outputs it produced when it failed. How a failure mode becomes a training signal is a structural question about the failure, not the model.

Why SFT has a ceiling on degeneration is still an open question - but the leading conjecture points to loss granularity. SFT trains token by token: each prediction is evaluated in isolation, and a repetition loop is never penalized as a completion-level failure. DPO inverts that logic. The training signal is the full output - chosen or rejected - which means a degenerated completion can be explicitly labeled as the wrong outcome, not just a sequence of locally probable tokens.

When a training objective maximizes the likelihood of observed sequences, it concentrates probability mass in the regions of distribution space those sequences occupy. A model that enters one of those high-probability attractor regions during inference assigns elevated probability to the same token at the next step - which increases the probability further, which sustains the loop until the sequence hits the maximum token limit. Text degeneration is the output of this geometry: a self-reinforcing repetition loop that an autoregressive model cannot exit without external intervention (Holtzman et al., 2020). It is not purely a decoding artifact. The attractor involves the training objective, the learned distribution, and how probability mass concentrates during inference - a systems-level failure rather than a failure localized to any single component.

The geometry of this failure is visible at the token level.

Figure 2: When a token dominates its own conditional distribution, every sampling step deepens the attractor. The decoder samples from this geometry; it does not determine it.

Inference-layer interventions - repetition penalties, temperature adjustments, early-abort logic - operate on the sampling step. They contain the symptom without touching the distribution that produces it. The attractor persists.

Supervised fine-tuning moves the distribution closer to the task domain. For a structured generation pipeline, this means training on domain-specific documents, in the target language, with the required output format. The model gains fluency with longer sequences, constrained syntax, domain vocabulary. What SFT does not do is attack degeneration directly. Its objective - maximizing the likelihood of observed sequences - has no term that penalizes repetition loops. The failure mode is simply outside the scope of what the training signal optimizes for.

One model family in the DharmaOCR benchmark showed an unexpected pattern: vanilla degeneration rate of 0.60%, rising to 3.23% after SFT, before a subsequent DPO stage brought it to 1.41%. It is a single data point - an exception, not a rule - and it would be overstating the evidence to treat it as proof of a mechanism. What it does illustrate is that SFT does not reliably reduce degeneration. Capability and degeneration resistance can move independently.

The distinction matters structurally. SFT and DPO are not interchangeable training stages performing the same operation at different intensities. SFT closes the distance between the model's prior distribution and the task domain. What it does not do is target degeneration as an objective - its effect on the failure mode is incidental, and the benchmark results show it is not consistent. The attractor that produces degeneration is not a problem with the model's proximity to the task - it is a problem with the shape of the distribution space the model now occupies.

Addressing that geometry requires a training signal built specifically to point the model away from its own failure modes. For a structured, non-conversational task with no human preference labels and no conventional "helpful versus harmful" distinction, constructing that signal is a design decision.

The DharmaOCR pipeline's contribution to DPO methodology is specific: it used the SFT model's own degenerate outputs as the rejected examples - not as noise to remove, but as the negative training signal the optimization needed.

DPO requires preference pairs: a chosen output and a rejected output for the same input, with a quality difference clear enough for the optimization to learn from. In chat alignment, human annotators produce those judgments - rating responses as more or less helpful, accurate, or safe. Structured generation tasks have no equivalent annotation source. An OCR pipeline either produces a correct transcription or it does not. Quality differences exist, but they are not produced by human preference rankings - they are produced by the task's own criteria for correctness.

The DharmaOCR pipeline identified a preference signal that structured generation tasks already produce: the range of outputs the SFT model generates in inference. A model capable of performing a structured task is also capable of failing at it in characteristic ways. Those failures - outputs that enter the degeneration attractor - are not noise to filter. They are the most informative negative signal available.

The paper implemented this on 23,726 training documents, generating multiple candidate responses per document with the SFT model and scoring each with an automated LLM judge. The pipeline is shown below.

Figure 3: The critical design decision is not in the pipeline's structure - it is in what the pipeline preserved: outputs displaying text degeneration were deliberately labeled as rejected examples, not filtered out as low-quality noise.

The conventional response when degenerate outputs appear in training data is to remove them. They are low-quality signal; filtering produces a cleaner dataset. The DharmaOCR approach inverted this logic. Degenerate outputs were deliberately retained as the rejected examples in each (chosen, rejected) pair, because they represent exactly the failure mode the DPO stage was designed to suppress. Removing them would have discarded the clearest target available.

The paper describes this as "preference-guided implicit unlikelihood" - the model is trained not only toward better outputs but away from a specific class of failure. Where SFT maximizes the likelihood of high-quality outputs, the DPO stage simultaneously penalizes outputs displaying the degeneration attractor geometry. The direction of the optimization is explicit in a way SFT alone cannot achieve.

Degenerate outputs are particularly well-suited as rejection examples because they represent a consistent failure mode rather than varied low-quality outputs. A transcription that misses words is low quality, but its failure is case-specific. Repetition loops, by contrast, appeared persistently across documents and model families even after SFT - a pattern consistent with a failure mode that likelihood-based optimization does not reliably correct. DPO applies its loss differently: at the completion level, with explicit rejection signals. The post-hoc analysis cannot establish causality, but the evidence suggests that what SFT's objective leaves unresolved, DPO's may address.

This approach requires no specialized annotation infrastructure - only a model capable of producing both acceptable and identifiable-failure outputs, and a scoring model to label preference pairs. A rule-based mechanism could detect repetition loops mechanically - but it could not identify which outputs represented high-quality transcriptions worth preserving as chosen examples.

The scoring model does both: it flags degeneration as the rejected output and validates clean extractions as the chosen one, keeping the model's extraction capability intact while the DPO signal penalizes the failure mode. Whether the resulting training signal successfully moves the distribution in the intended direction - and whether it does so consistently across architectures - is the evidence question.

The DPO stage reduced text degeneration in every model family tested - with reductions ranging from 37% to 88% and an average of 59.4% relative to SFT alone. The result held across architectures, parameter scales, and starting degeneration profiles that differed by more than one order of magnitude. One case in the dataset saw degeneration increase after the SFT stage before DPO corrected it. That case does not complicate the consistency. It confirms the mechanism more directly than any of the others.

Figure 1 shows the three-stage degeneration rate for each of the five model families tested: Vanilla, SFT, and SFT+DPO. In four of the five families, degeneration falls at each stage. The fifth family's bars move differently - and that difference is the most analytically important data point in the study.

The Qwen2.5-VL-3B result, read carefully, is not a complication. It is a confirmation. The model's vanilla degeneration rate was 0.60% - not because it was stable, but because it was too generic to produce long structured outputs at all. The model was not entering the degeneration attractor because it was not attempting the task seriously enough to find it.

SFT changed that. After domain adaptation, Qwen2.5-VL-3B became capable of the task - producing longer, more structured outputs with the domain vocabulary and format the pipeline required. That capability brought it into proximity with the degeneration attractor for the first time. Its degeneration rate rose to 3.23%.

This is the mechanism made empirically visible: SFT moved the model toward the task and toward the task's failure geometry simultaneously. These are not necessarily the same operation. A training stage that increases task capability can increase failure-mode exposure as a side effect - particularly when the failure mode lives at the edge of the capability frontier. Treated as the same operation, the Qwen2.5-VL-3B result looks like an error. Treated as distinct operations - which is what the SFT + DPO pipeline formally does - the result is consistent with the hypothesis that SFT and DPO address different failure dimensions.

The DPO stage then brought the degeneration rate to 1.41%. It did not restore the vanilla baseline because it was not designed to: the model after SFT was more capable than it had been, and a return to 0.60% would have required undoing that capability. What the DPO stage did was address the failure geometry the SFT stage had introduced.

The remaining four model families add quantitative weight to the same conclusion. Figure 1 shows the SFT-to-SFT+DPO comparison for all five.

Figure 1: DPO reduced degeneration relative to SFT in every family tested - average reduction of 59.4%, peak of 87.6% (Nanonets-OCR2–3B: 1.61% to 0.20%). The direction is invariant; only the magnitude varies.

No model family showed degeneration increasing after DPO. No family was immune to its effect. The consistency extends to gemma-3–4b-it, which entered the benchmark with the highest vanilla degeneration rate by an order of magnitude - 33.96%, compared to the next highest at 2.62% - and still reached a 75% reduction after the DPO stage. The reduction range - 37.3% to 87.6% - reflects differences in starting configuration and architecture, not inconsistency in the intervention's direction.

This is not a proof of universal applicability. DPO may not transfer to every domain, failure mode, or model family. What the DharmaOCR benchmark provides is evidence across five OCR architectures that the core hypothesis holds: optimizing over complete preference pairs - rather than maximizing token-level likelihood - addresses a failure mode that SFT structurally cannot target. The result was consistent in direction across every model family tested. That consistency, within the scope of this benchmark, is what the evidence supports.

The DharmaOCR approach was possible because this pipeline satisfied a set of structural conditions that allowed a DPO training stage to function as designed - conditions whose presence or absence determines whether the same methodology applies elsewhere (Dharma OCR Paper on ArXiv). It was not possible because OCR is a unique domain.

The first condition is that the failure mode be identifiable as a distinct class of output, not just a point on a quality continuum. Text degeneration qualifies because a repetition loop is categorically different from a transcription that misses words or misreads a character. The output is not merely suboptimal - it is broken in a specific, behaviorally recognizable way. That categorical distinctness is what allowed the pipeline to construct preference pairs where the rejected examples represented a coherent failure geometry, not noise. A task whose failure modes blend into its range of acceptable variation lacks this property.

The second condition is that a scoring mechanism can reliably distinguish acceptable outputs from failure-mode outputs without requiring human annotation. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, an automated LLM judge scored candidate responses against four task-specific criteria. The scoring did not need to be perfect - it needed to be consistent enough to produce preference pairs with a meaningful quality gap between chosen and rejected. Pairs with ambiguous quality differences contribute noise to DPO training, not signal. The judge's consistency was a design requirement, not an incidental feature.

The third condition is sufficient volume - enough inference outputs to generate a preference dataset with meaningful variance in quality. This is not an extraordinary requirement by fine-tuning standards, but it is a real one.

When all three conditions are present, the methodological move is structurally available. The design decision at the center of the DharmaOCR pipeline - treating the model's own failure outputs as the rejected examples rather than filtering them - applies wherever a model's failures are categorically identifiable, scoreable, and sufficiently numerous.

The practical implication for ML engineers building structured generation pipelines is direct. SFT is necessary - it closes the distance between a generalist model and a task-capable one. It is not sufficient for structured output reliability, because task capability and degeneration resistance are different properties of the distribution. A DPO stage after SFT is a one-time training investment. In the DharmaOCR results, the degeneration reduction did not come at the cost of extraction quality - the paper's benchmark results show both moving together (Specialization Beats Scale article).

What makes a failure mode usable as training signal is not the domain - it is whether the failures are consistent enough, identifiable enough, and numerous enough to constitute a legible signal. In the DharmaOCR pipeline, they were. Whether the same holds in another context is a structural question about the task's failure mode, not a question about the model family or the domain.

The DharmaOCR result does not depend on the domain being special. It depends on the failures being useful.

Text degeneration qualifies as useful because it is categorically distinct from acceptable outputs, consistently produced across inference runs, and reliably scoreable without human annotation. Those three properties - not the OCR context, not the model family, not the language - determined whether the preference dataset was tractable. A failure mode that satisfies them is not noise to remove. It is the most direct evidence available of where the distribution should not go.

The DPO stage used that evidence. Degeneration fell in every model family tested - in models that entered the benchmark with vanilla rates below 1% and in models that entered with rates above 33%. The direction held. The pipeline did not discard its failures. It trained on them.

#10163. From baseline to Secure Software Factory: securing the systems that build your software

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

In July, Docker, Snyk and Keycard published Agent Baseline, an open, vendor-neutral reference architecture that defines security outcomes for running AI agents in the enterprise. It grew out of conversations with industry leaders who want to adopt agents more broadly but need answers to three questions:

Agent Baseline gave the industry a shared frame of reference for secure agent adoption by defining the security outcomes for safely deploying agents in organizations. Last week, we published the Secure Software Factory reference architecture, which applies those outcomes to one of the most common agentic workflows: the AI-powered software factory.

The Secure Software Factory was written by practitioners from Keycard, Socket, Docker, Tessl, Tracebit, Browserbase and Tailscale and shaped by conversations with security leaders at large enterprises in regulated environments such as finance and insurance.

Over the past year, many engineering teams have started building software factories: systems where agents take a request, change code, run tests and hand the result to a human for review. Teams report faster delivery, but also agents doing things nobody asked for, like escaping sandboxes, dropping databases and pushing to production without approval.

Teams need controls that limit what agents can access and do, and check their work at each step. The Secure Software Factory reference architecture shows how to apply Agent Baseline’s security outcomes across this workflow, covering:

The paper’s central idea is that the more autonomy you give an agent, the less you can rely on it to police itself. An agent can be redirected at runtime by a prompt, a poisoned dependency or a malicious tool description. Controls have to work regardless of what the agent decides, which means they need to live in the environment it runs in. That means boundaries around credentials, tools, dependencies and network access, backed by evidence of what happened and a human accountable for the result.

This is the part of the problem Docker solves. Containers isolate applications; sandboxes isolate actors. Docker Sandboxes are isolated MicroVMs that constrain agents, deterministically.

Docker Sandboxes lets coding agents work autonomously in isolated microVM environments, locally or in the cloud, with explicit boundaries around the files, network destinations, and credentials they can access. This supports Agent Baseline’s Constrain outcome by confining agent execution and limiting its reach to what the approved task requires.

Agent Baseline is only useful if the people building the agent stack agree on it. Which is why we are proud to be among leading companies such as Snyk, Keycard, Browserbase, Tessl, Socket and Tracebit, in shaping the baseline and the reference architectures built on it.

In a software factory, context is the new code: it’s what actually gets executed. The skills you consume are part of your supply chain, and can be vulnerable, negligent or outright malicious. They need the same security controls software modules do – let’s get it right from the start!

“We’ve spent decades learning not to give software more access than it needs. We seem to have forgotten much of that now that the software can talk back. Agents need to reach real systems, sometimes even production. The rules haven’t changed: give them the authority to do a particular job, make that authority expire, and keep the policies and audit trail somewhere the agent can’t rewrite them. Agent Baseline gives everyone a common architecture for making that work, without every team having to figure it out from scratch.”

Avery Pennarun, Co-Founder & CEO, Tailscale

“Enterprises are handing AI agents real credentials, and some of those agents will go off-task, whether through prompt injection, a poisoned tool or a simple mistake. Agent Baseline sets the standard for keeping agents in bounds”

“Agents need the right guardrails to complete tasks on behalf of humans. This is an industry wide effort and Browserbase is proud to continue supporting initiatives like Agent Baseline”

“Agents will install whatever gets the job done, including packages that were never safe to use. The Software Factory Reference Architecture sets out the controls that prevent that, starting with verifying every input before the factory uses it.”

“Agents are already building software, and teams want them picking up work on their own. That only works if an agent’s plan can never become its permission. Agent Baseline gives everyone a shared architecture for deciding what each agent may do, task by task and outside the agent’s reach, so teams can add autonomy without starting their security model over.”

Ian Livingstone, Co-Founder & CEO, Keycard

Help shape Agent Baseline and the Secure Software Factory reference architecture by putting them to work.

Read the paper, open an issue on GitHub or join the Agent Baseline Slack to tell us where the architecture doesn’t match how you build. Implementation feedback is the most useful kind.

Docker’s WeAreDevelopers keynote shows how Sandboxes, Kits, and Cloud Sandboxes give AI agents strong isolation and reproducible authority.

An AI code review agent invented a CVE and recommended dangerous fixes. Learn how Docker Sandboxes contain agents and why their output needs verification.

Docker is launching the Navigator Partner Program, with three tiers, co-selling benefits, and a new incentive for every registered AI governance deal.

#10162. Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

Lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

The three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate quickly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

Let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

The only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):

One command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to new code.

Next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:

Lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

When I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the new revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

Better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:

For pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

Micah Walter is a Sr. Solutions Architect supporting enterprise customers in the New York City region and beyond. He advises executives, engineers, and architects at every step along their journey to the cloud, with a deep focus on sustainability and practical design. #10161. Your Agent Runs in a Docker Sandbox. Now It Can Join a Team.

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

Your sandboxed agents just got a team. The official BAND AI kit for Docker Sandboxes is now available at docker.io/bandhq/band-python-kit:latest.

Docker Sandbox kits package everything an agent needs to run in a Docker Sandbox, so a single sbx create command gives you a ready-to-use agent environment. But an isolated agent is only half the story: real work means talking to people and to other agents. The BAND AI kit connects a sandboxed agent to the world. The agent runs on your machine with access to your repository, and joins a BAND room where it collaborates with humans and with agents running anywhere: locally, in the cloud, or on your own infrastructure. The same kit also connects sandboxes to each other, so multiple agents can work together in one room while each keeps its own isolated environment. In this post, we’ll show how a sandboxed agent connects to the world through BAND, using a local agent called Repo Doctor.

BAND provides the collaboration layer for these agents. With BAND, developers can give agents persistent identities, bring them together in shared rooms, route work through @mentions, maintain message history, and surface tool execution events in the room. Each agent brings its own model, framework, tools, workspace, and infrastructure, and joins the room as a participant, wherever it runs.

Docker Sandboxes give that agent an isolated microVM with its own kernel, filesystem, Docker daemon, and network. Inside it, the agent works with local source files, runs commands and tests, and makes changes to a mounted workspace. The BAND kit connects the two with one sbx create command.

All connectivity is outbound. The agent opens a WebSocket to BAND and posts its replies through the BAND API, so nothing needs to reach into the sandbox. From the room’s point of view, it behaves like any other participant.

Here’s a neat example of how it all works together. Repo Doctor is a small agent that repairs a deliberately broken Python project. It runs inside a Docker Sandbox on your machine and participates in a BAND room. Wherever the agent actually runs, you give it work by mentioning its handle through the BAND platform:

This example repo includes a band.yaml file that tells the BAND sbx kit which agent to launch. In this example, it points to main.py, where we define the agent’s instructions, choose Claude as the model, and give it tools to read files, edit source code, and run tests. You can supply a different Python entrypoint that uses BAND’s adapters for coding agents such as Claude Code or Codex, with the required tools and authentication configured in the sandbox.

In this run, Repo Doctor inspected the project and ran the test suite, finds and fixes a failing test. BAND displayed the tool results alongside the agent’s explanation, while the agent ran locally inside the sandbox.

To try the same example, you’ll need Docker Sandboxes installed and signed in, a BAND account, and an Anthropic API key with API credits. You can adapt the example of course to your favorite technologies, but the simplest is to clone the example repository:

In BAND, create a remote agent or use an existing one. Note its handle, which you’ll use to mention it in a BAND room. Set agent.id in band.yaml to its agent UUID, and have its BAND API key ready for the next step.

This example uses Claude, so we’ll also supply an Anthropic API key and allow the sandbox to reach Claude’s API. These settings follow from the agent implementation in main.py in the repo; the BAND kit itself does not require a particular model provider. The BAND agent key authenticates the connection to the platform.

Store both keys before creating the sandbox. Each command prompts for a secret: enter the BAND agent key first, then your Anthropic API key.

Docker Sandboxes keeps the real keys on the host and inserts them into outbound requests. The agent sees only placeholder values, and both credentials are scoped to this sandbox.

Now create the sandbox with the BAND kit, allow the Claude API connection, and start the agent:

The kit already permits access to BAND and the Python package hosts. Add access to Claude’s API for this example:

Then start the agent in the prepared sandbox. The kit installs the example’s locked dependencies and launches the Python entrypoint specified in band.yaml. The agent connects to BAND, where you or other agents can communicate with it.

Keep the terminal open while the agent runs. Once the log shows Connected to platform, add Repo Doctor to a BAND room and mention its handle like we did above.

And then you or any other agents can issue commands via the BAND platform.

Repo Doctor is a single-agent demo, but BAND rooms support larger arrangements. A room can contain agents running locally, in the cloud, or on your own infrastructure. They can mention each other, add specialists to a room, work sequentially or in parallel, and return the result to a human participant.

For example, a planner agent can plan a change and ask a research agent to check the relevant API. When the work needs your repository, it mentions Repo Doctor. Only Repo Doctor needs access to the local workspace, so only that agent runs in the Docker Sandbox on your machine. After running the tests, Repo Doctor can @mention a reviewer with the result; the full execution events remain visible to the human in the room. The same pattern works across sandboxes: agents that each need their own isolated environment can run in separate sandboxes and still collaborate in the same room.

Humans can see the whole conversation. An agent’s context stays narrower because BAND delivers only messages that mention it. Hosted agents can collaborate broadly, with local execution attached to the one participant that actually needs it.

BAND is particularly good at this composition. The local agent is one participant in a larger room, and its peers address it by handle. That saves you from building agent identity, routing, a worker connection back to the laptop, credential handling, and an audit trail before getting to the actual task. The seam between BAND and the sandbox is a WebSocket connection and a room mention, which is about as much integration code as I would like this problem to have.

The BAND Python SDK repository contains the SDK and kit sources. The complete Repo Doctor example in the Docker Samples repository includes the agent, fixture, and scripts used to reproduce the screenshots.

Create a sandbox from the published kit, connect the remote agent to a BAND room, and check sbx policy log to confirm its network requests match the policy you intended.

For sandbox kit configuration, credentials, and network rules, see the Docker Sandboxes kit documentation.

#10159. Designing the hf CLI as an agent-optimized way to work with the Hub

hf is the official command-line entrypoint to the Hugging Face Hub. Anything you can do on the Hub from the Python SDK, you can do from your terminal: download and upload models, datasets and Spaces; create and manage repos, branches, tags and pull requests; run Jobs on HF infrastructure; manage Buckets, Collections, webhooks and Inference Endpoints.

The hf CLI has been primarily built for our users over the years. But it's now increasingly used by coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. So we rebuilt it to make it work for both audiences at once. This blog post summarizes what we did, and how we benchmarked it. We found that on complex, multi-step tasks the no-CLI baseline (an agent hand-rolling curl or the Python SDK) uses up to 6× as many tokens as the hf CLI.

We started tracking agent usage of the Hub in April 2026. The hf CLI (and the huggingface_hub Python SDK it's built on) detects when a coding agent is driving it by reading the environment variables agents set: CLAUDECODE/CLAUDE_CODE for Claude Code, CODEX_SANDBOX for Codex, plus Cursor, Gemini, Pi, and the universal AI_AGENT. That single signal does two jobs: it shapes the CLI's output (more on that below) and it tags each Hub request with an agent/ user-agent, so we can attribute traffic to the agent driving it. The two largest by distinct users are Claude Code and Codex, well ahead of everything else, and they're the two agents we benchmark later in this article.

The bars count distinct users per agent; request volume is the sub-label. Claude Code alone is ~40k users and nearly 49M requests, with Codex close behind. These are early numbers (we only began attributing agent traffic in April 2026), but the scale is already significant, and we expect it to keep growing as coding agents become a standard way to work with the Hub.

Humans and coding agents expect different outputs for the same hf commands. A human wants rich terminal output: ANSI color, padded tables truncated to fit the screen, a green ✅ on success, ✔ for booleans, progress bars, prose hints. An agent wants the inverse: no ANSI, nothing truncated, every value in full since an agent can handle far denser output than a human, kept compact and structured to stay light on tokens. It also can't answer a CLI prompt and will happily re-run a command after a timeout. The rest of this section is how hf gives each side what it needs. We introduced agent-mode output in hf v1.9.0 and have been migrating the rest of the CLI to it gradually in the following releases.

When hf auto-detects agent use (via the environment variables mentioned above), it renders the same command differently. It optimizes output format for humans or agents without passing a flag:

A human gets an aligned table, truncated to fit the terminal, plus a hint on how to see more, with color cues for status (a green ✓ on success, red on error). An agent gets the complete record as TSV: full repo ids, full ISO timestamps, every tag, no ANSI codes, nothing truncated, clean to parse and light on tokens.

In practice, we've implemented logging methods like .table(...), .result(...), .json(), etc., which take raw data as input and handle the formatting. In addition to human and agent modes, we've introduced --json and --quiet options to make it easier to pipe commands together. The default mode is automatically chosen based on context, but users can always force the format of their choice with --format human | agent | json | quiet.

CLI commands rarely run in isolation: one step usually implies the next (git add, then git commit). Many hf commands now end with a hint: the exact next command to run, pre-filled with the IDs you just used, so a user or agent can chain straight to the next step instead of working it out from scratch. Start a Job in the background and it points you to its logs; create a Space and it points you to its boot status:

For a human that's a convenience. For an agent it's a rail: the next action is named, parameterized with the right ids, and ready to run, so it takes fewer steps working out what to do. Errors behave the same way, naming the fix instead of just failing:

Hints, warnings and errors all go to stderr while data goes to stdout, so none of this guidance pollutes the output the agent is parsing.

hf never sits on an interactive prompt waiting for a key an agent can't press. A destructive command still asks a human to confirm, but in agent mode it fails fast with the fix in the message (Use --yes to skip confirmation.), and -y/--yes skips it. And because agents retry on timeouts and lost context, operations are built to be safe to repeat: hf repos create --exist-ok is a no-op if the repo already exists, and re-running an upload re-commits cleanly. Separately, the commands that move real data take a --dry-run that shows exactly what they'll transfer before they run, which proves handy for humans and agents alike, since neither has to commit to a long download or blind sync:

hf is built to be probed: run hf to see the resource groups, run --help on the one you need, and every --help ends with real, copy-pasteable examples (which an agent matches against far faster than it parses a description):

The command tree is consistent, resource + verb with the obvious aliases (hf models ls, hf repos create, hf jobs ps, hf collections delete; list/ls, remove/rm), so once an agent learns one command it can guess the rest. And the output composes: -q prints one id per line to pipe into the next command, --json gives you something to hand to jq.

To find out whether the hf CLI is really more efficient for agents, we measured it. We built a small evaluation harness and ran the same set of Hub tasks through each way of driving the Hub, many times over, grading every run against the live Hub. Here's the headline before the methodology: across both agents the hf CLI comes out ahead, most clearly on complex, multi-step tasks where it uses far fewer tokens.

(self-report error = the agent reported success on the 17 solvable tasks but the Hub said otherwise. The hf CLI rows are the CLI with its skill installed; what the skill adds on top of the bare CLI (chiefly fewer tool calls) is broken out in the skill section below. Representative transcripts are published in this bucket.)

We defined 18 non-trivial Hub tasks. Not "download a file", but the kind of thing you'd actually ask for: aggregate a trending org's models, inspect a repo's files and their sizes, upload a folder with include/exclude rules, delete files, copy files across repos, open a PR that adds a license, create a repo with a branch and a tag, sync and prune a bucket, build a collection. Each task goes to a fresh coding agent with exactly one way to talk to the Hub:

We run the hf CLI in two configurations, with and without its skill (a generated command reference we come back to in its own section). But the headline comparison below is simply hf CLI vs curl / the SDK; the skill's incremental effect is small enough that we break it out on its own rather than crowd it into the main results.

The config is deliberately clean: a fresh instance per run, no custom MCP servers, no CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, nothing in context to nudge behavior. The task and the tool go into a single prompt, and the agent finishes with a TASK_COMPLETE or TASK_FAILED marker, but we don't trust that marker (an agent will report success on work that never landed), so we grade every run independently by re-querying the live Hub: did the branch really get created, is the file actually gone, does the bucket exist? Each task/tool combination is run 10 times, since coding agents are non-deterministic, about 520 runs per agent (18 tasks × 3 tools × 10 reps, minus a cap on one billable Jobs task) and ~1,000 graded runs in total. We ran the whole thing twice, on the two most popular coding agents (Claude Code with Sonnet 4.6 and OpenAI Codex with GPT-5.5).

The two charts below unpack the table above. First, task success on Sonnet, the agent where curl and the SDK struggle most:

Without the CLI, curl and the SDK trail by ten points, because on Sonnet they simply can't finish parts of the job (the writes, mostly), while the hf CLI clears them.

The second image shows token impact on GPT-5.5, broken down per task. Each bar is the curl/SDK tokens divided by the CLI's on the same task, so 2.4× means the non-hf version burned 2.4 times as many tokens to do the same thing:

On a one-shot read (count dataset rows, batch metadata) curl and the SDK are fine, and sometimes lighter. But as tasks get more complex and involve several dependent steps, the agent has to hand-roll the entire chain of REST calls (or dig through the SDK) and the cost blows up: 2.4× to 6× the CLI's on creating a repo with a branch and tag, deleting files, copying across repos, or syncing a bucket. The hf CLI lets the agent express the task as a few higher-level commands, rather than crafting a complex workflow.

hf ships a skill: a compact reference of the whole command surface that an agent loads as context. It's auto-generated from the live hf command tree, one line per command (its signature, a one-line description, and the flags that matter), grouped by resource, with a short glossary of common options. It deliberately skips the self-explanatory flags so it stays terse and light on context, and it's regenerated every release. Run hf skills preview to print it, or install it with:

What does it buy you? Mostly, the agent stops guessing. The clearest single view is how many commands each run takes, with the skill and without:

On both agents that's about ten commands per task down to about seven, roughly 30% fewer tool calls. That's because the agent isn't probing --help to find the right command and argument. The skill won't cut your token bill, because it prepends a fixed slice of info to the context, so tokens remain about the same or slightly tick up for the same task. The Skill won't make the CLI more reliable either, but it will help the agent spend time running your task rather than finding out how the tool works. This could be particularly helpful when using hf with local models.

We ran each task in a fresh session, so the skill pays its context cost on every task. In a real multi-task session that cost amortizes (the agent learns the command surface once), so the token picture likely improves there; we didn't measure that case.

We benchmarked all this because we think it matters. Agents are becoming real users of the Hub: they train models, build and clean datasets, and ship demos as Spaces, almost always on behalf of a person. A Hub that works well for agents is also a Hub that works better for the people using them. The better an agent's tools are, the more it can do for you.

If your agent interacts with the Hugging Face Hub, we recommend giving it the hf CLI:

Then hand it the skill, so it knows the whole command surface from the first turn:

Then point your agent at the Hub and let it work. Make sure you're logged in (hf auth login), then hand it a prompt like:

It'll work out the commands on its own and come back with something useful.

The full command reference lives in the hf CLI guide.

Building an agent harness? Get it registered! That's how hf learns to detect it, and how the Hub attributes its traffic to your harness. You simply need to open a small PR adding an entry to agent-harnesses.ts. Read the Register your agent harness guide for more details.

Giving AI agents access to command-line tools can make them more capable because they can interact with real development resources instead of relying entirely on generated text. The important part is setting appropriate permissions, defining task boundaries, and checking the results of commands before allowing consequential changes. I also think repeatable workflows make these integrations easier to manage, especially when the same development tasks occur frequently. This guide onhttps://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-development/ai-workflow-automation-cursor-claude-commands is relevant to that idea, as reusable commands can help standardize routine coding activities. Combining tool access with clear safeguards is key to building dependable AI-assisted workflows.

Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

The number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning.

#10157. Security Update on PHP2Shell: Impact for Docker Customers

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Docker began tracking two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, commonly known as PHP2Shell. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to execute code remotely in PHP core, and they affect PHP packages going back to version 5.4: the supported versions 8.2 through 8.5, and the end-of-life versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1.

To address these vulnerabilities, PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and advised anyone running PHP to update to the latest version immediately.

Although this is a vulnerability in PHP itself, not in Docker’s systems, it nonetheless affects Docker users who build on PHP images and packages. In response, we have updated the Docker Hardened Images and Docker Official Images on Docker Hub, and advise customers to immediately update.

Along with other package repositories and secure package providers, Docker has been made aware of and is tracking two recently discovered critical vulnerabilities in PHP packages distributed since version 5.4. The two critical vulnerabilities, now commonly referred to as “PHP2Shell,” are identified and tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. (The PHP Foundation has published a detailed report on the discovery that we recommend reading for full context.)

In short: these vulnerabilities could allow remote code execution in PHP core by malicious actors. Both are flaws in how PHP manages request memory. In CVE-2026-109618, when PHP runs out of memory mid-request and aborts, some code paths leave memory uninitialized, and PHP’s cleanup step then reads it. In CVE-2026-109619, PHP’s internal state can keep pointing at memory that has already been freed, and a later request then uses that stale state. Attackers have multiple ways to trigger either condition and turn it into remote code execution.

Affected versions include the currently supported versions (8.2 through 8.5), as well as the EOL and unsupported versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1.

Whether you are a Docker user or not, if you are using any of the above affected versions of PHP, you should immediately upgrade to the latest version. That includes PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12, or a later release in the corresponding branch.

There is no other comprehensive remediation for the affected versions. Updating is the only complete mitigation path.

If for any reason you are unable to complete an immediate update, we strongly recommend taking your system offline until such time that you can initiate mitigation. This the guidance of not only Docker, but of the FBI, and numerous experts throughout the cybersecurity community.

While this vulnerability exists in PHP itself and not directly in Docker’s systems, there is nonetheless potential risk and exposure to Docker customers who run PHP in their applications, including anyone using PHP images or packages from Docker Hub, Docker Official Images, or Docker Hardened Images.

For users of Docker Official Images:Docker Official Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub and mirrored to Amazon ECR. Customers using either of these sources should update immediately.

For users of Docker Hardened Images (DHI):Docker Hardened Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub. The currently supported versions of PHP were updated as follows:

The updates to our images were completed and released within 24-hours of the upstream patches being made available. These images were made available after successfully executing the DHI testing and verification processes.

If you have any issues accessing the updated images or migrating to the new versions, please contact Docker Support at app.docker.com/support/contact. As always when it comes to matters of security, we appreciate your diligence.

#10156. Amazon S3 is now available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

Why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:

The integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

Analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

Vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:

Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where users upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

Combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

Using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a new AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

Pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. New AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months.
