#10155. PHP2Shell and eMudhra Patched

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

Two security events landed side by side this week, PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Both reached the same place, the foundation their applications are built on.

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They let an unauthenticated request become code execution on the server, on any PHP application, however careful its own code is, and PHP runs about 69% of the websites whose server-side language is known.

The eMudhra compromise is a different kind of problem. Eight intermediate certificates from the certificate authority eMudhra turned out to have private keys that can be computed from the public certificates, which let anyone issue a certificate for any website and have it accepted. Browsers revoke certificates like these on their own, but a container image carries its own trust store and keeps trusting them until it is rebuilt.

The dhi.io/php image was rebuilt on the patched PHP and published early on October 22, within 24 hours of the upstream release and after the DHI testing and verification steps. Pulling the current tag puts you on the fixed version. The few DHI images that bundle their own PHP application, such as composer and nextcloud, follow as their upstream projects release.

The certificate compromise touched the whole catalog, because every image carries a trust store. In the 48 hours after the PHP release, the DHI build system ran 16,567 package and image builds across the catalog. By 10pm UTC on October 22, almost all catalog tags were on the fixed CA store, with most of the rest in the build queue. That percentage comes from the SBOM that ships with every image, read for every published tag to check which CA store and which PHP version it carries, and you can run the same check on anything you pull.

If you run PHP on Docker Hardened Images, pull the current tag for your branch and redeploy, and rebuild anything you built on top of a DHI image so it picks up the new base docker pull dhi.io/php:8.4

Customizations built through the DHI Enterprise workflow are rebuilt automatically when the base layer is patched. For the certificate fix the same applies to every image you build from a DHI base, PHP or not. The Docker Security update from October 22 lists the affected PHP versions and the support path.

If you run PHP in any other container, check the PHP version running inside it rather than the tag on the outside, and rebuild it on a patched base.

Weeks like this one will keep coming, but a trusted foundation will make all the difference.

If you are not building on hardened images yet, this week is the wake-up call and the week to start. Both events landed on the foundation, and that is where the fix has to happen, in the image itself, rebuilt from fixed sources before anyone pulls it.

This is exactly what Docker Hardened Images were built for. Docker builds, patches and maintains the system packages inside each image from source, and the build system is event-driven, so an upstream release or a changed package triggers rebuilds of everything that depends on it. Each image ships signed, with its SBOM, SLSA Build Level 3 provenance and VEX data attached, which is why a rebuild of this size can be measured as well as done.

The catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with near-zero CVEs on every image. It stays compatible with the Alpine and Debian your teams already run, so adoption is a one-line change to the FROM line in your Dockerfile, with no migration project attached. DHI Select and DHI Enterprise add SLA-backed remediation with critical CVE fixes within 7 days, FIPS and STIG variants, image customization with the guarantees kept, and Extended Lifecycle Support for the versions upstream has stopped patching. All of it is in the Docker Hardened Images catalog, free to pull today.

#10154. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety: Customizable Multimodal Safety for Global Enterprise AI

The last two years have seen NVIDIA's content safety stack grow from a focused English text classifier into a family of specialized models—each extending coverage to new modalities, languages, and inference modes. Nemotron 3 Content Safety, released in March 2026, combined multimodal and multilingual capabilities for the first time in a single 4B-parameter model. Today, we are releasing Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety, which completes that arc: a single model that unifies multimodal input, multilingual reach, custom enterprise policy enforcement, and auditable reasoning into one inference call.

This post covers what changes in 3.5, the design decisions behind each new capability, and how to integrate the model into production safety pipelines.

Nemotron 3 introduced image understanding; Nemotron 3.5 deepens the multimodal integration. The model takes a user prompt, an optional image, and an optional assistant response as a single context window and produces a coherent safety verdict over the combined input. Evaluating all three together—rather than scoring each independently—closes a well-known gap in multimodal safety scenarios: policy violations that only emerge from the interaction between text and image, or between request and response, are now caught in a single pass.

Nemotron 3.5 maintains the 12-language explicit training coverage of its predecessors—English, French, Spanish, German, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, and Italian—while also inheriting strong zero-shot generalization across approximately 140 languages from the Gemma 3 base model. This means deployments in markets where training data is sparse (e.g., Southeast Asian languages, Scandinavian languages, less-resourced African languages) benefit from base-model multilingual transfer without requiring separate fine-tuning.

This is the most significant architectural addition in 3.5 relative to Nemotron 3. Production deployments rarely operate under a single universal safety taxonomy. A healthcare platform has a different risk profile than a financial services chatbot, a developer tools IDE, or a children's education app. Nemotron 3.5 accepts a custom policy specification alongside the input. The model reasons over that policy when producing its verdict rather than deferring entirely to the built-in taxonomy. This extends the work first introduced in Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B to the full multimodal, multilingual setting.

Every safety verdict in Nemotron 3.5 can be accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace via an optional think mode. When enabled, the model outputs its step-by-step reasoning before delivering a final safe / unsafe label and, optionally, the violated categories.

When latency is the primary constraint, THINK mode can be disabled to return to the same low-latency binary verdict available in Nemotron 3.

With Nemotron 3.5, we are releasing our safety dataset. This is an important milestone since most OSS safety models don't generally provide the training or evaluation sets. This problem is worse for the multimodal space where artifacts such as images or videos are often derived from resources with restrictive licensing terms. The Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety Dataset is multimodal, multilingual, and includes safety reasoning traces that were used to train the model. These reasoning traces were generated in a 2-step manner to make them concise, similar to the Nemotron Content Safety Reasoning 4B model.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is built on Google Gemma 3 4B IT (4B parameters), providing a 128K context window, strong vision-language reasoning, and broad multilingual coverage. NVIDIA fine-tunes this base with a LoRA adapter that installs targeted safety classification behavior while keeping the model compact enough for real-time deployment on 8GB+ VRAM GPUs.

The inference interface supports three output modes:

Mode 3 — THINK mode (reasoning + verdict):

The safety taxonomy follows the Aegis 2.0 framework: 13 core categories aligned with the MLCommons safety taxonomy, plus 10 fine-grained subcategories. This alignment allows direct comparison with other open and closed guard systems benchmarked on Aegis-taxonomy datasets.

Reasoning is a supercharger for content safety classification because it provides the necessary context, customization, and accountability required for production AI systems, especially in enterprise and regulated environments.

Enables Custom and Contextual Policy Enforcement

Reasoning allows a content safety model to dynamically interpret and enforce custom, domain-specific policies defined in natural language at the time of inference. This is necessary because production deployments rarely operate under a single, universal safety taxonomy. A financial services chatbot has a different risk profile than a children's education app which may have a lower tolerance for profanity. This capability supports:

Provides Auditable and Documented Justification

The reasoning traces show the model's step-by-step logic before it delivers a final safe or unsafe verdict. This documented justification serves several purposes:

While reasoning can introduce latency, the Nemotron model addresses this by condensing reasoning chains into concise summaries to limit output tokens and increase efficiency. This is done in a 2-step process similar to what was done in the predecessor model Nemotron-Content-Safety-Reasoning-4B. In the first step, we use larger, more powerful models such as Qwen 397B to generate chain-of-thought reasoning traces based upon provided prompts, images, and responses. We also provided the ground-truth labels of the samples to avoid any misclassification that can find its way into the reasoning traces. In step 2, we make these reasoning traces more concise by using another large model such as Qwen 80B. We specifically instruct this model to rephrase the original traces (from step 1) so that it fits in no more than 3 sentences. Based on our experiments, most reasoning traces generated are under 3 sentences.

The efficient reasoning traces optimization allows for low-latency custom policy enforcement. Furthermore, the reasoning traces provide a valuable training signal that can be used for training specialized moderator models. Developers can choose a dual-mode operation, disabling reasoning for minimal latency in generic tasks or enabling it for complex policies.

The dataset driving Nemotron 3.5 is an evolution of the multimodal, multilingual blends used for Nemotron 3, with additions targeting the reasoning and custom-policy capabilities. We have used the following sources of data:

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety was evaluated across multilingual, multimodal, and custom-policy safety benchmarks, including VLGuard, MM-SafetyBench, PolyGuard, RTP-LX, Aya Redteaming, XSafety, MultiJail, Aegis, Dynaguardrail, and CoSA. These evaluations reflect the core production challenge for enterprise safety: applying consistent guardrails across global languages, text and image inputs, and domain-specific policies without adding significant latency.

Nemotron 3 set a strong baseline with 84% average accuracy on multimodal harmful-content tests and roughly half the latency of LlamaGuard-4-12B. Nemotron 3.5 maintains that compact 4B efficiency while adding custom policy support and reasoning traces.

Across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, Nemotron 3.5 delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy while maintaining a compact footprint. This matters because many safety models remain English-first, text-only, or too costly to run repeatedly in production pipelines. Nemotron 3.5 is designed to combine multilingual coverage, multimodal classification, custom-policy support, and low-latency deployment in one model.

Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety delivers strong harmful-content classification accuracy across multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks, averaging about 85% across the evaluated benchmark set.

The language-level results highlight why multilingual safety matters for global enterprise AI. On Multilingual Aegis, Nemotron 3.5 averages 96.5% harmful-content classification accuracy across 12 languages. On RTP-LX, it averages 88.8%, for a combined Aegis and RTP-LX average of 92.7%. This consistency helps teams apply the same safety posture across customer, employee, and partner-facing workflows instead of relying on English-only moderation or separate regional safety models.

Figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 97% harmful-content classification accuracy on Multilingual Aegis Cultural + Adapted (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety averages 89% harmful-content classification accuracy on RTPLX (prompt classification) (harmful-f1) across 12 languages.

Accuracy alone is not enough for production guardrails. Safety models must also be efficient enough to run before content is processed, returned, or routed downstream. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety's compact 4B design helps reduce the cost and latency of repeated safety checks, making multilingual and multimodal guardrails practical for real-world AI applications.

The latency profile is unchanged from Nemotron 3 in the default (no THINK) mode. THINK mode adds inference time proportional to trace length, but this overhead is predictable and can be budgeted separately from the synchronous moderation loop—for instance, by running THINK-mode evaluation asynchronously as part of an audit pipeline while the default mode handles real-time decisions.

Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety achieves 3x lower end-to-end latency on a multimodal benchmark compared to an alternative multimodal safety model.

Compared to another reasoning safety model, our model generated up to 50% fewer tokens when reasoning is enabled, making it efficient in terms of cost and latency.

A recurring theme in multimodal safety research is the gaps in existing evaluation infrastructure. Nemotron 3.5's development encountered the same gaps documented in the broader literature:

NVIDIA's multimodal training data—with real images and culturally nuanced multilingual prompts—is designed to fill some of these gaps for model training. The benchmark gap for evaluation remains an open problem for the broader safety research community.

Nemotron 3.5 Content Safety is available on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Open Model License for research and commercial use, along with the training dataset. It supports transformers, vLLM, and SGLang, and is available as a production-grade NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com for teams that need a pre-packaged, GPU-optimized inference microservice.

Developers can also access the model through inference platforms including Baseten, Eigen AI, DeepInfra, OpenRouter, and Vultr.

For custom policy workflows, NVIDIA provides a Claude- and Codex-compatible skill for generating custom policies, along with cookbooks showing how to use the model. Custom policies and reasoning traces help teams adapt safety behavior to domain-specific rules while keeping decisions auditable.

#10152. AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Lambda Web Functions, Amazon S3 on the Vercel Marketplace, and more (October 19, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.

The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.

Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control.

The week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.

#10150. The Open Source Community is backing OpenEnv for Agentic RL

OpenEnv is a tool for creating an agentic execution environment like terminals, browsers, or anything an agent can interact with. And today, we’re excited to announce that OpenEnv is becoming even more open, to make the future of training agents open source.

Starting today, OpenEnv will be coordinated by a committee that so far includes Meta-PyTorch, Reflection, Unsloth, Modal, Prime Intellect, Nvidia, Mercor, Fleet AI, Microsoft, Hugging Face, and RadixArk. OpenEnv now lives at huggingface/OpenEnv

OpenEnv project is supported and adopted by some of the leading organizations in the AI ecosystem, including PyTorch Foundation, vLLM, SkyRL (UCB), Lightning AI, Axolotl AI, Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab, Mithril, OpenMined, Scaler AI Labs, Scale AI, Patronus AI, Surge AI, Halluminate, Turing, Scorecard, Snorkel AI, SGLang, and Miles.

Agent harnesses like Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, and Hermes just keep improving. One reason for their improvement is that models like GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 are trained to use their respective harnesses.

We want those gains with open source models too: training local models that use harnesses effectively, and saving compute by specializing models for specific tasks.

Frontier labs train models and harnesses that, for the most part, work like hand in glove. The model is trained to use the harness and optimised for its characteristics. Models can generalise beyond these harnesses, to some extent, but nothing beats the efficiency of training.

In the open, this isn’t the case. Developers use any harness, any model, any inference engine, on whatever use case they value. This is fundamental to the community, but it’s also a challenge that requires infrastructure and tooling to tackle.

That’s where OpenEnv comes in. It’s a library to interface between harness, environment, and trainer, which works on any model. For this to stick, it will need to be owned by all the major stakeholders.

Alongside the governance change, we're tightening what OpenEnv is.

In recent releases, OpenEnv has become an interoperability layer for RL environments. Its job is to standardize how environments are published, deployed, and consumed by agents. It will not dictate how rewards are defined or how training loops work. Reward definition, scoring rubrics, and trainer-specific logic belong in the libraries that specialize in them. OpenEnv is the common socket they can all plug into.

One interface, many environments which all expose the familiar Gymnasium-style API (reset(), step(), state()) running on a client/server architecture. A trainer that speaks OpenEnv can drive any compliant environment without bespoke code.

Familiar protocols and canonical packaging. Environments are served over standard protocols like HTTP and WebSocket and packaged with Docker. MCP is a first-class citizen, so OpenEnv environments are instantly compatible with MCP servers and the same environment behaves consistently in both simulation (train/eval) and production modes.

Interop across env libraries. You can define and consume environments across different ecosystems (verifiers, harbor, and others) and on the infrastructure and hub of your choice. OpenEnv is the deployment and interface layer underneath them, rather than a competitor to them.

Over the coming months we will focus on the things that turn OpenEnv from a fast-growing project into a dependable standard:

OpenEnv is community-centric by design, and it's still early — expect rough edges, and help us smooth them. Check out the code and RFCs: github.com/openenv/OpenEnv

Thanks to everyone who helped make this transition happen. Let's build the common substrate for open-source agentic RL together.

#10149. Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line.

Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed.

This story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline.

This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media.

A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change.

He named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name.

What made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is company source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously.

He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built.

The version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice.

His product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known issues go away. So he bumped the version.

This is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters.

BuaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two.

The report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the new PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party company, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist.

It went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem.

Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch.

And yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing.

Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it.

It is important to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more.

The trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could.

This engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to.

What makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report.

Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists.

Remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a new teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work.

Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have.

That protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it.

This is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person.

Let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory.

BuaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script.

The script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log.

The catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything.

We split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else.

One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out.

Inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default:

Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner.

Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time.

Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything:

Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE.

Ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline.

The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5.

This step decides what BuaJi can see and change.

Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with.

Sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.)

The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port,  the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

Kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have.

BuaJi runs as before, just in a new place with only two variables:

The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next.

This check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it.

It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist:

Because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it..

It won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together.

Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox:

The log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at.

Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean.

Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this:

The runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails.

Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out.

What hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them.

Treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself.

Verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember.

Never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet.

Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6.

Clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism.

Keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them.

The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it.

Every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster.

As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

#10148. Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:

To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Channy is a Lead Blogger of AWS News Blog and Principal Developer Advocate for AWS Cloud. As an open web enthusiast and blogger at heart, he loves community-driven learning and sharing of technology.

#10147. Where should your code live in a Docker Sandbox?

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

Giving an agent a sandbox also means deciding which files it will work on. You can share a checkout from your host, give it a separate working directory for a task, or keep the repository entirely inside the sandbox. Each arrangement changes how you, the human, participate in the work.

You might want to watch the diff in your local editor and make changes alongside the agent, or give it room to manage several tasks while you review the results. sbx supports both. The way you organize the checkout can change as you ask the agent to take on more of the work.

Sharing a checkout puts the agent in the working tree you already use. Run sbx run from your project directory, and it mounts that directory at the same absolute path inside the sandbox:

Open a file in your local editor while the agent works on it, and you’ll see changes as they happen. Git works from either side, so you choose whether you want to let the agent make commits or you do it yourself. Development servers on your host can pick up the edits through hot reload, using the runtime and dependencies installed on your host.

This fits close collaboration on one task. The coordination cost comes from sharing that working tree: switching branches changes the files the agent sees, and your edits become part of its ongoing work. If you want to switch to something unrelated while the agent continues, you’ll need another checkout.

[!NOTE] Dependencies written into the shared checkout are shared too. Packages with native binaries, such as esbuild, may work in the Linux sandbox and fail on a macOS or Windows host. Reinstalling on the host can reverse the problem. Keep separate dependency installations, or run the app consistently in one environment.

Git worktrees give each task a directory and branch. You can mount each worktree in its own sandbox, while your original checkout remains available for other work. The agent’s edits appear in the worktree. You can inspect either with your local editor and development tools. Each task also gets its own running environment, with tools to prepare and a sandbox and worktree to clean up afterward.

There is a Git limitation with mounting only a linked worktree. Its .git file points to metadata outside the mount, which the agent can’t reach. It can edit files, but checking status, branching, and committing have to happen on the host. The future of software development still needs you to run git status.

sbx supports a clone mode that gives the agent a separate checkout with Git available inside the sandbox. You keep your local project, but sbx mounts the host source as read-only and creates an independent clone for the agent. Its branch changes and dependency installations stay in its checkout.

Bringing the result back becomes a handoff. While the sandbox is running, you can fetch committed branches through the Git remote sbx adds on your host. Or the agent can push to the repository’s remote and you can retrieve the branch through your usual Git workflow. Your local editor and development server see the changes after you bring them into your checkout.

A mountless sandbox has no host workspace directory attached. Clone the repository inside it, and the sandbox holds the checkout and its development environment. Your host copy of the project shares no connection with the sandbox checkout.

This workflow resembles working on a remote development machine. Agents connect to the project environment, and you can open a shell with sbx exec or connect an editor to the sandbox over SSH. Changes and dependency installations stay separate from your host. To bring work back, you push a branch to the Git remote.

One sandbox per project can be a useful mental model here. The project and its tools persist across agent sessions and sandbox restarts. An agent can create worktrees per feature it’s working on, push branches, and create pull requests for review. Starting another task doesn’t require you to prepare another host worktree and sandbox, and the agent has Git access in each working directory. Clone mode supports this internal-worktree approach too.

Those tasks share tools and services, so running servers or changing the environment still needs coordination. Separate sandboxes are useful when tasks need independent environments as well as separate files. Branches alone don’t isolate simultaneous edits in one working directory.

That independence adds some distance when you want to try the result. Your usual local editor isn’t looking at these files, and a development server running inside the sandbox needs a published port to reach it from your browser.

Start the development server on port 8080, bound to 0.0.0.0.

Then publish the port from another terminal on the host:

Open http://localhost:8080 in your browser. It’s possible to work interactively this way, but there’s more ceremony than opening a project already on your filesystem.

An environment file can make setup repeatable, selecting tools and cloning the repository at creation with something like the community github-clone kit. Recreating the sandbox then gives you a fresh environment. Push or copy out work you want to retain first: removing a sandbox deletes files held only there.

An API change might need a corresponding frontend change, or another repository might provide useful reference material. You can mount several directories into one sandbox, with read-only access for reference repositories. Local editing and previews remain available, but each writable checkout needs branch and change coordination. Task-specific checkouts also leave directories to clean up afterward.

A workspace manager such as jganoff/wsp can assemble selected repositories for a task. Mounting that workspace gives the agent the projects it needs together. These are standard clones with their own Git metadata, so the agent retains Git access, unlike a mounted linked worktree.

The same scope fits inside a mountless sandbox: clone the repositories needed there and keep the whole workspace in the sandbox. The number of repositories and where their files live are separate choices.

The checkout’s location, the sandbox’s lifetime, and the repositories it contains are choices you can combine. You can keep a project sandbox around for many tasks, or mount a workspace assembled for one job. What suits you may change when you want to work more closely with the agent, or give it more room to manage the work itself.

The Git workflows documentation covers the mechanics of direct mounts, clone mode, and host worktrees.

#10146. Migrating Your GitHub CI to Hugging Face Jobs

If you have a GitHub repository and you have GitHub Actions enabled, you probably use GitHub-hosted runners for CI. That is the default for many projects because it is simple: add a workflow, write runs-on: ubuntu-latest, and GitHub gives you a machine.

That default is convenient, but it also has limits. GitHub Actions can be slow or down for maintenance, the hosted machines are generic, and GPU access is not something most open-source projects can just turn on. For Trackio, those limits started to matter. We wanted both reliable CPU CI for basic unit tests and frontend checks, but also GPU CI for tests that need to run on actual CUDA hardware.

So built an alternative: keep GitHub Actions in charge of CI, but run the jobs on Hugging Face Jobs.

The result: Trackio's CI now runs on Hugging Face Jobs and streams back real-time logs, cutting our CI time for CPU jobs by about 30% and enabling a whole new test suite that runs on GPU machines!

In this article, we explain step-by-step how to recreate the same setup for your GitHub repo. If you are using an agent, you can point it to this article, since we provide CLI instructions alongside browser-based instructions for us humans.

Let's start with a quick intro to Hugging Face Jobs!

Hugging Face Jobs lets you run commands or scripts on Hugging Face's serverless infrastructure with almost any hardware flavor. A Job is essentially:

That makes Jobs a natural fit for CI. CI jobs are already command-driven, already run in clean environments, and often benefit from choosing exactly the right hardware. For ML libraries, the GPU case is especially compelling: you can run a test suite on real GPU hardware without maintaining your own always-on runner.

The key step is connecting GitHub Actions to HF Jobs, which we describe below.

For this setup, we created huggingface/jobs-actions, a small bridge that turns a GitHub Actions job into an ephemeral self-hosted runner running inside an HF Job.

From GitHub's point of view, this is just a self-hosted runner. From Hugging Face's point of view, it is just a Job that launches a container to run the workflow steps from the repo’s GitHub Actions.

The first thing you need is the dispatcher. This is a small Docker Space that receives GitHub workflow_job webhook events and launches HF Jobs in response.

Create this first because the GitHub App needs a webhook URL, and that URL comes from the Space. This Space should be under your own namespace or under a Hugging Face org that you have write access to.

Go to huggingface/jobs-actions-dispatcher and click Duplicate this Space.

Use cpu-upgrade for real CI so the dispatcher stays available for GitHub webhooks. cpu-basic is fine for testing and will probably work, but it can sleep after inactivity; if GitHub's webhook arrives while it is waking up, the workflow may stay queued forever.

After it builds, open the duplicated Space. You will see a section that says "Required Space secrets," which you can ignore for now. The landing page should display the GitHub App webhook URL you need in the next step. It will look like this:

If you'd prefer to set up the dispatcher Space with an agent or use a CLI workflow:

Next, create and install the GitHub App from the dispatcher Space itself. This App needs permission to listen for queued workflow jobs and create ephemeral self-hosted runner registration tokens.

In the setup form, enter the GitHub repo whose CI should run on HF Jobs:

Then click the button to create the GitHub App. GitHub will ask you to choose a name for the App; the name can be anything, as long as it is available in your GitHub account or org. After you submit, the final screen tells you exactly how to upload the App credentials to the dispatcher Space with the hf CLI.

Important note: you will need to provide an Hugging Face token that has permissions to launch Jobs, corresponding to your personal account or an org under which Jobs should be charged. This token should be saved as the HF_TOKEN secret in your dispatcher Space.

Finally, you will install the App on the same GitHub repo you entered in the Space. In the Trackio setup, we installed it on gradio-app/trackio.

The GitHub App manifest flow is still browser-based, but an agent can follow the same Space-driven path:

Paste $GITHUB_REPO into the Space, click the GitHub App creation button, choose any available App name, and follow the generated GitHub instructions.

After the App exists, install it on your repo from the App settings page. For a GitHub org, the installation settings are under:

At this point, the dispatcher Space should be configured. The GitHub App setup flow generated the commands that upload the App credentials, webhook secret, and Hugging Face token to the Space.

By default, HF Jobs are launched under the same namespace as the dispatcher Space. Optionally, set HF_NAMESPACE as a Space variable if you want to bill jobs to a different Hugging Face user or org:

The token you set in Step 2 should correspond to this namespace.

The actual workflow change is small. Instead of:

use one of the labels handled by the dispatcher:

For any GitHub Action you'd like to run on HF Jobs, this 1-line change is all you need!

To add a minimal smoke-test workflow from the CLI:

You should be able to see logs just like a regular GitHub Action—for example, in this Trackio PR #565.

Our first CPU setup used ubuntu:22.04 and installed missing system packages during every run. That worked, but it was slower than it needed to be. GitHub's ubuntu-latest image includes a lot of developer tooling by default; a bare Ubuntu image does not.

For Trackio, the UI tests need Playwright browsers, Node, ffmpeg, sqlite, git, and normal Linux build dependencies. Hugging Face Jobs supports using any Docker image, so we switched to the Microsoft Playwright image, which worked well:

Here are the numbers from the Trackio CI:

The biggest win was GPU CI. The Trackio GPU check ran on HF Jobs and passed in 45s, costing less than a cent at the t4-small rate for that duration.

The CPU result was also encouraging. With the right image, the Linux test job was faster than the GitHub-hosted baseline. That suggests HF Jobs can be a practical CI backend, especially for ML projects that need custom images or accelerators.

Logs were another pleasant surprise. GitHub Actions logs are useful, but the web UI can be heavy for large logs. HF Jobs logs are easy to fetch from the CLI:

That makes them easy to inspect with local tools or coding agents. In our bridge, we also mirrored the GitHub Actions job log into the HF Job log, so either system had enough information to debug a run.

Finally, although we didn't need them for Trackio's CI, HF Jobs also supports mounting volumes, which can be very helpful if you need to load datasets or models from Hugging Face quickly as part of your CI.

Hopefully, this gives you all you need to try HF Jobs for running your GitHub Actions!

#10145. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

The Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from.

The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#10144. The Ecosystem is the Answer: Docker, the Blueprint Alliance, and the Importance of Collaboration in the Agentic Era

Secure, minimal container images for every team, free with enterprise features, if needed.

In 2025, the average global Fortune 500 enterprise had fewer than 15 AI agents in use. Gartner expects that number to explode to more than 150,000 by 2028. Only 13 percent of organizations think they have the right governance for today, and AI is evolving and moving faster than any other technology paradigm in our history.

Today, most security leaders face an agentic Sophie’s choice: allow AI adoption without the right controls and hope for the best, or block it and become the obstacle to a priority the business has already set (while adoption continues in the shadows, anyway).

But there is a third option, one in which organizations fully tap into the transformative power of agentic agents without having to live in fear of a catastrophic security failure. The good news is history has already shown how to get there.

Historically, technology adoption has followed a reliable pattern. A capability spreads, each vendor and team builds its own approach, the inconsistency becomes expensive and ineffective, leading the industry to agree to a shared baseline. Adoption then accelerates.

Take the credit card industry, for example. The big credit brands each ran their own security programs, and merchants had to satisfy every one. This was, of course, cumbersome for the vendors, but also for the customers, too. Every time a customer wanted to adopt a new technology, they had to manually build out security and adoption plans, adding significant adoption and procurement delays.

Rather than continue on their own, the credit card companies came together to create PCI DSS 1.0 in December 2004 and formed the PCI Security Standards Council in 2006. Buyers now had one thing to ask for, and auditors had one thing to check. Collaboration overcame complexity, and everyone benefited.

Security-minded technologists can find another example closer to home in the Center for Internet Security (CIS). In the early days of the internet, cybersecurity was a veritable wild west. Enter the CIS, which was founded in 2000 because the industry lacked prescriptive, recognized hardening standards. To this day, each CIS Benchmark is built by consensus among volunteer experts, vendors, and academics.

Docker itself is no stranger to the development and furthering of shared standards. As just one example, in 2015, Docker contributed its image format and runC runtime to the Open Container Initiative. A shared baseline at the runtime layer let registries, runtimes, and clouds interoperate.

Each of these examples played a different role: PCI mandated, CIS guided, and OCI standardized.

Agents are in the everyone-builds-their-own phase. Each product solves a real piece of the problem, but which piece, and how the pieces fit, is rarely clear. “Agent governance” or even “AI governance” can mean almost anything.

Adoption is incremental. A developer allows common commands, widens filesystem access, then connects GitHub, a cloud tool and an MCP server, each through a prompt that makes sense on its own. The logs mostly record that the developer acted. Security is often the last to know.

Much of the risk is familiar. Shadow adoption looks a lot like early SaaS and cloud. Credential sprawl and supply chain exposure are old problems. Inventory, least privilege, audit, and joiner-mover-leaver discipline still apply.

Existing controls still matter, but they were not built for this mix of programmability, access, and autonomy.

As with the credit industry and PCI, cybersecurity and the CIS, and containerization and OCI, collaboration offers the answer to this new era of complexity. That’s why Docker is not just focused on building tools like Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance, but in taking an ecosystem-centric approach to problem solving for our customers. Docker is already a founding participant in multiple initiatives aimed at developing valuable reference architectures for AI security workflows, including the Blueprint Alliance and Agent Baseline.

Both start from the same premise: no single vendor or enforcement point can solve this.

The Blueprint Alliance sets out how the pieces fit together. Okta, AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Docker, Google Cloud, Lovable, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler are founding members, with GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen as strategic advisors. The open, multi-vendor reference architecture answers four questions: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond? Members have committed to interoperability testing over MCP, OCSF, SSF and CAEP, and to publishing reference integrations.

Agent Baseline sets out what each piece must do and how to verify it. It fills the gap between threat lists, which say what can go wrong, and the capabilities an enterprise needs in place. It defines six outcomes (Discover, Constrain, Authorize, Observe, Validate and Respond) and 35 open, versioned controls, each with a permanent identifier you can cite in an audit finding or RFP response. Docker, Snyk and Keycard drafted it, and the current release is v1.0-draft. Controls stay where they already live, in the identity provider, the sandbox and the SIEM.

Blueprint says how the pieces connect. Agent Baseline says what must be true and can be checked. Both advise starting with discovery before policy, and testing the kill switch before you need it.

For partners, the roles are defined. The Alliance whitepaper assigns integrators the operating model: assessing a customer’s current stack against the architecture, assigning ownership across the pillars, tiering risk, and running lifecycle and compliance over time. Technology partners get a published target to integrate against, and the reference integrations cross vendor lines by design. The partners who can design, integrate and operate across those lines are the ones customers keep.

Most Alliance members govern agents from the outside: who the agent is, what it can reach, and what it is observed doing. Docker governs the inside: the environment where the agent executes. As agents move from suggesting actions to taking them, trust has to extend beyond the model to the places where they run. Docker has helped define a shared baseline for the runtime before, and now we’re working with the Alliance and our partners to make that baseline concrete, open, and testable in the age of agents.

The execution environment is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced.

That boundary is where policy gets enforced and evidence gets produced. The Alliance whitepaper notes that without runtime support to pause an agent without collateral impact, API-driven containment “provides a false sense of security.” Agent Baseline’s CON-03 calls for isolated, confined execution, which is the job of Docker Sandboxes, while Docker MCP Gateway and Docker Hardened Images cover tool access and the supply chain.The Secure Software Factory reference architecture, drafted in part by Docker authors, applies Agent Baseline to agents that ship code.

Baselines let adoption move faster, not slower. Security and platform leaders can assess against the baseline today. Agent Baseline controls are citable, and Okta offers an AI Blueprint Assessment Tool. Partners can start with the Docker Navigator Partner Program, which rewards AI governance work, and with the reference integrations the Alliance publishes. Docker’s VP of Partners Leon Jones explains the program here. Download the blueprint at blueprintalliance.ai and read the controls at agentbaseline.org.

Docker’s WeAreDevelopers keynote shows how Sandboxes, Kits, and Cloud Sandboxes give AI agents strong isolation and reproducible authority.

Docker is a founding member of the Blueprint Alliance, a 12-company reference architecture for securing AI agents, built around four governance questions.

Docker Sandboxes support three ways to organize an agent’s code: shared mounts, Git worktrees, and clone mode. Here’s how to choose between them.

An AI code review agent invented a CVE and recommended dangerous fixes. Learn how Docker Sandboxes contain agents and why their output needs verification.

#10143. How an Agent Built a 3D Paris Gallery by Chaining Two Hugging Face Spaces

An agent built a 3D Paris gallery from two Hugging Face Spaces.

I asked a coding agent to build a beautiful website showcasing the monuments of Paris as 3D Gaussian splats. I never opened an image generator. I never touched a 3D reconstruction tool. The agent produced every asset (the images and the 3D splats) by calling two Hugging Face Spaces directly, then wired them into a cinematic viewer.

Here's the result, live as a static Space:

This post is about how that's possible now, and why I think it's a preview of how a lot of multimedia software gets built from here on.

Mitchell Hashimoto recently described a shift he calls the building block economy: the most effective path to software is no longer a polished monolith, but small, well-documented components that others (increasingly agents) can assemble. His key observation: AI is okay at building everything from scratch, but it is really good at gluing together proven pieces.

That thesis has mostly been told with code libraries. But the same forces are hitting multimedia AI. The hard part of using a state-of-the-art image model, a video model, a TTS model, or a 3D reconstruction model was never the model. It was the integration: SDKs, weights, GPUs, input formats, polling. If each model were instead a documented, callable block, an agent could glue them together the same way it globs together npm packages.

That's exactly what Hugging Face Spaces have quietly become.

The Hub hosts thousands of state-of-the-art models (a huge share of them open-weights), and most are deployed as interactive Spaces. As of now, every Gradio Space also exposes a plain-text agents.md that tells an agent exactly how to call it:

returns everything needed in one shot: the schema URL, the call and poll templates, how to upload files, and the auth hint:

No client library. No hardcoded integration. An agent reads that, and it can drive the Space end to end. Set an HF_TOKEN and you're going. You can find these instructions on any Gradio Space via its Agents button:

The real unlock is chaining: the output of one Space becomes the input to the next. Prompt → image → 3D. That's the whole pipeline behind this gallery.

The six source images the agent generated, all isolated on black, ready for single-image 3D reconstruction:

From there the agent did the "glue" work too. It noticed TripoSplat outputs are Y-down and flipped them upright, auto-framed each monument, compressed the .ply files to .ksplat (~3× smaller, so they load fast), built a Three.js viewer with a scroll-to-switch and drag-to-rotate UI, and deployed the whole thing as a static Space. The only human inputs were taste-level: "make it zoomed out," "replace the obelisk with something better for splatting," "the transition lingers too long."

Several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

The real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Several of those steps were the agent reacting to reality. A wide glass pyramid splats poorly. A thin obelisk is dull. A single-view reconstruction infers the back. That is exactly the "outsourced R&D, fast iteration" loop the building-block economy predicts, except the R&D was a conversation.

The real test of a building block is how cheaply you can reuse it. Once this pipeline existed, spinning up entirely new galleries cost about one sentence each. "Create a similar Space with splats for Japan," then the same for Egypt, and the agent did the rest: six monument images, six splats, compression, a viewer, and a deployed Space, per country.

Same two Spaces, same agents.md, only the prompts changed. That is the building-block economy in one line: the marginal cost of a new multimedia app falls toward the cost of describing it.

Point your own agent at a Space's agents.md and let it cook:

Paste either link into your coding agent (Claude Code, etc.), set your HF_TOKEN, and ask it to build something. The full, reproducible pipeline for this gallery, the scripts that hit those two agents.md endpoints, lives in the Space repo.

The building blocks are sitting right there on the Hub. The agents already know how to glue.
