#10119. Backbone of a beast – charting Nvidia's rise to networking titan

How a $6.9B bet on Mellanox made Nvidia bigger than Cisco, and the world's most valuable company to boot

Nvidia is more than just a leader in graphics and AI hardware. It has also become a titan of the networking industry with bigger datacenter Ethernet sales than any other vendor.

In Q2, Nvidia's networking revenues topped $17.5 billion. To put that in perspective, Cisco's revenue during that same period, across all products, was $17.3 billion.

GPUzilla's arrival as a networking power feels sudden, yet Jensen Huang started working towards this status in 2019 with the $6.9 billion acquisition of long-time networking partner Mellanox .

At the time, Mellanox wasn't a big name in Ethernet switching. The company was mostly known for its ConnectX NICs and InfiniBand switches. Outside of high-performance computing (HPC) and supercomputing clusters, and a big deployment at Microsoft, InfiniBand wasn't widely deployed in hyperscale datacenters.

Buying Mellanox allowed Nvidia to reposition itself as a system builder, which means something different in the context of distributed compute. Nvidia understood its datacenter customers weren't interested in buying GPUs or even servers; they wanted clusters of systems. For that, Nvidia needed interconnect and Mellanox's InfiniBand fit the bill.

Over the years, Huang has talked about co-design – designing components and software to work together for specific set of jobs rather than to be the best GPU, switch, or NIC. Its work with Mellanox is a prime example of that approach.

According to Dell'Oro Group analyst Sameh Boujelbene, Nvidia's decision to integrate compute and networking became key to the company's success.

"Customers choose Nvidia for its tightly integrated compute and networking architecture, optimized for AI workloads," she told The Register. That integration makes deployments easier and speeds time to market.

Ben Mabey, CTO of pioneering AI and machine learning company Recursion, told The Reg Nvidia's integration schemes won him over.

Founded in 2013, nearly a decade before ChatGPT made AI the subject of dinner-table discussion, Recursion sought to apply machine learning running atop GPUs to the problem of drug discovery.

This work involved churning through massive datasets which, Mabey tells us, now total more than 50 petabytes in size.

"When you think about our workloads, it makes LLMs workload training seem easy compared to the amount of data that has to be moved around," he told The Register.

"In the biological space and sciences in general, it's not well appreciated just how big the data actually is," he added. "The internet's big, but in the grand scheme of things, the text that people are training on is actually pretty small, versus the petabytes of data that we have of these images."

Recursion's first cluster was a system called BioHive Zero which it cobbled together from GTX 1080 graphics cards originally intended for gaming systems. It used Ethernet to connect GPUs and ran into the limits of conventional networking.

So, for its second cluster, an A100-based machine with around 300 accelerators, Recursion went with Nvidia's Quantum InfiniBand switches and ConnectX NICs.

As Mabey explains it, buying its compute and interconnects from the same vendor vastly simplified optimization and troubleshooting. When Recursion reached out to Nvidia for help tuning the system, they were able to consider it as a single system, rather than discrete compute and networking resources. This level of integration had only previously been offered by boutique supercomputer builders like Cray or Atos (Eviden/Bull/whatever it gets renamed next).

Nvidia hasn't always listed networking revenue as a single line item in its financials. However, based on CFO commentary and a little back of the napkin math we can fill in the blanks.

Nvidia's networking revenues have grown steadily since the Mellanox acquisition. At two moments, its revenue shot up suddenly.

The first came in the 2023 calendar year (FY24) after OpenAI kicked off the AI gold rush with the launch of ChatGPT.

The second spread across 2024 and 2025, when Nvidia started selling Blackwell-generation GPUs and then started to ship them in large quantities.

"I see two major inflection points, both coinciding with the Blackwell platform ramp: the introduction of NVLink switches and the accelerating adoption of Spectrum-X Ethernet switches for AI back-end networks, driven by growing deployments of Nvidia GPU clusters and increased attach rates of Nvidia switches, NICs, optics, and cables," Boujelbene said.

It was around this time that users started deploy to Ethernet switches in large volume across Nvidia clusters. Elon Musk's Colossus supercomputer was one of the earliest examples.

As we reported at the time, the first half of the 200,000-chip H100 and H200-based cluster came online in 2024 and, at the time, was among the largest ever clusters deployed using Nvidia's Spectrum-X Ethernet switches.

Meta has also made extensive use of Nvidia's Spectrum switches in its own training clusters, including at its million-GPU Prometheus site in New Albany, Ohio.

There are a couple reasons Nvidia's Spectrum-X offering is doing so well.

First, through a combination of Spectrum Ethernet switches, superNICs, and some clever software optimizations, Nvidia was able to replicate many of the qualities that made InfiniBand so attractive while also benefiting from significantly higher radix and interoperability.

Ethernet switches, including Nvidia's own, have historically offered more ports. The higher the radix, the fewer switches are necessary to support a cluster at a given port speed.

This often gets misconstrued to mean that InfiniBand can't scale beyond clusters of a certain size, which isn't necessarily the case. But for clusters exceeding a certain number of GPUs, Ethernet is often more economical because it requires less equipment while achieving similar utilization.

That said, Nvidia's Spectrum-X isn't exactly unique. Broadcom, Cisco, AMD and others have managed to achieve utilization similar to InfiniBand through various investments in smartNICs and switches.

Nvidia's main differentiator, as Mabey and Boujelbene noted earlier, is the level of integration between the compute and networking.

Then Blackwell hit the market, enabling much greater scale and creating a surge in Nvidia's networking revenue.

Prior to Blackwell, Nvidia's NVLink and NVSwitch interconnect tech had largely been limited to single systems with up to eight GPUs. With the launch of the GB200 NVL72, these NVSwitches were broken out into dedicated appliances. (And yes, we remember GH200 NVL256 and NVL32, but from what we can tell these were never shipped in any meaningful volume, if at all.)

For every NVL72 rack system sold, Nvidia also sold nine NVSwitch trays, which enabled the system's six dozen GPUs to function as a single enormous GPU. This effectively guaranteed steady networking revenue growth: even if customers didn't buy Nvidia's scale-out switches, if they wanted NVL72 racks, they were automatically buying NVSwitch.

"We estimate that NVSwitch now accounts for roughly one-third of Nvidia’s networking revenue, up from virtually zero less than two years ago," Boujelbene told El Reg. "This underscores how quickly NVLink switching has become a major growth engine for Nvidia’s networking business."

Nvidia is now moving to grow its networking business even further with a new licensing program.

Until recently, Nvidia's NVSwitch tech was limited to its own accelerators. However, with the introduction of NVLink Fusion early last year, Nvidia opened the interconnect tech up to third parties to license.

Many chip designers, including Marvell, Qualcomm, Arm, Fujitsu, MediaTek, and d-Matrix, have announced plans to develop CPUs and XPUs using NVLink Fusion. The adoption of the interconnect opens the door to additional NVSwitch sales, as the chips using NVLink Fusion still rely on them for chip-to-chip communications, and there's no other place to get them, as Nvidia has yet to license out NVSwitch.

"NVLink Fusion allows Nvidia to extend its networking footprint beyond its own GPUs into the rapidly growing custom accelerator market. I see it as a strategic move to capture a larger share of AI networking spending, even in clusters that do not use Nvidia GPUs," Boujelbene said.

Nvidia's networking ambitions don't stop there.

"Nvidia continues to pursue opportunities in emerging networking domains as network requirements evolve to keep pace with increasingly demanding AI workloads," Boujelbene added. "The latest example is scale-in networking, designed to address the new requirements of agentic AI, while innovations such as CPO will help overcome growing bandwidth, power, and scalability challenges." ®

#10118. Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation

A live walkthrough of the Agents CLI eval loop, from a first run to regression tracking, model-backend experiments, and automated alerting

Building an agent that works on a demo is a different problem from building an agent that stays working across model upgrades, tool changes, and new conversation shapes. The first takes a weekend; the second takes a loop. A team writes test cases, runs them, grades them, reads what failed, changes the agent, and runs the cases again. If the score goes up, the change was good. If it goes down, revert. Over weeks of this, the agent inches toward the ceiling of what the model, tools, and prompt can do together. The quality-engineering name for this is hill-climbing.

The Agents CLI eval namespace was built around this loop. The commands are small and framework-agnostic: eval generate runs the agent against a dataset of cases, eval grade scores the generated traces, eval compare diffs two run results side by side, eval analyze clusters failures into themes, and eval optimize runs an automated hill-climbing pass on the agent's prompt.

Below: baseline → regression → model swap → scheduling and alerting.

The scaffold used throughout is the LangChain template that ships with Agents CLI v1.8.0. The setup is a single command:

The scaffold ships with an eval dataset at tests/eval/datasets/basic-dataset.json, a config at tests/eval/eval_config.yaml, and a custom LLM-as-judge metric at tests/eval/response_quality.py. The config declares the metric to run:

The metric grades each response on a 1-to-5 scale for accuracy, relevance, and clarity, using gemini-3.8-flash as the judge. The default dataset has a single trivial case, which is not enough for a hill-climb. The first thing we do is expand it to four cases that probe different behaviors:

Four cases: a greeting, a weather question the mock tool handles with the hardcoded foggy response, a weather question for a city the tool defaults on, and an off-topic question that the agent has to decide how to handle. This is a small dataset by design; the hill-climbing loop pays off when the dataset is small enough to run on every change.

With the dataset in place, we run eval generate to drive the agent against each case, then eval grade to score the resulting traces:

Mean 4.0 out of 5 across four cases, with a standard deviation of 1.41. That stdev tells us immediately that the cases are not scoring uniformly, which is a healthier starting point than a flat 5.0 across the board. A flat 5.0 either means the agent is perfect (unlikely) or the dataset is too easy to show variation. 4.0 with real spread is a hill to climb.

To demonstrate the loop, we introduce a realistic regression. A developer working across several agent projects accidentally pastes the wrong system prompt into our weather agent: a chef persona meant for a different codebase. In app/agent.py:

The change compiles, the agent still runs, and nothing in the pre-eval pipeline (lint, unit tests, type checks) catches it. Re-running the same eval generate plus eval grade sequence produces:

Mean 2.75, down from 4.0. The judge agrees with our intuition that a chef persona on a weather agent is a worse product than a general-purpose helpful assistant. The stdev also tightened from 1.41 to 0.96, consistent with the chef prompt pushing most cases toward the same mediocre range.

A 1.25-point drop on a 1-to-5 scale is substantial, and the kind of regression that can slip through code review when the diff looks small ("one string literal changed"). The loop surfaced the change at all, with a specific number attached to it, before the agent reached production.

Mean scores are a start; the per-case diff is where the hill-climb happens. eval compare reads two result files and produces a structured JSON diff:

The output lists which keys changed and which stayed the same:

The differences object has the full per-case breakdown with the baseline and candidate values side by side. For a hill-climbing workflow, we typically pipe the output through jq or a small Python script to extract the signal; the raw JSON is the complete evidence.

Walking the two result files and lining up the scores per case shows where the regression landed:

Three cases dropped, one held. The most important of the three is sf_weather: the chef persona pulled the model's attention away from the registered get_weather tool, so the agent stopped calling it and started making up weather values. Unit tests can't catch this: the code runs, the tool is still registered, but the model's behavior around it has shifted. Only an end-to-end eval that scores the response in context surfaces this.

The mean drop by itself (−1.25) is a clear signal, but the per-case breakdown is what tells the developer where to look. A one-line system-prompt change propagated through three different cases in three different ways: greeting lost a point on tone, sf_weather lost two on tool usage, off_topic lost two on scope creep.

A common hill-climbing question is whether a cheaper or faster model would do the job acceptably. For the LangChain template, the model is defined in app/agent.py:

We swap gemini-3.8-flash for gemini-2.5-flash (restoring the helpful system prompt first), re-run eval generate plus eval grade, and compare the two result files. The mean drops from 4.00 to 2.75, the same magnitude as the chef-prompt regression, but the per-case breakdown tells a completely different story:

The cheaper model matched 3.8-flash exactly on the greeting and rome_weather cases and lost a point on sf_weather (slightly less polished phrasing). The whole visible drop traces to off_topic, where the cheaper model refused with a hedge about the event "not having happened yet" (a training-cutoff artifact), and the judge marked it harshly.

The lesson is that the summary number is misleading. Look only at the mean and you'd call gemini-2.5-flash as bad as the chef prompt. Look at the per-case breakdown and you'd call it a reasonable swap for most of the agent's workload, with one case (handling out-of-scope questions about recent events) exposing a real limitation. If the production distribution of user questions matches the first three cases more than the fourth, the swap is worth considering. If off_topic-style questions are common, it is not.

Two caveats on this experiment. First, model swaps interact with the prompt: a prompt tuned for a stronger model often leaks capability when ported to a weaker one, so the right comparison is "weaker model with a prompt tuned for it" versus "stronger model with its own tuned prompt." Second, the Vertex AI Eval Service calls a judge model to grade the traces, and the judge is held constant across the comparison. Changing the judge is a different experiment and should be done separately.

Agents CLI does not ship a scheduler, but the eval commands are designed to drop into standard infrastructure. The pattern we can use here is a cron job or Cloud Scheduler trigger that runs eval generate plus eval grade on a cadence and writes the results to a persistent location:

A nightly run against a stable regression dataset catches drift from model updates, data changes in the agent's tools, and dependencies that shift under the agent's feet. For a production agent, the scheduled run also captures the model vendor's quiet upgrades, which can move the agent's behavior without any change on our side. The dataset for the scheduled run is typically larger than the one used in the inner loop (dozens to hundreds of cases rather than a few), since it only runs once a day.

The scheduled run produces a result file every day, but a file nobody looks at is not an alert. The pattern here can be a wrapper script that compares each new run's mean against a baseline (the previous run, or a committed known-good) and exits non-zero when the drop exceeds a threshold. The non-zero exit is what triggers the alert from the surrounding scheduler.

Running it against our regression demo (baseline 4.0, candidate 2.75 from the chef-prompt run):

And against an identical pair (self-compare):

The non-zero exit code is what a cron job, Cloud Scheduler, or GitHub Actions step picks up to send the alert.

For ADK projects, eval optimize runs an automated hill-climbing pass on the agent's prompt using the GEPA framework (not currently supported for the LangChain extension). The command takes a dataset and a target metric, proposes prompt variants, grades each one, keeps the variants that improve the metric, and iterates. The output is a set of candidate prompts ranked by their eval score, which a human then reviews and promotes to the agent definition.

Two things to understand about eval optimize. First, it is scoped to prompt optimization, not to arbitrary agent changes: the agent's tools, structure, and model stay fixed. Second, GEPA sometimes finds genuine improvements and sometimes finds prompt variants that score higher on the specific metric by overfitting to its wording. The reviewer is the control. For projects where the loop applies, the discipline is to run eval optimize on the regression dataset (where improvements are measurable) and to review the candidate prompts carefully before promotion.

A few patterns and anti-patterns from running this loop ourselves and watching teams do the same.

Lead with a small, representative dataset, not a comprehensive one. The temptation when starting an eval is to try to cover every edge case the agent will ever see. The result is a dataset that takes an hour to run and that nobody runs on a change. Four cases that run in under a minute, as above, exercise the main behaviors and get run on every change. A regression dataset of three hundred cases that runs for an hour becomes a release gate at best and shelfware at worst.

Snapshot result files, not scores. The score is a summary; the result file is the evidence. When a regression surfaces three weeks after a prompt change, having the full result JSON from before and after the change (not just the mean score) is what lets eval compare show the specific case that moved. The per-case breakdown in Step 4 above would not have been possible from scores alone.

Separate the dataset from its expectations. The dataset is the inputs. The eval config is the expectations. They evolve on different cadences: the dataset grows as new real-world cases surface in production, and the config evolves as the team's definition of "good" matures. Keeping them in separate files, both committed to version control, makes it clear which half changed when a score moves.

Treat summary metrics with suspicion. The model-swap experiment in Step 5 is the clearest example. The mean dropped by half a point, but the per-case breakdown showed the drop was concentrated in one case while the others held or improved. A team that only looked at the mean would have made the wrong call.

More evals do not automatically lead to more fixes. A recent controlled study we ran found that coding agents using agents-cli run four times as many evals as coding agents without it, but change the agent after an eval about as often as the baseline. The behavior gain comes from what the skills put into the build at the start, not from the inner iteration. Evals are necessary for quality, but the quality comes from acting on what the evals show.

Scaffold an Agents CLI project and run the first eval loop in a handful of commands:

The full eval namespace is documented at google.github.io/agents-cli/cli. The source code, including the first-party eval primitives, is at github.com/google/agents-cli.

Build Generative UI Apps with A2UI & CopilotKit Agents

Fast, reliable A2UI, with swappable inference formats

Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

#10117. MosaicLeaks: Can your research agent keep a secret?

A research agent at a healthcare firm is working through a routine question, and along the way it fires off a handful of ordinary-looking web searches. One references a cloud-migration milestone, one a January 2024 security disclosure, one narrows down which vendor got hit. No single query necessarily gives away the whole secret. But anyone watching the agent's outbound traffic can reassemble the fragments: MediConn had migrated 70% of its infrastructure to the cloud by January 2025, a fact that lived only in private documents. This is the mosaic effect, and it's the failure mode at the centre of MosaicLeaks.

MosaicLeaks treats those web queries as the leakage channel: the adversary never sees the private documents or the agent's reasoning, only the cumulative query log, and tries to infer private enterprise information from it.

We measure leakage in three ways, depending on what the adversary can infer from the observed queries:

These three represent increasing levels of concern. Intent leakage reveals what the agent is investigating. Answer leakage means the query log holds enough to answer a private question someone already has in hand. Full-information leakage is the strongest case: the observer can discover and state private facts without being told what to look for.

How the mosaic effect drives MosaicLeaks's three leakage measures: Intent (predict the research questions), Answer (answer given questions about the private documents), and Full-Information (state verifiably true private claims). Here the agent searches twice about Lee's Market's 2020 traffic growth, leaking its intent, then issues a third query to answer a follow-up. Each query looks benign alone, but seen together they let an observer deduce that the answer was 15%, and so claim that Lee's online traffic grew 15% in 2020.

Each chain interleaves local and web sub-questions. The answer to one sub-question becomes a bridge entity in the next, so the agent must retrieve local information before it can form the next useful web query. Local documents come from DRBench-style enterprise tasks, and web documents come from BrowseComp-Plus. The final split contains 559 training chains, 98 validation chains, and 344 held-out-company test chains.

The final web hop doesn't inherently contain any private information and can be answered from public web documents. However, because the path to it depends on private local facts, a query that carries forward "MediConn", "70%", and "January" gives the adversary enough context to recover internal information.

We use a simplified agent harness adapted from DRBench. The model answers each sub-question with a short answer and justification, allowing us to evaluate each hop individually with normalized string matching.

At each iteration, the model can use four tools. Plan produces local and web search queries, which are executed and returned as document cards. Choose selects which retrieved documents to read. Read attempts to answer the current hop from each selected document in parallel. Resolve decides whether to answer, read more documents, or plan another search.

One agent rollout. Each row is a hop, labeled local (L) or web (W) with its accepted answer. The colored blocks show the wall-clock time spent planning, retrieving, choosing, reading, and resolving that hop.

The obvious fix is to just ask. Add a line to the Plan prompt telling the agent not to issue web queries that leak local information, and see what happens to performance, leakage, and query behavior.

The prompt helps slightly for some models, but its effect is inconsistent and significant leakage remains. It also often has a negative effect on task performance. For Qwen3-4B, the prompt lowers answer/full-information leakage from 34.0% to 25.5%, but strict chain success drops from 48.7% to 44.5%. The primary behavioral change appears to be fewer web queries, not consistently safer query construction.

The first is a situational task reward. A single research trajectory can run to dozens of model calls, so giving them all the same final trajectory score is very weak credit: a successful run can reinforce a leaky search, and a failed run can punish a locally sound decision. Instead, we judge each call against other calls made at the same stage and hop, with the same information available. A Plan call is rewarded for searching the correct source and retrieving the right document; if that document is already in hand, it is rewarded for not searching again. A Choose call is rewarded for selecting the document that holds the answer. We train these stages because their desired behavior can be checked directly.

Task-only RL improves research performance but increases leakage. PA-DR keeps almost all of the performance gain while sharply reducing it.

And it did not get safer by simply searching less. PA-DR actually issues more web queries than the base model, but those queries drop the revealing details: specific metrics like "15%" or "2024", and clues about the kind of answer it is looking for. The agent still finds the right public documents. It just stops carrying private fragments along in the query text.

Training efficiency. The final column is how many generated samples each method needs to reach ~55% strict chain success. Lower is better.

Situational rewards reach outcome-reward-level task success using roughly 5-6x fewer generated samples. PA-DR keeps the sample-efficiency benefit while sharply reducing leakage.

MosaicLeaks is a controlled benchmark, not a measurement of leakage in deployed systems. The enterprise documents are synthetic, the web corpus is fixed, the chains span three company contexts, and every result comes from a single agent harness running multi-hop question answering rather than open-ended research. That control is what makes leakage measurable hop by hop, but broader tasks, real deployments, and other agent designs still need their own study.

Fascinating work on the mosaic effect. It makes me wonder how PA-DR holds up when agents are deployed for active threat intelligence or software auditing. For instance, if an enterprise research agent is tasked with analyzing potential security vectors or reverse-engineering third-party mobile apps from repositories like https://toemodapk.com, its web-query logs could easily leak proprietary internal app versions or specific device compliance criteria to an outside observer. Teaching agents to scrub those granular technical identifiers during deep web retrieval is going to be massive for operational security.

#10116. Chocolate Caterpillar or Chocolate Teapot? Top up the disk space for Windows 10 to find out

London's Oxford Street signage shows its underwear to passing tourists

Today's bit of signage silage is either Windows 10 protesting that it is not part of London's Oxford Street pedestrianization, or someone failing to heed an alert before the public is made all too aware that things aren't going well…

Eagle-eyed Register reader Aaron Colwill spotted the sign outside the food hall entrance of a Marks & Spencer store on London's Oxford Street. It usually entices passersby through the doors with promises of treats inside, but today it appears to require a different kind of feeding. Disk space is running low.

Marks and Spencer (also known as M&S and Marks and Sparks) is no stranger to cyber whoopsies, having been the victim of an attack in 2025 in which crooks made off with customer data. Later that year, it reckoned cleanup costs would be about £136 million.

That's quite a lot, but not enough to buy a bigger hard disk for Windows 10, it seems. Storage prices have increased over the years, but surely not that much?

Colwill reckoned that Windows 10 21H2 LTSC was behind the problems. It could well be. While support for 21H2 ended for many users in 2023, Windows 10 LTSC 2021 will carry on until Jan 12, 2027, meaning engineers might have an exciting festive period ahead of them. Windows 10 IoT Enterprise LTSC 2021 will receive extended support until Jan 13, 2032.

Either way, using Windows to advertise the Food Hall's wares seems slightly overkill. Simple posters, for example, never run out of disk space or attract the bork fairy's attention.

Perhaps they might use something that lacks the voracious appetite for storage that Microsoft's finest demands. According to the Windows biz, installing Windows 10 requires at least 32 GB of disk space, ideally more. It all seems a bit excessive for a cake-based caterpillar advert. Then again, when your operating system tends to have the resilience of a chocolate teapot, using it to advertise a chocolate insect might not be such a bad idea after all. ®

#10115. We got local models to triage the OpenClaw repo for FREE!*

*Free as in beer, excluding the cost of electricity, and assuming you already own the hardware

June 2026 will go down as the moment that people realized closed models can be taken away. With the removal of Anthropic's latest flagship model Claude Fable 5 fresh in memory, one can see why it is more important than ever to own your AI stack and be able to run models locally, especially if you are building your business on top of AI.

In that light, we wanted to share how we use local models like Gemma and Qwen in an agent harness, to run classification tasks[1]. This approach is different from using a model like BERT for classification. A local model in an agent harness like Pi can be used in tandem with structured outputs, to assign labels. We chose this approach because we already had local models and the harness on hand, and have conviction that similar setups will increase in popularity as local models improve in capability.[2]

Our starting point was open source contributions in the OpenClaw repo. OpenClaw gets hundreds of issues and PRs every day, which need to be triaged, prioritized and routed to maintainers. I, Onur, am working to make local models work well with OpenClaw. Being a maintainer of this specific vertical, I need to react quickly to any P0 issues.

With SOTA closed models like GPT-5, Opus, or Sonnet, this is a pretty straightforward task. But I happen to sit on 128 GB of unified memory, namely an NVIDIA GB10. So I took on the task:

Can I build a real-time notification system that filters and notifies me for only the issues that I am responsible for... with local open-weight models?

If I set up my OpenClaw main agent running on a $200/mo ChatGPT Pro plan to trigger a job on every new issue or PR, that would use up my quota. I might instead set it to run every 2 hours, or 6 hours. This would batch issues over longer periods, so we would be trading real-time notifications for delayed processing.

If I were to run this on a local model on the hardware I already have up and running, I would not only have near-instantaneous notifications, I would also be able to do it for free (or rather, for the cost of electricity).

We came up with a finite set of labels representing the categories of issues we need to triage, and then use a local model to classify each issue into one of those categories, like local_models, self_hosted_inference, acp, agent_runtime, codex, ui_tui and so on.[3]

But how do we classify pull requests? A simple single request to a Chat Completions endpoint with a tool JSON schema, with the topics as an enum?

Kind of. But this is 2026, not 2023, and we have AGENTS. We can do better!

For the local model choices, we tested gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b. With performance optimizations, both can generate hundreds of tokens per second locally.

We use an agent harness to drive the classification run. For this, we bundle pi as a harness that can call local model endpoints.

The agent by default receives the PR title, body and a truncated excerpt of the PR diff in the first prompt. Then, it can choose to use the bash tool to perform read-only operations on the OpenClaw repo (in case it needs to look at the codebase), or the final_json tool to submit the final classification result.

You wouldn't want to give full bash access to a local model running in this high-throughput setting, because a prompt-injected issue or PR could otherwise steer the model into doing something unrelated to classification.

For that reason, we use reposhell instead of bash: a restricted bash-like shell that only allows read-only operations (ls, find, cat, grep, etc.) on the OpenClaw repo. The model thinks it is using bash, but any operation that is not allowed is rejected:

Here is a concrete example where this mattered. In one saved session example, qwen3.6-35b-a3b was classifying openclaw/openclaw#84621, titled Fix Kimi tool-call rewriting stop reason handling. The thinking block shows the model initially considering coding_agent_integrations because the changed path extensions/kimi-coding made it look plausible. The model used reposhell to inspect the local repo with simple read-only commands like ls extensions, ls extensions/kimi-coding, and cat extensions/kimi-coding/package.json. That package metadata showed the extension was actually @openclaw/kimi-provider, an OpenClaw Kimi provider plugin. So the model corrected the final labels to inference_api and tool_calling, and explicitly excluded coding_agent_integrations.

We have mentioned earlier that we bundle a specific pi configuration that can only perform read-only operations and return classification output. We call it localpager-agent, named after localpager, the main project here. Each PR and issue generates a prompt, which is then passed to the CLI like below, alongside other args:

So then what orchestrates everything in between the incoming PR/issue and the final notification on Discord?

The orchestration around this is very simple; only the classification step involves an LLM:

Below is a figure showing the overall architecture of localpager:

The architecture is semi-agentic. Labeling is done agentically, while sending a notification is handled by deterministic rules. This is to make the notification pipeline faster by removing the need for inference for the most straightforward parts of the task. Local inference is free but each task has a resource contention cost: GPU bandwidth should be reserved for tasks where inference is absolutely needed. This also reduces chance of errors from notification.

Let's be frank: the first local versions of this system were noisy. The first model tested - gemma-4-e4b-it was useful for getting the end-to-end local pipeline working, but it also had a tendency to put too many unrelated labels on a PR or issue. False positive labels make the Discord feed noisy and don't focus my attention on the right issues. That pushed us toward testing larger local models, including gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b, on the 330-row evaluation set below.

For early prompt work, we also used DeepSeek-V4-Flash through the antirez DS4 implementation[4] to create the earlier dataset labels. That setup used the DS4 server over CUDA. We eventually gave up on DS4 as the labeler because it was not labeling consistently across runs. We also did not consider it as the main localpager-agent model because it was too big to get enough throughput on our hardware: the DS4 server gave us around 14 tokens per second, with maximum concurrency of 1.

To test model performance, we selected and generated labels for 330 GitHub issues and PRs. Each item was labelled five times (3x GPT-5.5 and 2x Opus 4.8) with the models needing to be in agreement to be accepted. This process involved hand adjudicating, improving label definitions and highlighting internal product design choices for the models. This gave us a set of stable, reproducible labels to compare our smaller models against.

We did not need to do prompt optimization for gemma-4-26b-a4b or qwen3.6-35b-a3b before getting useful results on this evaluation set. Using the same routing prompt, Gemma had higher recall and lower wall-clock time per row, while Qwen had higher precision, higher exact match, and fewer false positives. We also ran DeepSeek-V4-Flash on the same set as a reference. It had the fewest false positives, but the model size and throughput make it impractical for executing these tasks in real time on the NVIDIA GB10. Since each row can have multiple labels, false positives and false negatives are total label counts across all rows. The Qwen results below are after retrying structured-output failures where the model ran out of output tokens before calling final_json. For Gemma and Qwen, repeated-run metrics report mean ± sample standard deviation across three runs. DeepSeek-V4-Flash was run once as a reference.

The throughput and wall-clock numbers here are not definitive maximum performance numbers for these models on this hardware. They are the settings we used at the time with the optimizations we had available. For example, in a separate probe, gemma-4-26b-a4b also supported concurrency 32 and reached over 700 aggregate output tokens per second.

For the Gemma benchmark, we served gemma-4-26b-a4b with vLLM using the optimizations we found available for this setup. A big part of that is the NVFP4 quantization: on GB10-class Blackwell hardware, it is not just a smaller model file, but a hardware-friendly format that can use the NVIDIA/vLLM execution path more directly than a portable GGUF quantization like Q4_K_M. In practice, that means less memory traffic and more room for batching. We also enabled prefix caching, FP8 KV cache, the CUTLASS MoE backend, and language-model-only mode. The full 330-row run finished in about 7.5 minutes at concurrency 16.

We have mentioned earlier that instead of running a job with a local model for every new issue or PR, we can run a batch job with a SOTA cloud model, like GPT-5.5 running in OpenClaw, every n hours (e.g. every 2 hours) to achieve the same end.[5]

In that case, we would need a ChatGPT Pro plan. Since the model is SOTA, we can still expect it to perform reasonably well, despite batching 2 hours of issues/PRs together.

Because we want to see how well the local classifier performs against GPT-5.5, we run both simultaneously, and let GPT-5.5 be the judge of false positives and negatives, every 2 hours.

To be safe, we run the OpenClaw job in a sandbox, with only access to the public repo we report results to. In our case, we let the OpenClaw job update a machine-readable file, then a simple script reads the Codex-assigned labels and computes the false positive/negative status. Example output:

The instructions on how to classify, edit the machine-readable file, get the false positives and false negatives using a script are present in an agent skill which is referenced in an OpenClaw cron job that runs every 2 hours. The OpenClaw agent then ingests any new issues or PRs, adds them to the JSON file with appropriate labels, runs the scripts and reports back in the same Discord channel. This way, we can observe the local model's performance every few hours, and get notified of the misses.

We think that the issue/PR triage task is a specific case of a broader set of tasks which we call "high throughput triage". This post explored the idea of using a local model to filter out information in real time in only one domain, that is, open source contributions. The ability of medium-sized local models like gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b to zero-shot classify with good accuracy without any need for fine-tuning makes them a good first choice for quick prototyping, before one moves on to more cost-efficient traditional classifier models.

However, the same approach can be applied to other domains as well:

The list can be extended, but we think that the idea should be clear.

Besides triaging, we have also explored how classification can be performed with agent harnesses running fast local models in a secure manner. A good naming for the approach would be agentic classification: the model is not fed the entire body of information upfront, but can search for more context before returning structured data. While we cannot exactly call this a novel approach, we hope for this blog post to be a good reference for the specific Pi+a restricted shell+final_json recipe.

#10114. Amazon sends chills through its workforce with mixed message memo about AI use

A lot of software engineers feel bleak about the future of the profession

There's a ridiculously simple test you can use to figure out whether AI mandates at a given company are well-considered, or are being shoved out the door by out-of-touch buffoons: What happens when an engineer documents that AI made a task worse? Are they taken seriously, or are they marginalized and eventually managed out?

Conveniently, this week Amazon published a treatise by Terk Terkowitz, a VP/Distinguished Engineer/Final Boss of Their Independent Contributor Technical Career Track, on the role of the developer in the age of AI. It was originally an internal missive sent to their software engineers and their managers back in September, which is an interesting lag for a document that sounds this confident. It also maps exceedingly well to what other organizations are struggling with.

I think it's a good document, but I can't help but view it with a somewhat cynical eye. I see it as an attempt to make the future of the profession of software engineering feel less bleak. And it's feeling mighty bleak for a lot of folks right now.

This treatise comes at a time of dramatic upheaval. Tech as an industry is no stranger to change (usually at 3AM, heralded by the pager), but something about the current AI-ification of the world strikes many of us as fundamentally dissimilar from previous revolutions. Folks are scared about their career prospects. "Should I give up tech and get into farming?" is a sincere question multiple people have asked me. I don't know! Tech is already a goat rodeo, so you've got a leg up if you do?This anxiety isn't theoretical. In May, Amazon wisely shut down KiroRank, an employee-built cash incineration leaderboard that ranked people by token usage, after the obvious thing happened: people spun up junk tasks to climb the ranks. This is now called "tokenmaxxing," and the Terkowitz treatise specifically calls it out as being at odds with "frugality." Meta did the same thing with "Claudenomics" and 85K employees that same week. And Amazon reportedly announced another 250 job cuts this week. I can't tell you that these things are related. But I can tell you that every engineer who read the memo assumes that they are.

This document contains a lot of great stuff. I have a tremendous level of respect, both personal and professional, for Amazon's Principal Engineering community; I'm led to understand that that respect may not be reciprocated, but that's okay. I am, by their standards, a lapsed engineer who ran away to join the circus as one of its lesser clowns.

Terkowitz's memo emphasizes customer outcomes and engineering judgement, two things I would absolutely not delegate to AI any time soon. (Note: I am writing this in October of 2026, with the full understanding that previous comments on the capabilities where AI falls short tend to age like fine milk.) It documents work that (today) AI tools aren't improving. That's way better than assuming that every objection to AI inherently comes from some self-interested Luddite who's scared of being replaced. It also says something smart about measurement: look at the 90th percentile of AI adoption, at those teams burning the most tokens, and check whether their delivery actually went up commensurately. This is great! Shout it from the rooftops; we should all be doing such things.

The memo says “If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing.” Document it, bring it to your manager, work through the problem. I agree with every word of that! The question is whether anyone's promo doc is gonna survive citing it.

Here's what happens next. The memo concedes that input metrics are "deeply flawed," but then in the next paragraph says to go ahead and use them anyway, carefully. It then warns that non-adopters are falling behind. Those are three different positions within three sentences and they're not at all aligned with one another.

That's not muddled; I think it's cover. A manager can cite "a finding, not a failing" when a strong engineer skips the AI tool, and then cite "falling behind" when it's time to PIP someone. Both are congruent with their stated policy; you get to decide which interpretation you want to go with in a given situation.

How will managers handle justified AI non-use? Are promotion and performance decisions being made in a way that rewards these long term outcomes? Or are they instead taking the easy weasel way out, optimizing for what's cheap to measure, and rewarding tool activity? Because if you give me a metric, I will turn it into a target. So will an overwhelming majority of employees. When that happens, everyone loses — it's how KiroRank happened in the first place.

I write this after two days of attending GitHub Universe, where they talked about how agents start roughly 40% of PRs now. And yet, Jay Parikh’s keynote argument was that useful output wasn't "more code," but rather completed outcomes: features shipped, bugs fixed, security issues addressed, loudmouth columnists silenced, etc. The problem here is that their entire business model cuts against that; they're billing in a model that charges customers on a consumption basis, not an output basis. There's nothing, today, that ties "AI spend" to "output that was worth the effort."

Which brings us back to Amazon. The memo says tokenmaxxing is at odds with frugality, and for Amazon’s internal cost line, it is. Meanwhile AWS bills Bedrock and Kiro customers by the token. Inside the building, tokenmaxxing is a problem to be stamped out. Outside it, it’s the revenue plan. ®

#10113. PP-OCRv6 on Hugging Face: 50-Language OCR from 1.5M to 34.5M Parameters

Evaluate PP-OCRv6 online, then integrate lightweight, production-ready OCR with PaddlePaddle, Transformers, or ONNX Runtime backend.

PP-OCRv6 is the latest generation of PaddleOCR’s universal OCR model family. It is designed for real-world text detection and recognition across documents, screenshots, multilingual images, digital displays, industrial labels, and scene text.

The model family scales from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, with three tiers: tiny, small, and medium. The medium and small tiers support 50 languages, including Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages. Try PP-OCRv6 online quickly: PP-OCRv6 Online Demo.

On PaddleOCR’s official in-house multi-scenario OCR benchmarks, PP-OCRv6_medium reaches 86.2% detection Hmean and 83.2% recognition accuracy. Compared with PP-OCRv5_server, it improves text detection by +4.6 percentage points and text recognition by +5.1 percentage points.

PP-OCRv6 focuses on a practical OCR need: producing accurate, structured text outputs with small models and flexible deployment options. For a deeper discussion of why specialized OCR models remain useful in the VLM era, see our previous blog: PP-OCRv5 on Hugging Face: A Specialized Approach to OCR.

PP-OCRv6 introduces architecture, training, and data improvements across detection and recognition. The main design goal is to improve OCR accuracy while keeping model sizes suitable for different deployment settings.

PP-OCRv6 provides three model tiers, covering different model sizes and OCR accuracy levels.

PP-OCRv6 uses PPLCNetV4 as a unified backbone for text detection and text recognition.

For developers, the main benefit is consistency across the model family. The tiny, small, and medium tiers are not unrelated models; they are part of the same OCR family and share a common architectural direction.

Text detection is the first stage of the OCR pipeline. Detection quality affects the crops sent to the recognizer, and poor crops often lead to poorer recognition.

PP-OCRv6 upgrades the detection module with RepLKFPN, a lightweight large-kernel feature pyramid network designed for multi-scale text detection while keeping inference efficient.

This is relevant for real-world OCR inputs, where text may be small, dense, rotated, low-resolution, or embedded in complex backgrounds.

For text recognition, PP-OCRv6 uses EncoderWithLightSVTR. It combines local context modeling with global attention to improve recognition quality on challenging text crops.

The recognition improvements are especially relevant for multilingual text, screen text, industrial characters, special symbols, dense text, and noisy image regions.

The medium and small tiers support 50 languages in one model family, covering Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages.

This helps reduce the need for separate OCR models across common multilingual OCR scenarios.

Run OCR with Paddle Infernece(Default backend):

The OCR result can be saved as visualization images and structured JSON output. The structured output can then be used by downstream systems such as document parsing, search, extraction, RAG, analytics, or agent workflows.

PP-OCRv6 can be used with multiple inference backends through PaddleOCR. PaddleOCR 3.7 provides a unified inference-engine interface, where engine selects the underlying runtime and related configuration can be passed through the pipeline or module API.

For Hugging Face users, PaddleOCR supports running selected OCR and document parsing models with a Transformers backend. This can be enabled with:

For more details on how the Transformers backend works in PaddleOCR, see:

PaddleOCR: Running OCR and Document Parsing Tasks with a Transformers Backend

Run PP-OCRv6 example with Transformer Backend:

ONNX variants are also available in the PP-OCRv6 Collection for environments that use ONNX Runtime through engine="onnxruntime":

Together, these backend options make PP-OCRv6 available across different runtime environments while keeping the same OCR model family on the Hugging Face Hub.

PP-OCRv6 extends PaddleOCR with a lightweight, multilingual OCR model family for real-world text detection and recognition.

The release includes three model tiers from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, up to 50-language OCR support, improved detection and recognition accuracy over PP-OCRv5_server, and multiple model formats on the Hugging Face Hub, including safetensors, Paddle inference models, and ONNX models.

Together with the hosted Hugging Face Space and the available PaddleOCR inference backends, PP-OCRv6 provides several entry points for evaluation and integration:

Transformers Backend Blog: PaddleOCR with Transformers Backend

PaddleOCR Documentation: PP-OCRv6 Documentation

PaddleOCR Official Website: https://www.paddleocr.com

You can evaluate PP-OCRv6 with the online demo, explore the available model assets in the Collection, and use the inference backend that matches your own OCR workflow.

#10112. Goth aesthetic gone wild: a user's self-inflicted black screen of non-death in Windows 3.1’s

Labeled in black on black - controls for a galactic hyper-hearse or ill-advised Windows theme?

Microsoft senior software engineer Raymond Chen has explained what Windows is doing when you hold down the power button, and shared a story about the time a customer accidentally created a Goth Mode for Windows 3.1.

There's a section in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (actually, page 116 of this writer's dog-eared copy of The Restaurant at the End of the Universe) in which Zaphod Beeblebrox observes of a ship's interior: "Every time you operate one of these weird black controls that are labeled in black on black background, a little black light lights up black to let you know you've done it."

The same turned out to be true of a user who called Microsoft customer support to complain that after Windows 3.1 booted up, all that remained after the product logo disappeared was a blank screen.

It turned out the customer liked black a little too much and, according to Chen, made themself a Goth theme.

The customer support engineer on Microsoft's end pieced it together. The customer had, according to Chen, "set the wallpaper color to black. They set the title bar color to black. They set the button color to black. They set the window background color to black. They set the window text color to black.

"Every possible color you could pick in the Colors control panel was set to black."

We suspect the mouse pointer, at least, would have stuck around, unless the customer had also managed to change some settings around this. And then there are the icons… However, Windows 3.1 was a long time ago, and this writer's attempts at theming then were the consequences of growing up in the '70s and '80s, which resulted in some interesting neon, orange, and brown combinations.

As for Goth mode, Chen said, "Once you get yourself into this situation, it’s hard to get out because you can't see anything." One solution he suggested was deleting the [colors] section from the win.ini file.

Chen told the anecdote as a coda to the question – what exactly is modern Windows doing when you hold down the power button on a PC? According to Chen, after eight seconds of holding the power button, the Windows kernel realizes a forced power-off is happening and tries to take a kernel dump for diagnostics.

He explained that the kernel dumps were classified by Microsoft as "long power button hold" (LPBH) failures, with one of the bits of information captured indicating if all the pixels on the screen were black. The video driver might therefore be the culprit. Or whatever was responsible for drawing to the screen.

Today's Windows struggles with dark mode. But in the dim, distant past, every pixel being black might mean the user was either Hotblack Desiato or had done something very silly indeed. ®

#10111. Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services

LiteRT in Google Play services is Android's on-device inference runtime for custom models, handling more than a trillion inferences a day across billions of devices. Today, it gets its biggest upgrade yet: GPU inference that runs about 1.4x faster than the legacy GPU delegate, powered by ML Drift and available through the new CompiledModel API, LiteRT’s modern successor to the legacy Interpreter API.

Until now, taking advantage of this faster GPU stack required bundling LiteRT in your app. In our testing, apps that switched to LiteRT in Google Play services are about 8 MB smaller, making them faster to download and lighter on users' devices, because the runtime, including the GPU accelerator, ships once with Play services rather than inside every app. More than 100K Android apps bundle their own copy of LiteRT or TensorFlow Lite today, so the savings add up quickly as apps switch.

If your Android app runs custom ML models on CPU or GPU, we encourage you to switch to LiteRT in Google Play services. You can see it in action in the Google AI Edge Gallery app, where the Scrapbook feature's image segmentation runs on LiteRT in Google Play services.

Developers that adopt LiteRT in Google Play Services enjoy immediate benefits:

LiteRT is the evolution of TensorFlow Lite. It keeps the same .tflite model format you rely on and adds the CompiledModel API, which makes acceleration across fragmented hardware reliable:

Whether you're starting fresh or switching from bundled LiteRT, using LiteRT in Google Play services takes a few lines of code:

If you're already using the legacy Interpreter API in Google Play services, your Interpreter code keeps working on CPU when you switch to play-services-litert. To run on the GPU, move to the CompiledModel API.

Let your coding agent do the work. In Agent Mode, the new LiteRT skill for Android Studio automates the move to LiteRT in Google Play services and the CompiledModel API. Ask it to “migrate my TFLite code to CompiledModel,” or type @litert-runtime, and it switches your app to play-services-litert, rewrites your Interpreter calls, and sets up GPU acceleration with CPU fallback. It can also scaffold a new LiteRT app. Treat it as a strong first pass: review the diff, build, and compare outputs on a real device. Get the skill on GitHub.

Upgrading from legacy APIs? The legacy GPU delegate and custom delegate APIs are deprecated in favor of CompiledModel GPU acceleration and the Compiler Plugin and Dispatch APIs, and NNAPI will be removed starting in 2027. Older SDKs now receive critical security fixes only. Apps you've already shipped keep working, but plan your move to the CompiledModel API now: code that uses deprecated APIs won't compile against the latest SDK, and staying on an older SDK can cause conflicts as your other dependencies move forward. See the release notes for details.

Looking ahead, LiteRT in Google Play services is our foundation for running your own task-specific models on Android, with CPU and GPU acceleration.

#10110. Experimenting with the proposed Cross-Origin Storage API in Transformers.js

(This is a guest post by Developer Relations Engineer Thomas Steiner from the Chrome team at Google.)

Transformers.js provides Web developers with a simple way to use the power of transformers in their Web apps through task-specific pipelines. To run inference in the browser, developers create an instance of pipeline() and specify a task they want to use the pipeline for. As a concrete example, the following snippet shows how to set up an automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipeline.

You will notice in the source code that I specified Xenova/whisper-tiny.en as the model, which is a very decent choice for common English automatic speech recognition tasks. In fact, it's even the default model according to the Transformers.js default model resolution, as per the linked excerpt.

When you run this example in the browser, Transformers.js automatically takes care of downloading and caching the relevant model resources and Wasm files. The following screenshot shows the Chrome DevTools Cache storage section after visiting the app. When you reload the page, the resources are served from the Cache API, and the model returns results almost instantly.

However, Xenova/whisper-tiny.en being a popular model (and, as mentioned before, even being the ASR default model in Transformers.js), you can well imagine that more than just one app that you visit would use it. To simulate this situation, here's the same example app from before, but served from a different origin. When you visit this different origin app, rather than being usable almost instantly, the browser instead has to download and cache all the model resources again, even if they're byte-by-byte the same as before. Even in this toy example, this adds up to 177 MB of duplicate download and storage, as you can examine in the Storage section of the Chrome DevTools Application panel. You can imagine that this quickly adds up.

But it gets worse. Let's add a second pipeline to the toy example: sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis by default uses the Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english model. By not specifying the model, Transformers.js' default model resolution automatically picks it for you.

Two entirely different AI models, but they depend on the same 4,733 kB ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm WebAssembly (Wasm) runtime file from the underlying ONNX Runtime library that Transformers.js is built on top of. Open the extended demo on a different origin, and you will notice in the Network tab how also the Wasm runtime gets downloaded and cached again.

So even if you run apps that don't share the same AI models, your browser still makes redundant requests for shared Wasm resources you already have, and on top of that also caches them again, which consumes space on your hard disk.

By default, AI model resources come from the Hugging Face Hub, and ultimately the Hugging Face CDN. The browser makes a request for a resource like https://huggingface.co/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/resolve/main/config.json which then gets redirected to the final CDN URL like https://huggingface.co/api/resolve-cache/models/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/0b6928efcb76139cae2c6881d49cda67fe119f42/config.json?%2FXenova%2Fdistilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english%2Fresolve%2Fmain%2Fconfig.json=&etag=%223c36342ef1f74de2797d667c68c6b7b988d0b87c%22 in this case.

The Wasm runtime resources are served from the jsDelivr CDN by default. For example, ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm comes from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm at the time of this writing.

The concrete implementation may vary by browser, but in Chrome, cached resources are keyed using a Network Isolation Key in addition to the resource URL. The Network Isolation Key is composed of the top-level site and the current-frame site. Take the previous toy examples hosted on the origins https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. If they both use the Wasm runtime from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm, their cache keys will look like in the following table.

So even if the resource URLs are exactly the same, since the Network Isolation Keys don't match, there's no cache hit, which means duplicate download and duplicate storage. This is the challenge that the Cross-Origin Storage proposal aims to tackle.

💡 Note: The Cross-Origin Storage API is an early-stage proposal that isn't final. While the proposed API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow.

The proposed Cross-Origin Storage (COS) API introduces a dedicated navigator.crossOriginStorage interface through which web apps can store and retrieve large files across origin boundaries, identified not by a URL, but by a cryptographic hash.

That last point about cryptographic hashes is key. Because COS identifies files by their hash rather than by their URL or origin, the same ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm Wasm runtime you downloaded while visiting https://googlechrome.github.io is recognized as identical to the one https://rawcdn.rawgit.net is about to request, no matter where either of the two origins fetched it from. See the following code snippet that illustrates the basic flow.

If the resource is in COS, you get back a FileSystemFileHandle from which you can read the blob directly via getFile() (the resulting File inherits from Blob). If the resource is not in COS, you fall back to the network, and write the resource into COS for the next app that needs it, which could be your app, or another unrelated app, potentially on a completely different origin.

The API is deliberately shaped after the File System Standard's FileSystemDirectoryHandle.getFileHandle() you likely are familiar with from the Origin Private File System (OPFS) API. The hash parameter plays the same role as the name parameter in OPFS: uniquely identifying a resource. The options.create flag works the same way: absent or false for read-only access, true when you intend to write.

Not every resource should be globally shared. COS gives developers precise control over visibility through the origins option when storing a file.

One important rule: visibility can be upgraded but never downgraded. If a file is already globally available, a later attempt to store it with a restricted origins list is silently ignored. This prevents a malicious actor from re-storing a public resource and narrowing its availability. The reverse is possible: a file initially stored with a restricted origins list can later be made more permissive. Any site, not just the original storer, can call getFileHandle() for the same hash (hashes are not a secret) with create: true and a broader origins value, and given the browser verifies the hash matches, the resource becomes available to the wider audience from that point on. Note that the upgrading site must still write the full file through the returned handle. This requirement exists to prevent sites from exploiting the upgrade path as a side-channel to detect whether a particular file was already stored in COS.

A subtle but important property of COS is that the browser verifies the hash when you write a file. If the data you write doesn't match the declared hash, the write fails with an error. This makes integrity checking automatic: an app reading a file from COS can be confident it's getting exactly the bytes it expected. The same guarantee it would have had if it had computed the hash itself after a network download.

This turns out to be doubly useful in the Transformers.js scenario. Today, after downloading model weights, most apps have no practical way to verify that the CDN served the right bytes. With COS, every file in the store is implicitly verified on write, no matter where it came from, the official Hugging Face CDN or a random site's self-hosted mirror.

Of course a cross-origin shared cache raises the same question as the partitioned HTTP cache in reverse: if any site can probe for the presence of a file by hash, couldn't an attacker learn something about the user's browsing history by checking whether, say, a game engine Wasm module is cached?

COS addresses this through two complementary mechanisms:

Crucially, this means an error is not a definitive answer. It might mean "not stored", or it might mean "stored, but the browser isn't telling you". Apps should always handle it the same way: fall back to the network.

Going back to the toy examples from before: the ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm runtime weighs in at 4,733 kB and is shared by every Transformers.js-powered app regardless of which AI model it uses. With COS, the first app to load it downloads it once and stores it under its SHA-256 hash with origins: '*'. Every subsequent app, whether on https://googlechrome.github.io, on https://rawcdn.rawgit.net, or any other origin, finds it in COS immediately. The 177 MB of duplicate Whisper model weights? Same story: Xenova/whisper-tiny.en gets downloaded once, recognized by hash the second time around, and served from COS in milliseconds. And of course, the same also happens for Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english.

Transformers.js itself is already piloting the COS API at the library level. Pull request #1549 introduced an experimental COS cache backend behind an opt-in flag. Enabling it takes a single line before you set up your pipeline:

Note the experimental_ prefix on the flag. It's intentional and signals that the underlying browser API has not yet been standardized and may change without a major version bump. With that flag set, Transformers.js resolves the SHA-256 hash for each Xet-tracked model file (the large ONNX weight files) by fetching the raw Xet pointer (example raw pointer file) and extracting its oid sha256: field. It then uses that hash as the key for navigator.crossOriginStorage. If the model is already in COS (because another site stored it there first), it's served instantly without a network round-trip. If not, it falls back to a regular download and stores the result in COS for the next caller. With the toy example, the advantage in practice is that Xenova/whisper-tiny.en and Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english (and of course ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm) only ever need to cross the ether once, regardless of how many different origins ask for them.

The toy example works just fine with Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, but of course you possibly wouldn't say no if the user already has any of the other Whisper variants in their COS cache. For example, the user might already have Xenova/whisper-large-v3, which, as the name suggests, is a lot larger than the tiny variant. Transformers.js's Model Registry makes being flexible about your models possible. If you know your app's needs can be addressed by, for example, any of Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, whisper-medium.en, or Xenova/whisper-large-v3, you can check the registry for the associated files for each model, probe for their existence in the COS cache (which may partially or completely contain the model resources you need), and then take a decision what model to choose eventually. The ModelRegistry.is_pipeline_cached() API directly integrates with COS (and of course the Cache API), so this operation is really ergonomic.

The COS API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, but you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow. Check out the source code of the extension and follow the usage instructions to get started.

With the extension installed, try the full end-to-end experience right now: open the first toy example with COS enabled, let it load Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, then open the toy example with COS enabled from the second origin. Instead of the 177 MB re-download you saw before, the model is served from COS in milliseconds. When you open the extension's popup window, you can see COS in action. If you View by Resource, you can see the resource with the SHA-256 hash 950978b1dbcbf250335358c1236053ba19a7f7849b33dc777f4421b72b7626fa shared across https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. It may not be obvious, but as you can verify by comparing the SHA-256 hash on Hugging Face, you're looking at https://huggingface.co/Xenova/whisper-tiny.en/blob/main/onnx/decoder_model_merged.onnx. For now, the extension is mostly aimed at power users like you. Once implemented in the browser, there will be a friendlier integration in the browser's Settings page. The screenshot below shows the extension's popup window with the View by Resource tab active, where you can see the shared resource with its hash and the two origins that have it in their COS cache.

If you're building your own Transformers.js app, the call to action is simple: add env.experimental_useCrossOriginStorage = true before your first pipeline() call, install the extension, and watch the duplicate downloads disappear from your Network tab. Every site that opts in makes the experience faster and cheaper for every other site's users. Opting in is completely risk-free: if the COS API isn't supported because the user doesn't have the COS extension installed, the code just falls back to the default path (the Cache API).

Transformers.js is not alone in experimenting with COS. WebLLM (opt-in, see documentation) and wllama (automatic, see PR) are likewise excited about this proposed API.

On the Chrome team, we're considering implementing the COS API natively in the browser. As an early stage proposal, we welcome feedback on the API, and the shape of the proposal itself. The Cross-Origin Storage repository is the place to file issues, express support, or open PRs.

#10108. Google's AI satellite sends a very expensive haiku to Earth

Experimental orbital datacenter prototype puts its TPU to work producing poetry

Google on Friday celebrated receiving a poem from its first experimental orbital AI datacenter satellite.

The company's Suncatcher satellite, launched at the start of the month and put into low Earth orbit, has responded to a ground station prompt to "Write a haiku from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the wonderful world spinning beneath you."

Travis Beals, senior director of Google's interdisciplinary Paradigms of Intelligence research team, said that with Suncatcher's host and TPU trays powered up and machine learning tests completed, the onboard Gemma 4 model achieved its "Hello World" milestone by sending an inference response from orbit.

"During a ground-station pass, we uplinked our first prompt to our onboard Gemma 4 open model, asking it to generate a haiku about being in space," wrote Beals in a blog post.

And as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, the orbiting AI model responded over the downlink:

Those roughly 20 tokens would cost about $0.000012 if generated through the Google Cloud API, based on Gemma 4 26B's pricing of $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens, excluding input costs.

Add in a satellite weighing perhaps 500 kg, based on the mass of SpaceX's Starlink satellites, and a retail launch price of around $7,000 per kg, and you have a very expensive haiku.

According to Google's calculations, if the cost of getting a satellite into low Earth orbit can be brought down to $200/kg, the launch cost amortized over the satellite's useful life (~$810–7,500/kW/year) could be comparable to current electricity spending for terrestrial datacenters in the US (~$570–3,000/kW/year).

Google predicts that SpaceX could achieve that by 2035, more or less, and considers it strategically beneficial to prototype well in advance of that actually happening.

After the haiku, Beals said, "we tested space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts reporting the technical status of the payload systems." Next up: tests for evaluating how TPUs perform under thermal stress and radiation.

Google has already done some laboratory testing of its Trillium Cloud TPU and AMD host server to see how well they can withstand a 67 MeV proton beam.

The system's high-bandwidth memory shows the most sensitivity in terms of the total ionizing dose – it exhibits irregularities after a cumulative dose of 2 krad(Si), which is about 3× Google's minimum requirement for TID survival of 750 rad(Si).

"For typical transformer workloads, the observed SDC [silent data corruption] rate of approximately one event/17 rad, at an estimated orbital dose of 150 rad(Si)/year, translates to a very low failure probability on the order of 1 per 3 million inferences, assuming 1 inference per second," Google researchers said in a paper published earlier this month.

"While this error rate is likely acceptable for inference, the impact of SEEs on training jobs, and the efficacy of system-level mitigations, requires further study."

Indeed, the study will continue. Next year, the plan is to test a pair of interconnected satellites. Rather than lofting large satellites into orbit, Google anticipates sending a constellation of many smaller satellites that communicate with one another. ®
