#10077. Anthropic's IPO prospectus is big on promises, short on answers to tough questions

Pity Sam Altman: He's going to have a lot more explaining to do when OpenAI follows this work of abstract legal art

It's official: Anthropic is going public, and boy, are our eyebrows tired from poring over hundreds and hundreds of pages of questionable claims.

Anthropic is going to need to do a lot to make its massive IPO more than just a flash in the pan, as systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn tell host Brandon Vigliarolo on this week's episode.

For one, the company has nearly a trillion dollars in compute commitments to pay for, which is going to mean it'll be burning through more cash than a datacenter gas turbine turned up to 11. In addition to its massive spending for the foreseeable future, there's also the fact that much of its computing power relies on customers who are also competitors.

In short, we're skeptical, but you probably already knew that. It's El Reg, after all, and we're not just taking what the AI industry claims at face value - if it looks like a house of cards, it probably is.

Hey everyone, and welcome to the latest episode of The Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Reg reporter Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're focusing on what I think our contributor Carly Page aptly described as the peak of the AI hype cycle we've been in for the past few years, and that's the public release of Anthropic's initial public offering filing. With me to talk this over is our systems editor Tobias Mann and senior reporter Tom Claburn, both of whom I'm sure have plenty to say about this matter.

So, I'm sure we've got a lot to cover. 614 pages is a lot to go through. Tobias, I understand you were combing through this thing with a fine-toothed comb. Talk us through the hard numbers before we get into some of the more wobbly parts of this IPO.

Sure. At face value, going into any S-1 filing, it is a kind of mess of risk mitigation, kind of covering your butt. They all pretty much read like a doomsday prophecy.

The S-1 definitely did that. But on the numbers side of things, the takeaway for the market was kind of interesting because there were some people looking at the numbers and going, "OK, this actually seems reasonable." Their operating losses were only about 700 million dollars.

I think on 16.3 billion net [revenues], right? That was what they reported.

Now they also mentioned, I think, and I was going to ask you about this, $80.7 billion total losses, but I understand that was an accounting adjustment of some kind. Did they mention in the IPO what that meant specifically?

Not specifically. It's a little fuzzy, and it's always kind of like this.

Anthropic's business is extremely cash heavy, and so they had to go to partners and say, "Hey, we need capital in order to pay for compute to train these models. We can either take it in debt or you could also get repaid in valuation, our equity." And so I believe a large part of that loss is they're trying to write off a lot of the equity that they're going to have to pay off when they do go public. And so I do believe that's the lion's share of that loss. Because it does look huge, but when you think about how companies go public and how they raise capital as startups, it's not really that surprising. It's just a huge number because Anthropic is arguably the largest IPO in US history at this point.

Right. But bottom line is their actual day-to-day business losses were $693 million....It was $1.2 billion, I think, for the first half of the year or same time last year or something like that. So it's gone down.

And they're trying to go out at two trillion now? Is that the number?

Well, the number kind of depends on whether they're going to be able to sustain this. I was going to mention for the first time ever, their revenues outpaced their compute expenses two to one. This has never been true in the company's history, and it's one of the reasons that people are feeling more confident about this. The issue that really comes from all of this, and what has gotten missed somewhat in the more rosy interpretations of the S-1, is that they also are signed up to have to repay upwards of 800 billion dollars and counting of compute commitments out through the next two decades or so.

You outlined in your story just a whole host of people they owed billions of dollars to for compute. Like you said, it would be great. That $16.3 billion in [revenue] would be great if those compute costs were going to hold steady, right? But they're not. They're going to keep climbing and there are a lot of bills that are going to be due. So, profitability is relying on making more than that nearly trillion dollars in compute obligations, and that's a big if.

I mean, the big question mark is in terms of what the technology does for inference costs, because I think a lot of this is betting on being able to get the same hardware that is much more efficient down the road and maybe not drop your prices proportionately and profit on the difference. But it remains to be seen whether there will be enough competition to just have the price go do with the increasing cost. And you see that a lot. I think the inference costs have dropped pretty significantly over the year, on average. I mean, it's really hard to calculate inference costs because there are so many different factors and it's really situational depending on the workload and how much caching is going on and things like that. But overall it's a lot cheaper to do inference now than it was a few months ago.

But again, I feel like if you're betting this $2 trillion IPO on the fact that we're going to keep getting better and cheaper at inference, right? I mean, I know Moore's Law is kind of a thing of the past, but at this point, what if we run up against another compute bottleneck and inference stops getting cheaper before they need it to?

Obviously any IPO prospectus is one big document about risk, right? Like, "Hey, you might make a ton of money investing in this company, or we might go complete belly up and you lose everything," right? That's always a possibility.

Right. And they still haven't demonstrated that the use case for AI is wide enough at volume that they claim it is. I mean, in certain sectors it's pretty obvious now there's going to be AI for a long time. Coding, everyone kind of agrees that works and we know how to manage that. And then there will be adjacent fields to that. But once you start getting into more general office work and regular business tasks that are not super-compute heavy, I don't know. It's a good question. We'll see if people are going to use it that broadly, but I just see it being overly optimistic.

The big question I have right now is: Is there enough user demand to support even a $200 billion a year revenue stream? Because even going off just commitments that they can't get out of made in the first half of this year, that's $417 billion running out through about 2033 to 2036.

I think the upper end of your estimate was a total, including newer commitments, of about $807 billion. At the lower end, $782 billion at the lower end. That's not that much of a difference when you're looking at hundreds of billions of dollars.

But if they can't make a profit with a two to one revenue-to-compute ratio — if they have to make twice as much in revenue in order to pay for their compute and still not break even — you extrapolate this out and they're going to have to be making $200 billion plus, assuming no additional compute contracts are made during that period over the next year, which is definitely not going to happen. They've already said they're going to keep making compute contracts. So this number just keeps getting more absurd the further out you go, unless inference magically gets dirt cheap, which we haven't seen.

Right. And it could cap. You know, I think also you made a really good point in your story, Tobias, when you mentioned that some of their biggest customers are also some of their biggest competitors. They're leasing space from hyperscalers, they're making deals with people to host their compute. But these are also companies that are operating their own AI models. And you might end up in a situation where they're like an MVNO, which, if anyone's not familiar with a mobile virtual network operator, is cell phone companies that are not T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T. Anyone who's not those big three in the United States is operating a virtual network that piggybacks on someone else's infrastructure. And when that infrastructure is busy, you get less priority. So we could see them run into a similar situation there, I imagine.

There's an interesting trend that another piece I'm working on later today touches on. Some of the AI gateways like OpenRouter are now starting to move away from just focusing on price metering and looking towards things like fastest time to tokens and all the quality of service metrics in terms of the way that they price and deliver the models, because inference pricing has become very commoditized in terms of what they're dealing with. They're not necessarily serving all the frontier models at very high prices. They're dealing with a lot of open weight models. And if you just focus on the lower end of the market, there's not a lot of margin there. So it makes sense to go, "Well, maybe if we deliver this faster or have better reliability or service, we can move up the price and get a little profit." And I think everyone in the industry is starting to realize that the music is stopping and they have to take a seat at some point and make the business model work. So there's going to be a lot of pressure on that. And that's also showing up in things like the licensing of models. A lot of those open weight models have seen their licenses get more restrictive over time as companies realize, "Well, maybe we don't want someone competing with us with this thing that we've made." So I think there's a lot..

That reminds me of Mistral just releasing the open weight version of Large 4, "Le Chonk". And the licensing model basically said if you intend to use this for any down-market purposes, you've got to sign a fairly restrictive agreement with us so that you're not just using this open weight model without us benefiting from it, right?

A lot of the big Chinese models, like Kimi K3, I believe were among the first to move back in this direction, basically saying, "Hey, if you're just going to deploy this internally, we don't care." If this is just for your enterprise, fine, but if you're going to be selling an API service like OpenRouter around it, you gotta cut us in. So there is definitely that. And Anthropic in their S-1 – again, every S-1 reads like a doomsday prophecy. And this S-1 of the things that they raise: open models are a threat on multiple levels, one of them being that a lot of their customers are startups sensitive to economic downturn. So those customers will likely be the first to jump ship to cheaper alternatives that are maybe not as good, but they can afford if the economy runs into any issues.

I wonder if that'll happen or not, right?

Was it Elon Musk who was tweeting about the end of the neoclouds recently? With financing getting tighter, a lot of the neoclouds living on borrowed money are going to find it harder to sustain their loans and are not going to survive this. So there will be a shakeout at some point. Does it hit the big companies? I don't know. All the cloud providers look pretty happy because they get business regardless. Even if Google's AI models are not first in people's minds, they're still serving all of this stuff.

We've said that on multiple episodes, and in multiple articles we've written, right? Basically, if the AI industry does implode, Google's going to be fine, Amazon's going to be fine, Microsoft's going to be fine; these guys have other businesses. Anthropic and OpenAI, not so much. That's all they do. And in many cases they're renting compute space from these other providers. So they might take a bit of a hit there, but by and large, they're going to be okay. They've got compute, they'll turn it around, they'll find other people to use it. Which is interesting, from your article, Tobias, you kind of summarize that the entire pitch this IPO makes is that bigger is better, right? But as we were just talking about, there are a lot of reasons to say that's probably not the case. It makes me wonder if they're still living in the token-maxxing era, whereas I just wrote a story this week about AWS telling its engineers to back off, stop using so many tokens, be more judicious, use AI well, don't just use it. And Microsoft said this months ago in August – they were saying tokenmaxxing doesn't factor into how they want to do business. So you've got two very big consumers of AI basically saying, "Y'all need to slow it down and be more purposeful." So, bigger isn't necessarily...

Anthropic's business is predicated on the idea that more compute means more revenue. However, the disconnect is: Can revenue scale fast enough? Is there enough user base? Is there enough token demand to support the scale they need to cash the checks they've already written? And it really looks like a house of cards. They warn about this in the S-1 – they have to – that if their revenue can't keep up with their compute commitments, they could default. And that default could turn into a cascade where if they can't pay one bill, they can't get enough compute to generate revenue necessary to pay the next bill, and it all falls apart.

If it happens to Anthropic, the other AI frontier labs are not far behind, because that's going to be a symptom of a larger problem. And that's that people are basically saying what a lot of non-AI companies or companies that do AI along with other things, like AWS, are saying: We don't need these massive frontier models for the vast majority of business purposes. They're not necessary.

Right. A lot of the enterprise AI products you see now are about trying to figure out ways to reduce that cost, too.You have some sort of gateway or harness system that looks at your jobs and routes them to an appropriately cheap model so that most of the time you're not using top-tier intelligence; maybe you're using a decision model, a regular classifier, or something like Gemma to do language translation. You don't always have to use that expensive model, and that price pressure is going to hit them, too.

To Tom's point, Cadence Systems, which does a lot of electronic design automation and circuit board layout, just rolled out a new product line called Maestro that's built around Nvidia's Nemotron open-weights models. The idea is that they had been using proprietary APIs to power their agents that assist engineers with PCB layout and chip design, but those agents generate a ton of data that could be used to train and fine-tune open weight models. So their latest pitch is, "Hey, we know our customers like this, but it's getting expensive to continue using these proprietary models from OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. So we're going to give you a way to take an inexpensive model, use the proprietary model to generate training data that we can use to fine-tune this open model, and then you can decide how much of the work you want done on the expensive proprietary models versus the cheap open models. You can deploy those models on-prem, in our cloud, or on your preferred cloud. Just use our agent platform and pay the subscription fee."

I can't imagine most businesses are going to fork over all this money to proprietary model providers when they don't need those resources. It really makes me wonder how much of this IPO is forecasting the bursting of the bubble. I feel sometimes like we talk about the AI bubble bursting like doomsday prophecies: "It's happening now!" But there have been more signs recently. Chinese AI stocks have been hammered recently. There have been recent earnings reports from American companies that have not looked  Yeah.

Google was hammered; they lost like $500 billion in stock value based on the fact that their search was underperforming

That's that one I wasn't able to think of, that minor little blip, right?

AI overviews not monetizing as well. So there's a lot, yeah.

I would agree that Anthropic's survival depends fairly heavily on pushing the frontier forward. In order to do that, it needs a disproportionate amount of compute that it may not be able to afford on a continuing basis, especially if Microsoft, Google, and all of these cloud CSPs that provide compute for them and are among their biggest customers decide, "We don't really need cloud for this. We've reached a point where our own open-weights models or small proprietary models are good enough for drafting emails or generating code bases for our customers."

So they're going to start buying fewer tokens from Anthropic or OpenAI when they eventually IPO. They're likely to go through very similar challenges because they're also getting most of their compute from companies like Oracle and Microsoft at this point.

Which was one of the questions I wanted to ask as we wrapped up: Do you think OpenAI is going to be in any better position once their IPO comes out? Because neither of them owns a lot of their compute, and OpenAI's attempts to build its own compute seem to have fizzled out a bit. Could they be in a better position or is it going to be more of the same?

I don't know with OpenAI whether they're going to be able to overcome the same risks that Anthropic has. It does feel like Anthropic is sidestepping a lot of hard questions by pushing forward with their IPO now.

With Anthropic going public this year, if OpenAI goes public next year, I don't think they can avoid the scrutiny, because the world is going to have woken up to the risk factors associated with these giant model houses. And I think they're going to face a much harder time with this, even before they get there.

OpenAI has the distribution of ChatGPT, which is demonstrating itself to be a useful tool that people like to use. But that's not where their monetization gold mine is going to be, unless they become the Google of AI search, and Google is already trying to get to that space, too. So I don't know how they're going to make it into the enterprise business and get the margins they need to pay back all the money they've taken.

OpenAI also has a different business model than Anthropic, and to a pretty hilarious degree, if you recall the advertisements during the Super Bowl about injecting advertisements into GPT....

The point being that OpenAI's revenue streams may be sufficiently different to insulate them from this. They have been trying to position themselves as an AI advertising company as another revenue stream, which Anthropic has flatly rejected. So it's possible that OpenAI's business model is sufficiently different by next year.

12 months is a long time in this industry. If Altman takes them public this time next year, the conversation might be very different. Having said that, Wall Street's eyes are going to be open to a lot of the risk factors in a way that Anthropic is sort of sidestepping right now by being the first really big model house to go public.

Which is honestly kind of surprising to see OpenAI press the brakes while Anthropic presses the gas. I'm assuming they saw an opportunity to get out the gate first and avoid answering the hard questions. Because OpenAI basically said, "Hey, we're going to pause our IPO while we assess these risks," given they've been in the doghouse regarding AI behaving badly this year, giving Anthropic that opportunity to scoot past and not have to deal with these things.

I think the other tell with Anthropic is actually that two-to-one compute ratio, because that's the first time that's ever happened. And it will be very telling if in their first or second public quarter that just disappears. So the timing might be related to the fact that they can now claim their cash flows are on a positive trajectory towards being cash flow positive and moving towards profitability. OpenAI delaying their IPO, I suspect, is largely because they need to get to a similar point. Otherwise, people are going to look at this and go, "This has no possibility of ever being profitable." At least with Anthropic's S-1, halfway through 2026, it looks like they could be profitable. Whether that's true in in their first public quarter is another matter until

To close us out here, I think this statement from your article, Tobias: "The only way to justify this kind of spend and risk is if you believe the upside is enormous, like the biggest economic transformation in the history of humankind enormous." And that raises my final question for you both: Is it going to be worth it? And what's the chance that Anthropic is going to flame out spectacularly in the next year or two?

Tom, I'll let you take the first crack at that one.

Yeah. I mean, I don't know how spectacular it will be. I think it's gotten to the point where it's sort of too big to fail, but I could certainly see some desperation moves where one of these big AI companies strikes a deal with Apple for distribution, because they really need the kind of money that Google was paying Apple for, or sorry, that Google is paying Apple for for distribution. And I can see something like that happening because they really need revenue. I don't really see it blowing up because it's everybody. So they're going to figure out a way to do the least harm if things go downhill. And that may mean parting out part of their businesses. Who knows?

I would tend to agree with Tom. I think about what happened with the dot-com boom as an indicator. The situation is quite a bit different because the AI industry has wormed its way so deep that it's not the surface-level situation we saw with the dot-com boom. There was a ton of fiber laid during the dot-com boom that didn't get utilized until much more recently, but it did get utilized. So I think AI is probably bigger than the internet and going to go down in the history books as the next industrial revolution, in much the same way the internet felt like that.

After the dot-com boom, it was big, but it wasn't as big as people prescribed the value to. It took another 10 years for it to actually become the thing everybody wanted it to become. It eventually rose to that valuation, but it took much longer than the market could sustain. And I think we're probably in for that.

So in other words, don't buy during the IPO. Don't buy high and hope to sell higher, because you might have 10 years to wait before you get back to that IPO valuation or above. Who knows? Maybe it'll go faster. No matter what happens, there's a good chance we're going to be right here to talk about it because this sure can fill a lot of podcasts and articles. Digital ink is going to be spilled on this topic for years to come. We hope you'll join us to hear all about it on the Kettle. Thanks for listening. ®

#10076. PRX Part 4: Our Data Strategy

Welcome back! This is Part 4 of the PRX series. Parts 1 to 3 covered model architectures, training design, and a 24-hour speedrun. This time we're pulling back the curtain on the part that quietly underpins all of it: the data. Of all the things that shaped PRX's quality, the data pipeline was one of the least glamorous parts to build but nevertheless an important piece to get right. Here's what we did, what we'd do differently, and a few things we only learned the slow way.

In one sentence: we assemble training data from a mix of public and internal datasets, re-caption the images with a VLM, and turn the result into the streamable corpus we trained PRX on.

At a high level, the data pipeline looks like this:

In the following we will dive into it in detail.

The goal was to assemble a large, diverse dataset for pre-training. At this stage the model is learning how the world looks: the visual concepts, the objects and scenes, how things are composed and lit, and the sheer range of what images can contain. That is a problem of coverage and diversity, not of per-image perfection. A broad, representative corpus teaches the model far more about the structure of the visual world than a smaller, prettier one would, even if many of the individual images are ordinary snapshots or slightly compressed. Over-filtering for aesthetics at this stage would actually hurt, narrowing the distribution and costing the model concepts and compositional variety it cannot recover later. Making generations look polished is a separate, later concern, which we leave to fine-tuning and preference alignment on small, ruthlessly curated sets. Pre-training is for breadth; fine-tuning is for taste.

We assemble our pre-training data from a mix of public and internal datasets. The priority at this stage is breadth, diversity, and standing on curation that already exists rather than redoing it ourselves. Where a source already comes quality-filtered, deduplicated, and filtered for NSFW content and personal information, we build on that work instead of repeating it at scale. Sources arrive in different shapes: some come with the image data itself, others as metadata plus baseline captions that we bring into a common form. We took a pragmatic approach: rather than build a corpus entirely from scratch, we leaned on existing datasets and our own tooling to assemble one quickly. In hindsight it is not necessarily the absolute best dataset one could build, but it was a solid and lightweight starting point for pre-training a 7B model.

In our experience, what matters most for pre-training is to use long captions that accurately describe everything in the image. We saw this directly in Part 2, where switching from short captions to long ones substantially improved sample quality. If captioning is faithful, we don't need to worry about the occasional screenshot, advertisement, logo, or bit of text in an image, because those things get described in the caption too, so the model learns them as conditioned, controllable attributes rather than reproducing them unconditionally. Accurate captioning turns "noise" into something you can prompt for, or prompt away. This is precisely why the filtering we do later is deliberately light. We remove what is genuinely unusable, not everything that is imperfect.

We have been using Mosaic Streaming and Mosaic Data Shards (MDS) as a dataset format for distributed training for a while now. In combination with Mosaic Composer we found it to be a very low-maintenance, flexible, and well-performing framework for distributed training. Furthermore, MDS datasets can easily and effectively be mixed and shuffled and also allow for distributed training directly from object storage like S3 or GCS.

However, MDS datasets are very rigid. Adding a column or creating a subset for a given filter basically means that one has to scan and rewrite the whole dataset. That's why we use Lance for this kind of feature engineering and dataset curation. Lance is a columnar data format with cheap predicate pushdown, scalar indexes, and vector search, the right tool for building and exploring datasets with billions of rows.

These two formats play off each other throughout this post and the PRX data pipeline: Lance to build, MDS to stream.

For previous training runs, we used T5Gemma as the text encoder and pre-computed the text latents, storing them in MDS as bytes. This time around, after switching the text encoder to Qwen3-VL, we decided to compute text latents on the fly during training instead. Running the text encoder inside the training loop costs throughput, but how much depends on the model: for a small denoiser it can be significant, whereas at PRX's 7B scale the text encoder's compute is negligible next to the denoiser, and we measured only a roughly 3–4% throughput cost (about 1 extra day on a 30-day run). In return we get two things. Skipping pre-computation keeps our MDS shards much smaller, small enough to store the full pre-training dataset on the SSD-backed shared filesystem of our SLURM cluster rather than streaming it over the network from object storage. And it keeps us free to change the text encoder later without rewriting terabytes of stored latents, which is exactly the kind of switch we made when moving to Qwen3-VL.

We encoded all images as JPEG at quality 92, instead of a lossless format such as PNG. We did not just assume quality 92 was safe, we measured it. Real-world images have usually already been JPEG-compressed several times, so the real question is whether one more re-encode hurts. Across repeated decode/encode cycles on both high-resolution (1–2 MP) and lower-resolution (0.25–0.5 MP) real images, the first re-encode at quality 92 is essentially imperceptible. Each further cycle adds almost nothing, because JPEG quickly converges to a stable state, and even after 10 cycles the images stay well within the imperceptible range, while PNG would be 3–10× larger for no perceptual gain. The numbers, averaged over 100 images at quality 92 and measured against the original (higher PSNR and lower LPIPS are better):

Since most source images already arrive JPEG-compressed, storing them losslessly as PNG buys little, so we convert everything to JPEG at high quality (quality 92).

We also checked what matters most: whether training on JPEGs changes what the model produces. Our corpus is mostly JPEG anyway, so the only advantage PNG could offer is not introducing new artifacts. We deliberately drew the comparison from high-resolution sources, on the expectation that even originally-JPEG images carry few artifacts at high resolution. We trained two identical PRX models at 1024px on the same images, one stored as PNG and one as JPEG at quality 92. Both trained equally well on our metrics, and their generations were practically indistinguishable, including when we estimated how JPEG-compressed the outputs look using a known technique for estimating JPEG quality by matching quantization tables:

The detection rate is the fraction of generations in which any quantization structure is found at all. The mean and median estimated JPEG quality are taken over only those flagged images. The two models are practically indistinguishable: only about one generation in ten from either shows any detectable quantization structure, and the differences are small enough that we are confident the training image format has a minimal effect on output quality. So high-quality JPEG storage adds nothing measurable on top of what the sources already carry. For large-scale text-to-image training that is more than good enough. For artifact-sensitive data used to train other Photoroom models, such as our custom AI Shadows model, we still rely on PNGs.

You cannot interactively explore Parquet tables with hundreds of millions or even billions of rows. We therefore store the data in Lance, where we can index, query, and browse it. We run the ingest with Ray Data, reading the source tables in parallel and writing many fragments of a Lance table across the cluster.

One lesson worth sharing is about fragmentation. A Lance table is split into fragments, and several operations scale with the total number of fragments rather than the row count: a scan opens the files of every fragment, and some metadata operations are O(number of fragments). A table broken into too many small fragments therefore queries slowly no matter its size. The Lance performance guidance is to keep that count low (the rule of thumb is on the order of a hundred fragments even for a billion-row table) and to run compaction periodically to merge small fragments into larger ones.

We learned this the slow way. Our first ingest targeted only 100,000 rows per fragment, which left thousands of tiny fragments and made even simple filters and full-text queries crawl. After compacting up to roughly a million rows per fragment, which for our tables of several hundred million rows meant on the order of a thousand fragments, queries were fast and we stopped worrying about it. The right target depends on row width, query patterns, and how the data is written, and in hindsight fewer, larger fragments might have been a better default. Lance supports distributed compaction (for example via the Lance-Ray integration), so it is easy to adjust after the fact, but it pays not to over-fragment in the first place.

We chose to re-caption every image ourselves rather than rely on the captions some of the datasets happened to ship with. The reason is consistency: across a mix of sources, caption length, style, and quality vary a lot, and we wanted a single uniform standard across the whole corpus (more on the captioner in Section 3).

The metadata a dataset already carries is still valuable, though, just for a different purpose. Pre-existing captions, and the vector embeddings that sometimes come alongside them (for example CLIP embeddings), are what make a dataset explorable in Lance right away: full-text search over the captions and nearest-neighbor search over an embedding column let us navigate the data and quickly judge its quality and the filtering it will need, well before we have run our own captioning over it. So we keep both, joining them in when they live in a separate table, and lean on them for the browsing we describe next.

With the data queryable, we could quickly profile it. The resolution distribution, for example, told us where to set cutoffs. Our smallest training bucket is 512² pixels, and we cap upscaling into a bucket at 4/3 (about 33%), so the effective cutoff is 384² ≈ 147k pixels plus an aspect ratio in [0.5, 2.0]. Everything below that we discard.

Lance tables support full-text search on text columns as well as nearest-neighbor similarity search on vector embedding columns out of the box, and both can be accelerated by building indexes. We did exactly that for the caption and embedding columns, then built a small UI to browse the dataset: real-time text search over the captions as well as navigating clusters of visually similar images via vector search.

Browsing the data this way let us assess its diversity and quality qualitatively and spot issues early, simply by looking at it. We found uninformative baseline captions, a surprising amount of non-photographic content (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics), and some near-duplicate images. These observations shaped the rest of the pipeline directly: re-caption everything (longer, accurate captions describe even imperfect images well, and guarantee that the caption matches the exact image we train on), and add light filtering and deduplication passes later. In general, we believe this sort of exploration tool is invaluable for getting a feel for a dataset before committing to it.

We found that long, detailed captions are a very strong lever on output quality. In an early benchmark we trained a small diffusion model twice on the same images, once on captions we generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B and once on much shorter captions (produced with LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B), and scored both over training. The long captions generated with Qwen2.5-VL-7B won across the board, with lower FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD at every checkpoint (lower is better on all three).

A small diffusion model trained on Qwen2.5-VL-7B captions (red) versus the baseline LLaVA-1.5-LLaMA3-8B captions (blue), scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three metrics.

Here is an example image with both our long, VLM-generated caption as well as the shorter caption used as the baseline:

Our captioning runs as a streaming pipeline built on Ray Data: it reads the data from Lance, prepares each image, captions it on the GPU, and writes the caption back as a new column we can query and filter on. We prompt for a single dense, visually grounded paragraph rather than a one-line caption.

A tight schedule and limited resources meant that we couldn't spend too much time on ablations of different captioning models and system prompts.

We used the following prompts to generate the captions.

We shortlisted three VLMs as captioner candidates:

We benchmarked caption quality indirectly: we trained a small diffusion model for 100k steps on each caption variant and scored its generations with FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD. Alongside the three candidates we scored two reference captioners, to connect this comparison to the first benchmark: the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B (the same model as in the benchmark above) and a set of Gemini 1.5 Flash captions we had generated earlier for the 1M-image internal test set used here. The Gemini captions are a similar length but were produced with a different prompt (all others use the system prompt above), so its curve is indicative rather than a like-for-like comparison.

FID, CMMD, and DINO-MMD over training for the three captioner candidates and two reference captioners, scored every 10k steps up to 100k. Lower is better on all three.

Among the candidates, Qwen3.5-9B is best on all three metrics, with Qwen3-VL-8B close behind on FID and DINO-MMD (though weaker on CMMD) and the Relaxed captioner trailing on FID but competitive elsewhere. The clearest result is that the base Qwen2.5-VL-7B — the same model that beat the baseline in the first benchmark — is now the weakest of the five, which is exactly why we didn't just keep it: a caption-tuned or newer model measurably helps. (Gemini 1.5 Flash lands mid-pack, but with the different-prompt caveat above.)

We put less weight on throughput than quality, but at hundreds of millions of images it still matters, since it sets how much the captions cost to generate. We measured it only for the three candidates, all served through vLLM with no quantization or custom kernels. The tuning was at the pipeline level: one vLLM replica per GPU, with enough Ray Data pool workers to keep all eight GPUs on a node saturated. We first found Qwen3-VL-8B to be the fastest (20 img/s per H200) and chose it, for its speed, quality, and stable, release-grade vLLM support. Only later did we find that the Qwen2.5-VL "Relaxed" captioner reaches the same 20 img/s once fixed: it had been saved with the wrong architecture class, which broke vLLM's torch.compile hashing and forced slow eager mode until we re-saved it as Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration. Qwen3.5-9B produces great captions but ran slower (~6.5 img/s) and needed unstable nightly dependency builds at the time. A few months on, it is probably a great choice too.

At the end of the pipeline, we turn the captioned, bucketed stream into MDS, the format the trainer streams.

The Mosaic Streaming library packs samples into ~128MB shards streamed during training from object storage or a local filesystem. Lance does support simple distributed training as well, but we found that converting to MDS is the lower friction path for us. Mosaic Streaming gives us, for free, the distributed-training machinery we'd otherwise have to build ourselves:

Diffusion training runs on fixed-size tensors, so every image in a batch must share one width and height. Rather than crop everything square (losing the sides of portraits and landscapes) or pad (wasting compute), we use aspect-ratio bucketing: a small set of allowed (w, h) shapes, with each image snapped to the nearest one and only same-shape images batched together.

We bucket in two steps. First by resolution tier (pixel count): a 512px and a 1024px tier for most of the corpus, plus 2048px and 4096px tiers for high-resolution data. An image goes into the largest tier it can reach without upscaling by more than 4/3 (~33%), so each tier's floor is (size × 3/4)² (≈384² for the 512 tier, 768² for 1024); anything below the smallest floor is dropped. Then by aspect ratio within the tier: we enumerate the patch-aligned (w, h) shapes (both divisible by 16, AR in [0.5, 2.0]) that keep a roughly constant ~256-patch token budget, giving 13 buckets per tier, from 0.5 (tall) through 1.0 (square) to 2.0 (wide). At 512px that's 352×704 … 512×512 … 704×352; at 1024px the same 13 ratios scaled up. Constant patch count keeps per-image compute flat across shapes.

Each image is then resized to its bucket with a Lanczos filter and encoded as JPEG at quality 92, and Mosaic Data Shards are written into a tree keyed by resolution and aspect ratio so the trainer can stream buckets separately:

The exploration in Section 2 relied on whatever captions a dataset shipped with. Once our own detailed captions were in place, the same full-text search became far more powerful, and a few passes over the captions turned up things the sparser original metadata had hidden: more text-heavy images (screenshots, slides, documents, infographics) than we had estimated, and some NSFW content that had slipped through.

To turn those approximate searches into a filter, we ran a quick classification pass with Qwen3-8B in text-only mode: it reads each caption (never the image) and labels the sample visual, text, or nsfw. The whole heuristic is essentially one question, "Would you look at this image, or read it?" Classifying from the caption rather than the pixels is cheap (around 200 captions/s per GPU) and reuses work we had already done. A pixel-level image classifier would likely be more accurate, but this was good enough to remove the obvious cases at moderate cost and without having to annotate data and train a custom classifier.

Rather than rewrite the whole corpus to drop these samples, we added a skip-list feature to the MDS data loader: a small sidecar file per shard lists the sample indices to skip, and the loader unions them and skips those samples at training time. Nothing is deleted or rewritten. This turned out to be a flexible mechanism well beyond this one filter. We can exclude any set of examples identified after the fact, whether a newly discovered quality issue, a blacklist, or, importantly, data from users who later opt out of having their content used for training, simply by extending the skip list before the next run. It is also convenient for ablations: to measure a filter's effect, train once with the skip list and once without, off the same dataset, instead of storing two copies. The one limit is scale. Skip lists add a little per-sample work at load time, so once the skipped fraction grows large (we would estimate somewhere around 10%, though we have not measured the crossover), it becomes worth rewriting the MDS dataset without the skipped samples rather than carrying an ever-growing skip list.

The same explorer surfaced a fair number of duplicates: large image collections tend to accumulate exact and near-duplicate copies, which waste training compute and skew the distribution. We mainly targeted near-duplicates and exact copies, so we added a quick deduplication pass using perceptual hashes. If the goal is to identify duplicate concepts and balance them in a dataset, deduplication based on clusters of image embeddings is a more suitable approach.

We could have done an exact dedup on a byte hash like SHA-256, but a perceptual hash already subsumes that (it matches byte-identical images too) while also catching re-encoded or resized copies, so we used only the perceptual hash. It is a standard DCT-based perceptual hash (downscale to a small grayscale thumbnail, 2D DCT, threshold the low-frequency coefficients into a compact fingerprint), implemented in a few lines on top of OpenCV and SciPy. We consider two hashes a match if their Hamming distance is zero, so we only remove near-pixel-identical copies. Genuinely different shots of the same subject have different fingerprints (and different captions) and are kept on purpose.

Once every image has a perceptual hash (fingerprint), the dedup itself is just a hash-map lookup: scanning each aspect-ratio bucket across resolutions, we keep one entry per fingerprint, so any image whose fingerprint we have already seen is a duplicate of the one we kept, and when a cluster spans resolutions we keep the highest-resolution copy. The duplicates are written out as a per-shard skip list that the loader unions and skips at load time, so nothing is deleted and the dataset is never rewritten.

Across the corpus, deduplication removed on the order of a few percent of images, the caption-based text filter a few percent more, and the NSFW pass a small fraction of a percent.

The dataset described here is the pre-training corpus, where breadth and scale matter most. For supervised fine-tuning and preference alignment the trade flips entirely: quality matters far more than quantity, and the problem becomes finding and curating small, high-signal subsets out of this large corpus. To do that we have been building more powerful curation tooling, including a richer explorer that tags images with structured attributes predicted by a VLM so we can assemble highly targeted subsets for fine-tuning. We plan to dig into topics like fine-tuning and preference alignment as well as the data tooling we use for these in a future post.

Build something with PRX, or find a bug in our pipeline? PRX is Apache 2.0 and the model code lives at github.com/Photoroom/PRX. We integrated PRX into the diffusers library and there is a Hugging Face Space to try out our latest version PRX Pixel.

Come talk diffusion models and data with us on Discord.

Public test Space for pixel-space PRX t2i

Thanks so much, Photoroom team, for sharing your experiences from PRX so far!! Learned a lot.

AI, agents, voice, and physical controls are shifting software development from operating tools to expressing intent—and helping developers stay focused on building.

For most of my career, building software started with the same setup: keyboard, mouse, editor, terminal, browser, and an impressive number of tabs I was definitely going to look at later. The tools changed, but the relationship did not. Like most developers, I learned commands, memorized shortcuts, and adapted my thinking to the machine.

AI is changing that relationship and not because I can prompt my way to some workable code. It’s more because the system behind it can understand a repository, choose the right model, plan work, use tools, edit files, run commands, inspect failures, and keep going within boundaries the developer controls.

We’ve made it possible for a developer to describe an outcome, and GitHub Copilot can gather repository context, inspect symbols and dependencies, edit files, run tests, and revise the implementation. In the IDE, agent mode keeps that loop interactive. GitHub Copilot coding agent can take an issue into an isolated GitHub Actions-powered environment and return a pull request for review. This is not just faster coding. It is the shift from issuing commands to making intent executable. The developer still owns the outcome, but the work looks subtly different.

AI-assisted development compresses that chain of events. We spend less time navigating tools and more time setting direction, supplying context, defining constraints, and reviewing evidence. The development workflow now is about understanding the structure of codebases, the customer, and what a good solution should feel like.

This makes developers’ jobs even more important, and their time more valuable. It makes judgment more valuable. It makes taste more valuable. An agent can generate three implementations before you finish your tea, but someone still has to decide whether the abstraction belongs, the migration is safe, the tests prove anything useful, and the result solves the problem.

That is the most important change in the craft: the developer remains accountable for the outcome, even as more mechanics are delegated.

So what does this mean for the emerging developer workflow? The goal is to embed AI into the workflow, not beside it. It’s more of an ambient intelligence.

That requires portable context. MCP connects agents to tools and services; repository instructions and skills encode conventions; hooks enforce policy and validate output. Simpler interfaces need explicit context underneath.

I see three layers: modality captures intent; the harness plans and acts; the control plane lets developers inspect, redirect, and approve. The best products connect all three without surrendering control.

Together, they let developers move across text, voice, and physical controls without losing context.

I, and many others in the maker community, have been experimenting with ambient control devices, from inexpensive hackable picture frames to ESP32 devices with screens attached. Agentic coding is past just a keyboard and a terminal into alternative interfaces.

Getting this kind of technology into everyone’s hands is something that I’m very passionate about and so over the past 18 months we’ve been working with Logitech on their MX Keypad and how it can help this new way of working.

The Logitech MX Keypad turns familiar developer actions into programmable inputs to accelerate workflows that are ambient and contextual to the work devs are doing. In GitHub Copilot app, a key can submit a parameterized prompt, open or resume a Copilot session, invoke an IDE command, or trigger a multi-step sequence. The hardware earns its place only when that shortcut removes enough friction to keep you in the code, but still gives you control.

Physical controls work when an action repeats often enough that removing a few steps preserves concentration. Not every developer needs another device on the desk, and not every interruption deserves a key. However, with this experience the developer decides which actions earn that shortcut and when the keyboard, command palette, or voice is better. Maintaining flow is the key, and a good interface gives some of that attention back.

GUIs made software visual. Mouse made navigation easier. The web made it connected. Mobile made touch natural. Agents add intent and action. The interface now includes ambient control.

That is why GitHub worked with Logitech to integrate the GitHub Copilot app directly into the experience. Developers can run agentic workflows in control, map a repeated prompt, start or resume a session, and decide through real use whether a physical control helps you stay in flow.

This is still early, so the important questions are engineering questions. How much repository and organizational context should an agent retain? Which tool calls can run automatically? How should credentials, network access, and secrets be scoped? What evidence should accompany a change? How do multiple agents coordinate without duplicating work or creating conflicting pull requests? Products such as MX Keypad let us explore one practical part of that system: how developers invoke, steer, and resume agentic work without losing focus.

For decades, developers learned to speak computer: syntax, commands, APIs, shortcuts, and the occasional incantation copied from a seven-year-old issue comment. Now computers are getting better at meeting us halfway. The best interface will not have the most panels or AI buttons. It will understand enough context, preserve meaningful control, and get out of the way so we can build software that matters.

The goal is not to remove developers from the work. It is to remove friction around the work. Pairing MX Keypad with GitHub Copilot Pro+ gives developers a concrete experiment: choose one repeated interruption, map it to a control, and see whether it preserves focus.

If you want to try it, you can do so here and get three months of GitHub Copilot Pro+.

#10074. Frozen part II: Hackers remotely defrost produce in Euro supermarkets ... again

Let it go (bad): Dozens of stores report mass food wastage as managers start their week in puddles

The cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers in Europe continue, as a slew of grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden report widespread food wastage as a result of miscreants raising the temperatures to highs of 50ºC (122°F).

In Belgium, around 40 Delhaize stores were affected after the attackers reportedly switched fridges and freezers into defrost mode overnight, between Sunday and Monday, resulting in stock issues.

Diego Louwers, a Proxy Delhaize store manager in Overijse, near Brussels, told RTL Info that the consequences of the cyberattacks were "catastrophic," forcing the store to throw out the entirety of its fresh and frozen products.

"We can't have anything worse in our line of work," he said. "We have to throw away all of our merchandise, and it's both heartbreaking and very complicated operationally."

A Delhaize spokesperson said it took steps to ensure stores remain stocked, although fresh and frozen products are "temporarily somewhat limited."

"On Monday, 2 November, we identified an IT incident affecting the refrigeration systems in several dozen of our stores," they said.

"We immediately took the necessary measures to keep our stores operational and ensure that our customers can continue to do their shopping as usual.

"In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centres are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores.

"We are, of course, continuing to ensure that our products are stored and presented under optimal conditions, so that we can provide our customers with the quality and freshness they have come to expect from us."

Around 15 Carrefour stores are also reportedly affected, as are sites operated by Intermarché, Spar, and Shop & Go stores located at Q8 service stations.

Belgium’s De Laet & Van Haver chain of butcher shops reported temperature rises in its appliances too, but followed up with a statement on Monday saying there was no impact on its produce, and all stores remain open.

Simultaneously, similar issues have affected Swedish grocery chain ICA, which confirmed attacks on a "small number of stores."

"We can confirm that we have been informed of an incident overnight affecting a small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA’s central network," a company spokesperson said.

"The incident impacted the stores’ refrigeration and freezer systems. ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation."

ICA did not respond to questions about the scale of food wastage nor when normal operations are expected to continue.

One store, ICA Nära in Böda on Öland, said via social media that it is open today but has no fresh or frozen produce to sell.

"Unfortunately, we are one of the stores whose refrigerators and freezers have been hacked," it said. "We are open as usual, but unfortunately we have no refrigerators and freezers to sell.

"We have no status on when the refrigerators and freezers are expected to be up and running again."

The store manager, Mats Olsson, told SVT that he arrived to work on Monday morning and was greeted by a puddle of water and freezers set to 55 degrees C – a tale echoed by other managers across the country.

Coop stores are affected by similar attacks too, with six locations in central Sweden experiencing fridge-freezer issues, according to a company spokesperson.

Likewise, at least 13 SuperValue stores in Ireland are also affected, with fresh and frozen food being thrown out, according to parent company Musgrave speaking to RTE.

The news comes less than a month after various grocery chains in France resorted to discarding bucketfuls of produce after their appliances were remotely defrosted by cybercrooks.

Carrefour, Coopérative U, Intermarché, Monoprix, and others were hit with cyberattacks in mid-October, and hundreds of stores across the chains were reportedly impacted.

At least some of the affected stores were running outdated firmware on their Danfoss refrigeration controllers, and shortly after the attacks were confirmed, CERT-FR published an alert pertaining to numerous Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controller compromises.

Other retailers, such as Coopérative U, confirmed they were not Danfoss customers.

It remains unclear if the latest attacks across Europe used the same methods as those used for the disruption in France last month.

None of the companies that spoke to The Register on Monday responded to questions about who was behind the intrusions. ®

Learn how to move an agent session from the GitHub Copilot app into VS Code without losing the conversation, code changes, or working context.

The agent has finished the bulk of your change. Now you want to inspect one implementation detail, adjust a few lines by hand, and run the project locally before you ship it.

But the work is sitting in the GitHub Copilot app… and your editor is where you review diffs, debug code, and make final adjustments. Do you have to choose between staying in the session and starting over in Visual Studio Code?

You don’t. You can open the Copilot app session directly in VS Code and continue with its conversation, code changes, and working context intact. That means Copilot can handle the repetitive or time-consuming work, then hand control back to you for closer review, hands-on editing, and local testing.

This tutorial assumes you are already comfortable navigating VS Code, running commands in its integrated terminal, and working with Git branches and pull requests.

Open the session you want to continue. Before handing it off, take a moment to review the task and the work Copilot completed.

A session contains more than a collection of modified files. It also records the task, the plan, and the conversation that produced those changes. That context is important when you want to understand why Copilot chose a particular implementation or ask it to revise part of the work.

You do not need to summarize that history or copy it into a new chat before moving to VS Code.

From the session, select Open in VS Code. If the app presents more than one supported editor or VS Code installation, choose the one you want to use.

VS Code opens the project using the worktree associated with the session. It also displays the existing session in the Copilot sidebar.

That gives you three connected pieces of the original work:

You are continuing the existing session, not reconstructing it in a new editor window.

Before editing, inspect the diff in VS Code. Open the Source Control view to see the changed files, then select a file to review its changes line by line.

Review the implementation as you would any other proposed change. In particular, check that:

The preserved conversation can help explain how Copilot arrived at the implementation. If something is unclear, continue prompting Copilot in the sidebar. For example:

You can also ask Copilot to make another change. Because the session and worktree remain connected, you do not have to describe the task from the beginning.

Once you understand the proposed changes, edit any file directly in VS Code.

This is useful for adjustments that are faster or easier to make by hand, such as:

You are editing the session’s existing worktree, so your manual changes build directly on the agent’s work. You do not need to copy files between directories or manually re-create the branch.

Use the VS Code integrated terminal to run the project’s normal validation workflow. The exact commands depend on the repository, but some web app examples may include:

Treat agent-generated changes the same way you would treat code written by a person: run the relevant tests, inspect failures, and verify the behavior yourself.

If the development server prints a localhost URL, open it to test the change in a browser. When supported by your VS Code setup, you can open the URL in VS Code’s integrated browser and inspect the result without leaving the editor.

For a user-interface change, verify both the requested behavior and nearby states. For example, check the modified component at different viewport sizes and confirm that loading, empty, and error states still work.

At any point, you can choose the interaction that best fits the next step:

For example, after making a manual UI adjustment, you might ask Copilot:

Add a test for the updated label and run the relevant test file. Do not modify unrelated components.

Because you are still in the original session, Copilot retains the context needed to interpret “the updated label.”

When the implementation is ready, review the final diff one more time. Then commit and push the changes using the Source Control view or the integrated terminal:

Use your repository’s normal branch, commit, review, and approval practices. Because VS Code opened the worktree and branch associated with the session, pushing the branch updates the pull request already tracking that work.

There is no need to copy the finished files into another checkout or reconnect the work to the pull request manually.

Opening a Copilot app session in VS Code gives you a clean division of labor without splitting the work itself. Copilot can take on a larger or repetitive implementation, while you can move into the editor for detailed review, targeted changes, local testing, and final polish.

The session, diff, and worktree move with you. Start by directing the work in the Copilot app, switch to VS Code whenever you want hands-on control, and push the finished result through the same pull request workflow.

Ready to try it? Download the GitHub Copilot app, start a session, and open it in VS Code when you are ready to continue coding.

#10072. LeRobot v0.6.0: Imagine, Evaluate, Improve

This new release is about closing the robot learning loop: policies that imagine the future before acting, reward models that tell you when your robot succeeds, a deployment CLI that turns failures into training data, and six new simulation benchmarks to measure it all. It also brings depth sensing, VLM-powered dataset annotation, custom video encoding, cloud training on HF Jobs, and a much leaner install.

LeRobot v0.6.0 introduces world model policies (VLA-JEPA, FastWAM, LingBot-VA) that learn to imagine the future, a wave of new VLAs (GR00T N1.7, MolmoAct2, EO-1, EVO1, Multitask DiT), and a new reward models API (Robometer, TOPReward). It ships six new simulation benchmarks unified under lerobot-eval, the lerobot-rollout CLI with DAgger-style human-in-the-loop corrections, FSDP training, and cloud training on HF Jobs. Datasets get depth support, an automatic language annotation pipeline, custom video encoding, and up to 2x faster data loading, all on top of a leaner installation.

The robotics world is asking a big question: do world models actually help robot policies? v0.6.0 brings three policies to LeRobot to help answer that question. Each one learns to imagine the future as part of its training, and each takes a different path to keep that imagination affordable.

VLA-JEPA teaches a compact VLA (built on Qwen3-VL-2B) to predict the future in latent space while it learns to act: during training, a JEPA world model has to anticipate upcoming frames from the model's own actions. The trick is that the world model then disappears at inference, so you get world-model supervision at zero extra inference cost. Three ready-to-use checkpoints are on the Hub, including a DROID-pretrained base for fine-tuning:

Check out the VLA-JEPA documentation and the paper to learn more.

LingBot-VA goes one step further: an autoregressive video-action model that predicts future video and actions together, chunk by chunk, and feeds real observations back in to keep its imagination grounded. You can even save what the robot imagined (--policy.save_predicted_video=true) and compare it with what actually happened. Inference runs on a single 24–32 GB GPU. Check out the documentation and the paper for the technical details.

FastWAM asks the question in its paper title: do world action models need test-time future imagination? It pairs a ~5B video-generation expert with a compact action expert in a single network, so the model literally learns to dream its own rollouts. At inference it skips the dreaming entirely and directly denoises action chunks. Fine-tune it from lerobot/fastwam_base, and read more in the documentation.

We upgraded our NVIDIA GR00T integration to GR00T N1.7, the newest open generation of NVIDIA's cross-embodiment foundation model. N1.7 swaps the previous VLM for Cosmos-Reason2-2B (built on Qwen3-VL) feeding a flow-matching action head, and our integration is parity-tested against NVIDIA's original Isaac-GR00T implementation: same inputs, same outputs. Flash-attention is now optional, so pip install 'lerobot[groot]' just works, and you can load NVIDIA's published checkpoints directly.

GR00T N1.7 replaces N1.5 in LeRobot. If you need N1.5, pin lerobot==0.5.1.

MolmoAct2, the Allen Institute for AI's vision-language-action model, is now ported into LeRobot with the full lifecycle covered: fine-tuning (full or LoRA), evaluation, and real-robot deployment. Ready-made checkpoints with calibration correction baked in mean you can run it zero-shot on an SO-100/101:

Inference fits in ~12 GB at bf16, and LoRA fine-tuning fits on a single 24 GB GPU. See the MolmoAct2 documentation for the full deployment guide.

EO-1, a VLA pretrained upstream on interleaved vision-text-action data, joins LeRobot: a Qwen2.5-VL-3B backbone with a flow-matching action head, contributed by one of the paper's own authors. Train it with the standard lerobot-train workflow using --policy.type=eo1. Details in the documentation and the paper.

The Multitask Diffusion Transformer policy brings the TRI Large Behavior Models recipe to LeRobot: a ~450M-parameter diffusion transformer conditioned on CLIP vision and language embeddings, so one model learns many tasks selected via natural language. It supports both diffusion and flow-matching objectives, and it is small enough to train yourself. See the documentation.

VLAs don't have to be huge. EVO1 packs its policy into 0.77B parameters, an InternVL3-1B backbone with a flow-matching action head, small enough to fine-tune and run in real time on modest GPUs. It ships with two-stage fine-tuning and Real-Time Chunking support out of the box. See the EVO1 documentation and the paper.

Success detection and progress estimation are missing pieces in the robot learning loop, and v0.6.0 gives them a home. LeRobot now has a unified reward models API (lerobot.rewards), mirroring the policies API, with four reward models behind one interface - the HIL-SERL reward classifier, SARM, and two new additions:

Robometer is a pretrained, general-purpose reward model: point lerobot/Robometer-4B at any LeRobot dataset and it scores task progress and success from raw video plus a language instruction, with no task-specific training required. It is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and trained via trajectory comparisons over a dataset of more than one million robot trajectories (RSS 2026 paper).

TOPReward goes fully zero-shot: no reward weights at all. It wraps an off-the-shelf VLM (Qwen3-VL) and reads the log-probability of the token "True" given the trajectory video and the task instruction. Any capable VLM becomes a reward function.

Both ship with labeling scripts that write per-frame progress curves into your dataset, ready for reward-aware behavior cloning (RA-BC), dataset quality inspection, and progress-overlay videos. Check the Robometer and TOPReward docs.

Recording is no longer stuck with one hard-coded codec. The new --dataset.rgb_encoder.* options expose the full encoding surface (codec, quality, pixel format, GOP, presets), and vcodec=auto probes for hardware encoders like NVENC, VideoToolbox, VAAPI, and QSV before falling back to the default software AV1 encoder. For existing datasets, one command re-encodes everything:

Full details in the video encoding documentation.

Plug in an Intel RealSense, set use_depth: true, and LeRobot records depth maps end to end: captured in millimeters, compressed as compact 12-bit depth video streams alongside your RGB cameras, and decoded back to physical units at training time. Depth renders live during recording and in lerobot-dataset-viz, and it works across SO-100/101, Koch, OpenArm, reBot, Unitree G1 and more.

Your dataset stops being one task string per episode. LeRobot datasets now natively store rich language annotations (timestamped subtasks, plans, memory, corrections, speech, and per-camera VQA pairs), and the new lerobot-annotate CLI fills them in automatically using a VLM that watches your episodes:

A YAML recipe layer then renders these annotations into chat-style training messages at sample time: exactly the data tomorrow's long-horizon, talking robot policies will train on. Scale it up with HF Jobs, and read the annotation pipeline docs to learn more.

Training on video datasets is now up to ~2x faster out of the box: multi-camera frames decode in parallel, dataloader workers ship compact uint8 frames (4x less memory between processes), and persistent workers keep decoder caches alive across epochs. Loading a subset of a large dataset (episodes=[...]) went from minutes to milliseconds (275 s down to 0.06 s in our benchmark). Sampling is also deterministic and resumable now, so interrupted trainings restart sample-exact.

v0.5.0 planted the flag on LeRobot as an evaluation hub for VLAs; v0.6.0 makes it the real deal with six new simulation benchmarks, all runnable through the same lerobot-eval CLI, each with a docs page, a Docker image, and a SmolVLA baseline checkpoint smoke-tested in CI:

Simulator backends require specific system dependencies with their own install steps; each docs page has the exact recipe, and every benchmark ships a ready-made Docker image if you'd rather skip the setup.

Together with LIBERO, Meta-World, and NVIDIA IsaacLab-Arena, that makes nine benchmark families under one roof, and a new Adding a New Benchmark guide documents exactly how to plug in yours. Evaluation also got faster: parallel eval now defaults to async vectorized environments, benchmarked at up to 2x faster.

Deploying a policy used to be a hack on top of lerobot-record. The new lerobot-rollout CLI makes deployment its own workflow, with pluggable strategies and inference backends (including Real-Time Chunking for slow compatible VLAs). The base strategy just runs the policy. sentry records continuously, rotating episodes and uploading to the Hub as it goes. highlight keeps a ring buffer and saves the last N seconds when you hit a key, so an interesting moment is never lost. episodic mirrors the classic episode/reset recording workflow. And dagger turns deployment into data collection.

With the DAgger strategy, you watch your policy run, hit a key (or a USB foot pedal) the moment it goes wrong, take over with your leader arm to record the correction, and hand control back. Actuated leaders are driven to the follower's pose before you take over, so the handover is jerk-free. Every correction frame is tagged with an intervention flag, and the resulting dataset is ready for the next fine-tune:

Deploy, collect corrections, fine-tune, repeat: the robot learning flywheel is now a CLI flag. Read the deployment docs.

Robot foundation models are outgrowing single GPUs. LeRobot training now supports FSDP (fully sharded data parallel) through Accelerate: parameters, gradients, and optimizer state are sharded across GPUs, and checkpoints are gathered back into a plain single-file model.safetensors that loads like any other policy. You can even resume an FSDP run on a different number of GPUs. See the multi-GPU training docs.

No GPU? No problem. The exact same lerobot-train command now runs in the cloud by adding one flag:

LeRobot pushes your local dataset to a private Hub repo if needed, submits the job, streams logs to your terminal, and pushes the trained policy to the Hub at the end. Pick anything from a T4 to 8x H200 with --job.target (compute is billed pay-as-you-go). Check out the documentation

Check the release notes for the full list and migration pointers for the breaking changes.

Beyond these headline features, v0.6.0 includes hundreds of bug fixes, documentation improvements, and quality-of-life upgrades across the codebase, from smarter defaults to more reliable CI.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community. This release includes work from academia, industry and hobbyists teams who chose LeRobot as the home for their models and benchmarks. Every PR and bug report pushes open-source robotics forward.

Stay tuned for more to come 🤗 Get started here! – The LeRobot team ❤️
