#10049. Oracle gobbles $20 billion borrowing limit a week after setting it

In the middle of a datacenter capex binge, vendor promises no more borrowing until the end of 2030

The week after promising to cap new borrowing at $20 billion until the end of its 2030 financial year, Oracle launched plans to borrow all that in one go.

In notices to investors on Monday, Big Red said it is offering bonds worth $10 billion together with $10 billion in shares of its common stock.

It said it could use the money for working capital, capital expenditures, contractual obligations, acquisitions, dividends, stock repurchases, debt repayments and other matters. The most likely candidate is financing datacenters, as the tech giant is in the middle of capex binge which saw $55.7 billion spent in fiscal year 2026, which ended in May. The company plans to spend between $90 billion and $95 billion in fiscal 2027.

Last week, the company told investors it would limit new borrowing to $20 billion until the end of its financial year 2030, which ends in May that year. It promised to get more revenue from customers by charging for AI usage on top of seat-based subscriptions.

CFO Hilary Maxson also told an analysts' event that Big Red would look to borrow the $20 billion during the remainder of fiscal 2027, which ends in May, implying there would be no new borrowing for the following two years.

Maxson confirmed this was correct. “That's a real commitment. We don't expect other forms of structured financing or other things using our Oracle credit out in the market,” she said.

In July, Oracle said it could face more than $100 million a year in financing costs to guarantee the power commitments behind a nearly 1 GW datacenter campus it is developing in Wisconsin with Vantage and OpenAI.

In October, Oracle reportedly sent a force majeure notice to a Blue Owl Capital subsidiary developing Project Jupiter in New Mexico. Bloomberg reported that Oracle was seeking to defer payments if the campus failed to come online as planned, rather than withdraw from the project. Oracle says the development remains on schedule.

In September last year, Oracle's valuation rocketed after it boasted $455 billion in RPOs, $300 billion of which turned out to be for OpenAI, all largely based around leasing datacenters for AI compute. ®

#10048. The Real Lesson From Buffett's Famous Bet

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

Spend five minutes playing around with an award travel search tool.

If you've never used one before, I'd start with PointsYeah, especially their Daydream Explorer. Put in your home airport and see where your points could take you. You don't even need to have a trip in mind.

If you want to go deeper, Seats.aero and AwardTool are two other tools worth playing around with.

I was listening to Tony Robbins on the Modern Wisdom podcast that came out yesterday, and he was waxing poetic about sophisticated investors, private equity and opportunities outside the public markets.

Not because I think nobody can outperform the stock market. Of course they can. But whenever I hear about an investment strategy that supposedly gives sophisticated investors an edge, I come back to Warren Buffett's famous $1 million bet.

In 2007, Buffett bet that a simple, low-cost S&P 500 index fund would outperform a collection of hedge funds selected by professional investors over the next ten years, net of taxes and fees.

It would be easy to extrapolate from this that nobody can beat the market, so don't even try. But I don't think that's the real lesson.

There's a huge gap between knowing there are investors who will outperform and believing I can identify them in advance, gain access to them, and retain the advantage after their fees.

The first one is obviously true. It's the second one that's so difficult.

At the end of the next decade, there will be stocks that returned 20% or 30% per year. There will be fund managers with incredible track records. There will be cities where real estate prices exploded.

We'll know exactly what we wish we'd invested in. But that doesn't help us today, because we're making the decision without the benefit of hindsight.

That's one of the reasons I've always found index investing so compelling. It doesn't require me to figure out who the winners will be. I can admit that I don't know and still participate in their success.

There will absolutely be winners.  I just don't need to know their names in advance.

One of my favorite parts of writing this newsletter is spending the week with my eyes and ears open for things I think are worth sharing with you. It might be an idea from a conversation, something I read or listened to, a useful tool, or just something from my own life.

I listened to Vanessa Van Edwards on The Diary of a CEO talking about how much the quality of a conversation can change based on the question you start with.

Instead of the automatic “What do you do?” or “How are you?”, she suggests questions that give someone a chance to tell a story:

And once you know someone better, you can go a little deeper:

My current favorite: What have you changed your mind about recently?

I noticed recently that I was starting to pick up my phone more often than I wanted to, and when I paid attention to what I was actually doing, it was almost always one of two things: Reddit or the Google feed on my Android phone.

It started out innocently enough, as I was just looking for info on my favorite soccer team, Arsenal. But I started noticing how much time was disappearing into apps with infinite scroll.

I deleted Reddit from my phone, which was an easy decision because it is a cesspool. But the bigger win was something Erin figured out: you can turn off the Google Discover feed entirely.

On Android, open the Google app → profile picture → Settings, search for Discover, and turn it off.

Now when I open that part of my phone or go to Google something, instead of an endless list of stories, there's nothing there.

I don't make many guest podcast appearances these days, but I recently joined Robert Brokamp on The Motley Fool's Hidden Gems Investing podcast to talk about the current state of the Financial Independence movement.

We talked about why you don't see nearly as many FIRE articles in the news anymore. A decade ago, FI was novel enough to be a story. Now it's everywhere. To a large degree, the core ideas of FI have simply become personal finance.

Or, as I put it on the podcast: “We used to be (considered) these frugal weirdos. And we’re not so weird anymore.”

The fundamentals haven't changed: “For most middle-class people, there’s precisely one way to get ahead financially: live below your means.”

Listen to The Current State of the Financial Independence Movement.

We spent Saturday in Williamsburg for Family Weekend with Anna, including a scavenger hunt that had us running around town trying to decipher clues and find random landmarks.

It was ridiculous and surprisingly competitive, which is pretty much exactly what you want from a family scavenger hunt. We missed exactly one riddle that would have put us at the top of about 150 teams, and I’m embarrassed to report that we’re all still thinking about it.

It’s almost exactly 10 years since Jonathan and I first met in 2016, and lately I’ve been thinking about what ChooseFI has actually been about over that time.

I came across a line while reading Drownproof this week that put words to something I’ve been trying to articulate for years:

“Until you view yourself as the author of your life, you will be the victim of it.”

We’ve spent a decade talking about index funds, taxes, travel rewards, career moves, college, healthcare and hundreds of other topics. On the surface, that can look like a collection of financial tactics. But the people who seem to get the most out of ChooseFI don’t simply accumulate more tactics. They start approaching their lives differently.

They start questioning things they once assumed were fixed. If something looks complicated, they learn it. An expense that seemed unavoidable gets another look. If a career isn't what they hoped it would be, they look for another one. They stop assuming that the way things are is necessarily the way things have to be.

I think that’s why financial independence is so powerful. Money creates options, but the process of pursuing FI also teaches you to notice that you have options in the first place.

Ten years later, I think that may be the larger idea behind ChooseFI.

My sister came up with the idea of a girl cousins retreat. She reached out to all of our cousins on our mom's side of the family and invited them to come spend the Labor day weekend at her house to reconnect and build friendships. We have 22 cousins and in the end we had 6 show up. 4 which were my sisters. We had so much fun hiking, paddleboarding, laughing, sitting on the beach and everywhere we drove together was full of talking. There is a big age gap between our family and some of the cousins so it was a perfect opportunity to get to know them better. This was possible for me to go since I am retired and have the free time and finances to do. I also noticed that since I walk regularly I was able to keep up with the younger girls on our aggressive hike. Fitness, time and money have allowed me those freedoms.

Your podcast this week hit very close to home. I have been on a FI journey since 1989. I saved. I invested. I was patient. Teacher. Divorced. Remarried. One income. Etc. 12 years ago, in 2014 (60 years old), I was diagnosed with a very rare form of cancer. No cure. No treatment except emergency surgery to remove cancer cells and nearby lymph nodes. One year ago, the cancer returned. Now stage 4. I am currently 72, and I have lived long enough that there is a treatment (not a cure). I have set up my beneficiaries, invested, set up a family trust, funded charities, helped my grandkids on their paths, and lived my life the best I can. My advice. No one knows the future. Be prepared to change when necessary.

Last Black Friday, I bought an annual pass to my local museum. I bought the most expensive one (about $100) because I got 2 membership cards (one went to my sister), 4 guest passes, invitations to members only events, etc. But the best part is that the museum is a member of North American Reciprocal Museum (NARM) Association® which gives me reciprocity to over 1750 museums across the country! It's more than paid for itself and I'm looking forward to doing it again this year. Here's an extra tip: you can change museums every year if you'd like. There are 5 museums here that are all NARM museums and I could join any of them. I'm staying where I'm at but it is an option.

I had left my 31 year W2 in the summer and have begun work as a 1099. Today I opened my Solo 401K. That took minutes. Next comes the learning how to use and the funding -- but very soon, I will have truly self directed checkbook access to practically unlimited investment options from rental real estate to syndications & private alternatives + normal stocks and CDs. So excited to truly diversify!

I heard you talking about getting labs checked through function health and had a panel of labs checked through Superpower. I have been tired for a long time and figured it was chronic stress and getting older. Doctors would check my thyroid and hemoglobin and tell me labs were fine and to lose weight. Found out through Superpower that my ferritin was very low! This is a solvable problem that contributes to many of my symptoms. (Headaches, hair thinning, and fatigue.) Started iron supplements a couple months ago and ferritin is already almost up to normal. (I had been donating blood not knowing my iron was low because my hemoglobin was still fine!) Then - talking to Superpowers AI about my sleep data on my Garmin and my morning headaches it suggested a sleep study, which I did even though I did one a couple years ago - and found I have developed sleep apnea since my last test! Another solvable issue that could also be contributing to my fatigue. I imagine losing the weight will be easier with more energy with the low iron and sleep apnea addressed! And - my Health Savings through work paid for it all. Much more than 1% win.

I had a mindset shift. I was raised by my mom, who grew up in an extremely rural environment and who herself was raised by survivors of the Great Depression and WWII rationing. There was always a philosophy of "buy it just in case" in my family. This made sense when the nearest store was an hour away and you could be snowed in for weeks. But I live in an urban environment where the nearest store is 5 minutes away and the internet at my fingertips. So I've made myself some spending rules. I only buy if it's: (1) a necessity (utilities, clothes to replace outgrown ones for the kids, groceries); (2) Building freedom (shower organizers to make cleaning faster, precut garlic, scissors in every drawer); or (3) creates joy (travel, dining experiences, movies, books, artwork, exercise equipment, etc). There are exceptions to this rule, of course, but it's helped me see where my mindless spending was, like new clothes I didn't need. Not purchasing creates freedom, but so does understanding where I do and don't want to spend money.

#10047. Marvell wants to be a copper topper, bets $115B on photonics leader to push optical networking

IP house believes optics demand is going to explode as Nvidia and others eye bigger systems

Hoping to dominate the next phase of AI networking, Marvell Technology plans to acquire photonics giant Lumentum in an all-stock deal valued at $115 billion. The move will fill several key gaps in Marvell's photonics portfolio, particularly with regard to high-performance laser sources, optical transceivers, optical circuit switches, and specialized compound semiconductor manufacturing capabilities involving indium phosphide.

Higher speed interconnects combined with larger compute domains are the driving forces behind the move to photonics. As interconnects push beyond 400 Gbps per lane, copper interconnects are being pushed to their limit, necessitating denser, hotter rack systems. Optics offer a reprieve from these scaling laws.

Traditional copper wire can only maintain a 400 Gbps signal over about 1.25 meters. Every time the per lane speed doubles, the reach is halved. Photonics are largely immune to this and can push that signal over kilometers, enabling infrastructure providers to scale their systems across entire aisles, while also reducing the power and cooling requirements of each individual rack.

Due to close in the first half of 2028, the all-stock transaction comes as AI infrastructure builders, including Nvidia and AMD, eye larger rack-scale systems, which will rely heavily on optical interconnects to stitch hundreds and even thousands of GPUs together into a single compute domain for training or inference.

At Computex 2026 in Taipei earlier this year, Jensen Huang predicted that Marvell's long-term investments in photonics would catapult the IP house to a $1 trillion valuation. That hasn't happened just yet – the company’s market cap currently sits at just $180 billion – but it seems Marvell isn't above buying its way to the finish line by snapping up optics vendors before the AI boom sends their valuations skyrocketing.

As we've previously reported, the move to optical scale up networks has fueled a flurry of investment in optics, silicon photonics development, and manufacturing. Nvidia itself invested $2 billion into Lumentum just eight months ago to bolster its optics manufacturing capacity.

The limiting factor up to this point has been power. When Nvidia unveiled its first Blackwell-based rack systems in 2024, Huang noted the company specifically avoided optics as they would have added 20 kW of additional power draw to a system that already consumed 120 kW under load.

In the years since then, Marvell has invested heavily in next-gen optics tech. One of the most notable acquisitions came in February 2026, when the company paid about $3.5 billion for photonic interconnect developer Celestial AI.

Celestial's tech opened the door to more efficient optics integrations including near- and co-packaged optical interconnects that used a fraction of the power of conventional pluggable optics used in scale out networks.

Marvell's Lumentum buy will position the IP house as a one-stop shop for AI infrastructure providers' photonics needs. ®

#10046. Welcome Inkling by Thinking Machines

Inkling now comes in smaller size 🤗 Inkling-Small is out by Thinking Machines Lab. We have updated this post with performance, and deployment configurations for the Inkling-Small and the Inkling-Small-NVFP4 variants. Here’s the collection with all the Inkling models. We made it easier for you to deploy Inkling-Small with one-click on Inference Endpoints (getting up to 160 TPS). We also ship a real-time voice and image demo where you can interact with the model.

Inkling is a large (1T params!) open model to natively accept image, text, and audio inputs.

TLDR; Inkling by Thinking Machines is out on Hugging Face. Inkling is a huge multimodal LLM that understands all modalities (image, audio, text), has agentic capabilities, and supports 1M context. It comes in full BF16 and a well-calibrated NVFP4 variant, and includes speculative MTP layers for faster inference. There’s day-0 support in transformers, SGLang, vLLM, and llama.cpp. Thinking Machine Labs also released Inkling-Small with 276B total and 12B active parameters, as well as support for MXFP8 and NVFP4 weights, with the same architecture as Inkling.

Inkling is the first large open model with ~1T parameters and 1M context window to natively receive image, text, and audio inputs, trained on 45 trillion tokens of text, images, audio and video. It’s focused on reasoning across modalities such as audio, images, and text; and is intended for domain adaptation via fine-tuning. We’ve tinkered with this model to build some demos and explore the architecture, and we think it’s great for building a new wave of multimodal reasoning apps.

Inkling is a decoder-only multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 975B total and 41B active parameters. There are a lot of things going on, so let’s break each part down:

Here’s a quick glance of the architecture.

Relative attention: Instead of RoPE, which is the usual method to inject positional information in transformers models, Inkling uses relative attention to encode position information. Each attention layer learns position directly in the attention logits. Aside from key-query-values, there's a fourth projection producing a per-token, per-head relative feature R. This projection tensor is then tweaked with distance information (distance between the key and the query vector) and propagated into the attention module.

Hybrid attention: The decoder layers alternate between global attention (attending to the full context length at once) and sliding window attention (attending to a fixed context window in a sliding fashion). The architecture has a pattern of 5:1 sliding window to global attention layers. This hybrid attention scheme provides efficiency in computation. The final layer uses global attention to help build feature-rich representations.

Short convolution: The model uses a distinctive short 1D convolution, or SConv over the hidden states. SConv reads the current token and the previous W-1 hidden states, with W being the sliding window size. The intuition here is that SConv helps with local attention while freeing the attention and MoE modules from local representations.

MoE with shared experts sink: In Inkling, the router scores both routed experts and shared experts. Top-k selection is performed over 6 experts, plus 2 shared experts always active.

Vision understanding: The model includes a simple hierarchical MLP patchifier consisting of several linear layers. Each layer merges pixels progressively, until the final layer produces one embedding per patch.

Audio understanding: The architecture employs a discretized mel spectrogram, where each of the audio chunks (of 100 ms) are converted to the mel scale and then classified into the exact mel spectrogram bin.

The multimodal towers are relatively simple modules, unlike other models that employ separate encoders for each modality. Each image patch passes through the image embedding tower and the audio chunk is passed through the audio embedding tower to get both media embeddings. Image inputs also include an additional temporal dimension for video processing. We expect this capability to be useful for downstream fine-tuning, but we haven’t evaluated out-of-the-box video performance. The tower folds the patch grid, a small local block of neighboring tokens is stacked into the channel dimension and goes through hMLP. The audio waveform is converted to mel scale, which is then classified into a discrete mel bin. These mel bin values are embedded in the audio embedding tower and the embeddings are then summed to construct the final audio input.

Inkling comes with day-0 transformers support and is supported in major inference engines like SGLang and vLLM.

This model is huge. The bf16 checkpoint requires 2 TB of VRAM, while the nvfp4 version requires 600 GB of VRAM. You can try the model through serverless inference routers like Inference Providers, or use ggml quants for local deployment with llama.cpp.

The easiest way to infer with transformers directly is to use the any-to-any pipeline. You can use either the 16 bit "thinkingmachines/Inkling" on Hopper or later GPUs, or the quantized NVFP4 checkpoint "thinkingmachines/Inkling-NVFP4" on Blackwell Nvidia GPUs. Make sure to have the latest version of transformers (5.14.0 was released today) (pip install -U transformers).

After initializing the pipeline, you can pass in the prompt as follows.

Going one level lower, you can use Auto classes. For inference, you can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class for models and AutoProcessor class for processors. For different reasoning tasks, the tokenizer takes in a reasoning_effort argument. Existing options for reasoning effort are "none", "minimal", "low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", and "max".

For multimodal inference, you can use the same classes. We provide example snippets for each different modality in the model card.

Inkling also takes in audio input. Below is an example inference snippet, which still uses the same AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

For more realistic parallel deployment in a cluster of several nodes, please refer to the Slurm section below.

SGLang is one of the fastest deployment frameworks for Inkling at the time of release, as it includes a custom model implementation. The launch command below shards the model across 8 GPUs and serves an OpenAI-compatible API on port 30000.

Match --tp-size to your GPU count. Add --mem-fraction-static (e.g. 0.85) if you need to leave more headroom for the KV cache.

vLLM is strong for production serving. A single vllm serve command downloads the weights from the Hub, shards the model across your GPUs with tensor parallelism, and starts an OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000. You can view the vLLM Recipe for the model here to customize to your hardware.

In practice, you might need multiple nodes and a distribution tool like SLURM (see below). Key parameters are --tensor-parallel-size to the number of GPUs on your node, and use --max-model-len to cap the context window if you hit KV-cache memory limits.

You can infer with this model using several inference providers through Hugging Face. You can see all the code snippets to consume here. Below you can see how to use with the OpenAI client.

Using the “:auto” suffix routes to your preferred provider in your settings; you can also use “cheapest” or “:fastest” as well. For this release, we cover the inference costs for 2 hours within the release for everyone.

Note: audio support in Inference Providers is work in progress and will be added shortly.

You can use llama.cpp to run quantized versions of the model on limited hardware. Unsloth have quantized the model down to 1-bit precision, reducing VRAM consumption by 95% over the original model.

This starts an OpenAI-compatible server running at http://localhost:8080/v1 that you connect to in your preferred tool or clients. Heading there, you can start chatting with the model, and set it up with your favorite MCPs, pass in images or files conveniently and more!

Llama cpp also ships with a built-in UI that supports tools, mcp, and agentic workloads. Checkout Inkling running at 1-bit precision in the llama app:

Inkling GGUFs are also runnable in Unsloth Studio with dynamic 1-bit GGUFs which retain ~74.2% of top-1% accuracy whilst being 86% smaller.

Pi is a minimal coding agent harness you can use with different language models. You can use Pi with either an inference engine server endpoint, such as llama.cpp, or with Inference Providers on Hugging Face by adding this to your ~/.pi/agent/models.json after installation.

Then you can start Pi in your project directory by calling pi and you’re good to go! In this demo, we give the model a hard math reasoning problem and it uses tools in pi to solve it.

Inkling is focused on broad multimodality reasoning and low token consumption, so try it out with document processing or audio tasks.

MTP adds extra layers to the model that predict several tokens at once, not just the next one. During inference, the extra layers act as “drafters” for speculative decoding, speeding up generation without compromising performance. With MTP, you get the exact same generated outputs, multipliers in generation speed-up at small memory cost in VRAM (due to serving the drafter). Thinking Machines also provides an MTP drafter with this release.

We have prepared a small suite of reasoning questions from expert-level sources and university entrance exams. We have taken photos of the screen with watermarks in the screenshot to challenge the model. The model has solved all of them on high one, failed one in highest and medium reasoning efforts, so we provide a link to the model answers for you to check out how the model sounds and provide the number of tokens the model has taken to solve each of them. Note that we provide no system prompts in these vibe evals, and these reasoning questions should often be run with a good system prompt. The vibe eval images and results live here.

We have vibe-evaluated the model on some audio reasoning examples from BigBenchAudio and a few multilingual audio examples of GlobeAudio (Russian and Chinese multi-choice questions asking the last word in transcription). The BigBenchAudio examples we tested consist of logical statements and questions that either ask for formal fallacies (whether an argument can be logically deduced from the context given in audio) or object counting (stating multiple distinctive objects in the audio, asking for the total count of a certain one). Although this benchmark is initially made for speech-to-speech reasoning, we just want to see audio reasoning capabilities of this model. For GlobeAudio, the questions are relatively straightforward, so we ran with reasoning efforts of 0.1. We ran the first example of each language within GlobeAudio. All tests pass on all questions and efforts, except for second formal fallacy example on lowest effort, so we only provide the number of tokens spent in each question against reasoning effort. Vibe eval results and audio files live here.

If you would like to use Inkling for post-training, Thinking Machines have built tinker, a managed tool for post-training open weight models. Their cookbook includes examples for fine-tuning, distillation, and reinforcement learning.

We post trained Inkling with tinker and OpenEnv, an agentic RL environment tool. We used the ECHO algorithm that trains a model to predict the environment without a verifier, applying next-token cross-entropy loss to tokens produced by the environment, alongside the usual policy learning on agent actions. This teaches the policy an implicit world model without requiring a separate model, teacher, or additional rollouts. Check out the example.

If you’re working with Transformers Reinforcement Learning we suggest using Inkling as a teacher model in a knowledge distillation setup. For example, take advantage of Inkling’s document understanding abilities to improve the performance of a smaller (on-device) model. In this example, we use the transformer reinforcement learning library and the GOLD algorithm to distill knowledge. GOLD is handy here because it matches token logits between different tokenizers, so you can distill to any model on the hub.

Below you can find each Inkling checkpoint as well as their VRAM requirements.

To deploy Inkling on a cluster, we provide SLURM scripts serving with transformers API, as well as how to query the endpoint with different modalities. You can adapt these scripts to vLLM or SGlang by updating the commands. These scripts live here.

You can deploy an Inkling-Small NVFP4 checkpoint using Inference Endpoints. We provide a pre-tested configuration to deploy it on 8 RTX PRO 6000s with an aggregated VRAM of·768 GB, giving large space for KV cache, costs $ 22 per hourly uptime (scales to zero when unused). To deploy, run hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4 using the Hugging Face CLI or alternatively, head to https://endpoints.huggingface.co/new/thinkingmachines/Inkling-Small-NVFP4. With this setup, you can get 140 TPS (single user inference, prepared for multi-user support with continuous batching)

Once the endpoint is up, you can query as follows.

Releasing a natively multimodal model (text, vision, and audio) open-weights is a huge step forward for the open-source AI ecosystem! Having variable and controllable thinking effort built into a MoE architecture makes Inkling a really attractive foundation for fine-tuning. Excited to test out the smaller 12B active parameter variant for local agent workflows at https://geometrydashsubzero.io

#10044. Cops bust botnet of 1.3M infected Android TV boxes

Videostrong accused of shipping devices with a backdoor baked in

A coalition of private-sector security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries.

Google, Lumen, Human Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI participated in the disruption.

“We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology,” the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a Monday blog.

Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates, allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge.

The firmware’s pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices.

Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation.

The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. “Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices,” according to GTIG.

Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Videostrong did not immediately respond to The Register’s inquiries.

This backdoor and botnet operation is part of the same ecosystem as BadBox 2.0, another notorious botnet that infected more than 10 million TV boxes and other devices before Human, Google, and TrendAI disrupted it in March 2025.®

#10043. Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

Building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win. Send simple requests to cheaper models, reserve expensive ones for harder tasks, or route by specialty — Claude for code, Gemini for multimodal, and so on. A classifier or heuristic makes the call, costs go down, performance stays up. Done.

Except it’s not. Most routing systems assume that model selection is a classification problem. In our experience building routing into agentic systems, what looks like a model-selection problem quickly becomes a systems optimization problem. Three dimensions made this surprisingly hard for us.

We expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6. It wasn’t.

Across 417 tasks on the AppWorld Test Challenge using the same CodeAct agent, Sonnet cost $79 total ($0.19/task) while GPT-4.1 cost $155 ($0.37/task) — nearly double. On paper, this makes no sense. GPT-4.1’s token pricing is lower on both input and output, and Sonnet takes roughly three times as many reasoning steps to finish the same tasks. By sticker price alone, GPT-4.1 should win easily.

The explanation? Caching — something most routing discussions ignore entirely. Agent workloads tend to reuse large chunks of context across steps. When cache hit rates are high, effective input costs drop dramatically. Sonnet’s lower cache-read pricing meant it benefited disproportionately from this pattern, enough to overcome both its higher base pricing and its longer trajectories.

The takeaway: actual cost depends on the interaction between the model, the workload, and the serving infrastructure. A router that only looks at pricing sheets is optimizing against the wrong numbers.

A common routing strategy is to estimate how hard a task is and send harder tasks to stronger models. Intuitive, but it breaks down in two ways.

First, difficulty is often invisible at routing time. A request like "summarize this contract" looks simple, but might trigger retrieval, compliance checks, tool use, and multiple rounds of refinement before it’s done. Meanwhile, a highly technical prompt might be handled efficiently by a smaller specialized model. You often don’t know how hard a task actually is until execution is underway.

Routers aren’t solving one problem. They’re constantly juggling cost, quality, latency, compliance, and reliability all at once.

It’s tempting to think about latency purely in terms of model size — bigger models are slower, smaller ones are faster. But what the user actually experiences depends on much more than that.

Routing itself adds overhead. Infrastructure factors — which hardware a model is running on, whether the cache is warm, how busy the endpoint is — often dominate end-to-end response times. A theoretically faster model can still produce a slower experience if the serving conditions aren’t right.

Then there’s routing granularity. Routing once per task adds minimal overhead. But routing at every step — which gives you more flexibility to adapt mid-execution — means every additional decision point introduces latency and operational complexity.

A router that ignores the serving system is optimizing against the wrong reality.

These lessons shaped how we built our router. The key shift: we stopped treating routing as a classification problem and started treating it as an optimization problem. Rather than asking "which model is best for this task?", our algorithm optimizes across cost, quality, and latency simultaneously — while staying lightweight enough to avoid becoming a bottleneck itself.

The figure below shows the result on the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent. Each blue square is a different configuration of our router, tracing out a cost-accuracy frontier. The important thing isn't any single point — it's that the router gives you a range of operating points to choose from depending on whether you want to prioritize cost, latency, or accuracy. Configuration 1 (latency-optimized) lands at 84% accuracy for $93 and 83s — a 21% cost reduction and 9% latency reduction compared to running Opus alone, with only a 4% accuracy drop. Configuration 2 pushes cost even lower.

Notice that a standard difficulty-based router (the teal diamond) lands in a similar accuracy range but at higher cost — it doesn't explore the full tradeoff space the way an optimization-based approach can. And because the optimization itself is lightweight (roughly 6 ms and 2 kB of memory per task), the router doesn't become the bottleneck we warned about earlier.

The lesson we took away from this work is that routing isn’t really about choosing models. It’s about optimizing systems. Models are one variable — an important one, but just one among caching behavior, infrastructure state, compliance constraints, and workload patterns.

When routing works well, it’s rarely because it found the "best" model for a given task. It’s because it found the best operating point for the entire system. That’s a harder problem than classification, but it’s the one worth solving.

We’ll be sharing more about the technical details behind our approach in a follow-up post. In the meantime, if you’re building routing into your own agentic systems, we’d love to hear what tradeoffs you’re running into.

This post was influenced by numerous conversations with colleagues, whose thoughtful questions, feedback, and insights helped refine our thinking.

So I've always felt that model routing is a false proposition; it should have been part of the harness all along.

Agreed, routing should disappear into the harness and just be part of the system's execution logic. Our goal is exactly that—making model choice an intrinsic capability rather than a separate concern.

#10042. AI could break legal systems by finding previously hidden loopholes

If AI can find the holes in programming code, it can do the same with legal code, paving the way for chaos.

Felix Ringe, a visiting fellow at Stanford Law School’s liftlab and legal scholar, suggests large language models (LLMs) have become potent enough that they could break legal systems by identifying exploitable inconsistencies at scale.

"Legal systems encode the foundations of social order in natural language," Ringe and collaborator Linus Folkerts argued in a blog post last week. "Similar to computer systems, the written law can contain vulnerabilities that invite exploitation."

Ringe contends that while courts tend to pave over these text vulnerabilities through statutory interpretation, the ability to discover adversarially useful inconsistencies in the law in an automated way risks overwhelming the legal system's ability to bridge the gaps.

To buttress his thesis, he points to recent work by other legal scholars that frames laws as vulnerable code, such as "Legal Zero-Days: A Novel Risk Vector for Advanced AI Systems" and "Hardware and Software Bugs in the Legal System" [PDF].

The analogy dates back at least to 1999, with Lawrence Lessig's Code and Other Laws of Cyberspace [PDF] and Code Is Law: On Liberty in Cyberspace. Lessig credits William J. Mitchell, in City of Bits: Space, Place, and the Infobahn (1995), with the idea that code is cyberspace's law, adding that he "drew the metaphor from others as well."

Ringe has turned this on its head by proposing that law is code.

The analogy between programming code and legal code works reasonably well, up to a point. Law and code both have their share of formatting pedantry and ritual. The mapping breaks down when courts get cast as a runtime environment – non-deterministic trial outcomes don't work for production applications.

Discontinuities aside, Ringe's point is that AI models can surface statutory gaps at a scale that may bring the chaos currently seen in the software security ecosystem to the legal world.

To demonstrate that, Ringe and Folkerts cite several potential gaps in German law that they uncovered with the help of LLMs, noting that they're only sharing legal exploits they believe could not cause serious harm.

For example, an amendment to Germany's Occupational Diseases Regulation (BKV) is subject to a constitutional requirement to cite its statutory authority. But Ringe and Folkerts argue that the amendment omits a required reference. So, in theory, a journalist could request an unpublished statement submitted to Germany's occupational-diseases advisory council under freedom of information rules, challenging a confidentiality provision that the researchers argue may be invalid.

Another example cited describes a transit visa rule that may be invalid because the government failed to identify the authority under which the rule was made.

"We believe that with cheap legal reasoning proliferating, AI systems could jeopardize the functioning of today’s legal systems," they wrote. "In such a world, lawmakers would need to significantly harden the process of legislation, for example by leveraging advanced AI themselves."

Wendy Musell, a San Francisco-based employment law attorney and partner, told The Register that the use of AI in the legal field is expanding rapidly.

"Some California Courts, including LA Superior Court, are testing the use of AI as law clerks," said Musell. "Generally law clerks would assist the Court by researching and drafting opinions for the judge's review. That means AI is serving that role in certain courts.  Litigators now must consider how AI is analyzing motions and cases.

"This is the case even where I personally have found different AI sources to appear to have a slant or bias, and often fail to accurately analyze legal issues. It was just a matter of time before AI came for the legislative process."

Eric Goldman, associate dean for research and professor of law at Santa Clara University School of Law, told The Register that Ringe's argument has some merit.

"I think the methodology of using AI to identify potential statutory gaps is logical," said Goldman. "However, it will require careful human review to determine if the AI-identified gaps are in fact actually gaps. Statutory gaps also may have no legal consequence, or at least none of significance; and legislatures will often correct any major gaps once they are identified."

Goldman said the idea that legislators should use AI during the drafting process is ambitious, at least in the short term.

"Legislators often draft laws with a range of goals and priorities, and avoiding statutory gaps is rarely a high priority," he explained. "But many legislatures have legislative counsel who are responsible for converting draft bills into final legislative text, and I could see where legislative counsel could benefit from using AI to identify drafting gaps as part of their standard cleanup protocols." ®

#10041. These smart glasses promise to turn your silent mouth movements into text

Crazy person, or efficient employee? As always, it depends on what they're wearing

The next time you see a software engineer shaping silent words with their mouth, you may have to think twice before asking if they need a mental health day – they might just be wearing a pair of smart glasses that let them talk to their computer without uttering a sound.

Subvocal is a Y Combinator-backed startup aiming to produce these glasses, and already has working prototypes to show off in YouTube videos, including one with YC partner Dave Lieb trying them out and being impressed enough to offer funding. The headset isn’t what the final version will look like, the company notes, which is good: The demo headset is obviously 3D printed and far from fashionable.

Once the final product is available it should look a lot sleeker, based on mockups on the company’s website. It’s not clear when they’ll actually be released, though the preorder page says it’ll be sometime in Q1 2027 at an early bird price of $499. It’s not clear what the final full price will be.

As for how the glasses work, the founders, Georgia Tech computer science students Aarush Yadav and Arnav Kumar, explain in a launch post on YC that the device uses low-powered radio waves projected from the glasses toward a wearer’s face. Those waves are distorted by muscle movements and the change in a person’s face shape as they speak or simply mouth words, which the duo said can be picked up and translated into written text.

“We started working on this about four months ago after building the first version at a hackathon,” the pair explained in their YC post. “Since then, we’ve gone from a table full of electronics and antennas taped to our face to a semi-portable board and sleek glasses that can decode open-ended speech at 200+ WPM and a reasonably low error rate even at a small dataset scale.”

This is just a proof of concept, and many key details are still missing, like the accuracy rate, battery life, whether it will paired with an app, or what-have-you.

“The core thing we wanted to prove first was that the signal exists and that we can decode it,” Yadav and Kumar said.

In a Hacker News post announcing the company, Yadav and Kumar explained that they started the project during the hackathon by focusing on using EMG electrodes attached to Yadav’s face. They didn’t win the hackathon, but apparently the demo was impressive enough to earn some initial funding from San Francisco VC firm Afore Capital.

Shortly after that, the pair pivoted from EMG to RF sensing, as a commercial dictation product that required sticking electrodes to one’s face was unlikely to succeed.

“Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge,” Yadav said. “First we built an extremely low-noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face.”

They eventually got to the functional prototype they have now, and pre-trained the AI models doing the speech recognition to minimize setup time. According to the company, Lieb only had to read 20 sentences to calibrate the headset to his speech patterns.

“We think silent speech can become the next interface for interacting with computers, replacing voice and the keyboard,” the company says of its goal. “Emails, prompts, messages, code, notes, commands, all at the speed of speech without bothering anyone around you.”

With just four months of work under their belts, Subvocal could be a massive hit, ushering in a new era of silent muttering productivity for workers in a variety of industries, or it could flop as it tries to scale.

Those interested in finding out can preorder a pair now for $199, with the other $300 not due until the glasses ship.  ®

#10040. Security incident disclosure — July 2026

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the issue and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

We are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

#10038. OVHcloud GitHub Compromise Tied to GlassWorm Threat Actors

A developer's GitHub account that was compromised several months earlier was used to push malicious code to unsuspecting users.

GlassWorm threat actors appear to have snagged a big fish.

French cloud provider OVHcloud on Monday disclosed that one of its GitHub repositories was compromised, and that threat actors replaced existing assets in the company's open source command-line interface (CLI) tool with malicious binaries. Octave Klaba, chairman and CEO of OVHcloud, revealed the incident in posts on social media platform X, urging users that downloaded the latest version of tool to "update it again very quickly" or delete it.

"The hacker used the GitHub account of one of the developers and added a binary whose job is to retrieve secrets from the disk," Klaba wrote in an X post. "The quality of the binary is poor but it can go all the way. If you are affected, please change all the secrets on your disk."

According to OVHcloud's postmortem on the incident, the scope of the impact on the supply chain appears to be small because the malicious binaries were only available for one hour and 33 minutes, though they were downloaded approximately 250 times.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

However, the attack was tied to the threat actors behind the notorious GlassWorm, a self-propagating malware and botnet that first emerged in October 2025 and has since consistently targeted software supply chains, with previous GlassWorm attacks exhibiting long tails and extensive blast radiuses thanks to the worm functionality.

The attackers used a compromised GitHub account for one of OVHcloud's developers to gain access to the company's ovhcloud-cli project, according to the postmortem. For a brief period, the threat actors swapped out the legitimate releases with malicious versions of the tool.

A GitHub user downloaded a poisoned version of the tool on Monday and, after observing suspicious activity, quickly reported a GitHub issue to OVHcloud, which investigated the repository and removed the malicious binary in about 30 minutes. OVHcloud's security team also scanned all of the company's repositories and determined that no others were affected.

Additionally, the cloud provider noted that its main CI/CD platform for production is run internally on a private Git repository instance, not hosted on GitHub, and thus they were not impacted by the attack.

According to OVHcloud's security team, the supply chain attack was enabled by a simple misconfiguration.

"The main issue was that the GitHub repository was not appropriately configured to ensure release immutability," the company wrote in the postmortem, meaning assets could be altered after the software was published. "This misconfiguration has been corrected immediately and the repository is not [sic] longer at risk. The same configuration has been applied to every repositories [sic]."

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

It was initially unclear how threat actors obtained the compromised account used to access the CLI tool repository. However, in a blog post published yesterday on threat intelligence platform OpenSourceMalware, security researcher Paul McCarty tied the supply chain attack to GlassWorm threat actors via a Solana wallet address that was used in previous GlassWorm campaigns.

Perhaps more importantly, McCarty examined the developer account used to access the OVHcloud repository and found it has been compromised for seven months. "Its public repositories show a scripted history rewrite on 5 March 2026 and a hidden preinstall.js loader that decodes to a second stage using a Solana memo dead drop," he wrote. "The wallet is a known GlassWorm indicator, and the amend-and-force-push technique matches the ForceMemo campaign."

In that earlier campaign, GlassWorm infected dozens of extension packages on Open VSX, which is an open source alternative to Microsoft's Visual Studio Marketplace. However, OVHcloud's security team later discovered the developer installed a poisoned extension on a personal MacBook on Oct. 20, 2025.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Last October, researchers with cybersecurity vendor Socket flagged the exact extension version, [email protected], that OVHcloud referenced in its report.

"The extension's loader conceals executable code in invisible Unicode characters, queries Solana transaction memos to locate a remote payload, and downloads and executes that code," a spokesperson for the Socket Threat Research Team tells Dark Reading. "It also uses the same ivbase64 and secretkey response headers we documented in our GlassWorm themes investigation. Those behaviors are consistent with the GlassWorm loaders we've examined."

OVHcloud concurred and noted in its postmortem that the Solana wallet address points to GlassWorm. However, Socket notes that while the address matches what the vendor observed in its earlier Open VSX research, the extension file Socket retained embeds a different address. "We haven't established whether the address OVHcloud cites appears in a later payload stage, and we haven't independently analyzed the October CLI binaries," the spokesperson says.

Regardless of who the attack is attributed to, the Socket Threat Research Team stresses that a personal security lapse can lead to enterprise security risks.

"OVHcloud's account shows how an extension infection on a personal machine can lead to malicious software reaching an employer's users," the spokesperson says. "The company says its source code and build chain were unaffected, yet stolen credentials still allowed attackers to replace the binaries distributed through its official releases."

#10037. Max-severity bug in widely used OT programming tool exploited to deliver Linux malware

Your industrial IoT gateway isn't exposed to the internet, right? RIGHT?!

Unknown criminals are exploiting a maximum-severity vulnerability in Node-RED, a flow-based programming tool that is widely used in critical infrastructure, to deploy a flow that downloads and runs a Linux bot.

Node-RED is commonly used for workflow automation in industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT) environments. It’s built on top of Node.js and is used in commercial products including Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050. In August, Siemens assigned the vulnerability identifier – CVE-2026-58115 – to describe the bug and explain its perfect 10-out-of-10 CVSS rating.

Affected Siemens devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that can execute system commands on the device. This means unauthenticated remote attackers can create malicious flows, which is what VulnCheck researchers began documenting last Friday.

“On October 30, 2026, one of our canaries caught an attacker exploiting CVE-2026-58115,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity warned in a Monday advisory, adding that two Node-RED built-in nodes make this vulnerability “trivial to weaponize.”

One is an inject node, which fires a message either on a schedule or once at startup. The second, an exec node, can run shell commands. “Wire one to the other and the flow executes a command as soon as it is deployed, with no further interaction,” Garrity said.

Plus, these exploits come as criminals increasingly look to target internet-exposed OT and ICS devices, allowing their cyberattacks to impact the physical world and produce real-life harm. Case in point: the ongoing refrigeration controller hacks across Europe and the attacks on water systems across at least 12 US states over the summer.

The activity observed by VulnCheck came from a single IP address, 4.201.105[.]116, which sits in Microsoft’s AS8075 network and geolocates to Brazil. “It didn't just scan us. It sent the complete exploit, flow and dropper, in a single POST /flows,” Garrity wrote.

While there’s a lot that the researchers don’t yet know about the attacks - they didn’t retrieve a binary or staged scripts to analyze - the filename, bot-linux-amd64, indicates that the malware targets Linux running on AMD64 processors. It also suggests the malware operator may have other builds. “We did not fetch the binary, so we can't say what it does once running,” Garrity noted.

Between October 30 and November 1, the researchers saw this IP address target the same Node-RED vulnerability 16 times, and log 125 hits against eight different CVEs across their wider canary network. Among the targets of the attack were a seven-year-old Apache Solr flaw tracked as CVE-2019-17558 – affecting Camunda, Gitea, MLflow, Traefik, and Joomla, alongside Node-RED. All this suggests “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” according to the researcher.

One of these hits delivered a different payload pointing to a separate server (85.215.73[.]250), which VulnCheck now tracks - but doesn’t have any telemetry other than the URL. “Because the download host is a different machine from the one that sent the exploit, the likely setup is a scan-and-infect arrangement: the hosts that find and exploit vulnerable instances pull the implant from a separate, dedicated server,” Garrity wrote.

The mix of old and new bugs across unrelated products indicates “opportunistic mass scanning rather than a targeted attack,” Garrity wrote.

“If you run Node-RED anywhere, including inside OT environments, check today whether it’s reachable from outside your network, apply updates where available and implement detections to reduce the risk of exploitation,” he added in a LinkedIn post.

While the bug has been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, it hasn’t appeared (as of press time) in the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s KEV.®

#10036. 'PHP2Shell' Bugs Signal Red Alert for Security Industry

Security teams are scrambling to remediate two critical PHP vulnerabilities following leaked details and reports of exploitation attempts.

A pair of critical vulnerabilities tied to open source scripting language PHP appear to have significant consequences for much of the server infrastructure holding the Internet afloat.

These vulnerabilities, dubbed "php2shell" by some researchers, include CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. CVE-2026-109618 enables remote code execution (RCE) via out-of-memory corruption, and CVE-2026-109619 enables RCE via a stale global state. The vulnerabilities, discovered by infosec consulting firm Calif, were designated with a critical CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2.

According to a WatchTowr blog post, both PHP vulnerabilities let an attacker run their own code on a Web server without logging in. "It stems from stale internal data that survives after its memory is freed; a later request handled by the same worker can use that leftover data, and PHP confirms this can let an attacker run their own code on the server without logging in. Reaching the server over the network is enough; no account or prior access is needed," researchers said in the blog post.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

Organizations should update affected servers to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to protect against the flaws. As 8.2 through 8.5 are the supported versions of PHP, lower-numbered versions do not have a patch available, meaning organizations must either upgrade their PHP versions to a supported branch or use a backported fix. PHP's security advisory urges that while only an update is a complete solution, organizations can take certain actions to reduce exposure until that time.

PHP's maintainers initially said yesterday that an emergency security release was scheduled for Oct. 22 at 14:00 UTC alongside coordinated disclosure, but as WatchTowr's blog post explained, the embargo broke. A proof-of-concept tool called "PHP2Shell" came to light, and WatchTowr claimed to be able to recreate both vulnerabilities.

John Hammond, senior principal security researcher for Huntress, tells Dark Reading that there was a silver lining in the leak in that it "pushed defenders to inventory systems, prepare mitigations, and get ready to patch sooner."

On the other hand, "that same early warning was available to attackers, who were undoubtedly spinning up AI and LLMs to find the vulnerabilities, identify targets, and start developing or adapting exploits," Hammond adds.

This may not be theoretical risk, either; WatchTowr reported it has observed exploitation attempts of both flaws in the wild. Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for WatchTowr, tells Dark Reading that while no one has been successful yet, the company does not expect this to be the case for very long.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

The vendor said the potential for exploitation is broad across vulnerable PHP installations, and security teams should prioritize "internet-facing servers running PHP as an Apache module," as the PHP Foundation highlighted that configuration as having the highest risk.

"Every PHP installation that serves web requests is in scope, including PHP-FPM, Apache’s mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed, and PHP says the risk is highest on mod_php, where an attack can succeed before any application code runs," WatchTowr's blog post read. "Session Upload Progress, a feature turned on by default, offers one confirmed path to the problem, so most default deployments meet that precondition."

PHP is a common, highly supported programming language run on servers across the globe and used for Web development. The scope of organizations using PHP spans the Internet, from enterprises to small businesses, critical infrastructure, and municipalities. Many organizations, like the Netherlands' National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), took websites and services down to limit exposure and/or facilitate emergency patching.

Related:GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

As the Independent Federated Intelligence Network, a not-for-profit cyber intelligence group, warned in a Mastodon post, "If you are able to contact folks at local schools, governments, nonprofits, and other services to warn them about the PHP vulnerabilities, please consider doing so. These locations often do not have dedicated security staff and almost certainly have PHP assets exposed."

In a blog post, Huntress' Hammond recommended inventorying every PHP install, identifying end-of-life PHP installs, and alerting on "PHP worker processes launching shells, interpreters, or download tools."

Despite the leak and the resulting chaos, PHP maintainers acted quickly to give organizations lead time for two challenging vulnerabilities. Patrick Münch, chief security officer at Mondoo, praised the PHP Foundation's response. He worries, however, about the resources of open source organizations, which have to support this kind of work, often on a volunteer basis.

"I think the PHP team handled this well. They warned people a day ahead, Linux distributions got the patches early, and they even wrote fixes for old versions they don't support anymore. A lot of commercial vendors wouldn't do that," he says. "Where it gets harder is everything after php.net. PHP gets packaged and shipped by distributions, hosting companies, and software vendors, and a lot of those are volunteers or very small teams."

Indeed, the PHP2Shell flaws echo the Log4Shell vulnerability in Log4j 2 nearly five years ago, which similarly required the security industry to come together to collectively patch a major flaw in a popular open source project.

The terms living will, advance directive, and healthcare proxy are often used interchangeably, but they are distinct legal documents that serve different purposes. Understanding exactly what each one does is the first step toward protecting yourself and your family.

An advance directive is the broad umbrella term for any legal document that communicates your healthcare wishes when you cannot speak for yourself. It is the category, not a single document.

A living will is one specific type of advance directive. It documents the medical treatments you do or do not want when you are terminally ill, permanently unconscious, or in a persistent vegetative state. A living will addresses specific interventions:

A healthcare proxy (also called a medical power of attorney or healthcare agent designation) names a specific person to make medical decisions on your behalf when you cannot. This person can interpret your wishes in situations your living will did not anticipate. Many attorneys recommend having both a living will AND a healthcare proxy, because no document can anticipate every possible medical scenario.

A POLST form (Physician Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment) is a medical order signed by your doctor that translates your wishes into actionable medical instructions. Unlike a living will, a POLST travels with you from facility to facility and is immediately actionable by paramedics and emergency room staff. POLST forms are typically used by people with serious illness or advanced age, not healthy younger adults.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Most people associate living wills with elderly parents or terminal diagnoses, but this is a dangerous misconception. Consider these facts:

Without a living will, your family faces an impossible situation. They must guess what you would want during the most emotionally devastating moment of their lives. Disagreements between family members can result in court battles, destroyed relationships, and agonizing guilt that lasts decades.

From a financial independence perspective, the stakes are equally significant. An extended ICU stay for a patient on life support costs $10,000 to $30,000 per day. A prolonged legal guardianship dispute can consume $50,000 to $500,000 in attorney fees. These costs can devastate a family's financial plan and wipe out years of careful saving and investing.

A living will eliminates the guesswork. It removes the burden of impossible decisions from your loved ones and ensures that YOUR values — not a court's default rules — guide your medical care. This is not a morbid exercise. It is one of the most loving and practical things you can do for the people you care about.

Living will requirements vary significantly by state. Here are the key differences:

You have three primary options for creating a living will, ranging from free to several hundred dollars. The right choice depends on the complexity of your situation and your comfort level with legal documents.

The Five Wishes document is the most widely used advance directive in the United States. Created by the nonprofit organization Aging with Dignity, it covers five critical areas:

Five Wishes is legally valid in 44 states and the District of Columbia. In the remaining 6 states (Alabama, Indiana, Kansas, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Oregon), you can still use it as a guide but may need to attach it to your state's statutory form. The document costs $5 per copy and is available at fivewishes.org. It is written in plain language — not legalese — and takes about 30 minutes to complete.

Every state provides free advance directive forms through its attorney general or department of health. These forms are specifically drafted to comply with your state's legal requirements, so there is no question about validity. You can find your state's forms through the National Hospice and Palliative Care Organization (NHPCO) at caringinfo.org. These forms are more clinical than Five Wishes but are completely free.

An attorney can draft a living will tailored to your specific medical and family circumstances. This is worth the cost if you have complex medical conditions, blended families, or specific religious or cultural considerations that standard forms do not address. Many estate planning attorneys include the living will as part of a comprehensive estate plan package that also covers your will, power of attorney, and trust documents.

Regardless of which option you choose, you must distribute copies to your healthcare proxy, your primary care physician, your local hospital, and any close family members. A living will locked in a safe deposit box cannot help you in an emergency. Keep the original accessible and tell your family where to find it.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

A living will costs $0-$5 and takes 30 minutes to complete. Without one, your family could face legal bills of $50,000 to $500,000 and emotional devastation that lasts a lifetime. This is not about planning for death — it is about giving the people you love clear instructions so they never have to guess what you would want. If you are building a financial plan, a living will is as essential as an emergency fund. Do it this week.

No. A Do Not Resuscitate (DNR) order is a specific medical order signed by your doctor that instructs healthcare providers not to perform CPR if your heart stops. A living will is a broader legal document that addresses many types of medical treatments, not just resuscitation. Your living will can include DNR instructions, but a DNR alone does not cover ventilators, feeding tubes, dialysis, or other life-sustaining treatments.

Yes. You can revoke or change your living will at any time in any state. You can do so verbally, in writing, or by destroying the document. If you create a new living will, it automatically supersedes any previous version. Notify your healthcare proxy, doctor, and family members whenever you make changes, and collect and destroy old copies to prevent confusion.

Yes, having both provides the most complete protection. A living will documents your specific treatment preferences, while a healthcare proxy names someone who can make decisions in situations your living will did not anticipate. Together, they ensure your wishes are followed even in unexpected medical scenarios. Most advance directive forms combine both documents.

Most states honor out-of-state advance directives under either the Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act or their own reciprocity laws. However, some states have specific formatting or witness requirements that your document may not meet. If you split time between states or travel frequently, consider completing advance directives for each state, or use the Five Wishes document which is designed for multistate validity.

In most states, notarization is not required — two adult witnesses are sufficient. However, Missouri, North Carolina, and South Carolina require notarization. Even in states where it is optional, notarization adds an extra layer of legal protection and is recommended if you want to eliminate any potential challenge to the document validity.

Without a living will, your state default laws determine who makes medical decisions for you. In most states, the hierarchy is spouse, then adult children, then parents, then siblings. If family members disagree, a court must intervene — a process that takes weeks to months, costs thousands in legal fees, and forces deeply personal decisions into a public legal proceeding. Your family bears the emotional weight of guessing what you would have wanted.

A living will is one of the most important and most overlooked documents in any financial plan. It costs almost nothing, takes 30 minutes to complete, and protects your family from devastating emotional and financial consequences. Whether you use the Five Wishes document for $5, your state free forms, or an attorney for $150-$500, the key is to do it now — not someday. Talk to your partner about your wishes this week, choose your healthcare proxy, complete the document, and distribute copies. This is not about planning for the worst. It is about giving the people you love the clearest gift you can: certainty about what you want.
