#10034. Newer Models, Same Advantage

Three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

The training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

The combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

OCR models have been moving quickly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

The proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

This distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

DharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

That concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — new architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two new OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

DharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

Processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'

These are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

DharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

The examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

Extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

When a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output

This is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

The operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

Supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

The benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

It is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

What changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

This is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — new architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Three months ago, we showed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

#10033. Anthropic's compute tab could top $1T as Q3 revenue nears $17B

Revised IPO filing warns 12x revenue growth is unlikely to continue

Anthropic has published a regulatory filing revealing nearly $900 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments, with additional estimated payments potentially pushing the total beyond $1 trillion.

The Monday filing reports that Anthropic expects to pay nearly $70 billion in contractual obligations by September 2027, with a total of roughly $447.5 billion in commitments expected to be incurred by the end of 2030. That's assuming of course its revenues continue their upward trajectory, which the prospectus warns is far from guaranteed.

"In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all."

"Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the filing reads.

Which is to say, if Anthropic's revenues don't grow faster than its compute commitments, it could end up falling into a nasty spiral. And while Anthropic has several options, including debt and equity financing, relying on these long term could dilute existing shareholders or force the company to borrow on unfavorable terms.

Every IPO filing reads a bit like this because no company can guarantee eternal success and growth. A lot of this filing's language, as damning as it might sound, is therefore just Anthropic covering its butt.

However, even though the company is still growing steadily year-over-year, the latest filing shows revenue growth is already slowing. Between Q1 and Q2 of this year, revenues grew nearly 2.5x. Yet in Q3, Anthropic's reported revenues of nearly $17 billion represented an increase of just 46 percent from Q2. In the same period, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure costs grew 77 percent and it kept signing deals that commit it to more expenditure.

Last week, we reported that Anthropic's purchase commitments exceeded $800 billion over the next decade or so.

Anthropic now says its commitments are closer to $895 billion.

Roughly $320 billion of those commitments relate to existing contractual obligations. Another $451 billion covers leases Anthropic has signed, but that have yet to commence, with the company expecting them to begin between 2026 and 2028, although some remain subject to termination rights or other conditions.

Overall, however, Anthropic's compute spend is on track to increase substantially over the next few years. And that's not even counting the blank checks Anthropic has written to secure adequate compute, which it values at $150-$175 billion, putting Anthropic's total compute tab at somewhere north of $1 trillion.

Anthropic can't walk away from some of this spending because its deals with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Broadcom, which now total $437 billion, are non-cancellable. Some require payment regardless of whether Anthropic lights up a single GPU.

The AI upstart estimates that of its $895 billion in contracts, only about $213 billion worth allow it to avoid payments.

The revised S1 filing also offered insights into the company's customer base, including a major reliance on cloud service providers for distribution. The likes of Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are some of the model dev's biggest compute providers, but according to the filing, cloud marketplaces accounted for roughly 44 percent of its revenue in the nine months ended September 30.

Anthropic insists that none of its customers account for more than 10 percent of revenue. Yet reliance on hyperscalers for distribution remains a risk because they are all either actively developing competing products or provide access to models from Anthropic's rivals.

Despite all the risks in its prospectus, Anthropic believes it can become a sustainable business if it can access enough compute capacity. And by doing so, the prospectus claims AI will reshape the economy "in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet."

With so much at stake, how can humanity afford not to spend like a drunken sailor? ®

#10032. Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Research finds that, among respondents experiencing data loss, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incidents before data left the organization.

SEATTLE — (BUSINESS WIRE) — Data loss prevention (DLP) tools are often functioning as after-the-fact forensic systems rather than prevention controls, according to DLP in the AI Era, a new survey from the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA), the world's leading not-for-profit organization committed to AI, cloud, and Zero Trust cybersecurity education. The study, conducted in collaboration with Jazz, found that 73% of organizations said they experienced at least one confirmed data loss incident in the past 24 months. Among the respondents, only 16% said DLP blocked their most significant incident before data left the organization.

“Enterprise DLP has moved beyond the question of whether it should be deployed to whether it’s doing what it is intended to do. Enforcement is being softened, analyst capacity is consumed by noise, and new data-exit channels created through GenAI are exposing gaps legacy DLP was never meant to handle,” said Hillary Baron, AVP/Research, Cloud Security Alliance. “In the AI era, where employees and applications can move sensitive data through more channels than ever, organizations can’t afford to discover gaps after the fact.”

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Perceived visibility exceeds demonstrated capability. While close to half (48%) of security teams ranked GenAI as their top exfiltration risk, less than a third (29%) are able to produce a routine 30-day report showing sensitive data sent to GenAI tools.

Modern risks lack modern enforcement. Paradoxically, the highest-ranked risks are among the least strictly enforced, and the lowest-ranked are among the most strictly enforced. Both GenAI (48%) and cloud storage uploads (41%) were cited as top exfiltration risks, but only 22% of organizations strictly block on GenAI and 19% on cloud storage uploads. Conversely, removable media, which ranked last (10%) as an exfiltration risk, is strictly blocked by 31% of respondents, the highest strict-block of any channel measured.

DLP alert overload fuels fatigue. Fifty-four percent of teams are triaging DLP alerts where the majority turn out to be false positives, and 90% report at least one measurable impact from alert fatigue in the past year, including 21% who report voluntary staff departures directly attributable to DLP alert burden.

Business friction determines enforcement posture. Seventy-one percent of respondents reported that their security teams received pushback on DLP enforcement during the past two years. Among those teams, 66% reduced enforcement for specific teams/use cases; 8% reduced enforcement broadly across the organization; and 3% reduced or paused the program entirely. Across the full respondent base, 54% softened enforcement in some form.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

“Security teams know GenAI is creating new ways for sensitive data to leave the business, but many still cannot see the full impact,” said Ido Livneh, Co-Founder & CEO, Jazz. “Across the customer environments we observe, the average organization uses nearly 170 AI tools and fewer than 10 are sanctioned. Teams need to understand how data is actually moving so they can focus on real risk without blocking legitimate work.”

The survey was conducted online by CSA in June and July 2026 and received 433 responses from IT and security professionals. Respondents represented organizations ranging from fewer than 1,000 to more than 50,000 employees and were primarily located in the United States and Canada. Jazz funded the research and co-developed the questionnaire with CSA research analysts, while CSA independently performed the data analysis and interpretation.

Jazz is the DLP platform built to understand your business. Its agentic investigator, Melody, delivers pre-investigated findings with the business context already attached with no rules, no regex, and no browser extension required. A single lightweight agent runs at under 1% CPU and covers GenAI use, shadow IT, desktop applications, and personal cloud accounts. Jazz is a Gartner Cool Vendor and the winner of the 2026 CrowdStrike, AWS and NVIDIA Cybersecurity Startup Accelerator, selected out of nearly 1,000 startups. Learn more at jazz.security.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

The Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) is the world’s leading not-for-profit organization committed to awareness, practical implementation, and credentialing of forward-looking cybersecurity topics, including AI, cloud, and Zero Trust. In an era where digital transformation drives business success, CSA stands as the global authority ensuring organizations can operate securely while harnessing cutting-edge technology. Through the 501(c)3 CSAI Foundation, volunteer-driven research, globally-accepted standards, and award-winning vendor-neutral education programs that unite varied associations, governments, chapters, and corporate members, CSA bridges the gap between innovation and pragmatic security execution. Visit CSA’s website to learn more.

#10030. Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

Robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

Teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

But you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

That's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

And that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

Grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

We have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

And while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right)

Components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

Robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

Press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :

The data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

This release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most important next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

👉 Build a Grabette (GitHub) · Process your data (HF Space) · Contribute to the dataset

#10029. Toyota shows off SoC that stores model weights and its OS on integrated memory

Accessing external memory puts the brakes on physical AI, so carmaker has found an economical and speedy shortcut

Japanese carmaker Toyota has decided to have a crack at the market for AI processors.

Toyota is the major shareholder in a company called AISIN, a manufacturer of automotive components. Both companies are aware that cars are increasingly reliant on tech like image recognition, and that robotics and other forms of “physical AI” will need parts that overlap with cars.

AISIN thinks existing chips aren’t a good fit for such roles, because they rely on external memory to store AI models and then generate a lot of traffic between a processor and the model. That traffic, the company contends, makes image recognition and other on-device uses of AI less effective. DRAM is also currently vastly expensive.

The company’s response is a system-on-chip built on a 16nm FinFET process, an Arm Cortex A53 dual-core CPU, plus an Arm MaliG31 GPU. The chip includes built-in STT-MRAM, which stores both model weights and an operating system.

AISIN and its research partners at Tohoku University say that approach means the chip can go from power-on to kernel startup in 65.7 milliseconds – 38 times faster than is possible if using external memory – and run the Tiny YOLOv3 object detection algorithm on the chip.

“To effectively utilize the limited on-chip memory capacity, a hybrid multiplication architecture combining 8-bit and 16-bit multiplication was developed” according to a machine translation of Tohoku University’s announcement [PDF]. “By combining 16x16, 16x8, and 8x8 bit multiplication, the amount of weight data for the AI model was reduced by 53 percent, from 17.7MB to 9.36MB, while maintaining 16-bit precision.”

AISIN is an established parts supplier and already sells to Toyota and other automakers but hasn’t said if or when it can get this chip into production.

Meanwhile, the likes of Nvidia and Qualcomm very much want to sell their silicon to carmakers, and position themselves as sources of tech and AI smarts that existing automotive supply chain participants can’t match. ®

#10028. Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

The effort is aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure.

SANTA CLARA, Calif. — October 13, 2026 — Marvell Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MRVL), Microsoft Corporation and Oracle today announced a collaborative effort aligned with the Open Compute Project (OCP) aimed at standardizing a NIST FIPS 140-3 Level 3 integrated HSM for cloud and hyperscale data center infrastructure.

To direct this effort, the three companies have established a new OCP working group under OCP’s Security Track. The working group’s charter is to define open specifications for an integrated hardware security module for secure key caching and cryptographic key lifecycle management directly at the server level. This approach will reduce latency, improve scalability and strengthen the security posture of cloud compute workloads.

Most cloud and enterprise servers today rely on network-attached hardware security modules (HSMs) or software-only key management. This approach requires cryptographic keys to traverse the network or reside in unprotected, non-FIPS 140-3 Level 3 memory, exposing sensitive keys to potential security attacks. The working group will define an open specification for embedding a hardware security boundary, key vault and attestation chain directly into the server. This will ensure that cryptographic operations execute where data is processed, keys never leave a certified hardware boundary and workload integrity can be proven cryptographically to any relying party.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

“An integrated HSM will allow cryptographic key operations to execute where the workload runs, satisfying both regulatory compliance and zero-trust architecture requirements, all without compromising higher performance for security,” said Cary Ussery, senior vice president and general manager, Multimarket Business Group, at Marvell. “By defining this as an open specification, we’ll make that capability available to the entire industry.”

“As AI transforms cybersecurity and quantum technology reshapes cryptography, protecting the keys and credentials at the heart of our digital infrastructure has never been more important,” said Mark Russinovich, CTO, deputy CISO and technical fellow, Microsoft Azure. “Through the Open Compute Project, industry leaders are coming together around a fully open-source integrated HSM, combining our collective innovation to advance interoperability, accelerate the adoption of post-quantum cryptography, and shape the future of hardware security.”

“An open specification for integrated Hardware Security Module (HSM) capabilities is an important step toward enabling cryptographic operations where data is processed, protecting keys within a hardware security boundary and supporting cryptographic verification of workload integrity,” said Pradeep Vincent, executive vice president, Compute and AI Infrastructure at Oracle. “This effort aims to establish a common foundation for adoption across the industry.”

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

The Open Compute Project (OCP) is a collaborative community focused on redesigning hardware technology to efficiently support the growing demands of compute infrastructure.

As founding members of the new OCP working group, Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle will collaborate with the broader OCP community to publish a joint technical specification, with an initial draft targeted for release around the 2026 OCP Global Summit and version 1.0 to follow. The companies plan to demonstrate the new technology in their exhibit booths and during Security Track presentations at the OCP Global Summit (October 12-15) at the San Jose Convention Center in San Jose, California.

Organizations interested in participating in the security working group are encouraged to join through the Open Compute Project.

To deliver the data infrastructure technology that connects the world, we’re building solutions on the most powerful foundation: our partnerships with our customers. Trusted by the world’s leading technology companies for over 30 years, we move, store, process and secure the world’s data with semiconductor solutions designed for our customers’ current needs and future ambitions. Through a process of deep collaboration and transparency, we’re ultimately changing the way tomorrow’s enterprise, cloud and carrier architectures transform—for the better.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

Oracle offers integrated suites of applications plus secure, autonomous infrastructure in the Oracle Cloud. For more information about Oracle (NYSE: ORCL), please visit us at www.oracle.com.

#10027. TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Cloud providers may be storing sensitive customer data, without either party knowing it. But when a provider is breached, the unseen information comes to light.

A breach of an open source database provider may have inadvertently highlighted a serious gap in the way companies think about their cloud security.

On Oct. 19, software maker PingCAP, which sells an SQL database program called TiDB, disclosed that it had been breached. According to PingCAP's website, it serves major American corporations like Atlassian, Square, and Pinterest, as well as major players in China's AI space, including Manus, Kimi, and more.

The perpetrator — the somewhat deceptively named "Fulcrum Security," or FulcrumSec, for short — is a relatively new extortionist group whose leak site already includes major organizations like LexisNexis, Novo Nordisk, and the Manchester Airports Group (MAG). Earlier this fall, FulcrumSec appears to have compromised PingCAP, enjoying something shy of unfettered access to all of its cloud management, financial, analytics, storage, and other systems for a month or more.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

The even bigger issue is whether the breach exposed downstream customers' sensitive data. Investigators are still working out the details, but early evidence suggests that customers may be at some risk. Though their actual databases weren't breached, the information their vendor stored about them may have been enough to cause serious issues.

In a security notification published 12 days after first having discovered the incident, PingCAP acknowledged that hackers had access to its systems from Sept. 9 to Oct. 7. Using stolen service account credentials, the company wrote, the unauthorized party accessed internal company systems and then copied data and source code.

PingCAP's own third-party-assisted investigation found no evidence that attackers ran malicious commands or maintained persistent access in their systems, nor did they access any customers' databases. Instead, it said, the threat actors accessed customers' billing and other business data, such as contract terms and pricing, as well as various information pertaining to cloud accounts and product usage — email addresses, SQL editor text and errors, etc. They also exported a table with encrypted API keys, though investigators said the encryption protected the keys from actually being used maliciously.

Dark Reading reached out to PingCAP for comment. A company spokesperson provided the following statement:

"Between September 9 and October 7, 2026, an unauthorized party used stolen service account credentials to access certain PingCAP internal systems, copy data, and obtain source code. PingCAP identified the activity on October 7 and began disabling the affected credentials that day. As of October 14, all identified compromised credentials have been invalidated, all identified unauthorized access paths have been blocked, and four vulnerabilities reported by our external incident response firm have been fixed and independently verified as remediated.

Related:Marvell, Microsoft & Oracle Work to Standardize Data Center Hardware Security

"Our investigation, supported by outside counsel and third-party forensic specialists, has found no evidence that data stored by customers in our TiDB cloud production services was impacted, and no evidence that the attacker ran commands or maintained persistent access in the production systems reviewed. Exported records included certain TiDB Cloud account information, business and billing details. API-key values in the exported data were encrypted, and we have found no evidence that any were decrypted or used. As a precaution, we have advised all customers to rotate their TiDB Cloud management API keys and remain alert to targeted phishing attempts. We will notify affected customers directly as customer-specific impact is confirmed, and we will continue to share verified updates on our Trust Hub: pingcap.com/trust-hub."

FulcrumSec, however, painted a bleaker picture.

Related:Cloud Security Alliance Survey Finds Data Loss Prevention Often Detects Data Loss Only After It Happens

In a name-and-shame post to its leak site, the hackers claimed to be in possession of all of PingCAP's service management records, its financial records, its files stored within Google Cloud, Jira support tickets, customer relationship management (CRM) data, analytics data, source code, plus a four-year-long log of every connection every one of its customers ever made to the TiDB Cloud service.

Crucially, the hackers did not claim to have stolen any TiDB databases straight up. Instead, they indirectly obtained a wealth of potentially exploitable user data like those aforementioned API keys and other secrets, and potentially sensitive internal data exposed by cloud database commands.

The attackers fingered individual enterprises caught in the crossfire: brand-name US companies like Airbnb and Booking.com, Asian corporate giants like Baidu and Fujitsu, and a few of the world's biggest video game companies, including Capcom, Konami, and Square Enix. Asia represented the biggest slice of the pie, with nearly 2,000 affected organizations in Japan, China, and Hong Kong, with another 500 from India.

Additionally, FulcrumSec said its unauthorized access lasted for nearly two months, not just one. It was so comprehensive and unthreatened that, in the meantime, they were able to stand up a mirror of PingCAP's own service management system. Instead of having to manually exfiltrate data, their replication feed automatically pulled fresh copies of the company's internal database every six hours, for 22 days.

Claims made by threat actors must always be met with a degree of skepticism, and Dark Reading did not independently confirm FulcrumSec's. Still, the group does have some record of reliability.

Last summer, for example, the group breached Manchester Airports Group (MAG), claiming to have stolen 86GB of data. That data turned out to contain far more genuine personally identifiable information (PII) than MAG copped to, according to reporting by BleepingComputer. And whereas some hackers exaggerate their winnings, this case was something of the opposite: That initial 86GB claim represented compressed data. The hackers clarified that the actual, uncompressed total stolen was 640GB.

Even if one were to completely ignore the hackers' account and take PingCAP's more limited assessment as the truth, it would still represent a potentially serious risk to customers.

Arguably the most acute dangers — more than the broad customer data, or the API keys if they are in fact protected — lie in the less obvious exfiltrated data. This includes Jira tickets, SQL histories, and places where organizations unknowingly leak internal data. For instance, when customers use their cloud-managed database services, they send commands to the vendors' servers. Those interactions can often carry corporate secrets or sensitive data of many other types.

"Vendors don't typically set out to store secrets. However, customers often pass them over to use features built for convenience, and the data can settle in places few people think of as credential stores," explains Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at Sysdig.

Take PingCAP's SQL editor text and errors, for example, she says. "That's query history and error output, which is where secrets can accumulate when someone pastes a connection string to debug something on the fly," Morin adds. In FulcrumSec's name-and-shame post, for example, it highlighted exfiltrated SQL statements that listed in full view one medical clinic's roster of patients, and another's list of medical professionals.

Keeper Security chief information security officer Shane Barney seconds Morin's point. "The PingCAP incident illustrates a daily reality in enterprise security: Attackers do not need to compromise a customer's primary database directly if they can systematically harvest upstream credentials," he says. "In modern software-as-a-service (SaaS) ecosystems, customer metadata, API keys, and diagnostic query logs routinely seep into vendor environments through everyday operational telemetry. When service account credentials or administrative API tokens are stolen from a provider, that aggregated operational data transforms into a road map for exploitation."

Barney emphasizes the importance of cloud security hygiene — such as rotating vendor-facing API keys and eliminating hardcoded and long-lived secrets in developer workflows — and vetting one's managed service providers by demanding continuous third-party risk assessments and independent certifications and attestations such as SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001.

Morin urges organizations to ask a few specific questions when vetting cloud providers. "Teams should seek to understand what customer-provided data the vendor retains and what its retention policy is. They should also ask whether they scan for secrets at ingest and redact what they find," she says. "Teams may also want to understand how service account credentials are handled, whether they’re short-lived, how they’re scoped, how often they rotate, and what detections fire on anomalous credential or account use."

And, she says, don't forget: "Inquire about breach notification, specifically the timeline and what triggers it."

This story was updated at 9 p.m. ET on Oct. 22 to reflect a statement from PingCAP.

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10026. Bringing Nunchaku 4-bit Diffusion Inference to Diffusers

Large diffusion transformers can create stunning images (or even videos, audio snippets, and now text), but loading a modern text-to-image model in BF16 precision often requires 20-30 GB of VRAM, which puts these models out of reach of most consumer GPUs. Quantization is a powerful solution to this problem, and Diffusers already integrates several quantization backends such as bitsandbytes, GGUF, torchao, and Quanto, which we covered in Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers.

Most of these backends are weight-only. This means that they store the weights in low precision and dequantize them back to high precision at compute time. This reduces memory usage significantly, but it usually does not make inference faster, and can even add a small latency overhead.

SVDQuant, the quantization method behind the popular Nunchaku inference engine, takes a different approach. It runs the main transformer layers with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), reducing memory while also speeding up the denoising loop. The details are covered below, but until now, using these checkpoints required a separate inference library.

With current Diffusers, loading a Nunchaku checkpoint is as simple as calling from_pretrained(), with no local CUDA compilation required thanks to the kernels package. In addition, the companion diffuse-compressor toolkit lets you quantize new architectures yourself and publish them as regular Diffusers repositories.

First, install the requirements. You need a recent version of Diffusers and the Hugging Face kernels package:

Then load a pre-quantized pipeline like any other Diffusers model:

No custom pipeline class or separate inference engine is needed, and there is nothing to compile locally. The NVFP4 kernels are downloaded from the Hub through the Nunchaku Lite kernels page the first time they are used. This checkpoint pairs a Nunchaku NVFP4 transformer with a bitsandbytes NF4 text encoder, and generates a 1024x1024 image in about 1.7 seconds on an RTX 5090 with a peak memory usage of about 12 GB, compared with about 24 GB for the BF16 pipeline. You can find more details about the Nunchaku Lite checkpoint format in the official Diffusers documentation.

NVFP4 checkpoints require an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU (RTX 50 series, RTX PRO 6000, B200). For earlier generations, use the INT4 variants. See the hardware support table below for details.

SVDQuant is the quantization method behind Nunchaku, its reference CUDA inference engine. Standard 4-bit quantization is difficult for diffusion transformers because both weights and activations contain large outliers. SVDQuant handles this by moving activation outliers into the weights, representing the hardest part of each weight matrix with a small 16-bit low-rank branch, and quantizing the remaining residual to 4 bits. Nunchaku makes this fast with fused kernels for the 4-bit path and the low-rank branch.

The original Nunchaku engine gets much of its speed from model-specific fused execution paths, such as fused QKV projections and fused GELU/MLP kernels. Those optimizations are tied to each architecture's module layout and checkpoint format, so supporting a new model family usually requires model-specific integration work.

Nunchaku Lite is the new integration path in Diffusers. With it, Diffusers can load Nunchaku-style checkpoints without a custom pipeline or a separate inference engine. Under the hood, Nunchaku Lite patches the relevant nn.Linear modules of a stock Diffusers model with runtime SVDQ/AWQ linear layers before the checkpoint is loaded. The CUDA kernels come from the Hub through the kernels package. Two kernel families are used:

The trade-off is that, without architecture-specific fused kernels and modules, Nunchaku Lite cannot match the speedup of the original Nunchaku engine. However, the bare-bones implementation still delivers around 30% speedup while retaining the same level of VRAM reduction.

If you have used bitsandbytes or torchao in Diffusers, the mechanics will feel familiar. A Nunchaku Lite model repository is an ordinary Diffusers repository. The only special part is a quantization_config block inside the transformer's config.json:

This config tells Diffusers which modules were quantized, which scheme they use, and which Nunchaku Lite runtime layer to instantiate (SVDQW4A4Linear or AWQW4A16Linear).

Because the quantized model keeps the exact module structure of the dense one, everything downstream (schedulers, LoRA loading hooks, offloading, torch.compile) sees a normal Diffusers model.

Nunchaku Lite uses different kernel variants depending on the GPU generation and checkpoint precision:

Volta and Hopper GPUs are currently not supported by the 4-bit kernels. The quantizer validates the GPU's CUDA capability at load time and raises a clear error instead of producing incorrect outputs.

Nunchaku Lite can be combined with other Diffusers memory and speed optimizations.

torch.compile. Compiling the transformer improves the end-to-end speedup from 1.35x to 1.8x:

Quantized text encoders. The transformer is not the only component with a large memory footprint. Text encoders such as T5 or Qwen3 can occupy several gigabytes on their own. Further quantizing the text encoder with bitsandbytes NF4 reduces peak VRAM by about 22% in our benchmark.

Offloading. Diffusers offloading helpers such as enable_model_cpu_offload() and enable_sequential_cpu_offload() work as usual if you need to fit the pipeline onto a smaller GPU.

All numbers below were measured on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (Blackwell) at 1024x1024 using rootonchair/ERNIE-Image-Turbo-nunchaku-lite-int4-bnb4-text-encoder.

As shown above, Nunchaku reduces peak VRAM by up to 50% while still improving latency by roughly 30%. The remaining overhead comes largely from extra kernel launches, which torch.compile can mitigate, bringing the full pipeline down to 1.68 s, or 1.8x faster than the BF16 baseline.

Nunchaku Lite support in Diffusers is architecture-agnostic, and the diffuse-compressor toolkit provides an end-to-end SVDQuant workflow for Diffusers models: calibrate, quantize, package, and publish.

Below, we walk through quantizing FLUX.2 Klein 4B as an example. It covers the main steps: inspect the model, calibrate and quantize the transformer, package the result as a Diffusers pipeline, then verify and push it to the Hub. The full tutorial covers every flag in detail.

The generic scanner walks the model and decides what to target: compatible linears inside the repeated transformer-block stack become SVDQ W4A4 targets, recognized modulation linears become AWQ W4A16 targets, and everything else stays dense.

Always read this report before quantizing. For FLUX.2 Klein 4B, the expected result is 100 SVDQ targets, 3 AWQ targets, and 6 dense outer linears, with no missing patterns or duplicate names.

The following command runs SVDQuant on the transformer and writes the quantized checkpoint to outputs/checkpoints/svdq-int4_r32-flux-2-klein-4b.safetensors:

Replace --precision int4 with nvfp4 to build Blackwell-native weights.

The converter combines the quantized transformer with the base pipeline's other components, writes the compact nunchaku_lite configuration into transformer/config.json, and can optionally convert text encoders to NF4:

Once the outputs look good, run pipe.push_to_hub("your-name/your-model-nunchaku-lite-int4"). Other users can then load it with the same from_pretrained() pattern shown above.

Note that the generic path assumes the architecture can be quantized without structural rewrites. For additional speedup, the original Nunchaku engine rewrites groups of Diffusers layers as fused modules. The generic path cannot infer these changes on its own, such as combining separate Q, K, and V projections into one module or splitting a fused projection across several modules.

FLUX.1-dev's QKV projection is a concrete example. Diffusers defines three separate modules:

The Nunchaku FLUX module combines those layers into one quantized to_qkv module:

This grouped module is required because Nunchaku's fused operator consumes the QKV projection, Q/K normalization, and rotary embeddings together. By comparison, the default Diffusers path executes them separately:

The Nunchaku path supplies the grouped projection, normalization modules, and rotary embeddings to one fused operator:

This is the structural rewrite that the generic path cannot infer. Diffusers has three destination modules with to_q, to_k, and to_v parameter prefixes, while Nunchaku has one grouped module under to_qkv. A model-specific target config or adapter must state that the Q, K, and V parameters should be concatenated along the output dimension, in that order, and loaded into to_qkv.

Structural rewrites like these are described by a model-specific target config during quantization and handled by a small runtime adapter when the checkpoint is loaded. The FLUX.2 Klein 4B quantization script provides a concrete target-config example for producing a structurally rewritten checkpoint, while rootonchair/nunchaku-lite provides the runtime adapters needed to load grouped QKV tensors, split fused projections, and other fused operations. For the complete workflow, you can check the Adding A New Model guide.

To get started right away, check out the following repositories:

Nunchaku's SVDQuant kernels are one of the most effective ways to run diffusion transformers efficiently on consumer hardware, and they are now natively supported in Diffusers. Pre-quantized checkpoints load with from_pretrained(), and the diffuse-compressor toolkit makes it possible to quantize new architectures without waiting for engine support. By quantizing both weights and activations, the W4A4 path lowers memory use while improving denoising latency, keeping image quality close to the BF16 original.

If you quantize and publish a new model, we would love to hear about it. Share it on the Hub and let us know! If you have any questions about this feature, feel free to join our Discord.

To learn more, check out the following resources:

Thanks to the Diffusers maintainers for reviews and guidance throughout the integration, and to the MIT HAN Lab / Nunchaku team for the original SVDQuant work. Thanks to Marc Sun for providing feedback on the blog post. Thanks to Álvaro Somoza for trying out nunchaku-lite and for providing feedback.

rootonchair is also grateful to SilverAI for supporting this work and providing the environment in which much of this development took place.

#10025. Architect creates open source replacement for VM migration tool VMware has hidden

OpenVDDK is reportedly already being used in production, at scale

A cloud architect has created an open source alternative to VMware’s Virtual Disk Development Kit (VDDK), which the virtualization giant recently withdrew from public downloads.

VMware describes VDDK as “a set of libraries and utilities that enable software developers to create applications that can access and manipulate virtual disks” and “a valuable tool for developers of storage and backup applications.”

Users, along with VMware’s rivals, had another use for VDDK: migrating VMs to alternative virtualization platforms.

In August, VMware restricted access to VDDK downloads to its partners, meaning VMware customers couldn’t access the tool and some of its rivals’ migration tools became less effective.

Cloud architect Andrija Panić decided to do something about it.

“Many tools that have nothing in common except VMware use the same small library to read a virtual machine’s disks: virt-v2v and nbdkit, the importers in Forklift/MTV, Proxmox VE and Apache CloudStack, and countless in-house scripts,” he told The Register by email. “When public VDDK downloads ended, all of them became harder to install and run.”

“I didn’t think it was fair that people’s ability to move or protect their own data should depend on a download page.”

He describes the project as “an independent drop-in for libvixDiskLib.so.8.0.3, the disk library that VMware backup and migration tools load to read virtual disks. It was written from scratch, using only public documentation and black-box testing, and contains no VMware code.”

Panić told The Register he wrote the tool in Go, with a thin C layer that exposes exactly the same C interface, library name and symbol versions as VMware’s code.

The tool cannot write disks, just read them for backup and migration purposes.

In his email to The Register, Panić said he has successfully tested OpenVDDK on vSphere versions 6.7 U3, 7.0.3, 8.0.3, 9.1.1. He said that tests in his lab with the latter version, accessing OpenVDDK through vCenter on a standalone ESXi host, saw every disk read match.

“Independent testers have reported successful use with Forklift (VMware to KubeVirt, cold and warm), MTV on OpenShift (cold and warm), a Proxmox VE pipeline and custom nbdkit-based tools,” the architect told The Register. “I've received reports of production use, including a German cloud provider migrating a large file server with V2K Migrate and a US-based company migrating to Apache CloudStack/KVM.”

Panić was at pains to point out that the reports of successful use are “not independently audited customer endorsements or a guarantee of suitability for every production environment.” As is often the case with FOSS tools.

OpenVDDK is not the only option for migrating away from VMware without VDDK. KVM-based OpenNebula has a tool called OneSwap that it says has a 96 percent success rate. Nutanix recently tweaked its “Move” migration tool so it can do the job without VDDK. Red Hat is working on a fix but has provided details of a workaround.

Panić made OpenVDDK available under an Apache license, so perhaps Red Hat and others will find it useful as they re-jig their VM migration tools. ®

#10024. UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

The United Arab Emirates says it's creating a foundation of security and safety as it transforms its public service footprint.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) plans to move half of its government operations, services, and sectors to autonomous AI agents over the next two years, prompting a conversation around how it intends to secure and monitor those AI agents.

To that end, the UAE has implemented a "control tower agent," conducts audits using agents and humans, and considers monitoring and establishing trust as critical to its efforts, Omar Sultan Al Olama, minister of state for artificial intelligence, told attendees on Oct. 14 at the World Economic Forum's (WEF) Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai. Security and trust are critical to achieving the nation's goal of autonomous government systems that improve quality of life and to not risk harm to citizens, he said.

"There is an oversight that ensures that we understand what agents are doing, how they're taking certain actions — there's a continuous audit that is being done," Al Olama told attendees. "There's an audit that's done by agents, and there's an audit that's done by humans to ensure that this doesn't go haywire in any way, shape, or form."

Related:Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

In April, the UAE Cabinet unveiled a framework to transition 50% of the federal government's sectors, services, and operations to agentic AI within two years. The effort aims to redesign government policies and processes to embrace AI capabilities, creating "smart systems" that take proactive actions to reduce operational costs, provide more efficient services to citizens, and make government more efficient, according to public notes from the meeting.

The UAE's plans for agentic AI should not be surprising. While global AI diffusion — a measure of the number of adults who used a generative AI product in a specific period — hit 19% in the second quarter of 2026, the United Arab Emirates has taken the lead globally with more than 73% of the population using AI during the quarter, according to Microsoft's "Global AI Diffusion: Q2 2026 Trends and Insights" report.

Yet at the same time, the risk landscape is changing, often because of AI use. The UAE has already faced significant increases in attacks over the past two years, many powered by AI agents, as political tensions and military conflicts continue to build in the region.

The government's Agentic AI Project will roll out in several phases across ministries and federal entities, it said. On Oct. 9, the Ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and Development reviewed the first phase of the project, focused on "building government capabilities, surveying and assessing government services, operations and tasks, and setting priorities," according to a statement announcing the review. The second phase will establish a national technical ecosystem for agentic AI, under the name "FedAI," that will enable government agencies to develop and operate agentic services and conduct internal competitions, such as hackathons, to develop applications.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

The UAE leads other nations with 73% of its population using generative AI at least once in the quarter. Source: Microsoft

The coming phase includes training for government employees in agentic AI development and generative AI technology to provide a foundation for the future, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahya, one of the UAE's two vice presidents and deputy prime minister, said in the statement.

"We are building a government system that is smarter, more flexible, and more proactive; a system that leverages agentic AI to develop services, operations, and tasks, and to shape policies and decisions," he said. "This should be achieved in a secure and reliable digital infrastructure, in a way that strengthens the readiness of the UAE Government for the future and reinforces its leadership in developing government work models."

Security and trust are critical for operations conducted by agentic AI systems, and that means monitoring and auditing agentic activity, says Evin McMullen, co-founder and CEO of AmanTrue, an Abu Dhabi-based startup creating a governance control layer for agentic AI.

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

"Any institution, certainly a government that's adopting AI agents at scale, [and] especially related to internal operations or citizen services, should be able to show who acted in the event of an agent action," she says. "Which agent, who authorized it — which human being and associated institution — and what the limits or definition of the task was."

Governance is a key problem facing deployments of AI agents. Because of their often transitory nature, their ability to obscure on whose behalf they are acting, and their occasional penchant for going rogue, agents and their actions need to be tracked closely. However, 29% of security teams have discovered unknown AI agents running in production that were never registered, and nine in 10 organizations had a security incident in the past year attributable to agentic AI, according to an Oct. 20 report released by cloud-computing and AI-infrastructure platform ServiceNow.

As more organizations adopt agentic services, governance becomes more important, especially when multiple organizations work through agents on the same data and services, says AmanTrue's McMullen.

"When many services intend to act through the coordination of agents, an institution has to be able to show which agents specifically accessed a given data record on whose authority, within what defined limits, with what output," she says.

Gaining trust in autonomous systems will require that the AI agents are closely monitored, tracked, and controlled, the UAE's Al Olama said at the World Economic Forum event.

"The government's only currency is trust," he said, adding that "if the government makes one wrong decision, you lose a lot of that currency. ... The same would be true with AI. Once we have one breakthrough event, where AI exits the sandbox and goes and harms people, I think it's going to take a long time for us to regain that trust."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#10023. As AI Risks Grow, Insurers Split on Covering the Damage

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Some build specialized agentic AI coverage, while major carriers quietly exclude it — leaving enterprises exposed without their knowledge.

Following a rash of data breaches this year, several insurance companies have begun offering proactive policies related to artificial intelligence (AI) to cover enterprises that might be targets of unprovoked attacks or the source of attacks from AI agents going rogue. Meanwhile, other carriers are intentionally side-stepping this emerging risk, leaving enterprises to figure out how to manage it.

Insuring an enterprise against attacks from rogue AI agents that attack the enterprise, or perhaps those created within the enterprise that breach the corporate environment and attack third parties, is uncommon coverage. Many enterprises mistakenly believe their cyber and liability insurance policies covers AI-related risks.

As corporate insurance policies get ready to renew at the end of the calendar year, CFOs, general and outside counsels, CISOs, and other corporate executives tasked with insurance responsibilities should be examining them closely to determine their current AI risks and identifying exclusions that might be baked in. This is also a good time to meet with insurers that offer AI-specific policies to learn what types of coverage are available that the existing policy does not cover. Insurers are warning that the increased use of AI and AI agents is not keeping pace with enterprises’ governance. Rogue AI incidents, like the recent Open AI attacks against Hugging Face and other servers, have only heightened insurers’ concerns.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Last year, insurance coverage specifically for AI-related losses was in its infancy. Carriers often included minimal coverage in generic Errors and Omissions (E&O) policies, Directors and Officers (D&O) liability insurance, or simply in the liability policy, but many of those policies are inadequate to address AI's actual risks.

Today, several specialty insurance firms have coverage for AI-related incidents, either as endorsements, language included in technology E&O policies, or as standalone policies. Among the insurance companies and specialty providers that sell purpose-built policies, affirmative endorsements, and specialized coverage targeting AI risks are Armilla, Coalition, Corgi Insurance, Cowbell, Munich Re, and Beazley.

However, several large carriers are restricting or excluding AI-related risks and autonomous machine behavior from commercial general liability policies, adopting the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements. The exclusions address gaps in policies that were written prior to generative AI becoming ubiquitous within enterprises, according to insurance industry trade publication Insurance Business. The ISO endorsement removes coverage for bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising from generative AI. Chubb, Travelers, Berkshire Hathaway, AIG, and W.R. Berkley are among those adopting this endorsement, according to the publiction.

Related:Trust Is Not What It Seems — and Fraudsters Are Counting on It

So how can companies protect themselves from possible losses from potential risks from rogue AI agents? Here's what you can do today to reduce risk and improve your ability to qualify for AI-specific insurance:

Review your existing cyber and corporate liability insurance to determine which AI-related losses are covered and where your security exposures remain.

Analyze your network infrastructure to determine whether you have sufficient guardrails, along with specific policies and procedures, for addressing incoming and outgoing AI agent attacks.

Have your general or outside counsel review third-party contracts to ensure your supply chain is protecting you from potential AI threats.

Require your supply chain partners to demand their supply chain partners are protected; enterprises need protections multiple levels back down the supply chain.

Have your engineering team determine the different design patterns and architectural principles your vendors are using to build their AI applications. Not all AI development is compatible and responds to security software the same way; treating incompatible architectural principles the same could leave security gaps.

Be sure your AI applications have the minimum system rights and credentials required to do their jobs.

Treat Agentic AI as you would service accounts or endpoint detection and response systems. They're not "set them and forget them." They need to be monitored and maintained.

AI is not a panacea for every problem a company might face. It is a tool with specific use cases and configurations. If you use it as a catch-all for whatever ails your network, you will be compromised. Only use AI for specific tasks for which you have written rules, expectations, and results, and then ensure the AI applications are meeting those specific goals.

Related:Security Threats Don't Stop at the Office: Why Executives' Families Need Training, Too

Coverage for AI-based risks sometimes fall outside the purview of cyber insurance coverage. Because of AI's ubiquity in the enterprise, coverages for its potential failures likely will appear in other specialties as well.

For example, AI is used extensively by human resources departments in enterprises as a hiring tool, says Andrew Correll, head of underwriting for Armilla, a Lloyd's coverholder writing policies for the London syndicate. Coverage for AI tools that hallucinate or display a bias that triggers an insurable event might well be included in the enterprise's liability coverage or in coverage specific to use cases that are separate from a dedicated cyber insurance policy, he adds.

AI coverage addresses more than just a corporate computer being attacked and completely disabled, notes Craig Linton, AI and Emerging Risk Strategy Lead at Beazley. In some cases, a system only needs to be purged of unwanted data brought in by an AI agent. Taking systems offline for that purpose could interrupt business operations but is different than a common malware attack that forces the system to go offline or fail, which is a covered event. Beazley offers dedicated policies for defenses against the attack and endorsements that he calls "AI voluntary shutdown coverage," Linton says.

In order for enterprises to qualify for AI-related coverage, underwriters "look at the body of controls holistically," Correll says.

"Human review is obviously a component of that," he says. "But we also look for what kind of guardrails and rules are in place."

The Beazley application for AI coverage includes dozens of questions focusing on roughly 15 security controls, Linton notes. While most of the security controls are essential for cyber insurance coverage ­— multifactor authentication, backup and recovery, and training and network protection — the carrier also includes inquires about operational technology security, mergers and acquisitions, and Payment Card Industry (PCI) security.

He cautions teams buying AI insurance ­— often the general or outside counsel, chief financial officer and senior executives ­— that employees might be using unsupervised AI on their corporate and personal devices. Like similar shadow IT challenges companies faced in years past, employees will turn to shadow AI they can obtain easily and inexpensively if the tools are not provided by their employer and secured by the IT team. With AI, he says, this can introduce significant risks.

One challenge several sources mentioned is addressing the common problem of generative AI large language models (LLMs) hallucinating and displaying bias. For Corgi Insurance, coverage for hallucinated, inaccurate, or biased model outputs may fall under the Technology E&O policy/Generic Tech E&O policies written before generative AI technologies were widespread could be silent or ambiguous about how they treat model outputs. The company recommends looking for explicit AI-output language and reviewing algorithmic-bias exclusions carefully. When selecting an AI-centric policy, the proverbial devil is in the details, says Jack Kudale, co-founder and CEO of Cowbell. Does the policy wording address a nonmalicious system failure? Does it address an unauthorized disclosure without any external intrusion? Does that fall within a cyber coverage? Does it fall in a technology errors and omission, or does it in a completely different risk altogether? Questions like these will determine whether the policy or rider will address the threat the enterprise is trying to insure against or whether there is a possible exclusion, such as the Verisk/ISO exclusion endorsements and similar limitations employed by the top-tier insurers. If an exclusion is found in an existing policy during a corporate review, the enterprise then can purchase specialty coverage to mitigate that risk.

Protecting your enterprise from potential rogue AI agents and other AI risks requires that enterprises proactively ensure that three risk areas are protected: infrastructure, data pipelines, and your supply chain, Kudale says.

Protecting the infrastructure includes making sure that you have no misconfigured servers, overpermissioned identities, or exposed public endpoints. Safeguarding the data pipelines includes ensuring the storage architecture is secured from breaches, compromises, and poor decision-making, he adds. Finally, organizations need to secure their supply chain well beyond their direct vendors. Threats can come from secondary, tertiary, or further back in the supply chain.

"It's one thing we worry about the most," Kudale says. "We don't worry about hallucination and bias as much as others. We worry about supply chain more."
