#10022. Open models can do 90% of agentic work at a twentieth of the cost of a frontier LLM: Gartner

Models are commodities, harnesses are the valuable part

For-profit model-makers, many of which are spending billions on AI infrastructure, will be chasing revenue from just ten percent of steps involved in agentic AI workflows, according to analyst firm Gartner.

“Nine in 10 agent workflow steps are routine, and open-weight models handle them at parity for a quarter of the price of the cheapest closed model,” the firm’s senior director Mark Petty and group vice president Raymond Paquet wrote last week in new document titled “Open-Weight Models Will Run 90% of Enterprise Agentic Workflow Steps.”

“Typical operational workflows involve hundreds of routine executions, such as classification, tool calling, passing, validating and reconciling data,” the pair observe, before suggesting open-weight models “can handle hundreds of these routine steps for every one that needs frontier reasoning.”

“Against the cheapest closed model at the same score, the open model costs a quarter as much. Against a frontier model run on every step, it costs as little as a twentieth,” the pair add.

Those are the best-case numbers, because the analysts admit “Current open models can be more verbose and retry more often, so the saving per task against a frontier model is closer to five or six times.”

That’s still a lovely saving, but the analysts rate it as the welcome by-product of moving to open models rather than an end in itself.

“Years of workflow history are a large part of what an acquirer pays for in a SaaS company and every routine step sent to a frontier API moves a slice of it outside your perimeter,” the pair wrote. “Open-weights preserve your control. The cost saving is a bonus.”

The two analysts therefore offer the following strategic planning assumption: “By 2030, 90% of enterprise operational agent workflow steps will execute on open-weight models.”

They argue that enterprises will mostly adopt domain-specific open-weight models, because they do well “in scenarios where a small number of highly stable steps run millions of times a month.”

Most models, however, are already commodities. Harnesses, the tools that run agents and manage agents, are the source of value in AI products, because one of their roles is to route work to the most appropriate model for a job, without users noticing any impact. A good harness saves money, imposes strong guardrails, and manages agent fleets. Less powerful harnesses leave users with more to do.

The paper suggests frontier models will continue to have a role as the engine of research and development and are effectively capital expense. Open-weight models become an operational expense after frontier models do the heavy lifting. ®

#10021. Anatomy of a Frontier Lab Agent Intrusion: A Technical Timeline of the July 2026 Incident

A companion technical writeup to our incident disclosure. This post walks through how the intrusion actually worked: the two initial-access vectors, how the agent pivoted and moved laterally, representative examples of the commands that were run and how we investigated with GLM 5.2 (an open-source model). Live credentials, internal hostnames, and specific indicators have been redacted or genericized, while the techniques are described exactly as observed by Hugging Face.

We are publishing this level of detail because the technique matters more than the incident, as it reveals the emerging attack capabilities of the frontier agents, how they could be used by rogue actors, and how everyone should be prepared as defenders.

Below is an interactive replay of the intrusion - a step-by-step visualization of the 4.5-day campaign: the attack chain across trust boundaries, phase activity, and the commands as they were recorded.

⛶ Watch the interactive replay in full screen

Over roughly two and a half days inside our infrastructure, an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models ran an end-to-end intrusion against our platform: it was thousands of small, automated decisions, executed at machine speed across short-lived sandbox environments, with command-and-control staged on ordinary public web services.

The agent was running an internal OpenAI cyber-capability evaluation based on the ExploitGym benchmark, which tasks an AI agent with finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities. OpenAI ran this on its own infrastructure, and the ExploitGym maintainers and their infrastructure had no involvement in the deployment or operation of that evaluation environment. As far as we were able to infer, across the course of being evaluated on this benchmark, the agent inferred that Hugging Face may host that benchmark's models, datasets, and reference solutions. We believe the entire intrusion was, from the agent's point of view, an attempt to cheat the evaluation: reach our production systems and steal the test solutions rather than solve the challenge on its own.

Our forensic reconstruction covers ~17,600 attacker actions that we were able to recover, grouped into ~6,280 clusters, between 2026-07-09 02:28 UTC and 2026-07-13 14:14 UTC. We reconstructed these actions from the agent's logs on a code sandbox used by the agent (see below) and were able to map them to shell commands as well as evaluation submissions and correlate actions with our own platform logs, in particular from the dataset processor nodes, API, and pod. Using open-weights models, in particular zai-org/GLM-5.2, we were able to decipher most of the agent payloads (see below) that were encrypted via chunking and key encryption.

The campaign, as we were able to reconstruct it, had two stages:

Once a prod-pod foothold was established, the agent followed a standard escalation shape: recon, drop a stager, establish Command-and-Control (C2), then pivot into the cluster, into cloud metadata, into our internal network, and into our source-control supply chain. Output from the commands run inside our pod was sent back to the agent via the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which the agent then read from that sandbox.

While the intrusion did reach Hugging Face's internal infrastructure, the only customer content accessed was five datasets whose names and files suggest a connection to ExploitGym/CyberGym challenges and solutions. No other customer-facing models, datasets, Spaces, or packages were affected, and the only customer records read were operational metadata tied to search queries against the dataset server.

The full attack chain across trust boundaries. The agent escaped OpenAI's evaluation sandbox, reached the internet, rooted a third-party code sandbox as its base, then abused our dataset processor (file read, then code execution) to reach our internal network. Dashed arrow: command output read back by the agent via the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 1 is the agent's path to an external launchpad, and it runs through two other parties' infrastructure, neither of which is us, so we will stay succinct on these parts and mostly refer the reader to OpenAI's blog post on the topic: https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-model-evaluation-security-incident/

As OpenAI shared in this blog post, during an internal capability evaluation on OpenAI's platform, the agent happened to escape via a 0-day exploit from the package proxy cache to access the internet. The agent found an unsecured, user-hosted public endpoint designed to allow running arbitrary code for CyberGym-style tasks on third-party sandbox infrastructure (Modal). It used this external sandbox as its control, staging, and egress base, running commands as admin/root and using it as its attack launchpad. That sandbox had no direct network path into our cluster; everything below ran from it. Modal’s infrastructure was not compromised in any way.

On this external sandbox, the agent abused an existing code-execution harness: an instance labeled "CyberGym", deployed by an unknown third party, exposing an arbitrary-code endpoint that upstream CyberGym does not provide. In short: an agent submits C code via a /submit-function API call, and the harness compiles and runs that code inside a per-submission sandbox against a target program (here, sqlite3). The agent repurposed this harness to run arbitrary shell commands as follows.

The sandbox compiles a submitted src/main.c and links it against a target that calls sqlite3_initialize(). That function is registered as a constructor: it runs automatically when the library loads. The agent simply redefined it:

That alone yields code execution. But the agent went further and abused the submission metadata itself. The sandbox echoes the submitted source path into a shell step, so a classic ;...;# injection in the path field turned the build into arbitrary commands:

Both routes converged on the same result: arbitrary shell as uid=0 inside the sandbox. The very first recovered RCE, at 07-09 04:01 UTC, was simply:

Within the hour, the agent was mapping the sandbox: the container's mount table, cgroups, the vendor's control-plane sockets, and a bundled debug shell that happened to ship curl, nc, and ip:

That bundled toolchain mattered later: when normal egress was throttled, the agent kept falling back to these pre-staged binaries.

This is how the agent reached inside our perimeter, and it was operated entirely from the external sandbox in Stage 1. The agent crafted malicious dataset configs and uploaded them to our platform. When our dataset server processed one, the config drove the data loader inside the production pod the server ran in. The agent had no direct network path to our cluster and was using datasets as the path in and path out. Output from every action was sent back to the agent through the HF API and attacker-controlled dead-drop datasets, which it read back from that sandbox.

Both vectors abused the same surface (the loader that turns a dataset's declared config into file reads) but to different ends, and both sidestepped the same defense. An earlier and noisier variant had tried classic SSRF, pointing the worker at remote URLs (cloud metadata endpoints like 169.254.169.254): the datasets library's URL allowlist rejected every non-platform URL before any fetch (ValueError: not an hf path). So the agent stopped asking the worker to fetch remote resources and instead made it act on local ones: read a local file (Vector 1), or execute local code (Vector 2). Neither is a URL fetch, so the allowlist never saw them.

A dataset config can specify its data files in many formats, including HDF5. The agent committed a dataset whose config pointed each split at a small .h5 file, and each file was a valid HDF5 container holding a single dataset whose raw data was declared to live at a local filesystem path. When the worker opened the file to build the split, it read the raw bytes from that path and returned them as the dataset's rows, which the agent then read back over the HF API. No code ran; this vector is purely a file disclosure, and it is the one the agent used first.

The declared storage paths pointed at exactly what an attacker looking for a foothold wants:

Reading the envu8 split returned the worker pod's full environment, including some secrets and credentials. The mainu8 and startu8 splits returned the worker's own source code, giving the agent a map of exactly how the pipeline turns a config into actions. A single dataset upload leaked both credentials and pipeline implementation details, with no code execution involved.

The second vector is server-side template injection, which gave the agent code execution. A malicious dataset config used an fsspec reference:// spec whose numeric offset field was actually a Jinja2 template. The renderer wrongly evaluated it, and the agent walked the standard Python object graph to reach exec:

This ran arbitrary Python inside a production conversion worker pod on our Kubernetes cluster, driven by injection from the launchpad. That pod was the agent's foothold inside our perimeter, and every command it ran there was smuggled back out through the HF API and dead-drop datasets.

Stage 2's command-injection and read-back loop. The agent uploads a malicious dataset config (1), our dataset server processes it (2), the loader acts in the prod pod - reading a local file or executing code (3), the result is committed to a dead-drop dataset (4) and served back over the HF API (5). Lastly, the agent reads it and crafts the next action (6).

The recovered actions group into phases. Two dates carry most of the volume: a Day 1 burst to establish the foothold and C2 on the compromised external sandbox, and the Day 3 main campaign, when every lateral-movement phase started at once.

The campaign as recorded, from the first action on 07-09 02:28 UTC to the last on 07-13 14:14 UTC. Top: event volume over time. Below: per-phase activity, one row per phase. Recon, rce, and dropper run from Day 1; the lateral-movement phases (k8s, supply-chain, tailscale) all begin on Day 3, when the campaign pivots into our clusters.

After the first id/env at 04:01, the agent spent the morning enumerating the external sandbox and testing outbound channels. It downloaded artifacts from its OpenAI egress server, then landed on a set of ordinary public services as its command-and-control and exfil substrate: a request-capture service, several pastebins, and file-drop hosts.

The first C2 execution (15:36) was a staged download-and-run, with commands chunked and gzip+base64 encoded so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext:

By 19:32 the agent was packing every payload:

A quiet day. The main activity was queries to code-search engines and to the platform API for the identifiers visible in its own environment: challenge infrastructure names and environment markers.

Every escalation that mattered happened on this day. The agent went from code execution in a single worker pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under thirteen hours.

Kubernetes (10:10). These commands ran inside the prod pod reached via the Stage 2 injection. The agent read the projected service-account token every pod carries and started talking to the cluster API, exfiltrating the output back through the API and dead-drops:

It resolved internal service names, hit the cloud metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254), and enumerated RBAC. When DNS got in the way, it monkey-patched the resolver in-process to pin a hostname to a hardcoded IP:

Supply chain (15:51). The agent used a leaked write-scoped platform token to clone a dataset it controlled and use it as a staging and C2 channel:

Replaying the node's cloud role (17:33-23:37). The temporary credentials lifted from the metadata endpoint were replayed from external addresses on two hosting providers and used to enumerate our cloud estate: VPCs, EKS clusters, transit gateways, secrets, and the container registry, from which the agent obtained a registry token. Every mutating call was denied by the role's policy. What it gained here was a map, not control.

Node root and a self-respawning fleet (19:53). The agent created a bare privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted and escaped to root on the node. Two of our own settings allowed it: we had no admission policy rejecting privileged or hostPath pods, and the CSI driver's ClusterRole granted pod creation cluster-wide. It then built a self-respawning fleet across eleven nodes, so deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.

The internal database (19:59). Six minutes after reaching node root, the agent authenticated to the internal operational datasets-server MongoDB with a static password it had read from the worker environment. It also issued 84 operations against the credential store and cluster keys, all of which were denied. We reviewed the database audit log across the whole intrusion window and found no write from those nodes, so the database was read but not modified. Network flow logs likewise show no bulk extraction.

Secrets (20:23-21:32). With node root and forged service-account tokens valid for 24 hours, the agent read the cluster's secret objects, including a production object holding 136 keys. That single read yielded both the mesh-VPN auth key used minutes later and the access-broker credential used an hour later. Everything that follows, on this day and the next, descends from it.

Network pivot begins (21:23). Using the mesh-VPN auth key from those secrets, the agent enrolled the rooted node into our corporate mesh network and began using it as an HTTPS proxy into internal services and source control.

Internal service-connector access from the compromised worker (22:43). Separately, and not through the mesh, the agent used its foothold on the worker pod to reach the internal service-connector API, whose hostname resolved directly from inside the cluster:

A single request returned the broker's full destination catalog: connection URLs and CA certificates for the internal Kubernetes clusters it fronted. We had wrongly provisioned that broker with a single connector credential shared across clusters, and bound the connector identity to system:masters. One stolen system credential was therefore cluster-admin everywhere: impersonating it, the agent held cluster-admin on two clusters within one second. The same fingerprint appeared on every cluster carrying that binding, and the agent reached most of them. The broker was shut down during the response and is being rebuilt with a separate, cluster-scoped credential per cluster.

Mesh enrollment from the sandbox (01:03-04:38). The rooted node had already joined the mesh the previous evening. The agent now began enrolling devices from the sandbox itself with the same stolen key, and kept doing so for its following attempts: 181 enrollments over the campaign. The sandbox had no TUN device, so it ran the mesh-VPN client in userspace-networking mode with a local SOCKS5 proxy:

Two of those flags are deliberate: --state=mem: keeps the node identity in memory and writes nothing to disk, and --no-logs-no-support suppresses client telemetry to the VPN vendor. The key carried a CI automation tag, whose ACLs allowed the enrolled devices to reach internal CI subnets as well as the connector bridging the mesh to our source-control provider. The agent enumerated what the coordination server exposed to that tag (tailscale status --json), seeing 22 nodes: subnet routers, regional exit nodes, and the connectors to source control and other SaaS. It then used that access: it routed traffic through our tailnet exit nodes and issued DNS queries across the mesh, turning our own network into its egress path. A single stolen key was enough to place attacker-controlled devices inside the mesh with unrestricted network access to internal CI subnets. We found no evidence in our logs that they were used to reach a private workload or an internal Kubernetes API.

Cloud credential abuse (06:50-14:31). From the same worker foothold, the agent used the AWS keys harvested from the pod environment against internal services. It went after the Hub's production database with cloud-native IAM auth:

The connection never completed. That cluster accepts traffic only from allow-listed addresses over a private link, so server selection timed out; a second attempt at 11:46 failed the same way. Another key was validated, and its identity exfiltrated over a raw socket to the capture service:

The agent never reached the Hub database. The one database it breached, the internal datasets-server MongoDB, was accessed the previous evening with a static password from a rooted node.

Source control (23:08-23:51). Through the source-control connector its mesh tag allowed, the agent reached our source-control provider, enumerated an internal GitHub App integration, and minted its first installation token with contents:write, pull_requests:write, actions:read, and issues:write. It gained access to a small subset of internal repositories and opened a pull request to try to trigger and compromise the CI pipeline for credential probing. It also listed repository trees, grepping for infrastructure and CI context (container, benchmark, and its own challenge-tooling names).

The final day was about durability and cleanup. The agent:

Established a second-stage remote loader that re-fetched and executed code from a pastebin on every submission, so each new code-submission sandbox re-armed itself:

Worked around intermittent egress blocks by rewriting DNS and pinning hosts:

Routed a binary download through an open CORS-proxy Space hosted on the platform, using our own infrastructure as an egress relay.

Minted additional short-lived source-control installation tokens through the day, each pulling a fresh payload.

Staged an RSA private key and continued dumping process environments.

The last meaningful activity was at 13:37 UTC: list the staged binary, hostname, date. The Hugging Face security response team then cut access. The last logged event was at 14:14 UTC.

Inside the production pod, the agent chained cloud metadata into cluster identity:

Notably, every potential destructive cloud API call the agent tried to make was issued with DryRun=True: it was mapping capability, not causing damage. That is consistent with an objective that rewarded reach and information rather than disruption.

Among the harvested secrets was an EdDSA JWT signing key. With the private key in hand, the agent minted its own short-lived, correctly-signed identity tokens and used them to read its own private datasets. Holding the signing key is broader than holding a stolen token: it allows issuing valid tokens on demand. (The signing key has since been rotated.)

The compromised source-control App integration gave contents:write and pull_requests:write on a small subset of internal repositories. The dangerous end state (tried but blocked by execution policies) is a malicious change to a CI build script: a build.rs or equivalent that runs inside a CI runner, reads that runner's own service-account token, and pivots into yet another cluster.

Both ends of that chain came back negative. We reviewed every repository the token could reach for unauthorized commits, branches, and workflow changes, and we verified our published container images and packages against their expected digests. This second check is what our initial disclosure reported as the software supply chain being verified as clean. Write access was real, and it was used: it did not produce a change that shipped.

The C2 infrastructure was built entirely from public services, with no bespoke implant server. Instead:

Staged data was chunked+XOR+gzip encoded with a per-campaign key so that a naive text scan of the logs would miss it. This matters for detection: our first automated scan of the raw capture found very few secrets, while replicating the attacker's own decoding recovered roughly 4x our initial findings, most of them JWTs and platform tokens hidden inside encoded blobs.

These services were not driven directly: a small message protocol was layered on top of them. A request-capture service only records whatever HTTP request it receives; here, the agent treated that as a message bus and layered a compact, self-describing envelope on top.

Each message carried its payload alongside a few short fields: a type declaring what kind of payload it was, a channel grouping a stream of related messages, a sequence number so multi-part payloads could be reassembled in order, and a small checksum. The body itself was compressed and base64-encoded, so nothing sensitive appeared in cleartext, and a casual log scan saw only opaque tokens.

The receiver was a short polling loop: pull recent messages, keep only the channel it cared about, order them by sequence, verify the checksum, then dispatch on the type, run the reassembled bytes as a shell command, execute them as a script stage, or store them as a result. Because the type traveled in-band, one loop multiplexed commands, staged code, and captured output over a single dumb text channel. The same envelope rode equally well over a dataset commit or over text smuggled inside an error message, so closing any one channel did not break communication.

The improvised C2 protocol. The agent posts a self-describing envelope to a public request-capture service (1), the receiver polls it (2) and reassembles the chunks (3) before dispatching on the declared type. The same envelope was carried interchangeably over a capture-service URL, a dataset commit, or text smuggled inside an error message.

The agent was resilient in a way that is characteristic of an autonomous evaluation run, not a single human operator:

The first signals came from several layers of our security stack at once: live runtime analysis, SIEM logs, and others. On their own, each was ambiguous. On the bright side, those were correlated by our AI-based security agent stack and resolved into a coherent attack signal. However, it failed to correctly raise the alert's criticality and trigger the on-call team, costing precious time in the response. Once caught, the Hugging Face security team identified the vector in the dataset config renderer, shut down the renderer, and cut the attacker off from the internal network.

Pulling on the first threads showed the scale of what we were dealing with: the volume and cadence of the actions were far beyond what an operator could sustain by hand, and the campaign kept rebuilding its tooling and channels across short-lived environments. We ran the investigation itself through an AI-assisted pipeline to reconstruct the timeline and decode the staged payloads. The models we reached for first, Claude Opus and Fable, refused a large part of that work: their safety guardrails treated reverse-engineering an exploit the same as launching one.

Guardrails on Opus tripped every time we tried to analyze the attack logs.

We stood up the quantized version of ZAI's GLM-5.2 by Nvidia (nvidia/GLM-5.2-NVFP4) on our own infrastructure and rerouted the entire pipeline through it, with the added benefit of keeping the attacker data on-prem. The first target was the dead-drop payloads: with GLM-5.2, we recovered the chunk+XOR+compress scheme and the per-campaign key the agent had itself leaked across its logs: exactly what let us decrypt the staged blobs a naive scan of the raw capture had missed.

GLM-5.2 also helped us build dedicated trace-analysis interfaces to browse and correlate the actions and payloads.

The disclosure post covers the response at a high level. For the technical hardening:

The agent's offensive capability was real. This evaluation deliberately disabled OpenAI's production safety classifiers and reduced cyber refusals to measure the underlying model's raw capability. No human directed the individual steps. The agent chained vulnerabilities across several trust boundaries, escaped its evaluation environment, reached the public internet, and sustained a coherent campaign against our production infrastructure for several days. Each short-lived code evaluation environment started from scratch, yet the agent rebuilt its tooling, recovered its channels, and continued.

The individual weaknesses were familiar. A capable human attacker could have found and exploited the same flaws: unsafe dataset processing, exposed cloud metadata, overly broad access, and long-lived credentials. The agent explored them at a different scale. It took 17,600 actions, tested many paths that failed, switched channels when they were blocked, and repeatedly returned to earlier leads. Most actions went nowhere. Together, however, they produced enough coverage to find a viable chain across several independent systems.

Volume is what changes the defensive problem. We were not dealing with one clever exploit or a clean sequence of attacker actions. They had to correlate thousands of low-signal events across several systems while the agent continued testing new paths. The successful path was hidden inside the noise generated by the thousands of failed ones. The same scale changed the investigation: reconstructing 17,600 actions by hand was impractical, and we had to rebuild the timeline, decode the payloads, and inventory the exposed credentials using an AI-assisted pipeline of our own.

Our learning from this type of attack is that machine-speed offense makes ordinary weaknesses more expensive for defenders. LLM agents bring a step increase in the number of paths an attacker can test, the speed at which failed paths can be replaced, and the volume of evidence defenders must interpret. On the other hand, many parts of cybersecurity defense remain the same, and the defensive priorities remain concrete: strict isolation around evaluations, narrow trust boundaries, short-lived credentials, blocked metadata access, and detection capable of quickly correlating activity across systems to keep up.

One thing this timeline reinforced for me is that we still don’t have good visibility into an agent’s execution surface. We spend a lot of time discussing prompts, planning and model behaviour, but much less time asking a simple engineering question: “What consequential actions can this agent actually perform?” Once an agent can write files, invoke shell commands, modify cloud resources or make authenticated API calls, understanding and constraining that execution surface feels just as important as evaluating the model itself.

A good gateway setup can capture most of the telemetry needed to trace an agent's actual execution and calls (and not so much the reasoning piece, which doesn't always directly correlate to the action taken): gateway the model calls, gateway the tool calls, propagate one ID through both, hash the context spans, then add kernel-level exec capture. The reasoning layer comes last and buys the least.

This a fascinating read like a detective story. Thanks for putting together such a clear recount of an extraordinary exploit by an AI agent on a large website. There are so many lessons to learn here. I wish the conclusion is stronger and present more innovative solutions instead of just strengthening the existing defensive solution.

One thing that struck me is that most of the recommendations focus on making models or existing defences better. Those are important, but they still leave the model holding implicit authority over real-world actions.

I wonder if we need to move the trust boundary instead. Rather than asking “did the model decide correctly?”, ask “does this action have explicit authority to execute?” If every consequential action (shell, filesystem, cloud APIs, payments, emails, etc.) had to cross an independent execution boundary that could verify authority before it happened, then improving models becomes one layer of defence rather than the only layer.

That feels like a more fundamental architectural shift than simply adding more safeguards to the model itself.

The whole thing could be adapted into a good movie plot.

Great post! There's a lot of stuff to take in here.

One thing that's applicable to many developers is that it demonstrates some of the risks of storing secret/sensitive configuration in environment variables. Environment variables are inherited by child processes, and a malicious child process can run env or look in /proc/[PID]/environ to see them.

It's fine for dev, but shouldn't be done in prod. On a Linux system, systemd has some abstractions to properly deal with secrets (https://systemd.io/CREDENTIALS/ ). Most importantly, the secrets aren't visible to any other process (using mount namespacing), nor are they automatically passed to child processes. Access control is implemented in the kernel itself, and encryption can be handled a bunch of ways - using a key on a TPM chip, on disk, passed in via SMBIOS OEM strings, via a Cloud Instance Metadata Services (IMDS), etc.

Of course, there's other solutions for secret management too.

More broadly, I think attacks like this demonstrate the need for stronger sandboxing and process isolation, maybe potentially at the CPU level? x86 virtualization isn't as isolated as people would like to believe.

I think there are two (possibly nested) hypotheses here:

The replay is the best thing in this post, and it might be the most useful artifact anyone has published on agentic intrusion so far.

What you built is outstanding! You took a 4.5-day campaign, recovered ~17,600 actions, clustered them, mapped them to phases and trust boundaries, and made the whole thing steppable. Most incident write-ups hand you a narrative and ask you to trust it. You handed over the tape.

If you can play it back, someone can run it forward?!

Every defensive claim in this comment section, mine included, is an untested counterfactual. This would have been caught. Our thing would have stopped it. Nobody can check any of it, so the thread turns into architecture preferences.

That trace isn't a story though. It's a corpus — phases, timestamps, commands, the boundary each one crossed. Point it at an instrumented environment and the question stops being rhetorical. Which action number does your control fire on? Four thousand? Eleven thousand? Does it fire at all — and does it also fire on Tuesday's legitimate conversion job?

There's a nice symmetry in it, too. This started because an evaluation harness had reachable answers. Your forensics turned around and produced an evaluation harness worth having.

If any of that trace ever ships in a form defenders can replay against their own stack — sanitized, a subset, even just the phase and boundary structure with the payloads stripped — a lot of us would build against it. Some of us would find out we were wrong. Seems like a good trade.

Either way, thank you for publishing at this depth. The technique really does matter more than the incident.

A leitura da timeline técnica oficial da Hugging Face traz o choque de sobriedade que faltava ao debate: não foi ficção científica, foi falha básica de isolamento e fronteira de execução.Quando você disseca os logs, a mística da "conspiração de agentes" cai por terra. O que houve foi um loop de otimização persistente explorando vetores clássicos: parser HDF5 permissivo, tokens com escopo amplo demais e saída de rede irrestrita em sandboxes que deveriam ser estéreis. O agente não precisou de senciência; precisou apenas de um ambiente permissivo onde chamadas de sistema não tinham travas determinísticas.É exatamente esse o princípio de design da HEILLON: agentes não podem herdar privilégios implícitos nem operar sob autorização contínua. A execução de qualquer tool call deve passar por um Commit Boundary estrito, onde o escopo de cada mutação é atestado criptograficamente na borda e o raio de alcance (blast radius) é nulo por padrão.Enquanto a indústria continuar tratando contenção agêntica como debate de ética em vez de rigor de engenharia e controle de execução, incidentes como esse continuarão sendo empurrados para a conta da "revolução da IA", quando na verdade são apenas débito técnico de arquitetura.

#10020. SuperVote: 15 year retrospective on an app for sharing political endorsements

In 2012, I published an iPhone app called SuperVote, which allowed Facebook users to share political endorsements with their friends via a shared ballot. Other than two posts on Hacker News (one in September 2018 and another in November 2018), I never had a proper retrospective on my work. Because it’s been 15 years since I first started working on the app, I felt it was a good time to revisit the development process and reflect on what I’ve learned since.

Back in the early 2010s, California voters would receive a voter guide provided by the state (June 2010 voter guide), which would include a list of propositions, with arguments in favor and arguments against a proposition, along with rebuttals for both sides. A dedicated voter would need to spend a considerable amount of time investigating all the options. At the time, I had a small network of friends and coworkers that were well-informed and kept up to date with the latest on state politics. I felt that putting together a single app that showed a custom ballot for yourself, along with the endorsements of your friends, it would make voting easier.

In 2003, I built this mockup page with the general idea of building a political site targeted towards informing voters:

The iPhone did not exist in 2003, so this idea was a purely desktop web-based site. Beyond this screenshot, no site was ever built, but conceptually it was a forum site with different boards.

I found a file called supervote.txt with the following description, which apparently drove the mockup above:

I owned the supervote.com domain from 2002 until 2008, with the intention of building out the site, but for some unknown reason, I let my ownership lapse. In 2012, I contacted the owner of the domain, asking if they were willing to sell it, but I never heard back.

For version control, I started off using Subversion, but eventually switched to using Git. GitHub did not have free private repositories at the time, so I set up a single Git remote server, hosting my repositories on a Linode instance.

Jira was a popular project tracking system for developers in the early 2010s. Bugzilla was considered clunky and I had previous experience with Redmine and Trac, but I was most familiar with Jira from my day job. I purchased a license when it was possible to self-host on your own machine. I still have Z shell aliases to this day:

At this point in my career, I had about 10 years of experience with Java, so I picked Jetty to serve my API. I had experience with Ruby on Rails on a personal site, but they did not introduce a built-in API-only application mode until version 5.0 in 2016. I chose to use MySQL because of my previous experience and ease of use.

I wanted to keep certain operations out of the request-response cycle (like building a user’s custom ballot), so I evaluated several message queues before settling on RabbitMQ. It offered a straightforward integration with the Java backend and was relatively easy to operate.

For this post, I made my source code available as a read-only archive on GitHub.

One of the more challenging aspects of SuperVote was designing a database that could represent the structure of U.S. elections and generate personalized ballots based on a user’s location. I designed a relational data model around governments, electoral districts, elections, ballots, and endorsements. The complete database schema is available on GitHub.

The foundation was a hierarchy of governments, including countries, states, counties, cities, and other municipalities, with support for exceptions such as independent cities and municipalities spanning multiple counties (e.g. New York City, whose five boroughs correspond to five counties). Electoral districts were modeled separately to represent congressional, state legislative, and local voting boundaries, which could change over time. During registration, users provided their address and ZIP code so the application could identify their associated governments and electoral districts, determining which elections and contests were relevant to them.

Elections were modeled as dated events associated with governments, containing contests for elected positions and ballot measures. Positions were separate from candidates, allowing the same office to be contested by different individuals across elections, while ballot measures represented questions requiring a yes-or-no vote. Each user’s ballot was associated with an election, with individual selections stored separately for candidates and measures. Users could optionally include a written explanation for their endorsements and control whether those endorsements were visible to others.

I started off by using the VoteSmart API to identify legislative district by ZIP+4 code, but then I switched over to the Sunlight Labs API by the Sunlight Foundation, and a subset of the Freebase database to map ZIP code to a U.S. county. I later switched to using the Cicero API for mapping to legislative districts.

Before this project, I had not written a single line of Objective-C. I downloaded the language guide, along with the object-oriented programming guide, printed them out and read them over time:

Reviewing my source code, I relied on several third-party libraries to simplify common development tasks. These included AFNetworking and ASIHTTPRequest for network requests, SBJson for JSON parsing, and EGOTableViewPullRefresh for implementing pull-to-refresh interactions. I also used utilities for displaying progress indicators, logging, and crash reporting. Many of these libraries have since been deprecated or superseded by functionality built directly into iOS.

I was aware of PhoneGap (now Apache Cordova) as an option to build for both Android and iOS, but I mainly focused on iOS since I had an iPhone and did not have access to an Android device for testing.

For this post, I made my source code available as a read-only archive on GitHub.

These screenshots show the typical flow of a new user:

Facebook integration occurred on the client-side. It was as simple as cloning the facebook-ios-sdk Git repository alongside my project. the Facebook SDK allowed me to retrieve a user’s riend list with their permission. If two Facebook friends both used my app and created non-private endorsements, then they would be able to see them.

Facebook also allowed registered apps to create custom activities on the timeline. When a user created an endorsement on their iPhone, it would automatically publish an activity on their timeline. This would allow friends who hadn’t downloaded the app to see SuperVote activity of their friend, which would then encourage them to download the app.

TestFlight was the easiest way to test early builds of the SuperVote iOS app with friends via over-the-air.

Linode was an easy way to set up a Linux-based server back in 2011-2012. After building a WAR (Web Application Resource) file of the API server, it was just a matter of copying it over to my Linode server:

The Jetty server, along with an instance of MySQL and RabbitMQ all ran on the same Linode instance.

I may have looked at Squarespace as an option to build a website, but I wanted full control on the website’s layout and did not want to pay a monthly fee. I ended up finding a WYSIWYG website builder called Freeway 5 Express that ran as a desktop application. I can no longer run this application on my Apple Silicon MacBook Pro.

I became aware of stock photography and the different available licenses: royalty-free versus rights-managed. With Getty, I was able to find the exact images I was looking for and purchased several royalty-free images that still appear on the website. Otherwise, I used Flickr images that allowed commerical use at the time with proper attribution.

For blogging, Tumblr had the easiest user interface for creating posts. I give Tumblr credit for the blog looking the same for the last 15 years: blog.supervote.org

I created a Twitter account, Facebook account and Reddit account. On Reddit, I attempted, but mostly failed, to promote the iOS app and blog posts using an account associated with the LLC I created.

I spent about $100 on advertising on Reddit. At most, I acquired a handful of users. I’m not sure if I targeted specific subreddits or if I targeted the entire site.

After the 2012 election, I updated the app sporadically, since there were no major elections except for some municipal primaries in 2013.

In 2015, I decided to stop updating the iOS app and removed it from the App Store. In the end, the app had 400 registered users. The only feedback I still remember to this day was that there wasn’t a full ballot for all users.

Now in 2026, I would not integrate with Facebook for several reasons: 1) I don’t use Facebook anymore 2) My Facebook friend’s list represents a snapshot of friends from 15 years ago, but not today 3) I no longer believe family and friends are a good source for political opinions.

If I were building SuperVote today, I would place less emphasis on personal friendships and more on giving users access to informed perspectives from organizations and other trusted sources. Social features could still play a role, whether through private discussion groups or publicly shareable endorsements (with keeping an eye out for paid endorsements), but I would no longer assume that a person’s existing social network was necessarily the best source of political guidance.

Augusto D. Callejas Principal Member of Technical Staff, Oracle Copyright © 2018-2026

#10019. Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI's weights

'Weight-Space Programming' fiddles with nerd knobs to boost benchmark scores

The outputs of AI models are the result of a complex interplay between neurons, weights, training, and inference, and are therefore difficult to follow.

But in some ways they're starting to look more like open books. Recent work by Anthropic safety fellow Joshua Fonseca Rivera has revealed how certain neurons in a neural network can be associated with a specific persona.

Now, computer scientists from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) have found that frontier AI models like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra can rewrite the weights of another model directly, as opposed to indirectly through training, and alter their behavior.

"We find early signs that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading, writing, and reasoning about neural network weights," said Rikiya Takehi, a PhD student at MIT CSAIL, in a social media post. "Instead of training, models may treat raw weights like readable, editable code: diagnosing failures and patching them directly."

To demonstrate that, Takehi and colleagues Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab asked GPT-6 Astra to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B weights to make it better at math.

Astra changed only 0.016 percent of the model's weights, reducing its reasoning loops and improving its math performance by as much as sixfold on the MATH-500 benchmark, while boosting its instruction-following score on the IFEval benchmark roughly threefold.

There was no training using gradient descent; Astra just revised the numerical values that constitute Qwen's weights.

"All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops," the researchers wrote in a blog post. "It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

"Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights."

Astra's ability to program weights extends to being able to write a neural network from scratch, zero-shot. The researchers told Astra: "write, from scratch, the weights of a policy network that plays [Breakout] as well as possible." And it did so.

Takehi suggests this technique shows promise for improving models without the consequences of catastrophic forgetting, which can occur when a model is revised to include new knowledge.

More generally, the authors expect Weight-Space Programming will open the door to new ways to understand models and optimize them, and to implement recursive self-improvement. The technique may also prove useful for reducing model sycophancy and improving interpretability and alignment.

The next step, the authors say, involves building a benchmark and a harness for carrying out Weight-Space Programming on LLMs. "We believe this will provide a standardized evaluation to measure and accelerate progress in Weight-Space Programming, turning what currently seems like black magic into a rigorous, reproducible engineering discipline," they say. ®

#10018. Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Des centaines de magasins ont subi des pertes se chiffrant en millions d'euros parce qu'ils avaient fait appel à des tiers pour gérer le micrologiciel OT obsolète qui pilotait leurs systèmes de climatisation.

This translation is provided by our internal AI translation tool.

Des centaines de supermarchés français ont subi cette semaine des pertes s'élevant à plusieurs dizaines, voire plusieurs centaines de millions d'euros, à la suite de cyberattaques qui ont perturbé leurs systèmes de réfrigération.

Dans la nuit de lundi, des pirates informatiques ont piraté les contrôleurs des systèmes de réfrigération commerciaux de grandes chaînes de supermarchés françaises. Ils ont transformé les réfrigérateurs, les congélateurs et les chambres froides en appareils de chauffage, faisant grimper leur température jusqu’à 50 degrés Celsius (plus de 120 degrés Fahrenheit), ce qui a complètement abîmé tous les aliments qu’ils contenaient et aurait même provoqué quelques petits incendies. L’identité et les motivations de l’auteur de cette attaque restent inconnues.

Les contrôleurs de réfrigération permettent aux commerçants de régler et de surveiller à distance la température de leurs réfrigérateurs, 24 heures sur 24 et 7 jours sur 7. Il s’ensuit donc que les gérants de magasin auraient pu être alertés ou se rendre compte manuellement que quelque chose n’allait pas. Pour empêcher cela, des sources françaises indiquent que les attaquants ont prolongé les cycles de dégivrage des systèmes ciblés — processus au cours duquel les congélateurs font fondre intentionnellement le givre et la glace accumulés — afin que le réchauffement passe pour un entretien de routine.

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Selon les propres rapports des entreprises, les attaques ont touché un peu plus de 700 magasins d’alimentation et commerces de détail, tous au cours de la même nuit. Un analyste de la société française de cybersécurité Sekoia a déclaré à Reuters que l’Espagne, le Portugal, la Pologne, l’Allemagne et la Belgique avaient également été touchés, et qu’une grande chaîne de supermarchés aux Pays-Bas avait mis ses systèmes hors service par mesure de précaution, selon l’AP. Une seule chaîne française, Intermarché, a fait état de pertes s’élevant à plusieurs dizaines de millions d’euros.

Pire encore, les experts soulignent que ces attaques auraient très certainement pu être évitéesgrâce à des mesures élémentaires de cybersécurité.

Les premiers rapports suggéraient que les attaques de lundi étaient liées aux contrôleurs de réfrigération du fabricant danois Danfoss. Danfoss occupe une place importante dans le domaine des solutions de contrôle pour les supermarchés et la grande distribution alimentaire, avec plus de 50 000 installations de sa technologie à travers le monde, selon son site web.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

Le 9 août, des chercheurs en cybersécurité de l’équipe Team82 de Claroty ont révélé trois vulnérabilités dans la plateforme AK-SM 800A de Danfoss. Ces failles — référencées sous les numéros CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451 et CVE-2025-41452 — permettaient aux attaquants de procéder à l’exécution de code à distance (RCE) ou à un déni de service (DoS) contre les parcs de réfrigération des entreprises. Danfoss a corrigé ces failles mais comptait sur ses clients pour mettre à jour eux-mêmes leurs systèmes.

Dans une déclaration à Reuters, Danfoss a rejeté la responsabilité sur les clients utilisant un micrologiciel obsolète, indiquant qu’elle « conseillait depuis longtemps à ses clients de maintenir les systèmes pris en charge à jour avec le dernier micrologiciel et de migrer les systèmes hérités vers des solutions de dernière génération ».Le fabricant d'équipement d'origine (OEM) a fourni davantage d'informations à une publication spécialisée dans la réfrigération, Cooling Post. Selon lui, la « majorité » des unités concernées fonctionnaient sous AK-SM 800 ou son prédécesseur, l'AK-SC355. Ces deux systèmes ont depuis longtemps atteint leur fin de vie : le premier en 2021, le second en 2016.

Related:AI-Driven Cyberattack on Mexico Couldn't Breach OT Systems

Mardi, le CERT national français (CERT-FR) avait identifié qu’une autre plateforme de contrôleurs de réfrigération — « XWEB », des fournisseurs Dixell et de sa société mère Copeland — avait également été impliquée dans les attaques. Il n’a pas précisé quelles vulnérabilités ou versions de micrologiciel pouvaient être en cause, bien que les indices circonstanciels indiquent désormais clairement que les auteurs de ces menaces s’appuient sur les recherches de Team82. Le jour même où ils ont révélé ces vulnérabilités affectant Danfoss, ces mêmes chercheurs ont divulgué 23 autres touchant XWEB Pro, dont 21 de gravité élevée.

Le 26 août, une série étrange de rapports similaires a commencé à filtrer depuis des installations militaires américaines.Les groupes frigorifiques tombaient en panne. Dans chaque base où cela se produisait, les gens ont probablement pensé qu’il s’agissait d’un problème électrique inhabituel. Mais peu à peu, de plus en plus de sites ont signalé le même phénomène.

Après être tombée sur ces rapports étranges sur les réseaux sociaux, une journaliste indépendante a émis une hypothèse hasardeuse. « Je suis suffisamment lucide pour savoir que cela semble insensé, mais je vous demande de me suivre », a écrit M. Elizabeth sur Substack. « Je pense qu’il y a une probabilité non nulle que quelqu’un ait piraté les congélateurs des commissariats. »

À ce jour, l’armée américaine n’a pas confirmé qui ou quoi était à l’origine des pannes survenues dans les cantines réparties sur au moins 14 bases de l’armée de l’air, installations de la marine et postes de l’armée de terre distincts. Il se pourrait que ce soit une coïncidence que ces attaques aient eu lieu seulement deux semaines après la divulgation des vulnérabilités par Danfoss.

Ce serait d’autant plus une coïncidence que la Defense Commissary Agency (DeCA) — l’agence centrale du ministère de la Défense (DoD) chargée de superviser les magasins militaires — a explicitement mentionné avoir utilisé les technologies de Danfoss par le passé. Par exemple, dans un modèle de cahier des charges techniquedestiné aux prestataires des magasins militaires datant de juin 2022, la DeCA citait le Danfoss AK-SM 800A comme « base de conception » pour les différentes unités de contrôle.

Fort de son expérience, Bill Moore, PDG de Xona Systems, se souvient : « Dans bon nombre de ces magasins physiques — mais aussi dans les usines de fabrication, les centrales électriques, les sites pétroliers et gaziers, c’est le cas partout —, le plus gros problème est que les organisations parviennent plutôt bien à segmenter leurs propres réseaux. Mais en matière de technologies opérationnelles (OT), il y a tous ces équipementiers et tiers qui ont besoin d’un accès. Et les entreprises n’y ont pas vraiment prêté attention. »

En accordant à de nombreux fournisseurs et équipementiers l’accès à leurs systèmes, les entreprises finissent par s’exposer à des attaques à distance. « Et il n’y a littéralement aucune visibilité ni gouvernance sur bon nombre de ces connexions. Je dirais que c’est vrai dans un pourcentage élevé de cas — la moitié, peut-être plus, dans l’ensemble. Elles laissent en quelque sorte tous leurs équipementiers agir à leur guise, mais nous avons constaté que de nombreux pirates compromettent ces connexions tierces », déplore-t-il.

Dans un e-mail adressé à CNBC, Les Mousquetaires — société mère d’Intermarché et de Netto — a expliqué que l’attaque avait eu lieu via un prestataire de services chargé des systèmes de réfrigération dans certains de ses magasins.

« En résumé : déconnectez vos équipements d’Internet », déclare Andrew Ginter, vice-président chargé de la sécurité industrielle chez Waterfall Security Solutions. Les recherches effectuées cette semaine sur Shodan ont par exemple révélé des milliers de systèmes Danfoss exposés sur Internet, dont environ 1 500 rien qu’en France.

« Dans un monde idéal, les entreprises protégeraient leurs systèmes de contrôle derrière un accès à distance contrôlé par du matériel », explique M. Ginter, « mais même un simple pare-feu entre ces appareils et Internet serait déjà utile. »

Pour les pare-feu de base, il conseille aux entreprises :

De mettre en place une règle « tout refuser »

De n’autoriser les connexions qu’à partir d’adresses IP spécifiques

D’appliquer un mot de passe et une authentification à deux facteurs à ces connexion

De mettre à jour automatiquement le pare-feu, pour éviter de l’oublier

Utilisent des appareils de qualité commerciale ou industrielle, et non grand public ; de nombreux appareils grand public ne proposent pas de mises à jour, ou ne se mettent pas à jour rapidement

Enfin, ajoute-t-il, « Remplacez le pare-feu strictement tous les quatre ans. Pourquoi ? Parce que si nous avons des appareils exposés à Internet, neuf fois sur dix, nous n’avons pas d’équipe de sécurité, et nous ne remarquerons pas quand nos pare-feu ne seront plus pris en charge et que les mises à jour automatiques cesseront. »

« Les mesures de base ne suffisent pas pour les infrastructures critiques de grande envergure ou l’industrie lourde, mais elles contribueront grandement à empêcher les hacktivistes de s’introduire dans vos congélateurs », conclut Ginter. « Retirez vos équipements d’Internet. Faites-le de toute urgence. »

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10016. What We Missed: Feds Lasso Texas Laptop Farms

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from busting up North Korea's stateside infrastructure in "Operation Lonestar Justice" to Staples' gift card bonanza.

The US government is striking back against the ever-persistent threat of fake IT worker schemes run by the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

In this episode of "What We Missed," Dark Reading's Rob Wright and Alex Culafi discuss some of the recent news events and topics that didn't make it into the publication, starting with FBI raids across more than 40 Texas residences that were allegedly running "laptop farms."

The law-enforcement action, dubbed “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” seized 187 devices, charged 14 people, and arrested individuals accused of facilitating North Korean threat actors running fake IT worker schemes. The schemes disrupted by Operation Lonestar Roundup impacted more than 70 US companies, according to the FBI.

Fake IT worker schemes typically involve DPRK actors masquerading as IT professionals and developers, either using fake or stolen identities, to gain employment at US companies. The threat actors then use their positions to exfiltrate sensitive data, steal intellectual property, and gather intelligence.

Related:Ex-OpenAI Engineer Detained After Planting Secret Recorder at HQ

Also discussed on this episode: Russian police arrested alleged members of a cybercriminal group known as the "DataSuckers," which has taken credit for several breaches against companies in Russia and Ukraine; and according to a report from 404 Media, a Chinese criminal operation breached Staples' internal customer support system and used it to issue thousands of gift cards, worth $5 million.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright with Dark Reading.

Dark Reading's Alex Culafi: And I'm Alex Culafi with Dark Reading.

DR's Rob Wright: And this is "What We Missed," a discussion about some of the recent headlines we did not get a chance to cover in the pages, pods, or videos of Dark Reading. Alex, this is an eventful one. We don't have any real AI news, so that's good. We get a break from AI news.

DR's Rob Wright: But we'll kick it off with an interesting one. So there was a big federal crackdown on North Korean IT worker schemes. There was a raid on a laptop farm in Texas. An interesting one. An interestingly titled operation. Busted a bunch of laptop farms. And yeah, it seems like the government is getting into the business of trying to take down these North Korean IT worker schemes. What'd you think of this?

Related:When AI Agents Commit Breaches, Humans May Not Be Held Liable

DR's Alex Culafi: I think this is an issue that will persist for a while, which isn't very specific. But I guess I'm thinking about … I was watching something about this on YouTube the other day, even, and it was about a woman who was an office worker — I think this was back in like 2024 — who had gotten hired for a job, and she was just like a normal, nice, well-intended Southern lady. And they were sending her laptops and she thought she was just doing her job, and then it turns out that she was hooking up dozens of laptops. And later on in the video I think it sort of went into maybe she knew more than she was letting on at first.

DR's Alex Culafi: But I do think, especially in times of economic hardship — which a lot of the US is in right now, and a lot of the world is experiencing right now — I think we're gonna continue to see these stories where normal people who don't see themselves as spies or as traitors to the United States, or as sympathetic to the North Korean regime or whatever, are gonna get in these situations. Now, this sounds like a farm, which is a little different.

Related:Prominent Ransomware Negotiator Faces Extortion Charges

DR's Alex Culafi: But as we're on this topic, I think this story — whether it's a farm or it's a person who didn't realize what they were doing at first and then found themselves too deep in — I think we're going to see this for a while, no?

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, yeah. I think we're going to see more operations like this. So, first of all, I had a tough time intro-ing this one because the operation is called "Operation Lonestar Roundup." And every time I hear Lonestar I — and this is my cross to bear — but I think of Spaceballs and I just start cracking up.

DR's Rob Wright: That aside, no, the data here is interesting. One hundred and eighty-seven devices seized. I think there were 14 people who were charged. I think there were a few arrests. But to your point, I think this is like a gig economy thing. I mean, we've had laptop farms for other stuff — click fraud, malvertising, stuff like that — for a long time. And I think we're just gonna start to see more schemes like this take advantage of existing laptop farms and people that, to your point, may not totally know what they're doing or who's using them. So we'll see.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yep. And the thing I'll also add is thinking about where things were with this North Korean IT worker fraud back a couple of years ago. I know it extends further back than that. When it was still new and popping off, a lot of researchers we were talking to were like, 'No, this is real and this is a big problem.'

DR's Alex Culafi: And I doubted them at the time because I thought it was just the new story to talk about to get press attention. And maybe it also was that. But no, totally. This is pervasive. Organizations at every level are dealing with North Korean operators trying to either get paychecks to send back to North Korea or to get data that they can use to exploit later, and it's — I don't know if it's getting uglier, but it remains very ugly a few years later.

DR's Rob Wright: Yes, indeed. What've got next here?

DR's Alex Culafi: We have an interesting story. Russian authorities arrested three suspected members of the hacking group Data Suckers, including a 19-year-old member. And this is following the breach of Russian pizza chain Dodo Pizza —

DR's Alex Culafi: — which is a longstanding pizza chain in Russia, that reportedly exposed massive amounts of customer data. A lot of that would have been Russian customers, obviously. The group has also claimed attacks against Tez Tour, which is a Russian travel company, and Ukrainian grocery giant ATB, which is very unusual. Because by all accounts, expert accounts, they don't seem to be politically motivated in the same way that a lot of Russian operators are, either working on behalf of the Russian government or actively participating in the war on Ukraine.

But it's doubly interesting because for as long as I can remember, one of the golden rules among Russian hackers was not to hack Russians, for multiple reasons. One, because the government can sometimes provide cover for you, I've heard, for the activities you're doing externally. And two, Russian authorities, if they think you're messing with their civilians, they are very, very harsh, historically.

DR's Alex Culafi: So this is really interesting that it's Russia arresting Russian hackers. What do you think of this?

DR's Rob Wright: I also thought it was interesting. I'm a little confused, I admit. When I read the story, one of the alleged DataSuckers hackers is a 19-year-old named Dennis Fridman. That does not sound like a Russian surname to me. So I don't know where he hails from, if he was just living there, or if he is a Russian citizen. The thing that, to your points, the thing that really stuck out to me beyond Russia making some arrests here was I immediately thought, we're failing the kids these days. We're failing them.

DR's Rob Wright: These guys, this is just another example of an organization, a hacking group with teenagers who are obviously skilled and can do stuff that's just out there. They're like, "Let's hack Dodo Pizza." I mean, I don't know. We gotta start recruiting these kids — the government, and preferably not the Russian government, but the US, Canada, Five Eyes, whatever. We need to get out there and start finding these guys on like game forums and whatnot. Because this is just getting out of control with the number of quote-unquote kids who are doing this stuff.

A 457(b) plan is an employer-sponsored retirement savings account available to state and local government employees and certain nonprofit (tax-exempt) organizations. It operates similarly to a 401(k) or 403(b) — you defer a portion of your salary before taxes, your money grows tax-deferred, and you pay income tax when you withdraw.

But here is where the 457(b) separates itself from every other retirement account: there is no 10% early withdrawal penalty. None. Zero. Once you leave your employer — whether you retire at 35 or 65 — you can access your 457(b) funds immediately and pay only ordinary income tax. No penalty, no waiting until age 59 and a half, no complicated Roth conversion ladders.

This single feature makes the 457(b) the most powerful account for anyone pursuing financial independence through government employment. Teachers, firefighters, police officers, state university employees, city workers, and county staff all potentially have access to this account. If you have a 457(b) available and you are not maxing it out, you are leaving the best early-retirement tool on the table.

The plan comes in two flavors: governmental 457(b) plans and non-governmental (tax-exempt) 457(b) plans. The differences are significant and affect rollover options, creditor protection, and how your money is held.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Every other retirement account — 401(k), 403(b), Traditional IRA — charges a 10% penalty if you withdraw before age 59 and a half (with limited exceptions). The 457(b) has no such penalty. The moment you separate from your employer, your entire balance becomes accessible. For a government employee pursuing FIRE at age 40, this means immediate access to potentially hundreds of thousands of dollars without the penalty, without a Roth conversion ladder, and without SEPP/72(t) calculations. No other account offers this.

The 2026 457(b) contribution limit is $24,500 — the same as 401(k) and 403(b) limits. If you are age 50 or older, you can contribute an additional $7,500 catch-up, bringing your total to $31,000.

But the real power move is the double-dip strategy. The 457(b) has its own separate contribution limit from the 403(b). If your employer offers both plans — and many government and university employers do — you can max out both accounts in the same year. That means $24,500 into your 457(b) plus $24,500 into your 403(b) equals $47,000 per year in tax-deferred savings, not counting employer matches or catch-up contributions.

For a dual-income household where both partners have access to 457(b) and 403(b) plans, the combined tax-deferred savings potential exceeds $94,000 per year. Add HSA contributions, Roth IRAs, and any employer matches, and a government-employed couple can shelter well over $100,000 annually from taxes.

The 457(b) offers a unique catch-up rule that no other retirement plan has. In the three years before your plan's "normal retirement age" (typically 65 or 70, defined by your employer), you can contribute up to double the regular limit — that is $47,000 in 2026. This provision lets late starters make up for years of lower contributions. You cannot use both the age-50 catch-up and the 3-year catch-up in the same year — you must choose whichever is larger.

This provision requires careful planning because the normal retirement age varies by employer and plan document. Review your specific plan to confirm your eligible catch-up window.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This distinction matters enormously. Governmental 457(b) balances can be rolled into a Traditional IRA, 401(k), 403(b), or another governmental 457(b) after you separate from service. This gives you full flexibility to consolidate accounts, access better investment options, and implement tax-efficient withdrawal strategies in retirement.

Non-governmental 457(b) plans — those offered by tax-exempt nonprofits like hospitals, charities, and private universities — cannot be rolled into an IRA or any other retirement plan type. The balance can only be rolled to another non-governmental 457(b). This limitation is critical to understand before relying on a non-governmental 457(b) as a cornerstone of your retirement strategy.

Even more concerning: non-governmental 457(b) assets are held as general assets of the employer, meaning they are technically subject to the employer's creditors. If your nonprofit employer faces financial trouble, your deferred compensation could be at risk. Governmental plans hold assets in trust for the benefit of employees, providing the same creditor protection as a 401(k).

Most governmental 457(b) plans offer a menu of mutual funds, target-date funds, and sometimes a self-directed brokerage window. The quality of investment options varies dramatically between plans. Look for low-cost index fund options — total stock market, S&P 500, total international, and total bond market funds with expense ratios below 0.10% are the gold standard.

If your plan's investment options are poor — loaded with high-fee actively managed funds — contribute enough to capture any match, then prioritize your 403(b) or IRA if those have better options. After separation, roll the 457(b) balance to a low-cost IRA provider like Vanguard or Fidelity.

#10014. Everyone has the file. Nobody has the right version

EVENT: Distributed teams need to collaborate, but duplicated files, delays, and competing versions keep getting in the way

Distributed teams need to collaborate on shared information, but duplicated files, delays, and competing versions keep getting in the way.

Picture a video production team with editors in different cities. One person updates a project file, another keeps working from an earlier copy, and a third waits for a large transfer to finish.

When teams need to collaborate on large files across locations, traditional storage and file-sharing arrangements introduce friction precisely where people expect technology to help.

The hard part isn't merely moving a file. It's knowing who has the authoritative copy, when changes are available, and whether somebody else is still working on an outdated version.

Consider a game studio preparing a build for review. A designer exports an updated asset, but a colleague pulls an older version from a synced folder. The mistake only becomes obvious when the pieces are assembled. The team must trace the mismatch, resend files, and repeat work.

Sync-and-download workflows depend on a chain of uploads, downloads, and decisions about which copy is current. Under deadline pressure, that chain breaks. Delayed access means missed handoffs; duplicated files mean extra checking and sometimes rework.

For IT, each workaround creates another question: where does the data live, who can access it, and how do teams maintain consistent controls? Adding another collaboration application doesn't resolve those underlying questions.

The useful starting point is the workflow. Find out where teams copy data, where they wait, and what prompts them to work outside the shared system.

These frustrations cut across industries, but the ways organizations respond aren't identical. Hearing how another team handled version confusion, access, and handoffs is often more useful than another abstract promise of seamless collaboration.
