#10013. NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams: Bringing Real-Time Generative Simulation to Surgical Robotics

Surgical robotics is moving quickly from teleoperation toward increasingly capable vision-language-action policies. But evaluating and training these systems remains difficult. Physical robotic platforms are expensive to operate, experiments are slow to reproduce, and failures can damage instruments or biological material. Conventional simulators provide a safer alternative, but surgical scenes are exceptionally difficult to model: deformable tissue, fine instrument interactions, specular surfaces, sutures, needles, smoke, and occlusions all matter.

World foundation models offer a different path. Instead of manually authoring every object and physical interaction, they learn visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics. NVIDIA's Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator demonstrated this approach by generating future surgical video from an initial scene and a sequence of robot actions. It enabled faster-than-physical evaluation and synthetic data generation across the Open-H-Embodiment ecosystem.

Today, we are introducing the next step: Cosmos-H-Dreams, a real-time, action-conditioned generative simulator for surgical robotics. Cosmos-H-Dreams distills the capabilities of Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator into a causal, few-step student model and serves it through FlashDreams, NVIDIA's accelerated streaming-inference library. Running on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU, the result is an interactive environment that a person or a learned policy can control in a closed loop.

Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator is an action-conditioned world foundation model built on NVIDIA Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B and post-trained on the Open-H-Embodiment dataset. Given a surgical context frame and a future robot trajectory, it generates video showing the likely visual consequences of those actions. This makes it useful for offline policy evaluation and synthetic data generation. A recorded or policy-generated trajectory can be sent to the model, the corresponding rollout can be generated, and the result can be inspected or scored without repeatedly executing the motion on a physical robot.

Cosmos-H-Dreams moves the model into the real-time regime. Starting from the multi-embodiment surgical priors learned by Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator, we specialize the model for da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK) tabletop suturing and distill it into a causal student that generates the scene autoregressively. The released model receives an initial RGB frame and a live stream of robot kinematics, then produces the next chunk of frames before continuing with the following action block.

We have also demonstrated the versatility of Cosmos-H-Dreams by collaborating with CMR Surgical and Cambridge Consultants to integrate it with the Versius surgeon controller, enabling real-time operation on the Versius platform.

The key challenge is preserving useful surgical dynamics while reducing the cost of generation. Cosmos-H-Dreams uses a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long, autoregressive rollouts.

The bidirectional teacher begins from the Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator Open-H checkpoint, which uses a unified 44-dimensional action representation. For the released dVRK tabletop model, the dual-arm dVRK action content, consisting of relative end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper state, is mapped into this common representation.

The teacher is then fine-tuned on the JHU dVRK tabletop mixture, including successful demonstrations as well as failure and out-of-distribution episodes such as needle drops, missed throws, and unsuccessful knot ties. These failures are important: a simulator intended to evaluate policies must reproduce the consequences of poor actions, not only ideal demonstrations.

To improve stability during long rollouts, the training process progressively increases the teacher's temporal horizon. We start training on a 12-frame horizon and progressively increase this number until 72 frames. At each horizon bump, we initialize the warmed-up model with pretrained weights.

The teacher's denoising trajectories are first precomputed and cached. A causal student is initialized from the teacher and trained to imitate these cached trajectories. This warmup stage teaches the student to operate with causal attention and a streaming key/value cache before it begins learning from its own generated history.

Autoregressive models face a familiar problem: during training they may see clean, ground-truth context, while during deployment they must condition on their own imperfect outputs. Small errors can therefore compound over time.

Cosmos-H-Dreams addresses this mismatch with self-forcing distillation. During training, the student rolls forward using its own generated context. Distribution-matching supervision from the frozen teacher then guides those self-generated rollouts toward realistic surgical video. This prepares the student for the same conditions it will encounter during interactive inference.

The resulting model supports few-step diffusion, with as few as two denoising steps per latent frame, rather than the many-step process used by the full teacher. It combines the teacher's surgical priors with the causal structure needed for streaming.

Model distillation is only part of the real-time story. Cosmos-H-Dreams is served through FlashDreams, an accelerated inference library for autoregressive world and video models.

FlashDreams turns the distilled student into a low-latency streaming system through several complementary optimizations, such as streaming KV cache, CUDA Graph capturing, or model compilation.

Together, these techniques bring the distilled surgical world model fine-tune from the roughly ten-frames-per-second regime of standard Cosmos-H-Surgical-Simulator inference to interactive operation (~160 frames per second) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000.

Cosmos-H-Dreams also provides the human-machine interfaces that turn generation into interaction. A browser client can send keyboard commands and receive generated frames over WebRTC. A Meta Quest client can map tracked controller motion into robot actions and display the synthesized scene through WebXR. The same model can also be connected to a learned surgical policy, with generated observations and predicted actions exchanged inside a closed loop.

While Cosmos-H-Dreams includes a pre-trained checkpoint for tabletop suturing, the system is designed to be extensible to your specific embodiment. To train a real-time student model for your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide.

Cosmos-H-Dreams opens a new frontier for surgical simulation: environments learned from real robot data that are responsive enough to be inhabited.

The immediate next step is to evaluate more than visual quality. A useful surgical simulator must respond correctly to actions, preserve instrument and scene structure over long rollouts, and support conclusions that transfer to the physical robot. This motivates a new family of closed-loop benchmarks: tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action diversity, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and real policy outcomes.

Real-time world models can also become active partners in surgical policy development. They can generate rare failures on demand, provide scalable environments for reinforcement or imitation learning, and enable rapid evaluation of new policies without tying every experiment to scarce robotic hardware.

Further ahead, real-time simulation enables a series of downstream applications such as latency-aware telesurgery, where the world model helps maintain a more stable display; or interactive surgical rehearsal, procedure planning, and intraoperative decision support. Cosmos-H-Dreams is a research and development platform, not a diagnostic system, a replacement for intraoperative imaging, or a controller for a physical surgical robot. Yet it provides a foundation for exploring these possibilities safely.

As model fidelity, temporal stability, and hardware efficiency continue to improve, real-time generative simulation can help connect surgeon education, synthetic data generation, policy training, and policy evaluation within one shared Physical AI environment.

Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos-H-Dreams:

Cosmos-H-Dreams brings action-conditioned surgical world modeling into the real-time loop, creating a new environment for people and policies to practice, explore, generate data, and evaluate what happens next.

This is a fascinating leap for surgical robotics. Real-time generative simulation could greatly reduce risks in training and planning. The concept of distilling a large model into a causal student model is clever. If you're also exploring video generation from images, check out the Seedance 2.5 image-to-video tool for creative applications.

Assessing more than just visual quality is the immediate next step. A practical surgical simulator must enable findings that translate to the real robot, maintain instrument and scene organization during extended rollouts, and react appropriately to actions. Tool-tip reach and pose accuracy, gripper-cycle fidelity, idle stability, counterfactual action variety, long-horizon drift, and agreement between simulated and actual policy outcomes are some of the new closed-loop benchmarks that are motivated by this.

The progress in surgical robotics is genuinely exciting! 🏥🤖 Being able to train and test advanced vision-language-action systems in realistic simulations without risking expensive equipment or delicate procedures could make development much faster and safer. The level of detail needed for tissues, instruments, smoke, and lighting really shows how challenging this field is. 👏

It’s impressive to see technology moving beyond simple teleoperation and towards smarter, more capable robotic assistance. 🚀 Better simulation environments can help researchers refine these systems before they ever reach an operating room, which is a win for both surgeons and patients. 😊📱

Looking forward to seeing how projects like NVIDIA Cosmos-H-Dreams shape the future of healthcare. 🌍💙 If these simulations continue becoming more realistic, they could play a huge role in improving surgical training, reducing costs, and ultimately delivering better patient outcomes. Amazing work and an exciting glimpse into what's ahead! 🙌✨

#10011. Microsoft Links Storm-0940 to ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack

The China-linked actor used an AI-enabled penetration-testing tool to automate and accelerate its attack on more than 2,200 tenants.

A China-linked threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940 used an agentic AI penetration-testing framework to accelerate a supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

The attackers used compromised application credentials associated with the service to attempt to access the Microsoft 365 environments of more than 2,250 downstream customer tenants. In multiple instances, the attackers obtained privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure in less than three hours after initial targeting, Microsoft said in an analysis published this week.

The activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and scaling their operations exponentially, Microsoft researchers wrote. "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," they said.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

ConnectWise provides software and IT management technology that managed service providers use to deliver a broad range of services to their customers, including backup and recovery for Microsoft 365 data. Delivering these services requires the company to have authorized application access to customer Microsoft 365 environments to back up and restore data.

On Oct. 16, ConnectWise disclosed unauthorized access to application identities associated with its Cloud Backup product. The company subsequently published additional details and containment guidance but has not publicly explained how the attackers initially gained control of the application identities.

Microsoft described the incident as part of a broader Storm-0940 campaign that began as early as September and targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide across several industries including manufacturing, aerospace, chemicals, energy, defense, and financial services. The threat actor has been using an AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX to automate and accelerate its operations.

"In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access," Microsoft said.

In the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate reconnaissance and scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. The threat actor used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, generating as many as 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. That pace left defenders with little time to detect and respond to the activity, Microsoft noted.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

"Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations," the company said.

ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service and also took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline following the incident. In an Oct. 22 update, the company noted it was continuing work on restoring disrupted services and urged customers to keep affected ConnectWise application connections offline until further notice.

"Investigation and monitoring continue alongside restoration. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise," the company said. ConnectWise called on customers to review their individual Microsoft 365 environments using the company's technical investigation and remediation guide and related information.

Microsoft meanwhile highlighted its own mitigation and protection guidance, which included recommendations like reviewing every Microsoft 365 tenant that might have been tied to ConnectWise and to preserve logs and other forensic evidence before making any changes.

Related:PapRAT Cyber-Espionage Campaign Leaves a 'Bitter' Taste in South Asia

Ross Filipek, CISO at Corsica Technologies, says that before reconnecting with ConnectWise, affected organizations should have a clear understanding of what might have happened inside their environment. He pointed to Microsoft's discovery of application credential changes that could give attackers a way back in to compromised environments. Organizations are going to need to investigate whether their Microsoft 365 environments are safe before they reconnect, he says.

"Keep affected connections disabled in line with vendor guidance. Investigate unauthorized changes that could leave another way in. Preserve evidence without delaying containment," Filipek tells Dark Reading. "There's also an immediate business question: Are backups still running? Assign someone on each side to check coverage during the interruption. A restored connection needs verification that backup jobs are completing and recovery works."

Going forward, organizations need to have a recovery plan that takes into account the potential of their losing access to a service that they normally would depend on for recovery, Filipek adds. Incident responders should know which applications connect to the organization's Microsoft 365 tenant and how to quickly sever those connections when necessary, and exercise that scenario with their service provider.

"Establish who checks backup coverage during containment and who decides whether the business can tolerate the interruption. Leaving those responsibilities implied is how both sides end up assuming the other has checked," he says.

Jon Baker, vice president of threat-informed defense at AttackIQ, wants affected organizations to preserve sign-in and audit records and to investigate application sign-ins, Microsoft Graph activity, new credentials, privilege changes, and unusual data access. "Remove confirmed unauthorized access and verify vendor and tenant remediation separately," he advises. "After containment, controlled validation can test whether comparable application behavior can still reach sensitive resources or establish another foothold."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#10010. Raspberry Pi hikes prices again, barely a month after the last round

Memory crunch pushes 16GB Pi 5 to $385, more than triple its launch price, just a month after the last round of hikes

Raspberry Pi has announced yet another round of price hikes, this time adding $80 to the cost of its 16GB Pi 5, which now sells for more than three times its original launch price.

The latest bump, announced by Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton, takes the 16GB Pi 5 to a whopping $385. The 16GB Compute Module 5 variants are also getting $40 more expensive, although the Raspberry Pi 500+, which packs the same amount of RAM, has escaped this particular round.

Upton blamed a familiar culprit: soaring memory costs, worsened by a lack of alternative suppliers for 16GB DRAM and ongoing shortages of other components.

"Unfortunately, a lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages, means we now need to make further price increases on some of our highest-density products," Upton wrote.

It's becoming an expensive habit for Raspberry Pi customers. The 16GB Pi 5 cost $120 when it launched in January 2025, which seems almost reasonable now. Raspberry Pi added $25 in December, another $60 in February, and a further $100 in April. With today's $80 increase, buyers are being asked to cough up $265 more than they were less than two years ago, a price hike of 221 percent.

And it's barely been a month since Raspberry Pi raised prices on its 2GB Pi 4 and Pi 5 models by $12.50 apiece, taking them to $67.50 and $77.50 respectively.

The repeated markups come despite Raspberry Pi reporting record first-half results in September. Revenue jumped 90 percent to $256.9 million, while gross profit rose 79 percent to $59.4 million. Gross profit per board climbed 53 percent to $12.20, helped partly by memory purchased before prices went through the roof. That stockpile advantage has since largely disappeared.

For customers unwilling to pay nearly $400 for a single-board computer, Upton advises buying something with less RAM, using an older Pi, or optimizing applications to make do with less memory.

He also warned that some sellers are exploiting the shortages by charging inflated prices or offering products that aren't what they appear to be, urging customers to stick to approved resellers.

“We’re aware that a few bad actors have been taking advantage of the current memory supply circumstances to sell Raspberry Pi products at inflated prices or shift products that aren’t what they seem,” he said.

There is, apparently, some good news, as Raspberry Pi continues to insist the increases are temporary. "As we've said from the beginning, the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again," Upton wrote.

That could be a long wait. Micron has previously warned that memory shortages could drag on into 2028 or beyond, so anyone hoping to see a $120 Pi 5 again probably shouldn't hold their breath. ®

#10009. State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Relatively small data breaches in India can turn quite serious, thanks to a sophisticated underground market for trading PII.

An anonymous hacker has leaked a small batch of sensitive customer records from the State Bank of India (SBI), with potentially serious consequences for the thousands impacted.

SBI has been posting a lot about cybersecurity on social media lately. In August it introduced a new CGI mascot named "Captain Y." Captain Y from SBI is "your Cyber Protector," he says in his promo video, "with awareness as his superpower." SBI's best plug for cybersecurity awareness came on Wednesday, though, when it publicly disclosed that it had suffered a breach of customer data.

In a notice to India's National Stock Exchange, the organization's compliance and company secretary acknowledged that 3,897 customer records had been leaked online. They did not specify whether those records belonged to 3,897 individual customers. In a public notice to customers, the state-run bank emphasized that the incident really only impacted "a very, very small number of customers."

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

For a bank that serves north of 500 million people, a few thousand records does indeed qualify as very, very small. Cyber experts note, though, that for those affected, the consequences could be significant thanks to India's sophisticated underground economy for buying and selling personally identifying information (PII).

Last week, a new account with the name "Siriusim" published a post to the mainstream data breach website BreachForums. They had new user data from SBI, they claimed, including personal user information, new account and loan applications, and more. The data included a table with 375,000 rows, and 2,722 PDF files. Importantly, neither figure necessarily indicated the total number of individuals impacted.

As part of the post, Siriusim featured a few documents with handwritten personal information. Mumbai's Free Press Journal verified that PII from the breach samples was valid, belonging to real Indian citizens. One individual, for example, lost their mobile number and know your customer (KYC) documentation in the breach, and the WhatsApp photograph associated with their number matched the passport photo included in the KYC file.

SBI acknowledged that leaked data included names, genders, mobile numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth, bank profile IDs, metadata associated with loans, and "other files." Follow-on reporting out of Mumbai suggested that this extra data included Central KYC numbers — a single identifier for financial accounts in India — and video KYC verification data, and the kinds of files one might have to submit in the process of creating a new bank account, or filing for a loan. For instance, one published document included an individual's employment and income declaration, with details about their current employer, work experience, and salary.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

Exactly what precipitated the leak, and why it affected only 0.0008% of the bank's customers, remains unclear. In its formal declaration, SBI emphasized that "the bank's core business functions continue to operate normally without disruptions." Altogether, these clues might point to a breach of some peripheral digital service or data-handling system, rather than the core bank system.

In fact, SBI's last major customer data leak followed just such a script. In 2019, it exposed customer account data through a single server at a Mumbai data center, which was missing password protection. The server supported its "SBI Quick" system, used to text and call customers about basic account information. That one machine put millions of customers at risk, perhaps highlighting just how minor this new leak really is.

"If the data is genuine, the main risk is not direct account theft but credible-sounding phishing, vishing, and identity or loan fraud, since attackers who know someone’s details can impersonate the bank convincingly," explains independent security researcher Sushant Bhardwaj.

Related:Warlock Ransomware Hits Large Spanish, Portuguese Orgs

Email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth carry fairly obvious risk in the hands of bad actors, and less common kinds of PII can add color to otherwise generic identity attacks. For instance, "KYC details are hard to change, so they can support identity fraud, such as applying for credit in someone else’s name or answering account-verification questions," Bhardwaj notes. And with regard to loan metadata, "a caller who can quote real loan details can pose as the bank or a recovery agent and pressure a borrower into paying a 'fee' or sharing a one-time password (OTP)."

Brian Hussey, senior vice president for Cyderes' Howler Cell, goes deeper. Last month, his team reported on an Indian data broker selling personal records for only about 5 rupees (6 cents or so) per lookup, through a Telegram bot and business application programming interface (API) platform. Using these simple lookups, cybercriminals targeting Indian citizens can obtain vast stores of PII belonging to regular citizens in an instant. And data breaches like SBI's, Hussey notes, can feed into this underground economy. "A breach dump goes stale the day it's posted. A live lookup service is always current, because it is asking the authoritative source in real time. India’s underground data market has both, and they work together," he explains.

"India built one of the most connected identity systems in the world, and an entire industry exists to query it," he warns. "That connectivity is what makes a leak in one place so impactful and useful somewhere else."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10008. Work on GEFS (the Good Enough File System) for OpenBSD progresses

Home Archives About Submit Story Create Account Login

Contributed by Peter N. M. Hansteen on 2026-11-01 from the most excellent file shredder dept.

Now Ori has followed up with more evolved code that includes several important steps towards makin the new file system fit for general use. In a message to tech@, Ori writes: List: openbsd-tech Subject: Re: GEFS on OpenBSD: A very early preview From: ori () eigenstate ! org Date: 2026-10-31 17:08:42 So, it's probably time for a few updates. First off, thanks to Martijn, and everyone else who tried it out and sent patches. Everything is updated and rebased, and the diff has been regenerated with all of the lastest. I've gone through a the error handling code. In theory the filesystem will handle errors mostly correctly. There are probably still places where theory diverges from reality. I've also forward ported most of the important bugfixes from 9front. The file system now leaves the first FS block unused by default -- we can put disklabels there, which makes it hard to put the superblock there as well. Some userspace tools have been done (you can now mkfs on openbsd!), but snapshot control hasn't. I'm thinking we have a userspace 'gefs' program that lets you handle this, trying to keep the interface similar to the 9front ctl file. The commands below should suffice: gefs debug [0|1] gefs usereserve gefs retain snap timespec gefs snap name newname gefs fork name newname The consistency protocol is still the biggest missing piece; I've been reading the old code for softupdates, since it had the same flavor of problem. what gefs wants, in the ideal case, is some way to put ordering barriers in the commit phases, while still accepting new block i/o, something like the following sequence of steps: 0) normal use, generate dirty blocks and write back in any order. holding mutlk { 1) barrier(), ensure that all blocks written before the commit will be on disk before the commit finishes 2) enqueue free list/deadlist data 3) prepare arena header/footer + superblock } 4) enqueue arena headers 5) barrier() 6) enqueue superblock 7) enqueue arena footers 8) wait for enqueued blocks to hit disk 9) free blocks no longer used by previous gen on 9front, I have a priority queue of blocks that are sorted by (gen, addr) tuples, which means that writes within a generation are flushed to disk as sequentially as they can be, while not crossing generation boundaries. I'm currently thinking I'll implement the same in OpenBSD -- launch syncer kprocs that do synchronous I/O to the block device. If we kick things out of cache and write it back to disk early, that should generally be safe -- The only blocks the buffer cache must not reorder are the arena headers and superblocks, so a flag to pin them unwritten may be all that's needed here. I'm open to other ideas, though. Quoth ori@eigenstate.org: Followed by a quoted part of the previous message that has the links to the code and documentation. If you are as excited as we are about this new file system development and are in a position to test, please do.

#10007. GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

Extract text and tables from document images

The next frontier is managing an entire fleet of agents and there is nothing stopping it.

Agreed. And the part that isn't priced in yet: a fleet of agents makes per-token cost scale linearly with the business. At some point large enterprises stop paying that curve and bring the models in-house — which doesn't remove the cost, it just trades a vendor price list for a utilization number. And agent fleets are brutal on utilization: real-time inference under latency SLAs, batch jobs, retraining, evals — all bursty, all fighting over the same finite pool. Managing the fleet is going to be, in large part, a GPU scheduling problem.

Scheduling is the core bottleneck of this problem. A CPU-like isolation mechanism, or a sandbox-based architecture on GPUs, could significantly alleviate this issue.

Good point, isolation is a real part of the picture. CPU-style boundaries (and the GPU sandboxing now landing, like the Kata Containers work) are what make it safe to co-locate unrelated workloads on the same card without fault or memory-contention risk, which widens the set of placements a scheduler is even allowed to make.

Taking that a step further: once co-location is safe, we have to decide which workload runs on which GPU, at what time, at what priority, given that each one wants something different from the hardware (memory footprint, latency tolerance, duration). Isolation gives you a bigger, safer decision space; something still has to pick the right point in it. And rigid partitioning can even cut utilization, since an idle slice can't lend capacity to a busy neighbor.

That's exactly the direction we're taking next: an intelligent solution for job scheduling. We've got a follow-up article on it in the works, which will be published next week. Would be curious to get your read when it's out.

I expect we will see GPU rental systems become a thing. There are a lot of high-end GPUs sitting in consumer computers doing absolutely nothing for 90% of the day. Imagine if individuals could allow a training model to access their GPU remotely and in return pay them something in return. Yes, remote GPUs is not optimal, but with the consumer taking on the maintenance, power bill, and ownership of the GPU, any use the training model gets is a net positive.

#10006. UK.gov lacks understanding of climate impact, says watchdog

Risks of changing climate and cost of transition to low-carbon energy poorly measured by government departments

Public bodies in the UK expect higher operating costs and energy charges as a result of climate changes and the transition to lower carbon energy, but few have a good picture of the risks, according to government auditors.

A new report from the National Audit Office (NAO) says some public bodies expect financial impact from the risks they identified, although bodies were often not able to cost these – even approximately.

"Bodies anticipate costs to arise from damage to assets and infrastructure, driven by physical damage from extreme weather, as well as from chronic shifts to higher temperatures and more precipitation. Bodies also expect higher maintenance and repair costs, potential asset upgrades, and transition costs. Many bodies expect increased operating costs, including energy charges. Bodies controlling significant property or infrastructure are particularly concerned with decarbonization and adaptation costs," the report stated.

His Majesty’s Treasury (HMT) has set out rules for climate-related financial disclosure in larger central government bodies' annual reports, which produced their first set of reports for the 2025-26 financial year. Other rules for disclosure have been in place since 2022.

However, the NAO found [PDF] that understanding of the risks in the impact of climate change –  increasing temperatures, higher risk of flooding, higher winds and longer droughts – was poor, as was insight into costs of moving to a low-carbon economy.

"Bodies did not articulate transition risks as well as physical risks in the strategy disclosures. In the disclosures we reviewed, while several transition risks were listed, few specifics were given, unlike physical risks, which were explained in greater detail," the report from the watchdog stated.

"The transition risks most frequently identified included the financial cost of transition, and supply chain disruption. Anticipated transition costs included the costs of: switching to lower-carbon energy sources, including investments in new technology; complying with new regulations; and of fluctuations in the price and availability of materials, water, energy and specialist skills," it added.

Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "UK public services will need to adapt to the impacts of climate change. Parliament needs clear information on the resilience of infrastructure, service provision and finances to climate change, and on how these risks are being managed."

"Although public bodies are still learning how best to report their most pressing climate risks, the requirement on all large central government bodies to make such disclosures from 2025-26 is an important first step. We expect this reporting to become more useful over time."

Earlier this year a report from Global Action Plan, a climate charity, claimed 84 percent of proposed datacenter developments were in areas that are already water stressed or projected to be water stressed by 2040.

Water consumption by datacenters could intensify strain on the UK’s water systems already stressed by climate change, it argued.®

#10005. AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may compound — not contain — the risk.

Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

Jeffrey Schwartz is a New York–based freelance writer specializing in information security and enterprise IT. Focused on the constant pace of technological change, Jeff has covered the evolution of technologies, including professional broadcast, computing, networking, the Internet, mobile communications, modern cloud infrastructure and software development for over 30 years.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. Earlier contributions include Pro Sound News, Television Broadcast, Videography, Sound & Communications, Post magazine and Crain’s Electronic Media. Jeff holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in Communications and Journalism from Adelphi University. More details are available on Jeff’s LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeffaschwartz.

#10003. Broadcom denied names of cloud providers backing VMware merger challenge

EU court's confidentiality ruling clears a procedural hurdle, not the merits of CISPE's case against Commission approval

Euro cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom following a ruling by the EU General Court.

Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe filed an action last year seeking to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of the cloud and virtualization giant.

CISPE believes the Commission erred in allowing the purchase to go ahead without imposing any conditions on Broadcom to protect the many European cloud providers and their customers who depend on VMware's software.

Broadcom sought access to redacted information identifying members supporting the action, arguing that it needed the information to challenge the action's admissibility. CISPE says the ruling allows the case to proceed without disclosing those identities to Broadcom.

"It is a procedural ruling on confidentiality rather than a decision on the substance of the case, but it removes the immediate obstacle to the action moving forward," a CISPE spokesperson told The Register.

CISPE argued that identifying the members, which are or have been VMware customers, would expose them to a significant risk of retaliation because of Broadcom's market power. Those members had supplied information about their commercial relationships with VMware.

As far as the case itself goes, CISPE says it warned the Commission that Broadcom would use VMware's pre-eminent position in the private cloud market to rewrite licensing terms and reshape the market in its favor.

Just a month after Broadcom's acquisition concluded in November 2023, partners were informed that VMware's channel program was to end in early 2024, and that Broadcom was also ditching the majority of VMware's Cloud Services Providers, keeping only a select few that had the largest turnover.

Despite Broadcom CEO Hock Tan publicly stating that inflating prices was not his strategy, that is what happened. AT&T says that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent price increase, for example. Meanwhile, nine out of ten respondents to a recent survey of VMware customers said they were considering moving to alternatives.

CISPE, which represents 48 cloud infrastructure service providers across the EU, says fewer than 20 European providers remain authorized to offer VMware-based services, down from more than a thousand.

Commenting on the latest ruling, CISPE Secretary General Francisco Mingorance declared it a good day for the organization and for the rule of law in Europe.

"The case matters even more today than when we filed it. In the three years since the European Commission waved this deal through without conditions, Broadcom has dismantled the European VMware channel," he said.

"Those excluded have until 31 March, 2027, to sell their infrastructure or their customers to a competitor chosen by Broadcom, or to close. This is the foreclosure the European Commission was warned about."

We asked CISPE what outcome it hoped to achieve, nearly three years after the acquisition closed.

"The immediate objective is to have the Commission's unconditional clearance annulled, on the basis that it failed to properly assess the effect of the acquisition on European cloud providers and the VMware channel," CISPE's spokesperson told The Register.

The Commission did impose conditions concerning interoperability with rival hardware, but CISPE argues these did not address the risks to cloud providers.

"We appreciate that it's a long shot (although there is precedent)," the spokesperson continued. "We have (along with others) also filed a competition complaint with the Directorate-General for Competition against Broadcom for its actions post-merger."

The precedent referred to is the EC approval given to the merger of Sony and BMG's music divisions in 2004, which was ruled to be not of "the requisite legal standard" two years later. The deal was subsequently reassessed and re-cleared.

"Ultimately, we want to do whatever we can to bring Broadcom to the table to negotiate and ideally end some of its most egregious practices so that European cloud providers can once again support cloud customers in a commercially fair and viable manner," the spokesperson added.

The Register asked Broadcom to comment The European Commission declined to comment on procedural matters . ®

#10002. Cyber Insurance's New Reality: Underwriting Isn't Enough

Rising AI, social engineering, and cloud risks are pushing carriers beyond risk transfer and deeper into cybersecurity itself.

The relentless evolution of the threat landscape has pushed cyber insurance companies to follow suit with a continuous expansion of cybersecurity posture requirements as well as taking an active hand in the defense process.

While cyber insurance has existed for years, the ransomware boom of the late 2010s and early 2020s transformed it from a niche risk transfer product into a central component of many organizations' security strategies. Today, policies cover everything from incident response and business interruption to legal costs and, in some cases, ransomware payments. Some of the names you'll see pop up around this space include Coalition, Chubb, AXA XL, Cowbell, and Resilience.

The threat landscape, especially when discussing enterprises, was never moving at a slow pace. But compared to the business email compromise and conventional ransomware attacks of five or 10 years ago, techniques are now evolving faster than ever, meaning insurance agencies must work harder to keep up.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled threat actors to orchestrate complex attacks, streamline malware and exploit development, design phishing lures without typos, and operate at a scale never before possible. AI introduces uncertainty into threat models built largely around ransomware and data extortion attacks, which insurers have accumulated years of claims data around. Social engineering advancements could alter both attack frequency and severity faster than historical loss data can account for.

While outside of AI, attackers are also coming up with new social engineering tactics all the time, and cloud resource consolidation means compromised credentials or a single stolen API key can lead to devastating consequences.

Thomas Pytel, vice president at Cowbell, tells Dark Reading his firm believes in underwriting that continuously adapts to risk. "AI is changing the speed, scale, and credibility of phishing and impersonation, so historical loss experience alone is insufficient. Underwriting must assess how a business verifies identities, authorizes payments, and controls its own use of AI," he says.

According to a 2025 report from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), cyber insurance premiums reached nearly $15 billion in 2024, up 7% year over year. Additionally, direct written premium (DWP) for the US market reached roughly $9.14 billion in 2024, compared with a market that was only a fraction of that size several years earlier. This underscores how cyber insurance has evolved to become a highly significant segment of the cyber-risk ecosystem.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

On the other hand, that same NAIC report cited nearly 50,000 claims across the US in 2024, the highest on record and a nearly 40% increase year over year. This could speak to the increasing number of customers choosing insurance, the aggressiveness of attackers, or both.

What remains to be seen is whether the industry's growth has outpaced its ability to accurately model the threat landscape.

Increasing insurance popularity also gave way to the rise of certain requirements for coverage, primarily demanding insurance customers uphold a certain quality of cybersecurity posture.

George Gerchow, IANS faculty and chief security officer at Bedrock Data, tells Dark Reading that a few years ago, these requirements were contained on a short form that "no one checked," but insurers now expect multifactor authentication (MFA), endpoint detection and response (EDR), immutable backups, and privileged access controls, while "some are moving to continuous telemetry instead of a once-a-year attestation."

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risks at Coalition, agrees. He says legacy underwriting models based on point-in-time questionnaires cannot keep pace, and this has been true since the ransomware epidemic took hold around 2020.

Related:Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots

This occurred amid concerns that organizations would use cyber insurance as a replacement for patching, practicing defense in depth, or using strong data and authentication controls.

Better posture may be an objective net good no matter where it comes from, though it also risks turning security into a compliance exercise. Gerchow says these requirements can feel like that depending on who you ask.

"Insurance did more to get MFA and EDR deployed in the mid-market than any of us standing on a stage, and that part worked," he says. "But the application is a snapshot, and too many teams treat passing it as the goal. The carrier finds the gap for you at claim time. Lapsed MFA or an untested backup you attested to is now one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied."

Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of cyber loss prevention vendor Root Evidence, says insurance carriers are requiring more to be implemented, steadily, year over year, and "it seems to be working well for many." However, he says, "The issue is that organizations tend to not have the data to properly measure and model their risk, and their carriers are often in a better position to do so."

One relatively recent development in this space has been the rise of insurance organizations as active participants in the security process. While insurers these days broadly require MFA, security products like EDR, managed detection and response (MDR), and validated backups, insurance firms will also offer security products and services directly to their customers.

Coalition's offering includes access to an automated detection and response product, for example, while Resilience offers risk management tooling and Cowbell offers services including risk assessment, penetration testing, and training. All of these firms also work with other security vendors to recommend preapproved products and incident response services. While on the other end, traditional security vendors like Arctic Wolf offer products specifically for insurability.

Coalition argues its "Active Insurance" model has resulted in 73% fewer claims than the industry average and is why 56% of claims reported in 2024 were resolved with no out-of-pocket expense to those insured. Woods says that as the threat landscape intensifies, insurers that passively issue policies and hope claims do not exceed premiums will face increasingly worse results.

"The solution is for insurers to bring threat researchers and security experts in-house to monitor the threat landscape and actively support customers in improving protections during the life cycle of their policies," he says. "Risk transfer is still a fundamental component of cyber insurance, but so is ongoing protection and prevention."

Some risk remains difficult to model. Gerchow argues that if a crisis were to occur tomorrow where a major cloud or identity provider was taken down or compromised, the market would struggle to absorb it, and, he says, "the carriers know it."

"Look at where policy language is moving: war exclusions applied to nation-state activity with no declared conflict, widespread-event carve-outs, and small sublimits for dependent business interruption. CrowdStrike in 2024 was a bad update with no attacker anywhere in it, and it still grounded flights and stalled hospitals in a single morning," he says. "A real compromise of a major identity provider means every downstream customer needs forensics, counsel, and notification at the same time. If I'm a CISO this week, I'm reading the systemic-event exclusions in my policy first and assuming a big piece of that loss stays with me."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#10001. Apple's Mac business is booming, but the memory market has other plans

New CEO John Ternus toasts record sales as soaring RAM costs threaten supplies and squeeze margins

Apple says it sold more Macs in fiscal 2026 than in any previous year, but soaring memory prices are threatening to spoil the Cupertino-based gadget maker's record-breaking run.

The warning came during Apple's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, the first since John Ternus took over as CEO.

"What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus told analysts.

Apple has already raised prices across much of its hardware lineup, including Macs and iPads in June and iPhones in September. Those increases, along with existing inventories and cheaper components elsewhere, have softened the blow. Unfortunately for Apple, memory prices haven't finished climbing.

"For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs," Ternus said, adding that Apple expects to pay more for memory beyond the end of the year.

Mac buyers haven't been deterred so far. Apple pulled in $10.8 billion from Macs in the September quarter, up 24 percent year-on-year, following $10.35 billion in the June quarter, up nearly 29 percent year-on-year. The MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro accounted for much of the latest growth.

"We have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time," Ternus said.

Whether Apple can keep enough of them on shelves is another matter. COO Sabih Khan said the company had already experienced supply constraints across iPhone, Mac, and iPad during the September quarter, largely because of limited availability of advanced chipmaking capacity. Now memory is taking over as the chief headache.

"For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected," Khan said.

Apple isn't sitting idle. Ternus revealed that its manufacturing purchase obligations jumped by $33 billion between June and September as it bids to secure supplies, although he offered no indication of when the memory crunch might ease.

Higher memory costs are also squeezing Apple's margins. CFO Kevan Parekh said gross margin fell by roughly one percentage point between the June and September quarters, excluding tariff effects, entirely because of memory costs. The damage would have been worse without existing inventory, cheaper non-memory components, and those price hikes.

Apple expects its gross margin to fall from 47.9 percent in the September quarter to between 45 and 46 percent in December, primarily because of higher memory costs. Costs associated with rolling out Siri AI will also weigh on the figure.

Parekh said Apple had "reluctantly" raised hardware prices, but supply constraints made it too early to assess how customers were responding.

Meanwhile, Ternus is keen to sell customers on the Mac as an AI machine, particularly for running models locally.

"Mac mini and Mac Studio in particular are pushing the boundaries of local private AI," he said, pointing to workloads that previously would have been difficult to run on desktop hardware.

Apple has also refreshed its Mac lineup with M6-powered machines and a touchscreen MacBook Pro, giving customers more reasons to upgrade, provided there's enough memory to build the things.

Not that the wider business is struggling. Apple reported September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year-on-year, while iPhone revenue climbed 17 percent to $57.6 billion. Services brought in $31.6 billion, up 10 percent.

Apple forecasts revenue growth of 7 to 10 percent in the December quarter despite the supply constraints. Even with memory prices running wild, it isn't expecting to go hungry. ®
